AFM has teamed up with AMC Century City (directly across from the confab’s Fairmont Century Plaza headquarters) and the fan-driven B-List Movie Club to expand market screening opportunities for the upcoming session.
All AFM screenings will take place at AMC Century City and this year will offer a more flexible menu of options and enhancements, including World and Market Premieres, Slate Showcases, Amplified Screenings incorporating hospitality and concessions, and red-carpet moments with talent and photo opportunities.
In addition, the 5,000+ members of the L.A. chapter of the B-List Movie Club can access to screenings and slate presentations from exhibiting companies that are looking for audience feedback from a group of dedicated moviegoers. The Club will work directly with filmmakers and companies to bring in select audience members for the AFM during the week. B-List Movie Club members can sign up for screenings organized directly within The B-List Movie Club Discord Server.
AFM’s 47th edition unspools November 10-15 with more than 215 exhibiting companies already confirmed and the number continuing to grow.
Watch on Deadline
Buyer registration is also tracking ahead of last year, with companies from 55 countries registered to date, representing all forms of distribution.
“We’re seeing tremendous participation from across the global industry, and all signs point to a very strong AFM this November,” said Jackie Brenneman, new president and CEO of the Independent Film & Television Alliance (IFTA) of the org’s flagship annual event.
“We’re excited to collaborate with AFM and engage communities like The B-List Movie Club to give movie fans access to special screenings, discover upcoming films, and experience content that isn’t typically available to general audiences,” said Carrie Trotter, AMC Theatres SVP, Marketing.

Imagine walking into a neighbourhood medical store with a prescription in hand. The pharmacist checks the medicine, packs it and hands it over. But what happens when there is no prescription? According to a nationwide survey, for a large number of consumers, the answer is that the medicine may still be sold. The finding comes as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed installing CCTV cameras at medical stores to make prescription-medicine sales traceable.
The survey, conducted by LocalCircles, saw about 1.06 lakh responses from consumers across 327 districts of India. Of the total respondents, 63% were men and 37% women. Besides, 52% of them were from tier-1 districts, 29% from tier-2 districts and 29% from tier-3, 4 and 5 districts.
The survey found that 64% of consumers said their chemist never or rarely asked for a doctor’s prescription before selling medicines in the past 12 months. Only 15% said their chemist mostly or always refused to sell medicines without a prescription. The survey also found that only 31% of consumers were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated a draft notification proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at every medical store that dispenses drugs sold on a doctor’s prescription. Under the proposal, the supply, other than by wholesale, of any drug sold on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner would have to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the premises.
The proposal also comes against the backdrop of intensified enforcement in multiple States against chemists selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, operating without registered pharmacists and failing to provide proper bills.
Neighbourhood chemist remains the main source
The survey found that the neighbourhood chemist remains the primary source of medicines for most consumers. The question on how respondents had primarily purchased medicines in the previous 12 months received 16,822 responses. This revealed that 86% of the respondents primarily depended on local chemists, followed by 14% on ePharmacy apps.
Who is actually behind the counter?
The survey then looked at whether consumers were receiving assistance from qualified pharmacists when they needed help with medicine or disease-related queries. The question received 19,409 responses. 31% of the consumers said they were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always. 27% of them said they never or very rarely received such assistance.
Home delivery is not free of the prescription gap
The survey also examined prescription checks when medicines were delivered to consumers’ homes. The question received 15,473 responses. 41% of consumers surveyed said a prescription was never or rarely asked for during home delivery.
A missing bill can mean a missing trail
Consumers were also asked whether they received proper bills when buying medicines from local chemists. Of the 20,573 respondents, 26% said they were not provided a GST bill. “A bill is not merely a tax document. It carries the batch number, expiry date and identity of the seller and provides a record if a medicine turns out to be expired, defective or counterfeit,” it said.
The survey also sought to establish whether consumers had purchased medicines that later turned out to be counterfeit or ineffective. The question received 18,457 responses. 15% of consumers said they had bought medicines that were later found to be fake or counterfeit.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

భారత స్వాతంత్ర్య ఉద్యమ సమయంలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నారంటూ ఒక ఫోటో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమవుతుంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నప్పటి ఫోటో.
ఫాక్ట్: వైరల్ ఫోటో రెండు వేర్వేరు సందర్భాల్లో తీసిన ఫోటోలను జోడించి ఎడిట్ చేసి సృష్టించబడింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ ఫోటోలో RSS కార్యకర్తలు నిలబడి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో (ఆర్కైవ్) లభించింది. ఈ ఫోటోను ‘డెక్కన్ క్రానికల్’ వార్తా సంస్థ తమ వెబ్సైట్లో 2016లో ప్రచురించిన ఒక కథనానికి ప్రతీకాత్మక చిత్రంగా ఉపయోగించింది. ఈ ఫోటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి లేరు.
ఇక వైరల్ ఫొటోలో బ్రిటన్ రాణి ఉన్న భాగాన్ని రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, దానికి సంబంధించిన అసలు ఫోటో ‘Getty Images’ వెబ్సైట్తో పాటు ‘History Ville‘ అనే ఎక్స్ (X) ఖాతాలో లభించింది. ఆ వివరాల ప్రకారం, 1956లో ఎలిజబెత్-II రాణి నైజీరియా పర్యటనలో నైజీరియా సైనిక దళాలను తనిఖీ చేస్తున్నప్పుడు ఈ ఫోటో తీయబడింది. దీన్ని బట్టి, సంబంధం లేని పై రెండు ఫోటోలను ఎడిట్ చేసి, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా తప్పుడు ప్రచారం చేస్తున్నారని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
చివరిగా, RSS కార్యకర్తలు బ్రిటన్ రాణికి గౌరవ వందనం చేస్తున్నట్లుగా చూపుతున్న ఈ ఫోటో ఎడిట్ చేయబడినది.

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

18 suspects accused in the July 2021 killing of Haiti's president being extradited from Haiti to US
Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse are awaiting extradition to the U.S. It marked the end of a drawn-out judicial process in Haiti for a killing that shocked the troubled Caribbean country
PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti -- Eighteen suspects who were arrested in the July 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse were awaiting extradition to the U.S. on Sunday, marking the end of a drawn-out judicial process in Haiti for a killing that shocked the troubled Caribbean country.
The suspects will face trial in Florida, according to Jason Reding Quiñones, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
“Today marks the next major phase in our pursuit of accountability for the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse,” he wrote on X. “We will follow the evidence wherever it leads, to those who financed it, facilitated it, supported it or committed crimes to make it possible. Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished.”
Quiñones did not identify the suspects, but those who remain in Haiti awaiting trial include more than a dozen Colombian soldiers, a former Haitian police officer and a former Haiti Ministry of Justice employee who was part of an anti-corruption unit.
Quiñones said that 30 people have been indicted in Moïse’s killing, with FBI Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles noting that there were multiple arrests in the U.S. and abroad on Sunday.
He said that the FBI and others “remain steadfast in ensuring that all individuals who allegedly sought profit from the assassination of a head of state are held fully accountable.”
Relatives of some of the Colombian soldiers didn't immediately respond to requests for comment on Sunday.
They had previously complained about the repeated delays in the Haitian judicial process following their arrest in 2021, with the investigation stalled by gang violence, death threats and a crumbling judicial system.
In October 2025, justice officials in Haiti asked the U.S. and Canada for help after a local court of appeals ordered a new investigation into Moïse's killing, the third inquiry of its kind since he was fatally shot at his private residence in July 2021. The previous investigations were stalled because Haitian judges kept resigning from the case, fearing for their lives, and gangs seized control of the downtown Port-au-Prince courthouse where the judges were interrogating suspects.
The extradition comes as the U.S. continues to prosecute and sentence multiple other suspects in the case.
In May, a jury in Florida convicted four men in the killing, and at least five others have pleaded guilty and are serving life sentences.
Those recently convicted include Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages, all of whom pleaded not guilty. A jury found them guilty of conspiring to kill or kidnap Haiti’s elected leader and providing material support for the plot.
Still awaiting trial is Christian Sanon, a Haitian-American citizen whom authorities said was initially picked by the alleged conspirators to replace Moïse. Once in power, the plan was for him to award contracts to a company known as CTU for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment.
Ortiz and Intriago were principals for CTU, which stood for Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security. Meanwhile, Veintemilla was a principal of Worldwide Capital Lending Group. Both companies were based in South Florida.
Suspects who previously pleaded guilty in U.S. federal court include a retired Colombian army officer and a Haitian-Chilean businessman who was once an informant for the U.S. government.
Authorities said that key fugitives in the case include Dimitri Hérard, ex-head of security at Haiti’s National Palace, who escaped last year after a powerful gang federation stormed Haiti’s two biggest prisons.

Dánica Coto reported from San Juan, Puerto Rico.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) asked the Centre to respond on whether it was contemplating formulating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.
A bench of Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Amit Sharma said it would hear a PIL seeking the constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms after three weeks. It asked Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma to take instructions on the issue.
Mr. Sharma said that it would be in the domain of the policymakers to consider some of the issues raised in the plea and suggested that the petitioner could submit a representation to the government.
The counsel for the Centre and certain social media platforms also took objection to the maintainability of the petition in view of some orders from the Supreme Court and high courts which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.
Addictive architecture
Petitioner Vikas Kathuria, a professor of law, said the fulcrum of the issue is not what content social media platforms carry, but how such platforms are architecturally designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, algorithmically curated and personalised feeds, notification systems, and variable-reward engagement metrics, such as “likes”, to capture, retain and repeatedly re-stimulate the attention of the user.
The plea said the concern assumes significance in the Indian context as statistics reveal that Indian youths aged 18-24 spend more than an average of 120 minutes daily on social media.
It has been clinically proven that long hours on social media are linked to suicide and depression among adolescents, the petition said.
The plea sought the court’s direction to the Central Government and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights to restrict, prohibit, or regulate the use of these features.

New Delhi, Sep 21: A Delhi court on Monday set aside a magistrate's order refusing to probe the allegation that Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's name was included in the electoral roll three years before acquiring Indian citizenship in 1983.
Special Judge Vishal Gogne was hearing a revision plea against the magisterial court's order on a complaint filed by advocate Vikas Tripathi, vice president of the Central Delhi Court Bar Association of the Rouse Avenue courts.
Pronouncing substantive portions of the order orally, the judge said, "An order of the court must maintain fidelity towards the law, and not flirt with facts. This court finds itself unravelling the impugned order rendered by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate (ACJM) on this yardstick."
The judge said Tripathi's complaint was that Sonia Gandhi's name was unlawfully entered in the electoral roll of New Delhi Parliamentary Constituency in 1980, whereas she attained Indian citizenship only in 1983, and although the name was deleted in 1982, it was re-entered in 1983.
"It alleged that even this re-entry was prior to the acquisition of citizenship by her on April 30, 1983," the judge noted.
He said the magistrate's order dismissed the complaint, saying that it was based on bald assertions, unaccompanied by essential particulars of cheating and forgery, and based on a photocopy of the photocopy of the uncertified electoral roll in 1980.
"The sanctity of the electoral roll is an article of faith for every citizen in a parliamentary democracy. The mightiest in the land may only be a voter or citizen at par with others less powerful," the judge said.
"Any allegation of tampering with the electoral rolls, fraudulent inclusion of the name of a voter, inclusion of the name of a non-citizen, and possible use of false declarations or documents merits a reasoned order to determine whether allegations relating to cheating and forgery have been disclosed," he said.
He said the ACJM's order recorded no discussion on the sequence in which Sonia Gandhi's name was included, deleted, and again included in the electoral roll in 1980, 1982 and 1983 respectively.
Rather than finding whether these allegations constituted a cognisable offence, the impugned order simply branded the complaint as lacking essential particulars, the judge said, adding that the extract of the electoral roll was casually dismissed as being "a photocopy of the photocopy of the alleged extract of the uncertified roll of 1980."
He said, "The limited prayer before the ACJM was to consider the extract of the electoral roll and other allegations as being adequate, or otherwise to direct investigation for the allegedly fraudulent entry of the name of Sonia Gandhi."
In effect, it is a non-speaking order on the question of disclosure of a cognisable offence, the judge said.
"The order suffers from a manifest error in law on account of non-compliance with Section 175(3) of the Bharatiya Nagrik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), inter alia, not hearing the submissions of the concerned police officer and non-calling of a status report from the concerned police station," the judge said.
Section 175(3) empowers a magistrate to order police investigation into a cognisable offence.
The judge said the magistrate failed to consider the twin options permissible in law: one, directing the registration of an FIR; two, the conduct of proceedings under Section 223 of the BNSS (which governs the magistrate examining the complainant and witnesses after taking cognisance of an offence).
Regarding the issue of citizenship, the judge said the ACJM had only to decide whether the allegations disclosed a cognisable offence and whether it called for a police investigation. However, he conflated this with the jurisdiction of the Central government and digressed towards the issue of citizenship.
The court said it was unable to fathom why the ACJM considered the Election Commission's powers to include or exclude persons from electoral rolls to be a bar on the police to prove fraudulent inclusion of names in electoral rolls or the use of false documents.
The judge said the magisterial court did not perform its "core function" of discerning the disclosure of a cognisable offence.
"The court finds the four pillars of reasoning adopted in the impugned order to be perverse and improper, as well as an incorrect appreciation of law and allegations. In fact, the impugned order is liable to be set aside," the judge said.
He remanded the matter back to the magisterial court to "pass a speaking order in light of the specific requirements of 175(3) of the BNSS" and directed fresh hearing of the complainant's arguments.
The matter has been posted for further hearing on September 29.

The man who would be king - the rise and fall of 'the next Prince Naseem'
- Published
Boxer Daniel Teasdale was hailed as the heir to the legendary Prince Naseem Hamed, but his promise never materialised into fame, fortune and films.
"He's better than Naz at the same age," said trainer Brendan Ingle.
Hamed had won his first world title aged 21. Teasdale was still a teenager.
Ingle, from his gym in Sheffield, moulded the careers of a conveyor belt of world-beaters and title winners. He guided both of the fighters from childhood.
Before super-middleweight Teasdale's first professional bout, the Rotherham fighter had been featured in national newspapers, books and was being documented by photographers and film-makers.
He won a succession of national titles, establishing himself as the next contender to emerge from the Ingle gym.
Photographer Simon Roberts travelled to the Ingle gym in 1997 hoping to photograph Hamed.
"Brendan said 'don't worry about Naz, start photographing that kid in the corner. He's going to be bigger than Naz'. That was Daniel," Roberts said.
Roberts began to follow the young sensation, hoping to capture his rise on camera.
Filmmaker Stuart Mitchell had a similar brief.
"We were selling the documentary as 'who's the next Prince Naseem?'," says Mitchell.
He recalls Teasdale being the subject of similar headlines in national newspapers, and later accompanying him to an event gathering together the best British prospects from every sport for the new Millennium.
Attention on Ingle's latest protégé was more than just hype.
"He was like Oscar de la Hoya," recalls former stablemate Amer Khan.
"Teasdale was exceptional as a junior, he was stopping everyone."
Teasdale learnt both ballet and gymnastics to develop his footwork and skills in the ring and was seemingly set for stardom.
"I was very teachable, could talk, had the looks and could box," says Teasdale, who took up the sport aged six.
The bitterness of Hamed's split from trainer Ingle in 1998 has been well-documented, with both sides seemingly losing.
"Brendan lost the focus with the up-and-comers," Teasdale says.
He followed Naz in leaving the gym, linking up with one of its greatest exports, three-time world title challenger Herol 'Bomber' Graham.
The exit was said to have been spearheaded by Teasdale's father who "essentially gave up his career" to help his son fulfil his potential, Roberts says.
It was funded by a businessman with no prior experience in boxing, but a thirst to be part of Teasdale's rise to the top.
Teasdale remembers Graham's influence as "a breath of fresh air", but the presence of others was less helpful.
"People started to try and feed off Daniel," says Roberts.
"I photographed [Mike] Tyson and Lennox [Lewis], I have seen all of this stuff before."
'Everybody wanted a piece'
Mitchell was also filming future Olympic bronze medallist Darren Sutherland when he arrived at the Ingle gym from Ireland.
"Daniel was probably more talented than Darren, the trouble with Daniel was he was always being wooed," reveals Mitchell.
Teasdale's tag as the next Prince Naseem also hung heavy.
"I was like catnip for cats, everybody wanted a piece," Teasdale explains.
While the career of some talented prospects is carefully nurtured, Teasdale may not have been as well protected.
"To some extent Daniel was used because he was seen as a big potential and was a good scalp for somebody who wanted to get through the ranks," Roberts says.
Different trainers, managers and promoters followed, but Teasdale admits instability harmed his progress.
His debut had been a disaster - abandoned due to rioting in the crowd - while the following year he received death threats before a bout.
Despite undeniable talent, those early misfortunes could now be seen as an omen of what was to come.
After filming Teasdale across five years, Mitchell shelved his documentary when commissioners lost interest.
He too lost faith after a training session in Graham's garage.
"It felt very small and I didn't think this was going anywhere," he says bluntly.
Many have since raised doubts over whether the "pretty boy" was made for a career getting punched in the face.
"Everybody has a weakness and mine was women," Teasdale confesses.
"I lost the edge and my focus wasn't where it should be."
He walked away from the sport in 2005 after he was stopped in the first round of a light-heavyweight contest - his first professional defeat.
He returned in 2010 and reunited with Ingle, winning his one and only comeback fight.
"After that I just gave it up, I thought 'I'm not going to be second best to the first me," says Teasdale, whose professional career ended after just five fights over a seven-year period.
"At 27 I should have been a world champion defending my title."
Roberts continued to photograph Teasdale.
"There were a lot of unfortunate circumstances with him which meant he didn't fulfil his potential," Roberts says.
"There was a lot of bad advice and a lot of people wanting something from him, and not necessarily for the good."
Mitchell did some "soul searching" over his role in Teasdale's journey.
"There was so much clamour around him - then it just evaporated," he recalls.
"That must be very difficult to deal with when expectations are that you are going to be a successful and famous boxer."
Teasdale says "everything went up in the air" as a professional, in contrast to the stability of his early years.
Bad management played a part in not fulfilling his potential, but he admits "living for other people's dreams and ambitions."
Still, there are no regrets about how his career turned out.
"It's made me who I am," says Teasdale, now enjoying an altogether different career as a support worker.
"I'm doing the job that I love, it's not the profile that I was but it's all about being stable in your life."

11 things we learned from the Neil Peart documentary
Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple spotlights the late, legendary Rush drummer
Drummers often get short shrift. Hidden behind the kit, they remain mysterious, even anonymous.
Not so for Neil Peart, who was a tour-de-force for the Canadian rock band Rush and is widely considered one of the best drummers of all time.
In Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple, co-directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn celebrate Peart's life, extraordinary musicianship and lasting influence through interviews and musical performances.
Bandmates Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson, along with Peart’s fellow drummers and friends — including Stewart Copeland of the Police and Chad Smith of Red Hot Chili Peppers — share insights into the wizard behind the kit and perform Rush songs together as a tribute to his enduring legacy. The film debuted at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sept. 16. Here are 11 things we learned:
1. His name is pronounced 'Peert'
"It's not 'Pert' like the shampoo," says Dunn, correcting a mispronunciation that has even appeared in films such as School of Rock and I Love You, Man.
2. He moved to London at 18 to pursue music
After leaving high school, Peart moved from St. Catharines, Ont., to England determined to become a musician. He lived in cheap rooms and shared flats, experiencing what he later described as "anonymity and poverty" — an early test of the focus and stubbornness that would define his career.
3. He was an enthusiastic reader
When his bandmates first met Peart, he was reading "five or six books a day," according to Lee, who said it soon became obvious that their new drummer should also be writing lyrics.
4. He loved The Lord of the Rings
Peart’s imagination was shaped by fantasy, mythology, science fiction, comedy and classical music — influences that found their way into Rush’s songs and lyrics. His love of J.R.R. Tolkien influenced songs such as The Necromancer and Rivendell.
5. He rehearsed before rehearsal
Peart studied, practised and took lessons throughout his career, always approaching the drums as a student.
"I think it matters for me to play better all the time," he says in archival footage, "to play my best all the time, to keep it fresh and changing. It’s kind of my responsibility."
He would rehearse for at least an hour by himself before rehearsing with the rest of the band. As the filmmakers put it, he was continuously trying to get better — even after becoming one of the best in the world.
6. He helped build Rush’s big, theatrical sound
Peart played a major role in shaping Rush’s intricate arrangements and dramatic instrumental passages, which became central to the band’s sound.
His influence is especially evident in 2112, the 20-minute title suite from the band’s 1976 album.
"It was Neil’s idea to do an overture," says Lifeson, to "take all these pieces and put them together in one really cool opening." The movement weaves together themes that return throughout the piece, reflecting Peart’s operatic and orchestral approach to percussion.  
7. His whisky pours got bigger
During studio mixing sessions, Peart reportedly enjoyed a glass of Macallan whisky at 5 p.m. — a pour of about "two fat fingers," according to Lee. Over their 40-year friendship, Lee jokes, Peart’s "fingers got fatter."
8. He was an air drummer's drummer
Copeland notes Peart’s solos were so intricate, physical and theatrical that audiences didn’t just watch — they played along in the air.
"I asked him one time, how do you get the air drummers? I want that," Copeland said. "It's amazing at a Rush show to see them."
"The middle part of Tom Sawyer is every air drummer’s fantasy section," adds Smith. "If you hear Tom Sawyer, they’re all air drumming."
9. He was intensely private
Peart was uncomfortable with fame and fiercely protective of his personal life.
"If I go off to do my job, I’m a professional," he says in an archival interview. "If I’m not doing my job, then I’m a person, so don’t get that mixed up."
10. He took bikes very seriously
Lee recalls Peart riding his bicycle from Milwaukee to Chicago, some 150 kilometres, on his day off and then performing a three-hour concert.
He later became a devoted motorcyclist, chronicling his travels, which followed devastating personal losses, in his memoir Ghost Rider: Travels on the Healing Road.
11. He nearly retired, but came back for one more tour
After the deaths of his 19-year-old daughter, in a car accident in August 1997, and his wife, from cancer 10 months later, Peart took a five-year hiatus. He returned to make the album Vapor Trails in 2002 and tour.
Following that, Peart took part in the albums and tours for 2004's Feedback, 2007's Snakes & Arrows and 2012's Clockwork Angels.
Although he considered retirement in 2015, he agreed to return for one final tour.
'Respect the drummer'
"Drummers are the backbone," of bands, Dunn told CBC News, "and Neil was taking drumming to a whole other level."
That appreciation drives the film, which serves as the tribute Peart never received: a proper farewell concert or memorial, made impossible by the pandemic after his death from brain cancer in January 2020.
Instead, Lee and Lifeson reunite with four of Peart’s musical "brothers" for a musical, funny and emotional tribute.
"It’s a very joyous celebration of a complex individual," McFadyen said.

Lee jokes that Peart "would say we were idiots" and might be "a little embarrassed" by the attention. He adds that he remembers him as "a very wise, quick thinker, philosopher" and gifted lyricist.
The film ultimately asks audiences to do exactly what Dunn recommends: "respect the drummer."

In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters. He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016. But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent, where it was at the beginning of his second term.
Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
The Latino backlash to Trump is a major bellwether.
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy.
It was the same in 2024. During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today. In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos. Today, the blame is falling on Trump.
America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them.
“I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.”
That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics. Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections?
Yes, it absolutely has to do with that. Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary.
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election. A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election.
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are. It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume.
I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are?
Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors. I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that.
Look, I’m Latina. I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio. I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León. A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do.
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish. And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word. There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate.
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community.
Exactly. So that’s mistake No. 1. Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings. So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.”
So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings.
Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting. Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube.
So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community. That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.”
We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos. It matters that much.
Let’s stay in 2024 for a second longer. Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy. I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly.
Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign?
I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming.
What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals.
And so that’s what people bought. Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration. They feel like there was a broken promise there.
They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that.
And then add that to the litany of broken promises.
I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump. But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office.
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course. Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months.
You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy?
It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration. It’s those three things.
One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job.
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy. It’s almost been a complete and total reversal.
Listen, you tell people you’re going to fix egg prices and gas is going to go down, and then you do the opposite, and we’re hearing that story universally across different electorate groups.
You’re saying that’s still the main story when it comes to Latinos also?
Yes, it’s still the main story. I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup. What that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.
We have less savings. We have lower rates of home ownership. So the safety nets that other people might have, we just don’t have.
That really has exacerbated the kind of impact that people are feeling right now as they’re trying to make ends meet.
You mentioned the exponential growth in the terms of people who now regret or are disappointed with their vote for Donald Trump. Does that mean a preference for Democrats? How should we think about the binary choice between D and R versus what is a clear story about a backlash to Donald Trump’s actions?
I think it is a huge mistake for Democrats to rest on their laurels and think that because of what people are feeling about Trump and Republicans and the sense of disappointment and promises broken that that is automatically going to translate for them as a party and as a brand.
Right now, the Democratic brand has suffered a repeated set of blows among Latino voters. Twenty years of comprehensive immigration reform hasn’t been delivered. It’s a thing that comes up in almost every focus group.
And part of what the build-up to 2024 was, was not only 20 years of a promise undelivered; it was the chaos at the border, it was feeling like Democrats were focused on everything but Latinos and their families, or everyday Americans and their families, and that they had lost that thread.

LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

PHOTOS: The precarious life of fisherfolk
He works from 2 a.m. to 7 a.m. every day. In pitch darkness, he carries baskets of fish on his head from boats in Kasimedu harbor to the auction house, navigating slimy and damp pathways littered with fish scales and wet with seawater. It's a third of a mile each way. He makes the trip 40 or 50 times during his shift for the daily auction, which begins at 4 a.m.
Pavadairayan, who is 60 years old and goes by one name, is one of hundreds of workers known as basket men. It's a tough job. Each basket weighs about 35 pounds. Their bosses don't trust them: "If supervisors think that fish are missing, they can dock your pay and fine you several thousands of rupees. Basket men have few rights," he says.
They earn about $5 a day.
Despite the hardships, Pavadairayan says he loves the job because the rest of the day is his own. He spends his mornings sleeping and lounging.
"Many other basket men go out and do other odd jobs," he says. "But I always refuse. This money is enough for me. Sleeping with a full belly under open skies, a salt sea breeze fanning your face: that's what I call heaven."
A smuggler's story
Pavadairayan is one of around 30,000 people who are part of the bustling scene at the Kasimedu harbor in the southern Indian city of Chennai. In addition to basket men, there are fishermen, auctioneers, fish hawkers and wholesalers, transport workers, ice suppliers. The harbor itself is overcrowded, built for fewer than 600 boats and now estimated to be serving over 1,000.
They have stories to tell about their labors and their lives. Their experiences testify to the struggles they face — and to their undying love for the sea.
Nandu Kumar, who is 65, says he used to be a smuggler.
Dressed in a grey shirt and a checkered lungi (a traditional garment men wear, made of light cotton and wrapped around the waist), Kumar is seated on an overturned boat on the harbor's sandy shores. In the pale light of early dawn, he looks vulnerable, almost fragile, with a wispy white beard and contemplative eyes.
He's always worked as a fisherman. But in the early '80s, desperate to make a living, he says he'd help smuggle in imported alcohol and cigarettes on his boat. This was the time when India imposed steep customs duties and limits on consumer-goods imports. Smuggling was profitable until 1991, when economic reforms began taking effect.
So Kumar gave up on his illegal cargo and went back to battling the sea for fish.
Years later, in December 2010, tragedy struck., Kumar says. His daughter's husband, who drank heavily, toppled off his boat and drowned. "This fishing life — it's harshest on the body," Kumar says. "Your shoulders ache all the time. Sometimes, alcohol is the only way you can cope and forget the pain."
His daughter struggled to come to terms with her loss. Months later, she took her life, ingesting the pesticide she had bought to weed the garden.
After his daughter's death, Kumar took in her infant daughter and son — and soon realized that spending weeks at sea was no longer practical. Fishing was a gamble. A group of ten fishermen would go out to sea for three weeks or months in a boat, and sometimes, come back empty-handed. Kumar needed a steady income to care for his grandchildren. "With the support of my two sons, I decided to start selling fish," he says.
Today, he runs a shop at the harbor and does brisk business.
A risky business
Members of fishing communities in Kasimedu are well aware of the risky nature of the business, says Bhagat Singh, a researcher, social worker and member of the Coastal People Rights Movement, a grassroots campaign led by fishing and indigenous communities to protect their traditional marine livelihoods against corporate displacement and unregulated development.
Singh's own father was a fisherman, and he knows the community well. ""It's feast or famine. That is the rhythm of life at the harbor. For workers and fishermen here, earning a living is hard enough. One bad season, one poor catch, or one spell of illness can be enough to push a family into dire poverty. There are no safety nets. Worse, they have little access to government support and their labor remains largely invisible, " he says.
On an average, the fisherman at Kasimedu earn around $200 a month, he says — if they have good catches. The precariousness of the job is a reason why the younger generation seeks out more reliable employment. But that need for independence that is so inherent to their personalities eventually surfaces, he says. "Many of my friends are not happy in corporate jobs or in related industries. Eventually, they do find their way back fishing again, and many make this career change mid-life."
Nizamuddin, 25, belongs to the younger generation of fishermen. He's also the only man in the entire harbor wearing a wet suit. When he's not out fishing, he helps repair nets, dock boats and haul fish from the hold to pass onto the basket men.
The power of the sea
He is aware that young people his age are conspicuously absent from Kasimedu, but he's always embraced his job. "It's a hard life but I wasn't very good at studying," he says. "This is the only work I know and it has helped my family survive." He's put two older brothers through school and college. They now have good jobs, he says, but he's never regretted his own career choice.
The fisherman-turned-fish vendor Kumar knows all too well that the seas hold power over those who've worked there. "It's like your mother's lap. You may travel far and wide, and don't need it anymore, but you will return for the warmth and comfort it gives you," he says.
Every now and then, in the early hours of the morning, Kumar sits in the stillness to watch the fishermen return with their catch and feels a pang of longing. "Life on a boat is hard, but it is also exhilarating," he says. "There are moments when you never know what will happen next. I quite miss that."

Three dead and eight injured in Philippines school shooting
- Published
A 16-year-old gunman has shot two students dead and injured eight others at a Philippine high school, before killing himself.
The two deceased victims were 14-year-old pupils at a school in Banga in the southern province of Mindanao, the local mayor told the BBC.
Albert Palencia said four of the injured were in critical condition.
The education department said in a statement it was "deeply concerned" by the reported incident which took place on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education department said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time (06:00 GMT) and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.
