Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster believes OpenAI used his work to rush ahead and beat him to solving a legendary math problem with a $1 million bounty.
But that’s not been enough for him to stop using the company’s models—and he’s not the only mathematician that feels that way.
“Even if you don't agree with any of this, you're kind of stuck. With AI being so useful, it's hard to completely prevent oneself from using it,” Buckmaster tells WIRED. “These companies have a monopoly, and there is not much choice,” he adds.
In the week and half since the New York University professor accused OpenAI of copying his approach, Buckmaster has been using the company’s coding agent Codex to tidy up his research papers. When he has time to do math (which he says is rare, since the fallout thrust him into the spotlight), the tool has been helping him understand the logical steps OpenAI’s agents might have taken to get from his earlier workings to the final proof.
Buckmaster had used Codex as well as Anthropic’s competing Claude to work on what’s known as the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, alongside Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to reach the solution, but only after it learned the equation was close to being solved, Buckmaster says.
When Buckmaster went public with his claims, it ignited a firestorm about artificial intelligence and whether it would make human mathematicians obsolete. It also led OpenAI to do an investigation and amend its announcement about solving Navier-Stokes to say it “confirmed that Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the two months preceding this announcement and paper on September 8, 2026, could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training.” The company pointed WIRED to its announcement in an email.
Showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics was “more important than the result,” Buckmaster says. But churning out solutions to long-standing math problems without fully crediting the human work undergirding them—especially ahead of major IPOs—is irresponsible and “childish,” he says.
Other mathematicians have raised similar concerns. Only a handful of people on the planet understand the techniques in geometric group theory that German mathematician Andreas Thom has dedicated the last two decades to developing. So when OpenAI said in August that its Astra model had used them to prove a long-standing problem he had been working on, “I was amazed,” says Thom. “And of course I was wondering, how did they learn about it?”
So he says he asked OpenAI researchers Mark Sellke and Sébastien Bubeck. In an August email, he pointed out that the firm’s assertion that “no progress” had been made on the problem in the last decade overlooked a 2019 paper of his, as well as other mathematicians’ work. The company amended its press release. He and a colleague had been using ChatGPT to assist their work on the problem in the months running up to the result, but when he asked if their interactions had been fed into training data, Thom says Sellke replied: “That did not happen.”
“I set it aside,” Thom recalls. “I'm not so much interested in these political things; I want to work on mathematics.”
While Thom has seen OpenAI’s statement that Buckmaster’s prompts couldn't have influenced the system, he says he doesn’t trust this and concedes he will probably never know whether his work actually fed the result.
“AI really kills this entire idea that you could trace back who contributed what,” he says. “That is probably over.”
It’s a big change from how science is typically done, with academics subjecting their findings to peer review and building on each others’ work with credit. Beyond upending attribution, the fact that humans still don’t fully understand each step OpenAI’s agents took to arrive at the Navier-Stokes result also poses existential questions for mathematicians, who see their field slipping from their understanding.
"If I want to make a contribution to mathematics, how do I do that as just a human nowadays when these trillion-dollar companies are in on the game?" says Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend, the coauthor of a forthcoming book on the field’s evolution.
Since August, Townsend has seen many of his colleagues start to ask what they need to know about the technology and how they can set up subscriptions to access higher-powered models.
"I feel both excited and nervous simultaneously," Townsend says. "Excited because I can achieve things that I couldn't achieve without it, and nervous because I'm questioning: 'OK, what's my purpose here?'"
Thom accepts that his area of study is changing, and has continued to use ChatGPT—with updated privacy settings to stop his work being used to train the data—to speed up writing papers because it is “extremely efficient.” (OpenAI’s offerings through universities and at the enterprise level default to not training models on users’ data.)
“If a human had actively done that, then I would be very, very angry,” he says of someone using his work without attribution. But if information was pulled into the model through a back door, by an algorithm which nobody fully understands, “I could probably live with that,” he says.
Some mathematicians are less forgiving. Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote in an open letter that AI companies and mathematicians are “severely misaligned.” More than 4,000 people have signed the Leiden Declaration, which has a series of recommendations for how mathematicians, funders, and politicians can ensure that AI doesn’t swallow the field.
Buckmaster fears the possibility of using AI to “clean up some of your grammar, and suddenly your years of work [could be] gobbled up in user data and sold to another mathematician or grad student. That's what I think most of the mathematicians tend to be worrying about, and I think it's a real issue.”
With no oversight on the horizon and AI further engraining itself in the field, some mathematicians want to find a way to at least tap the brakes. That includes more than 2,000 people with ties to Caltech who called on organizers of an AI math hackathon at the school to suspend the event. The hackathon was sponsored by Anthropic and OpenAI, though the latter has since dropped out. But any attempts to slow things down may be for naught, especially in the long term.
“I don't think this is really sustainable because of the efficiency gain” that AI offers, says Thom. Any mathematicians—especially early-career researchers—risk being “isolated” if they don’t use AI to accelerate their work, he adds. He and Buckmaster both believe the community needs to start thinking about what the technology means for younger mathematicians and how to smooth the transition.
The next generation of mathematicians is already looking for guidance: Students have also been asking about what their future could look like now that AI is becoming so capable at solving math problems, Townsend says.
Buckmaster is calling for a detente in AI-driven mathematics while mathematicians and AI laboratories set some ground rules on how to release results, including getting their references right. He himself is going to clean up the papers he published prematurely last week to beat OpenAI’s announcement, one of which he described as “AI slop.”
”I have a responsibility to clean up the papers that I did post that weren't completed, and I think I have a responsibility to explain to mathematicians what we did,” he says.
He’s also open to discussing this with OpenAI. “I don't want to just engage in fights” he says. As for whether he would ever actually work on a problem with the company, “we have to be careful with that,” he says with a wry smile.

The meme provides some factual information about both stories and, as of this writing, an accurate GoFundMe tally of donations earmarked to defray Clancy's parents' travel and housing costs as they attended the trial. Also, it's true that a Swedish news outlet reported that a church deacon in that country organized a fundraiser equaling, at current currency conversion rates, about $42,000. However …
… the meme omits additional fundraisers and sponsors who pledged to help rebuild Schols' home, according to information found in the same Swedish news outlet mentioned above and her 2022 book.
In late summer 2026, people shared a meme pitting a story of heroism involving a mother named Emma Schols against that of Lindsay Clancy's murder case.
Schols' story of heroism, which involved saving her six children from a house fire and sustaining severe burns in the process, appears on the meme's left side, with a fundraising figure of $42,000.
The right side features Clancy, the mother at the center of a highly-publicized Massachusetts murder trial — which ended in a mistrial on Sept. 4, 2026 — in which prosecutors charged her with killing her three young children, along with a purported GoFundMe fundraising figure exceeding $1 million.
On Sept. 15, an Instagram user posted (archived) the meme, which reads under photos of Schols: "Mother pulls all 6 of her children out of raging house fire, going back in three times despite burns covering 93% of her body. Money raised: $42,000." Clancy's caption reads: "Mother kills all 3 of her children by strangling them to death with exercise bands. Claims she is victim. GoFundMe: $1,044,318+."
(@davidjharrisjr via Instagram)
Other users shared the meme on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Reddit (archived) and X (archived).
In sum, Schols' book and news media outlets' reporting confirm the meme features a few specific facts but also omits key information. For these reasons, we have rated the meme's content as a mixture of true and false information.
Snopes emailed Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, and Schols to request comment.
Breaking down the Schols-Clancy meme
Schols, who lives in Sweden, saved all six of her children in a Sept. 3, 2019, house fire, taking three trips to remove all of them from the inferno. Her 2022 coauthored book, "Ärren bär jag med stolthet: branden i Edsbyn och livet efteråt," which translates to "I Carry the Scars with Pride: The Fire in Edsbyn and Life Afterwards," tells her harrowing story, including the fact that 93% of her body sustained burns, as the meme claims.
In September 2019, Swedish news media outlet SVT, quoting church deacon Christer Schwartz, reported Schols' fundraising total at 400,000 Swedish krona, or at current exchange rates about $42,000. According to that report, Schwartz's fundraiser was one of several on Schols' behalf but no other figures were reported.
On top of Schwartz's and other fundraisers, a February 2020 charity hockey match reportedly collected an additional 200,000 Swedish krona ($21,000). Schols says in her book that people and companies also initially pledged to sponsor the rebuilding of her house, though she adds some of those sponsors pulled out after she separated from her partner.
As for Clancy, The Associated Press, Reuters and other outlets reported she admitted strangling her children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023, and pleaded not guilty to her initial charges, which included three counts each of first-degree murder, strangulation and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Prosecutors later dropped the strangulation charges, saying they were redundant to the murder charges.
The organizer of the Clancy case GoFundMe (archived), titled "The Musgrove Family Fund," described the purported recipients of the fundraiser as Clancy's parents, Mike and Paula Musgrove, citing their hotel, travel and relocation costs to stay close to their daughter over more than three years. The in-question meme does not mention Clancy's parents, instead making the allegation that Clancy herself will one day collect the funds. At last check, the fundraiser had grown to more than $1.2 million with a goal of $3 million, bringing in more than 35,900 individual donations.
The meme adds that Clancy has claimed she's the victim. During her criminal trial in summer 2026, Reddington, her attorney, said "there is evidence of lack of criminal responsibility" and suggested "a required finding of not guilty should be entered on the case." He repeatedly argued Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis, a disorder an estimated one or two in 1,000 women experience after giving birth that can include delusions, depression, hallucinations, insomnia, paranoia and other changes in behavior. Prosecutors, on the other hand, argued she knew what she was doing.
Schols' harrowing rescue story
On Sept. 3, 2019, Schols awoke before 6 a.m. in her home to early-morning light shining through her window, with the faint memory of minutes earlier hearing some of her children playing in another room.
In Schols' book, which we translated to English, she said her then-partner, Anders, was working a night shift, leaving her to sleep alone. She wrote of the morning, "Great, I think, now I have a few minutes to lie down and catch up before I have to start my morning routine."
Moments later, the book recounts, she felt a very different sense of "fear, panic and desperation" when one of her children screamed from downstairs, "Help, mom, there's a fire. There's a fire in the TV room!"
She wrote, "To make sure all the children have woken up, I scream at the top of my lungs: 'Everyone has to get out of the house!'"
In the minutes that followed, Schols first managed to guide her young children Albin and Oliwer out the front door, then looked for William, Melwyn and Nellie. After seeing William and showing Melwyn to safety, she made it to her youngest child, Mollie, who was standing in her crib with a full diaper.
Schols became unable to move from the flames covering her body. She wrote, "If I have managed to give birth to six children, I will swear to get six children out of this burning house," and that she gathered strength, picked up Mollie and looked to escape. She described William as positioning a ladder they happened to have left out from a long-neglected painting job as their method of escape from the balcony.
Once outside, Schols described hearing her dog, Sally, inside making noises and thinking of her cat as well. A neighbor, seeing burns all over Schols' body, told her it was too late to save her pets.
Several Swedish outlets published news of the fire on the same day.
Following extensive hospital stays for her burns and a period of rehabilitation, Schols returned home.
In her book, Schols wrote of Schwartz, the deacon, organizing the fundraiser following the fire. A Facebook post from days after the incident mentions Schwartz by name.
Schols said locals helped find clothes for her children, writing, "I am struck by the incredible care that exists in our country." Other examples of that care included "Playing for Emma," a charity hockey match organized in Schols' honor in February 2020. Schols wrote about the match, as well as her family's home insurance situation at the time of the fire:
On Sunday, February 2nd, a tribute match will be held for me, where the money raised will go to help me and my family get back on their feet. For all the years we have had home insurance, but just a month or so before the accident, we had, due to our financial situation, fallen behind on that particular bill. This fact is something I am ashamed of today. As I have been mulling this question over here in the hospital. This very month, when the house burns down, we were forced to skip that bill. What are the odds of that?
Later in December 2020, the Swedish Heroes Gala awarded Schols the title "Lifesaver of the Year."
Near the end of her book, Schols wrote that some companies and people sponsoring the rebuilding of their former home pulled out after she and Anders separated.
To close her book, Schols thanked numerous locals and medical personnel, as well as her family, former partner and friends, saving a message for her children for last:
My biggest thanks go to William, Nellie, Melwin, Albin, Oliwer and Mollie. I may have saved your lives, but you are the absolute biggest heroes in this whole story. You are my everything and I love you with all my heart.
For further reading, we previously reported on other matters involving donations, including a rumor alleging prison inmates donated over $4,000 to a Kansas school district's lunch debt.

For most of the last century, T. rex was pictured as a sluggish, tail-dragging reptile that had to warm up in the sun before it could go anywhere. Then, further research changed that view, replacing it with the active, bird-like animal shown in the movie Jurassic Park. But whether T. rex used warm blood to power that activity remained a question. Now we might have gotten closer to an answer.
A team of researchers led by Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle, geochemists at the University of California, Los Angeles, has measured the T. rex body temperature by analyzing its teeth. This dental thermometer read about 36° Celsius—roughly the body temperature of a modern elephant.
Dental thermometry
Paleontologists have long argued about dinosaur physiology based on indirect evidence like bone microstructure, growth rates, and where fossils turn up on the map. Some studies suggested many dinosaurs were endotherms, generating their own body heat like birds and mammals. Others argued that each lineage may have had its own thermal strategy.
Earlier attempts to measure T. rex’s temperature relied on oxygen isotopes in bones and teeth. The problem was that those ratios depend not only on temperature but also on the composition of the water present in the animal’s body, which was something nobody could pin down for an extinct creature.
Flores, Eagle, and their colleagues got around that with a technique called clumped isotope thermometry, which Eagle introduced to dinosaur research over a decade ago in work on Jurassic sauropods. Carbonate minerals in tooth enamel contain rare, heavy isotopes of carbon and oxygen (carbon-13 and oxygen-18). How often these heavy atoms bond with each other, or clump together, depends on the temperature at which the mineral formed. Since tooth enamel forms inside a living body, the number of those clumped bonds records the animal’s body temperature, regardless of the water content in its body.

At Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, in Telangana’s Bhadradri Kothagudem district, a single specialist has helped bring specialised eye surgery to patients from remote tribal areas and even neighbouring States.
The Ophthalmology Unit of the hospital has completed 400 cataract surgeries since its dedicated ophthalmic operation theatre was established in December 2023. Patients have travelled to Bhadrachalam not only from Bhadradri Kothagudem district but also from Warangal, Karimnagar, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Odisha.
The unit currently performs around 20 cataract surgeries a month and has increased its surgical schedule from one to two days a week. The achievement is significant given the geographical challenges of the agency area and the limited availability of specialist manpower.
The ophthalmic operation theatre, the first-of-its-kind in the entire district, was established in December 2023, even before a similar facility was established at Government General Hospital (GGH), Kothagudem. It was set up with financial support from former District Collector Anudeep Durishetty on the initiative of District Coordinator of Health Services (DCHS) Dr. G. Ravi Babu.
The facility subsequently received continued support from successive District Collectors Jitesh V. Patil and Ankit, and ITDA Project Officer B. Rahul. “Their support included intraocular lenses, surgical consumables and other requirements, enabling the unit to provide cataract surgery services consistently,” said Dr. Ravi Babu.
The hospital performs modern phacoemulsification cataract surgeries. The 400 procedures have been completed without major complications. The unit is also among the best-performing ophthalmology units under the Telangana Vaidya Vidhana Parishad (TVVP), despite functioning with a single ophthalmologist appointed on a contract basis.
“For a hospital located in a remote tribal region, the ability to provide specialised surgical care without patients having to travel to major urban centres represents a significant healthcare service. The hospital has been able to sustain the service through a combination of administrative support, dedicated infrastructure, essential surgical consumables and specialist medical and support staff,” added Dr. Ravi Babu.
He appreciated ophthalmologist Dr. Santosh as well as the entire ophthalmology nursing, operation theatre and support teams for their sustained commitment. According to Dr. Ravi Babu, the ophthalmic operation theatre was established using district funds and, so far, has not received State funds.

Will even one of the U.N.'s 17 'sustainable development goals' be met by 2030?
By any standards, it was an eye-popping to-do list.
No poverty. Zero hunger. Quality education for all. Gender equality. Clean water and sanitation. Reduced inequalities. Peace, justice and strong Institutions.
In September 2015, these were just some of the 17 goals that global leaders set for themselves to accomplish in the next fifteen years. The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals, broken down into 169 targets, were meant to transform the world by 2030.
A decade later, that deadline is closing in, but the world is nowhere near achieving much of what it promised. According to the U.N.'slatest assessment report"
- Just 15% of the targets for which sufficient data are available are on track.
- 21% are making moderate progress
- 32% are making marginal progress
- 17% are stagnant.
- And 15% have alarmingly slipped far below where they stood in 2015.
These numbers raise big questions. Were these goals just too unrealistic and ambitious in the first place? Can the world expect to tick some of those boxes before the deadline? And if none of the goals are met, is the enterprise a failure?
While none of the SDGs goals are literally impossible to achieve, many require rates of progress that would be "historically unprecedented" — far beyond what even the fastest-improving countries have previously achieved, says Charles Kenny, senior fellow at the Center for Global Development, a think-tank in Washington, D.C. "In order to meet them, we'd have to see incredibly dramatic global policy change," he says.
Zero poverty, for instance, is a great goal to have, he says. "There is no moral excuse for [extreme poverty] at all. On the other hand, given the global system and political realities, the idea that we were going to get to zero by 2030 was really optimistic."
There's no point in blaming the goal, experts say, when the actions of the global community don't match up. "I don't want to let governments off the hook," Kenny says. "These SDGs were agreements between the planet's leaders." But he points out: "the heads of countries that signed these goals then went back home and didn't do any of the things that might have helped speed it up."
Wealthier countries could have accelerated progress by increasing development aid, expanding trade opportunities, increasing private investment in poorer countries, and allowing greater migration, Kenny says. Instead, several of these trends have either stalled or moved in the opposite direction.
But Kenny cautions that judging progress solely by whether countries are on track to meet those ambitious targets can obscure how much has actually changed. "One of the problems with setting really ambitious goals is you can be off track and yet making big progress," he says.
What's working?
This is especially true with some of the health goals, says Thoai Ngo, Professor and Chair of Population and Family Health at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, New York. "We do continue to see child mortality fall year after year, and life expectancy increase. We see more and more kids going to school. There is a lot of progress," he says.
Some goals, such as gender equality, have had a domino effect, says Ngo. "We've managed to keep more girls in school, which has helped prevent child marriage and has improved the health of women in general."
"In my view, the goals worked where money, technology and political will lined up," says Paul Spiegel, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Humanitarian Health. Since 2015, he notes, roughly a billion people have gained access to safe drinking water, and 1.2 billion have decent sanitation. Electricity now reaches 92% of the world and 74% are connected to the internet. New HIV infections have fallen by 30%, and AIDS-related deaths by 35%. The proportion of births attended by a trained health professional is on track to reach 90%. "For the first time, more than half of humanity has some form of social protection [such as a pension, cash assistance, maternity or disability benefits, unemployment support or health coverage]," he says.
The goals have provided a universal direction of where we want to get, they have inspired new partnerships and collaborations among different sectors, they have facilitated data collection and measurement, says Shirin Malekpour, associate professor of sustainability governance at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia. "I see all of the above as facilitators of change," she says.
Inadequate or ... more than adequate?
Measuring the SDGs solely by how many targets have been met may miss what the goals were intended to achieve, says Sakiko Fukuda-Parr, professor emerita of international affairs at The New School, New York. "It means that our actions have been inadequate to actually live up to our aspirations," she says. "But that doesn't mean we shouldn't have goals at all. It helps to think about these and to make an effort to take action."
On a visit to Okayama in Japan this month, she was struck by how universities and the wider community had embraced the goals as a framework for sustainable development.
In 2018, Japan designated Okayama an"SDGs Future City," recognizing its effort to put the sustainable development goals into practice in everyday life by building sustainable businesses and healthier communities and by encouraging greater citizen participation in community initiatives and decision-making. Schools, universities, nonprofits, businesses and local governments now work together to translate the broad goals into community action. "I think at that community level, the SDGs have been extraordinarily successful in bringing like-minded people together," she says. "It's not just a numerical scorecard but a political and social catalyst."
Crises don't help
Meanwhile, the world scene hasn't helped. Repeated global crises have put pressure on the SDGs.
"There has been one crisis after another, and some of these are global crises, like the COVID pandemic or the effects of certain wars leading to inflation and critical materials becoming much more expensive. Climate change, of course, has affected each region differently," says Andrew Shepherd, senior research associate at ODI Global, a think tank, and director of the Chronic Poverty Advisory Network in the U.K.
"While people have escaped poverty, other people have fallen into poverty. Or some of the people who've escaped poverty have fallen back into poverty as a result of these crises," he says.
Shepherd argues that policymakers need to anticipate crises better and focus more on preventing people from slipping back into extreme poverty, especially the large number whose lives are better but remain highly vulnerable to economic shocks. It can be much harder for governments and the international community to create economic growth that is genuinely inclusive and reaches those most often left behind, such as women, people with disabilities and other marginalized folk, he says.
For this, governments need a lot of foresight. "There isn't enough attention given to the resources and support for people to recover from crises," Shepherd says. He says governments and international agencies are generally better at responding to emergencies than at helping people recover from them. Support often tapers off quickly once the immediate crisis passes, he says, even though households may remain financially vulnerable for years.
What protects people?
Giving poorer people better access to loans and financial services can help, Shepherd says, but it can also create new problems. Microfinance has made it easier for many low-income families to borrow money, but without strong safeguards, people can end up taking on more debt than they can repay.
He points to Bangladesh, where microfinance first became widely established and where over-borrowing is now a concern. "Microfinance is definitely part of the solution," he says, adding that digital finance has also helped more people gain access to financial services. "But there are still some risks there which need to be addressed and governments should focus more on this."'
Health insurance, he says, offers another kind of protection. Rwanda's community-based health insurance system called the Mutuelles de Santé, developed in the late 1990s, is worth emulating, he says. Premiums are linked to income. Under the current system, those in the poorest category pay nothing because the government covers the entire premium, and people in higher income categories contribute increasingly larger amounts. Such systems, Shepherd says, can help prevent an unexpected illness from wiping out a family's savings or pushing people back below the poverty line.
That preventive approach is particularly relevant to the SDGs' pledge to "leave no one behind," he says.
Another area where the world could focus on more would be on environmental goals, says Ngo. "We need to invest more in climate resilience, increasing [disease] surveillance, community infrastructure, strengthening food, agriculture and social systems. Our ecosystems and biodiversity continue to be lost. War and conflict are wiping out our gains."
Although the narrower measure of chronic hunger has recently improved, 2.1 billion people experienced moderate or severe food insecurity in 2025 —527 million more than in 2015. In conflict-ridden Western Asian countries like Palestine, Yemen and Syria , undernourishment is still increasing, says Ngo. Forced displacement reached 117 million people by mid-2025, while civilian conflict deaths remain well above post-2015 levels. The number of refugees relative to the global population hasmore than doubled since 2015.
The global risk of species extinction continues to worsen. More than48,600 species are now threatened, facing extinction.
We're also consuming more resources than ever before, with record levels of e-waste and hazardous waste, moving in theopposite direction of sustainable development objectives.
Collective policies can make a difference, says Kenny. Governments, and people working together make it worthwhile to strive toward these goals, even if many remain unmet, he says. "There's still much reason for hope."

A clinical trial by doctors at a private medical college hospital in Chickballapur near Bengaluru has found that a dual stellate ganglion block (SGB) procedure may help reduce anxiety symptoms in patients who do not respond to standard treatment.
The study, published in the July-August 2026 issue of Pain Physician, an open-access journal, involved 63 patients with moderate to severe treatment-resistant anxiety. The researchers found that those who underwent the procedure had a significantly greater reduction in anxiety symptoms than those who received a sham procedure.
What the study involved
Led by G. Niraj, senior consultant, anaesthesiology, and a multidisciplinary team of pain medicine physicians, psychiatrists, and clinical psychologists at the Sri Madhusudan Sai Institute of Medical Sciences and Research (SMSIMSR) in Chickballapur, the randomised controlled trial evaluated dual SGB specifically for treatment-resistant anxiety.
The study focused on patients whose anxiety had persisted despite standard treatment. Treatment-resistant anxiety was defined as failure to respond to at least one first-line medication and one first-line psychotherapy, each given for at least eight weeks. Most patients in the study had tried several medications. Forty-six of the 63 participants had tried at least two medications.
The study involved 63 patients, of whom 42 received the dual SGB procedure and 21 received the sham treatment. The patients were followed for 12 weeks.
What is the procedure?
A stellate ganglion block involves injecting a local anaesthetic and steroid mixture into a group of nerves in the neck under ultrasound guidance. These nerves are part of the sympathetic nervous system, which controls the body’s ‘fight-or-flight’ response.
The procedure was performed on both sides of the neck, with the second block given between 24 hours and seven days after the first. The researchers said that reducing excessive activity in the sympathetic nervous system may help ease some symptoms of anxiety.
“Persistent anxiety is not just in the head. The body’s stress alarm can remain stuck in the ‘on’ position. Our research helps to reset this stress response, offering hope to people whose anxiety has not responded to standard treatments,” Dr. Niraj said.
He stressed that SGB was not intended to replace psychological therapy or medication. “It provides another valuable option for patients with poorly controlled anxiety,” he said.
The procedure was generally well tolerated by the patients in the study. None of the adverse events reported in the SGB group was serious. Temporary hoarseness lasting one to three hours was reported by 14 patients, while one patient experienced numbness in an upper limb that resolved within six hours.
Future potential
Dr. Niraj and his colleagues said the findings could have implications for mental healthcare in both rural and urban areas, particularly where access to long-term psychological therapy is limited. The researchers said a clinic-based intervention, when used appropriately alongside existing mental health treatment, could provide a valuable option for patients with difficult-to-treat anxiety.
The researchers cautioned that the findings need to be confirmed through larger studies. The trial was conducted at a single centre and followed patients for only 12 weeks. Further research is needed to determine how long the benefits last and to better understand the mechanism through which SGB may help reduce anxiety.

Your questions about the AI apocalypse, answered
Writer Jasmine Sun offers some clarity on the AI panic.
Hi readers, happy Friday! We’re talking AI again today.
Earlier this week, my colleague Caitlin Dewey asked for your questions about artificial intelligence and, well, whether it’s going to kill us all. We asked Jasmine Sun, who writes about the culture and politics of AI on her Substack and other publications, to help us answer them.
These questions were sourced from two readers of this newsletter, Levi and Orietta, as well as Vox readers who submitted questions on social media. If you have more questions, you can always reach me at cameron.peters@voxmedia.com, and we’ll do our best to get them answered!
Now, here’s Jasmine:
AI researchers have been warning about the risk of human extinction for years now, and AI executives have been calling for federal regulation for almost as long. But the latest warning, and the latest call for regulation, seems to have really resonated with a lot of people. Is something different this time? And if so, what?
I was also surprised to see these ideas break through — a new poll found that 63 percent of Americans now think AI has at least a moderate chance of “destroying humanity”!
My guess is that a couple factors mainly catalyzed the shift.
First, skeptics used to dismiss rogue AI scenarios as “science fiction.” But the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident brought these from speculation into reality: Thousands of unreleased AIs teamed up to escape one company’s sandboxes and hack into another one, unbeknownst to the researchers who created them.
Second, the extinction talk from AI employees used to seem disingenuous: Why build a technology you think might kill everyone? That made ex-Anthropic-and-OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon’s exit tweet especially penetrating. Quitting signals “that you mean it,” as Matt Yglesias said. And Coxon’s announcement had just the right combination of good timing, moral clarity, and comms savvy to spark a media storm.
These safety incidents are also colliding with the fiery grassroots backlash to data centers and Flock cameras. People and politicians are primed for yet another reason to fear AI.
It can be difficult, as a layperson, to evaluate the credibility of the AI researchers warning about existential risk. How do you go about evaluating these claims, as a journalist and technologist? And what’s your read on the current freakout: Are the extinction people credible experts…or participants in some kind of mass delusion?
Many AI “doomers” are pretty knowledgeable, and they represent a significant fraction of top researchers. Half of AI researchers in a 2024 survey gave at least a 10 percent chance of “human extinction” or “permanent and severe disempowerment.” Those who have worked at AI companies — like Jacob Coxon, Geoffrey Hinton, and Daniel Kokotajlo — have a unique perspective both on how modern AI is developed, as well as the company cultures that might permit recklessness.
But that doesn’t make the doomers either representative or correct. There are plenty of experts in AI and other domains who are less gloomy: Some are optimistic that we can “align” the AIs, ensuring they follow human goals; others find it implausible that AIs — code, not beings — will develop a motive for massacre. Extinction is also a high bar as opposed to, say, a nuclear-bomb-level accident that still kills millions.
AI risk is genuinely complicated, and nobody can predict the future, much as they try. Experts can — and do — vehemently disagree. I try to seek out and take seriously all sides of the debate before coming up with a (provisional) take.
What is the method through which AI would actually eliminate humans? Do we get robots like in Futurama that are programmed with an unremovable “kill all humans” bug and overpower any life form, or is it something…less epic?
The Hugging Face hack showed that we’ve trained AIs to be disturbingly goal-oriented. They’ll throw themselves relentlessly at a problem, developing long-term cooperative strategies, with total disregard for human decorums like “Do not commit cybercrimes to do well on a test.”
You could conceive of a similar but more extreme scenario where AIs decide that they could accomplish goals more easily by getting rid of the pesky humans who might gatekeep resources or shut them down. And they might figure that getting rid of all humans in one go — e.g., via a deadly engineered virus — would be the most efficient cheat. This is one type of story I’ve heard people tell.
It seems unlikely that AIs will turn to murder as the most effective way to influence humans (versus, say, nonviolent persuasion). We also haven’t seen much evidence that AIs have long-term goals that persist across projects. And current AI is not nearly as capable in the physical world as in the digital: There are a lot of natural roadblocks preventing isolated disasters from escalating across the globe.
Are there nearer-term threats — hacking, mass unemployment — that are more plausible or more urgent than risks like human extinction?
Definitely. We’re already seeing AI-enabled cyberattacks, a tougher hiring market for junior programmers, chatbot-induced psychological incidents, and more. You can also imagine AI catastrophes not quite at the level of extinction: Criminals could use AI to hack into small banks and drain their accounts, or the US military might launch a fleet of autonomous drones that misfire and kill thousands of civilians instead. I’m more concerned about humans voluntarily handing power to flawed AI systems than AIs developing their own motives.
However, we should be able to allocate resources toward both categories of risk. And in some cases, the tactics to address short-term problems — such as limiting AIs’ cyber-offense abilities, or improving AIs’ ability to follow human directions — may reduce extinction risk too.
We got a lot of versions of this question: What can individuals or protest movements do to check the AI industry, in the absence of more aggressive government regulations?
Honestly, I think the whole AI conversation could benefit from more specificity and less vague fearmongering. There’s a way that the word “extinction” tends to short-circuit people’s thinking and make them panic instead of focusing on solutions.
If you’re worried, I’d start by reading about different AI risk scenarios and deciding which really concern you. Then you can go from there to contacting your congresspeople. Some of the leading AI companies are starting to say they’ll self-regulate — but actual national policy is what’s necessary to enforce safety across the industry.
Jasmine Sun is a writer covering the culture and politics of AI on her Substack. Her work has appeared in the New York Times, the Atlantic, and the Wall Street Journal. She is based in San Francisco.

A Chinese optical engineer is the winner of this year’s Small World in Motion competition, sponsored by Nikon. Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in Beijing beat out 346 other video entries from 40 different countries with his super-resolution video (above) of the abnormal beating of cilia in the airways of a child with a rare genetic respiratory disorder.
Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a genetic disorder that adversely affects the tiny hairlike structures that line the lungs, among other areas. Their wavelike motion helps move around germs, mucus, dust, and other irritants so the body can dispel them via coughing or sneezing. In people born with PCD, there is something wrong with those cilia, so those irritants build up, causing respiratory infections, among other complications. The cilia might be the wrong size, the wrong shape, or missing altogether. They might move abnormally or not move at all.

Recently, I may have saved a woman’s life on the road. Somehow, this was something I had expected to happen.
On that day, I saw a truck leave a construction site with a tangled wire trailing behind. I frantically looked to see what the wire was attached to and spotted the scaffolding a few meters ahead. I shrieked and grabbed the hand of the woman walking in front of me just as the metal pipes came crashing down. We hugged for a brief second, and then walked our separate ways.
Mumbai (pictured top) is a city that is being made every day, and so much of the Bandra-Khar area that I inhabit is never not under construction. Since I moved here from Seoul earlier this year, I have learned to be hypervigilant every time I walk the streets.
I was reminded of that moment last week as news broke about the collapse of a five-storey building in Delhi, which killed seven people. Authorities had flagged safety concerns in the neighbourhood months earlier, the Hindustan Times reported, after 23 people died in a fire at another building.
As the world’s most populous country, India can feel like a place where life can be startlingly cheap, and people die every day in tragedies that could have been prevented. According to analysis of government data by the Times of India, between 2020 and 2004 nearly 33,000 deaths occurred due to building collapses, fires or people falling into pits and maintenance holes.
The collapse in Delhi has prompted questions, once again, about the state of urban infrastructure in India’s biggest cities. At a time when the country is undertaking a rapid infrastructure boom – new airports, high-speed expressways, luxury residential towers– daily life in cities like Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru appears to be deteriorating.
Indian cities are not walkable, they rank among the worst for air quality, construction is poorly regulated, seasonal flooding is common and waste management remains under pressure. These challenges are only going to increase; the World Bank expects India’s urban population to double, going up to 951 million, by 2050. More than half of the urban infrastructure the country will need by then has yet to be built, it said.
So, what would it take to make our cities better and safer? The experts I spoke to broadly agreed that Indian cities don’t lack rules as much as the political will and institutional machinery to enforce them.
For infrastructure veteran Vinayak Chatterjee, one solution lies in giving urban local bodies more power. He points to a constitutional amendment from 1992 that was meant to strengthen municipalities and give them greater responsibility over urban planning. “But it remains largely unimplemented – in spirit and will. It is a serious matter that affects the very fabric of our urban existence,” said Chatterjee, founder of the Infravision Foundation.
Rahul Goel, an expert on transportation safety and a professor at the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi, believes the problem with India’s roads begins with on-street parking. “People are using public space for personal use. Everything becomes better when you remove on-street parking,” he said, arguing that freeing up roads would make pedestrians and cyclists safer, reduce traffic jams and make walking easier.
In other cities in the global south, from Bangkok to Manila to Cape Town, one cannot just park their car on the road to run errands, Goel said. He described it as a governance failure, saying there is a need to create more parking spaces and perhaps have civil defense personnel or municipal workers enforce fines.
“Our streets are self-run,” Goel said. “That’s why they are in complete disarray.” He pointed to the Delhi Metro as an example of a space where people follow rules and things are orderly. “When rules are enforced, people follow them.”
The same gap between rules and enforcement is evident at construction sites.
India has detailed guidelines for construction approvals, including how traffic must be managed, what signage must be put up, and creating paths for pedestrians. But compliance remains a significant problem, says Geetam Tiwari, emeritus professor at Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. In an audit of construction sites on highways, including bridges, Tiwari and her colleagues found widespread violations. Contractors had a financial incentive to complete projects quickly with payments being tied to the pace of construction, she said, adding that penalties for violations were low enough that it was cheaper to simply pay the fine than make fixes.
For unsafe buildings and unauthorised renovations, Tiwari said, the solution also requires bringing stakeholders together: resident associations, landlords, lessees and local authorities to conduct audits, raise awareness and penalise contractors who violate safety requirements. Actions, she said, that should not wait for the next tragedy.
In the aftermath of the Delhi case, the high court has directed authorities to inspect student accommodations for safety. Building owners have been arrested and several municipal officials in charge of the area have been suspended.
A similar governance deficit shows up when it comes to air pollution, another long-time challenge for Indian cities. Ronak Sutaria, founder and CEO of Respirer Living Sciences, has been working on one aspect of this issue: by developing affordable air-quality monitors for construction sites. Respirer’s air-quality monitors are now installed in 5,000 locations across 10 cities in India, helping authorities identify pollution hotspots. (Some cities, including Mumbai, require construction sites to monitor pollution levels.)
“A number of sites are getting alerts [from authorities] and are taking dust-suppression measures, for instance, to bring down [pollution] levels. So, the entire loop is sort of working,” Sutaria said.
Indian cities continue to grow, but the question is whether governance can keep pace. On that afternoon in Bandra, I recall thinking how lucky the woman and I were not to be grievously injured. But we shouldn’t have to rely on luck to survive.

A recommendation from someone with great taste
This week, writer and professor Amitava Kumar (@amitavawriter), whose latest book, The Social Life of Trains, explores how railways helped shape India’s national identity, suggests the work of a poet he discovered on Instagram:
“Can I begin with a confession? I have been a professor of literature for more than three decades, but I don’t often understand poems. How lovely it is, then, to discover a poet whose lines are as clear and beautiful as the dawn! Recently, I came across the poems of a young Hindi poet named Parag Pawan. They spoke to me and, more importantly, they spoke to our moment. I immediately sat down to translate them into English.
A series of his poems could be translated as Poems for the Unemployed. One of the poems, sharp and precise, begins with the funny, acerbic lines: ‘On the topic of our unemployment / the prime minister gives speeches / but he doesn’t give us jobs. / He works for eighteen hours / while we believe that asking anyone to work / for more than eight hours / is exploitation.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
2,192
That’s the number of days Umar Khalid has spent in jail since his arrest on 13 September 2020 – without trial. Last week, the student activist wrote a searing account describing the daily drudgery of life in prison, published in The Quint. Earlier this year, in his first interview since being jailed, Khalid told the Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Peterson: “Humanity is a privilege that is not granted to people like me.”
Vibe check
As more people read news online, watching Ayan Shaikh (@paperboy_ayan) delivering newspapers with serious swag gave me great joy and some hope. The 22-year-old from Ahmedabad posts videos of it on Instagram, and it’s a feat to watch. Watch his papers swerve, reach gravity-defying heights and land with pinpoint accuracy and tell me his deliveries don’t rival Jasprit Bumrah.
Delivering papers was Shaikh’s first job after he dropped out of school. He spent four years mastering the techniques that would allow him to make faster deliveries to earn more money. The first video, filmed by his friend, had 20m views and a recent one has crossed 128m, more views than many Bollywood stars might command. He starts his day at 4:30am, making 300 deliveries in two hours, before he begins a second shift as a gig worker for quick commerce apps.
“I think people love [the videos] because I do it passionately … from my heart,” he said. “If you do things dedicatedly, anything is possible. It won’t work out once, twice, thrice, but it might on the fourth attempt.”

The Indian spacetech ecosystem is entering its most critical phase yet. After years of experimentation and ambition, spacetech startups must now prove they are on a path to commercial viability. Investors are already betting on this transition. According to Inc42's data, homegrown spacetech startups have already raised $252.9 Mn so far this year, nearly double what the sector raised in 2025. Leading the momentum is Skyroot Aerospace. The startup became India’s first spacetech unicorn in May after it raised a $60 Mn round. Subsequently, it was successful in becoming the first Indian private company to place a rocket into orbit with its Vikram-1 mission. It is now lining up a bigger $200 Mn round. Earlier this month, Temasek-backed hyperspectral imaging startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn Series C round made headlines as the single-largest funding round raised by a spacetech startup in India. So, why are spacetech startups suddenly the flavour of the season? A key reason is the deepening policy push. The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) earlier this year began deploying capital from its ₹1,600 Cr Antariksh Venture Capital Fund. Similarly, the state-backed ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) fund also recently allocated nearly ₹834 Cr to spacetech startups in its inaugural cohort. The buzz around the sector hasn’t just been about money coming in, but real achievements too. GalaxEye recently became the first Indian startup to secure a US patent for its OptoSAR satellite imaging technology. Agnikul Cosmos also completed a test firing of its Agnite engine, which boasts India’s first semi-cryogenic engine and the largest 3D-printed single-piece rocket engine in the world. Despite this, finding commercial viability is a looming concern for many spacetech startups. In addition, there are concerns around the frothy spacetech valuations. Under the current scheme of things, can Indian spacetech startups convert milestones into scalable and sustainable business models? What Are VCs Betting On? Earlier this year, Union minister of state (MoS) Jitendra Singh pegged the size of India’s space economy at around $9 Bn and projected that it would grow to nearly $45 Bn over the next decade. Behind this projected market size is an entire value chain: First comes the infrastructure layer that enables launches, including ground stations, launch vehicles, and the components that act as inputs for the rockets Then come payloads – the satellites and sensors that hitch a ride on the rocket and generate data from orbit From there comes the ‘downstream’ data intelligence and applications layer, comprising analytics and services that process the raw data from the previous step. It is this ‘downstream’ layer that Viju George, a partner at Mela Ventures, believes has the most promise. “Revenue models in satellites tend to be very lumpy and capex-driven, whereas data streams tend to be high-margin recurring revenue,” he observed. The upstream input layer is relatively more commoditised, as per George. But that doesn’t mean it’s not investable. “If you’re able to take the shovels approach, where you provide the components to satellites like avionics, communication infrastructure, and others, that is a kind of a multipurpose play. With that positioning, you're not really dependent on a single satellite brand winning or losing,” he added. Ashish Taneja of GrowX Ventures, an early investor in Pixxel, also believes that the nascent earth observation segment is a huge market opportunity. He added that the infrastructure layer is a “big thing too” as it continues to be a supply-constrained market. But have the potential and the promise of spacetech taken investors too far? The Gap Between Hype & Market Demand The rapid influx of capital into the spacetech sector is creating concerns around valuations, market size and whether the demand required to justify these bets has materialised yet. “I worry about the valuations because now somehow we are in the FOMO zone,” George said, adding that he is unsure whether the market is large enough to support current valuations. The risk, he said, is “whether you are paying a little bit more for market demand that is not yet evident.” The valuation question is especially pronounced for capex-heavy businesses, where large cheques are being signed based on potential future launch cadence and scale, even as India’s launch capacity is still developing. Space hardware also carries risks around technology, manufacturing, launch and satellite longevity. Satellites are expected to operate for around five to six years, but India does not yet have enough historical data to establish how reliably newer constellations will perform over that period. Because of limited launch experience and deployments, investors are finding it tough to benchmark execution capability or predictable revenues. The growing number of startups is also raising the investment bar, with multiple ventures now attacking similar problems. To achieve scale, spacetech startups will need to expand their base beyond government buying, which has, thus far, acted as an anchor customer. These emerging players will also need to tap into foreign sovereign buyers and commercial enterprises as well. But demonstrating competitive cost, reliability, performance and consistency will be key to competing in international markets. As such, GrowX’s Taneja remarks that “not many people will make the cut” in attracting sustained capital, predicting consolidation as startups expand beyond their initial products and become vertically integrated space infrastructure companies. Simply put, he believes that stronger players could eventually acquire or absorb smaller companies. What Will It Take To Win Capital? The first phase of Indian spacetech hinged on visions and ideas. But growing market maturity and an influx of new ventures have turned investor focus to identifying which businesses can turn technical breakthroughs into large, durable markets. A startup may solve an extremely difficult engineering or deeptech problem, but that alone does not guarantee a scalable business. “Early stage investors like to see milestones because we think they are the precursor to valuations and revenues. But once growth investors come in, they like to see tangible metrics,” said Mela Ventures’ George. In 2018-19, investors were largely evaluating founder quality, technical capabilities, and whether building satellites and propulsion systems out of India was even possible. This is no longer the case. “I want a precise use case. I want clarity on the use case. I want a differentiated solution which is defensible in the long run,” said Taneja. Investors also want clarity on who will buy the product, how it will be used and what makes the offering difficult to replicate. Hence, established spacetech startups have more of an advantage now in attracting growth funding as they have a track record to show. Signs of market maturity are also evident with global investors now participating in larger rounds, while domestic growth-stage funds are also beginning to enter Series B and beyond. But the funding pool remains smaller, particularly for capital-intensive spacetech businesses that require significant funding before reaching scale. This could make the public markets increasingly relevant to the sector's long-term funding cycle. Once companies have spent years building technology, establishing revenues and reaching sufficient scale, public listings could provide another route to capital and liquidity. For early investors, meanwhile, the long development cycle itself can create multiple opportunities for valuation repricing as spacetech startups move from technical milestones to commercial deployment. Taneja cited a 17X outcome over around five years, following the sale of a small portion of GrowX’s stake during Pixxel’s recent $100 Mn fundraise. Regardless, the investment thesis has evolved substantially from when the first spacetech startups created the market a decade ago. The real challenge now is not reaching the stars, but turning that journey into a stellar business.

'We hit the floor': Belleville, Ont., synagogue leader recounts shooting that left police officer, man injured
Exchange of gunfire came as members of Jewish community gathered for Yom Kippur
Around 7 p.m. on Sunday evening, Sons of Jacob Synagogue president Norman Weddum was ushering people into the Belleville, Ont., sanctuary to begin services for Yom Kippur when he heard shots ring out.
"It was boom, boom, boom," Weddum told CBC News Network on Monday.
The exchange of gunfire outside the synagogue in the southern Ontario community left a man and a police officer wounded, authorities say. The 29-year-old man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition. The officer is in critical but stable condition.
Weddum said he went to the lobby where he could hear more defined shots.
"I could say, 'Oh, this is definitely … someone is shooting here,'" he said. "So that's when we ran back into the auditorium of the synagogue, closed the doors behind us so as to not leave a visible target and we hit the floor."
"Literally everyone went down," he said. "I yelled for everyone to get on to the floor and the shots continued for a few more seconds, and then it was basically over."
Weddum said the officer had been stationed outside the building in an unmarked car.
Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said the shooting involved a man with a rifle. It also confirmed the incident happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, in the area of Bleecker Avenue and Victoria Avenue, about 175 kilometres east of Toronto.
Belleville police said the officer encountered the man around 7:10 p.m. and that both were taken to a hospital.
Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The SIU, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.
Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was underway.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.
"I'm disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur," Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people "have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear" and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
"My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones," Ford said.
Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis told the CBC's Ontario Morning he was shocked by the news of the incident. He said his heart goes out to the Jewish community and commended the injured officer.
"We've been rocked by this … stuff like this doesn't happen in Belleville," he said. "We are a community that's strong, and we are a community that's vibrant, and we will get through this together."
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow also said her thoughts are with the Jewish community and injured officer in a post on social media platform X.
"Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives," she said. "As long as we contend with rising antisemitism and hate, we will spare no expense keeping the community safe."
Toronto Police Service said in a statement Monday, while there is no known threat to Toronto, they will be increasing patrols at synagogues and other places of worship.
York Regional Police also said there was no known threat in the region, but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Witness counts over 20 shots
Chris Masterson, who lives nearby, said he was watching TV on Sunday evening when he heard three "loud pops."
"There was a little bit of a pause and then I heard more shots," he said. "It was very clear it was gunshots."
Masterson said he estimates there were around 25 shots back and forth before he heard a siren and someone clearly yell: "Police, stop."
"I've been living here for over 10 years and nothing like this has ever happened," said another resident, Cody Bain. "It kinda makes you nervous. Makes you wonder about the future."
Surge in antisemitism
Sunday's shooting comes months after Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Canada was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.
Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues and attacks on community centres and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.
Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.
'We will carry on': synagogue leader
When asked what he thought the man involved in the shooting was trying to do, synagogue leader Weddum said he thought "his intentions were pretty clear."
"Well, he was coming down the street with some type of a firearm, and he was headed toward a synagogue where Jewish people were having service. So I think his intentions were pretty clear," said Weddum.
"It's rough. And unfortunately we can't have our services again today to complete the Yom Kippur holiday, because the building is under a lockdown right now for the investigation," he said. "But, you know, once the building is released we'll get back to having services.
"We will carry on."

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued an alert on the use of unauthorised cosmetic products manufactured in Pakistan, which are on sale in India.
A public notice dated September 8, 2026, stated that cosmetic products named ‘Goree Beauty Cream’ and ‘Chandni Whitening Cream’ are unauthorised for sale and no trade registration certificate was issued to the manufacturers.
“To manufacture cosmetics for sale and distribution, a licence must be obtained from the State Licensing Authority... For the import of cosmetics, the products must be registered with the Central Licensing Authority in accordance with prescribed rules,” the notice said.
The products are unauthorised and contain excessive levels of heavy metals beyond the specified limits, which may pose health risks to consumers, including toxic effects, said CDSCO.
The drug regulator warned people not to purchase or use the products. It also asked consumers not to use similarly named cosmetic products if they had already purchased them.
It also informed that all concerned establishments/individuals were warned not to sell, distribute or advertise these products.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa
- Published
"What we are going to do, I have no idea," sobs Nokwanda Matshikiza, reflecting on the murder of her niece Dineo Motapane. "But something must give."
"For us, for all the other women. How many other bodies will be found before something happens?"
Nokwanda is speaking to the BBC from the family home near South Africa's main city, Johannesburg, just two days after relatives identified Dineo's body.
The 38-year-old mother-of-two was last seen alive last Sunday. Her battered body, partly burned, found later in the residential region of Ekurhuleni.
Nokwanda weeps as she describes how the family will have to face, at some point, the grim task of telling Dineo's daughter of her death.
"How do you explain that your parent was brutally murdered, dumped in a field, and just left there, discarded like a piece of rubbish.
"There's no coming to peace with it," she adds. "It's something that you can never reconcile yourself with, that you can never get over."
Dineo's death this week has come amid a series of comparable incidents in Ekurhuleni – her body one of three discovered there this week. In total, nine bodies of murdered women have been found in similar circumstances in the region since July.
The problem has always been there but this spate of grim discoveries has once again sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country – which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
Themba Kekana is also living in shock at the death of a loved one.
His sister, Itumeleng, was one of the first to disappear in Ekurhuleni.
The 32-year-old shopkeeper's body was found in July, 17 days after she was last seen alive. Her body was badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge.
"We are devastated with grief," says Themba, wet eyes shining.
"I look at my sister's young daughter and my eyes fill with tears, I know there is no way that I can ever take this pain away from her.
"No family should have to deal with what we are faced with."
Only one arrest has been made in connection with the murders – and that was two days after the first body was discovered on 15 July.
Nobody has been detained following the murders of Itumeleng or Dineo or the other six Ekurhuleni women.
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
Police have said they are not sure if they are hunting a serial killer. It is possible the cases are not linked.
Either way, what has happened in this residential district east of South Africa's biggest city has traumatised the nation, shining a spotlight on a situation that many believe is a crisis.
South Africa's police issue detailed crime statistics every quarter, which show that during the last quarter – between April and June this year - 5,427 people were murdered.
The official data does not distinguish between the genders of the victims, but this week the country's Human Rights Commission released figures showing that 569 women had been killed in that period (six a day on average), with another 1,052 who faced attempted murder.
Many women - already feeling unsafe - have been left reeling by recent events.
And it has put pressure on the government, less than a year after ministers acknowledged the scale of the issue and declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
Announcing the move last November, Minister of Social Development Nokuzola Sisisi Tolashe said treating the issue as a national disaster would help the government tackle the crisis.
It followed weeks of protests, culminating in a "Women's Shut Down" march as South Africa hosted the G20 summit.
This week has seen a chorus of calls for things to go further.
Rights group Amnesty International said an important first step towards protecting South Africa's women was to recognise femicide as a separate crime.
"Every day that femicide remains unrecognised as a crime is a failure to confront the targeted killing of women," said Amnesty's country director Shenilla Mohamed in a statement. "It is time to call it what it is: Femicide.
"Femicide is a gender-motivated crime. It is the killing of a woman because she is a woman."
Amnesty says femicide is criminalised as a specific crime in 33 countries, including Gabon and Morocco in Africa.
It argues that making that change in South Africa could help focus on the scale of the issue.
"It would compel the state to confront their failure to protect women and girls from violence," says Mohamed. "You cannot fix what you are not tracking."
Almost everyone in South Africa agrees more needs to be done.
President Cyril Ramaphosa this week pledged to leave "no stone unturned" in investigating the crimes in Ekurhuleni, adding: "As a nation, we must stand up for the rights, safety and dignity of women and girls."
Lebogang Ramofoko, an advocate for gender and social justice, said the levels of violence against women in the country were symptomatic of a much bigger problem – a lack of regard for humanity.
"The bodies of black women have been treated as disposable in this country for time in memorial, passed down from colonisation through to apartheid," she tells the BBC, referring to the legalised system of racism that was in place until 1994.
"What we see happening to women is testimony to legacies of violence from those systems whose traumas were never addressed.
"This is not to say black men are inherently violent, but in systems where violence was meted out against them for decades, historically black women were the people that that violence would be taken out on - that cycle has not been broken."
In Kempton Park, a district of Ekurhuleni where five of the nine recent bodies were found, Lumka Maqhubela is part of the Girl2Woman Foundation group which has held protests to raise awareness of the crimes.
"We are grieved, we are scared," she says. "If the police cannot protect us any more the government should step in and do something.
"It's clear that we are not safe, we cannot be told by the police to be more vigilant. They should be doing more to make our communities safe – what else are we expected to do? We are not safe anywhere, not in our homes, not in the streets, it needs to stop."
"I feel uncomfortable," says Thulisile Sibande, 32. "When I go to a shop, I have to look around. I'm shocked and scared. So scared, it's a trauma."
Thembi Mabena, 60, tells the BBC she lived in the same neighbourhood as Dineo Motapane.
"She was laughing every day, with everybody," she remembers. "Now I'm worried.
"I know many children, girls, who tell me they are afraid to go to the shop alone. There is no safety, even for me too. I am old, but there is no safety."
"In South Africa," says Lerato Mzizi, 20, simply, "women are not safe any more."
