Britain’s Burnham is set to meet Trump for the first time at the UN in New York
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to meet U.S. President Donald Trump for the first time
LONDON -- LONDON (AP) — Andy Burnham once said he would refuse to meet Donald Trump.
Now Britain’s prime minister is about to hold his first meeting with the U.S. president, with Ukraine and the soaring cost of conflict in the Middle East at the top of his agenda.
U.S. officials say the two leaders will hold talks on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Burnham is set to address the annual gathering of world leaders on Tuesday, setting out his vision of Britain’s place in an increasingly fractured world order.
Burnham’s only other foreign trip since taking office in July was to Kyiv, and he has said he will urge Trump to send interceptor missiles to bolster Ukraine’s air defenses ahead of another winter of war.
The British government also wants to discuss ways to restore free movement of ships through the Strait of Hormuz, largely blocked since the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February. The closure of the key route has sent oil prices spiking, complicating Burnham’s efforts to jump-start Britain’s sluggish economy and ease the cost of living.
Like many Labour Party politicians, Burnham was strongly critical of Trump in the past. In 2017 Burnham, as the mayor of Greater Manchester, said the president wouldn’t be welcome in the city. Two years later he said he would refuse to meet Trump if he visited.
After becoming prime minister in July, Burnham said he always tries to find “common ground” with other politicians.
Burnham and Trump have spoken twice since Burnham replaced Keir Starmer at the helm of the center-left governing party. Trump has called Burnham “a nice guy,” but has also recently needled U.K. officials by expressing support for Irish unification and musing about the future of the Falkland Islands that are claimed by both Britain and Argentina.
Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Burnham would be “pragmatic.”
“We won’t agree with the U.S. administration on everything,” Phillipson told Times Radio on Sunday. "We are from different political traditions, we have different approaches. But maintaining that relationship is critical for our national interest and I know that that’s the approach Andy Burnham will always take, putting our country first.”
Starmer went out of his way to flatter Trump, presenting him in the Oval Office in February 2025 with an invitation from King Charles III for an unprecedented second state visit to the U.K.
British officials felt Starmer’s approach was vindicated when the U.K. struck a trade deal with the Trump administration. But Trump soured on Starmer over his refusal to join the Iran war. The president also has repeatedly criticized the U.K.’s immigration and green-energy policies, urging the country to open more of the North Sea up to oil drilling.
Burnham is expected to announce a decision soon about whether to approve new oil and gas fields off Scotland.
U.K. officials also are braced for criticism of Britain’s ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and efforts to regulate big American technology firms.
Trump’s threats to seize Greenland alarmed the U.K. and other European allies earlier this year, and Burnham was among leaders expressing relief at the announcement of a deal between Greenland, Denmark and the U.S. to bolster the American military presence there but keep the Arctic island under Danish control.
Trump has other, more high-profile, international meetings this week, including one at the White House with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Burnham’s trip comes as middle-sized powers, led most vocally by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, try to forge closer alliances in the face of Trump’s “America first” foreign policy. Burnham’s government wants Britain to be bolder on the world stage, and to restore some of the ties with Europe severed when the U.K. left the European Union in 2020.
Ed Davey, leader of the centrist Liberal Democrats, urged Burnham to “do what the Europeans are doing, what the Canadians are doing, and start saying to Donald Trump, ‘the way you’re treating our country, the way you’re treating the world, is not acceptable.’”
“I want him to stand up to Trump. It’s really clear that’s the only language the president respects,” Davey said.

On Wednesday, US government officials removed a Chinese AI search tool that was briefly deployed on the Federal Register website, Reuters reported.
The change came after social media users noticed an apparent contradiction: The National Archives was using one of Alibaba’s Qwen AI models, even as top US law enforcement claimed that such models illegally copy US frontier models. Earlier this month, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) named Alibaba among six leading Chinese firms allegedly conducting “industrial-scale distillation” that the agency says is helping America’s biggest competitor cut costs and development time in the race for global AI leadership.
It’s unclear when exactly the National Archives, which runs the Federal Register website, began offering visitors the option to use a Qwen model to search public comments on proposed regulations. So far, the independent agency tasked with increasing public access to federal government documents has not commented on the removal and did not respond to Ars’ request for comment. The White House and the FBI have also not commented.
On X, a user with the handle “tleilax___” posted a widely shared screenshot showing the option displayed on the government website on September 15. Reuters’ report noted that an archived version of the site’s source code confirmed that the Qwen model was taken down on Wednesday, so the service was available for at least a day.
Daniel Castro, president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, told Reuters that it is an “insane” disconnect for a US agency to use an Alibaba model while the FBI encourages stakeholders to use only American models.
Use probably posed no security risks
Whether the government use of the Qwen model posed a security risk depends on how it was trained, Georgetown University Law Professor Anupam Chander told Reuters. It also matters if any US data was processed by “Alibaba-controlled systems,” Senator Marker Warner (D-Va.) said.

KYIV/URBANA, Illinois/BERKELEY, California – Twelve years ago, Ukraine was sleepwalking toward catastrophe. Now Europe is.
Before 2014, Ukraine’s military had been hollowed out by decades of neglect and disarmament. That was a choice. Why spend scarce resources on defense when the 1994 Budapest Memorandum offered security assurances in exchange for Ukraine surrendering its nuclear arsenal? Why prepare for a conflict that the prevailing intellectual consensus said could never happen? Liberal democracy had triumphed, great-power conflict was a relic and the arc of progress bent toward peace, liberalization and economic convergence.
Worse, Ukraine allowed Russia to penetrate its information space, promote pro-Kremlin narratives, cultivate political allies and meddle in Ukraine’s elections. Under President Viktor Yanukovych, a former Russian citizen served as minister of defense. The army was sabotaged from within.

For decades, astronomers thought rings were something only giant planets had. That changed in 2013, when a small, dark body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus passed in front of a star and blinked twice on either side of the main event, revealing two narrow rings around an object barely 250 kilometers across. “It was a surprise,” says Pablo Santos-Sanz, an astronomer at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Granada, Spain. Ever since, the question has been what such rings are made of and how long they can last.
In a recent study, Santos-Sanz and his colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope to watch the same body, now known as Chariklo, pass in front of a background star again. They found one of its rings had grown denser and the other had almost vanished. We don’t know exactly why.
Shadowing a star
The technique behind the observation is simple. “We predict when a Solar System object passes in front of a star,” Santos-Sanz said. The starlight dims for a moment, and the shape of that dip reveals the size, shape, and surroundings of the object that caused it. “This is particularly challenging for minor bodies, and more challenging for distant minor bodies,” he said.
The difficulty is that the target’s silhouette on the sky is minuscule, and knowing when it will cross a particular star requires very precise positioning data for both. Still, in 2013, we used ground telescopes to discern Chariklo’s two rings, C1R and C2R. These sat 390 and 405 kilometers from its center and were only a few kilometers wide and about 7 kilometers apart.
Doing this with a space-based telescope, though, makes lining things up considerably harder. JWST sits at the L2 Lagrange point, and controllers need to nudge the telescope every few weeks to keep its orbit stable. “It’s a kind of tricky task,” Santos-Sanz said. His team identified a possible Chariklo occultation in August 2022 and redid the prediction every week. Between the first prediction and one of the last, the projected line of sight shifted by about 110 kilometers, which was enough to move it off the body entirely. Unfortunately, JWST requires observations like this to be planned at least 14 days in advance.
“We did this maybe a bit blindly, because we didn’t know exactly where the line of sight was,” Santos-Sanz said. “I’m going to move one of the biggest, best telescopes in space, and we don’t know if finally we will catch this or not.” But it all worked out.
The occultation came on October 18, 2022. The reconstructed geometry shows JWST’s sightline to the background star skimmed 7.4 kilometers above Chariklo’s surface, missing the body but catching its rings.
The ring that thickened
JWST recorded the event simultaneously in two near-infrared bands, at 1.5 and 3.2 micrometers, which made it the first time anyone has caught a minor body’s rings in a band beyond three micrometers—a range Earth’s atmosphere puts out of reach for ground telescopes.
The inner ring showed up unmistakably, with abrupt, distinct edges, but it was much darker than before. Averaged over roughly 10 previous ground-based occultations, C1R’s normal opacity (the fraction of starlight it blocks) sat at 0.303. JWST measured it at 0.431. “We didn’t believe it at the beginning, so we fought a lot with the data,” Santos-Sanz said.
The most straightforward explanation was geometry. Rings are not always uniform, and JWST might simply have cut through a denser clump. To rule this scenario out, the team built a lumpy ring model and ran 10 million simulated occultations. Reproducing an opacity as high as JWST recorded came out at a roughly 1 in a 1,000 chance at 1.5 micrometers, and 4 in 100,000 at 3.2 micrometers for a single measurement. The telescope caught the ring twice, going in and coming out, which made the odds even smaller than that.
Santos-Sanz concluded that the inner ring most likely got thicker. At the same time, the outer ring did the opposite.
The ring that faded
C2R barely registered at 1.5 micrometers and did not appear at all at 3.2, even though the telescope was recording the same stretch of ring in both bands at the same instant. “At the beginning we didn’t even see the outer ring in the light curve,” Santos-Sanz said. “We had to use models. It was really barely visible, so we said, ‘What is happening here?’”
The team came up with two possible explanations. The first is that JWST, looking at wavelengths where almost no occultation has ever been recorded, is simply seeing grains that scatter light differently in the infrared. The other is that the rings really have physically changed. Santos-Sanz argues radiative transfer models point toward the latter. The older visible-light observations were consistent with a mixture of ice and silicates, but once the JWST data points are added, no combination of materials and grain sizes could explain what the telescope has seen.
“We are witnessing a real evolution of the rings with time,” Santos-Sanz said. “Of course it is not a certainty, but for me it is the preferred explanation.” What’s more, this evolution most likely was not just the material from the fading outer ring migrating inward to the inner ring. Measured as equivalent width, the inner ring gained about 10 times more than the outer ring lost.
“We don’t know where the extra material is coming from, but there are some hypotheses,” Santos-Sanz said.
The ghost moon
The leading explanation, Santos-Sanz explains, is a small shepherd satellite sharing the outer ring’s orbit. Such an object should explain the rings’ stability and their sharp edges and could also shed debris that replenishes C1R. “This satellite has not been detected yet, if it exists,” Santos-Sanz said.
A computer model based on JWST data also hints at what the two rings are made of. Santos-Sanz, though, makes it clear that this part of the work is unfinished. “Our feeling after this model is that the inner ring should be composed of bigger particles than the outer ring. The outer ring we think is more dusty,” he said. “But this is a work in progress. I can’t say with certainty, well, this is dusty, this is not.”
The best test, the team argues, would be to catch another Chariklo occultation, this time using visible light, which would separate genuine change from a wavelength effect. “We are searching for new occultations,” Santos-Sanz said. Understanding how rings around small bodies evolve over time, he explains, matters, because Chariklo is not the only one to have them.
Rings are now known around another body from the same category as Chariklo, called Chiron, the dwarf planet Haumea, and the trans-Neptunian object Quaoar. Giant-planet rings are already known to shift over months and years; Saturn’s D ring has measurably shrunk, and Neptune’s Adams arcs rearrange themselves. Now small bodies appear to do it as well.
“I think this work is just a piece of the puzzle,” Santos-Sanz said, “but it could be an important clue for broader studies about the rings around minor bodies and around giant planets.”

US President Donald Trump called his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in order to persuade Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russia's oil refinery centres, a move that Trump thinks could further deepen the global diesel shortage and the consequential price increase, Financial Times reported citing people familiar with the matter. Trump's message to Zelensky was about “diesel, diesel . . . diesel” and he has urged the latter to stop drone and missile attacks on key Russian oil infrastructure, a senior official who was on the call with the two leaders told the publication. Trump is worried about the price rise of diesel and wants to ensure that Russian oil is reaching the global markets to provide a relief to the rising prices, another official told FT. Zelensky issued a statement after the call, in which he said that it was an 'important conversation', and that his talks with Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week "could change a lot". As per the Ukraine president's office, the meeting will likely take place on Tuesday (local time). "I thanked the President for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s visit to Kyiv. We went through the key details thoroughly, and they saw the situation in Ukraine firsthand. The peace track is our number one priority," Zelensky also said. While the United States is not worried about Russia losing revenue from oil, it is concerned about the knock-on effect lower supply of Russian refined petroleum products could have on the global refined-fuel market, especially diesel. Russia is one of the biggest exporters of refined petroleum products. As per the International Energy Agency (IEA), Russia has around 6.5 million barrels/day of refining capacity. It has been the third-largest producer of refined petroleum products historically. Russian refinery throughput has been reduced almost 30 per cent year-over-year, thanks to strikes by Kyiv. The IEA has also said that global seaborne diesel/gasoil exports averaged 4.7 million barrels/day in the first eight months of 2026, down 10% year-on-year. The Russian and the Middle East diesel exports have also fallen substantially due to the two ongoing wars. More than 1000 drones were fired by Ukraine on Russia on Sunday in the middle of the Russian parliamentary elections. The mayor of Moscow called it the "largest ever" drone attack on the city and said that the Moscow Oil Refinery had also suffered damages. The attack led to two deaths and injured 20, as per local governor Andrei Vorobyov. Zelensky himself shared a video of the damage caused, He called Russia's oil facilities, one of which was hit by Kyiv's drones, as "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine". Russia has not made any comment on Trump's call to Putin to halt attacks on Moscow's oil infrastructure. Neither has Putin said anything after Trump's statement that Ukraine would pause attacks on Russia's oil refineries if Moscow also promises the same. Putin is not likely to agree to this before the winter, when he is planning to launch a major aerial bombardment of Ukraine's energy infra, FT reported citing people briefed of the Russian president's plans. “They are hitting ours. They’ll get an answer. That’s basically how it is,” the Russian president said. A study by Chennai-based diabetologists has attempted to find out how India has managed to reduce the prices of new and expensive diabetes drugs and what lessons this could possibly hold for other low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). The study, ‘Making Modern Diabetes Medications Affordable and Accessible: Lessons from India for Other Countries’, was led by V. Mohan, chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, and was published in the journal Diabetes Care.
What did the study find?
Of the 589 million adults in the world with diabetes, 80% live in LMICs, the study noted. Modern diabetes therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while analogue insulins help reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. However, affordability remains a barrier: diabetes requires lifelong care and management of complications.
India’s ability to maintain low medication prices is closely linked to its role as a major pharmaceutical exporter, the paper stated, noting the strategic legislative history of maintaining critical safeguards to prevent ‘patent evergreening’ and allowing for generic manufacture of drugs. It also found that the country has increasingly focused on strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. There are concerns over global trade policies affecting prices and the availability of raw materials. A government incentive scheme has been introduced to promote domestic manufacturing of raw materials, and as of 2025, production has commenced for 26 molecules that were previously imported.
The paper notes that metformin and sulfonylureas continue to form the foundation of type 2 diabetes management in India - both are included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). While DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4) inhibitors, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA have all been introduced, they are not currently in the NLEM. Initial uptake of these drugs was constrained by pricing. Following the competitive entry by multiple domestic manufacturers, the price of semaglutide, for instance in India, has dropped considerably now, and there has been a huge increase in sales; however, absolute monthly costs remain high relative to the household income in India, and, crucially, these are not covered by insurance, as they are, to a great extent, in the U.S.
Quick availability of generic and biosimilar drugs, deliberate regulatory and distribution strategies such as the government’s Jan Aushadi Kendras, and market competition have allowed for affordable drugs in India, the paper highlighted.
What does it propose for other LMICs?
Building local manufacturing capacity as a strategic public health investment, balancing patent governance that encourages easier access to newer molecules, predictable and structured price regulation, good distribution networks at reasonable retail prices and aligning pharmaceutical policy with health financing and ongoing monitoring of medicine quality, prices, prescription patterns and patient access can all help with improving access to affordable medicines, the paper noted. These core principles could also apply to high-income countries facing drug prices, the paper said.
Challenges ahead
Challenges that remain include urban-rural disparities in distribution and availability of medicines; tight regulations potentially affecting chances of drug innovation; differences in quality between generics and difficulties in maintaining strict pharmacovigilance; as well as limited formal evaluation of government schemes to look at their long-term impact on clinical outcomes.

As European militaries adapt to the use of AI and drones in modern warfare, a NATO-backed startup is helping to deploy AI-driven target detection and selection that can run on small drones for surveillance and attack missions.
The company Scaleout Systems was originally founded by researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden in 2018, and initially focused on training and deploying machine learning models directly on the hardware available in commercial trucks and other vehicles. But once Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company pivoted toward defense applications.
“With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world, we realized that this technology can be very important to operationalize edge data and sensor data for machine learning to make sure that NATO allies have found that strategic advantage,” Andreas Hellander, cofounder and CEO of Scaleout Systems, told Ars.
Instead of using frontier AI models from OpenAI or Anthropic, Scaleout is harnessing leaner ones, such as machine learning models that can perform computer vision tasks on the hardware of drones or computers used at forward bases. “They need to fit on forward-deployed hardware and edge hardware, which can vary quite a bit from small embedded devices to quite powerful edge workstations,” Hellander said.
Scaleout was selected to join NATO’s Defence Innovator Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) Challenge Program in 2025. There, it has worked on the Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon project to adapt machine learning models for the edge computing hardware found in drones, drone pilot tablets, and field command posts.

Welcome to Edition 9.11 of the Rocket Report! The most interesting story of the week, in our view, is a deep dive by Stephen Clark, linked below, into the dwindling fortunes of United Launch Alliance. As recently as a decade ago, the launch company, co-owned by Boeing and Lockheed Martin, could claim dominance over the US industry. But those glory days are fading fast. So what’s next for a company that is tied to an expendable rocket?
As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don’t want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Avio seeks to cash in on Falcon 9 retreat. Italian launch services provider Avio has seen an influx of customers who were unable to secure launch opportunities with SpaceX, European Spaceflight reports. “I can tell you SpaceX has already gone captive because we have a whole bunch of customers coming to us and saying, ‘Oh my God, can you fly us?’” Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo said during the company’s September 10 earnings call. In recent months, SpaceX told multiple prospective customers that it was no longer accepting new orders for commercial Falcon 9 launches.
Europe’s answer to this, a subsidy? … According to Ranzo, some customers who had been turned away by SpaceX used the International Space Summit in Paris last week to lobby European institutions for financial support that would help offset the higher cost of launching with a European provider. Although prices for Avio’s Vega C rocket are not public, it likely costs about $60 million for a launch on the solid-fueled rocket. In our view, subsidizing launches on expendable launch technology is a poor plan. The continent should increase investment in developers of more competitively priced rockets.
Vega C successfully lofts two satellites. Speaking of Avio, a Vega C rocket launched on Tuesday from French Guiana, successfully carrying the European Space Agency’s FLEX Earth Explorer satellite and the Copernicus Sentinel-3C into low-Earth orbit. It was just the second launch of the Italian-made Vega rocket this year. A new launch adapter called Vespa allowed both satellites to be stacked inside the rocket’s fairing, the European Space Agency said.
Two for the price of one … An evolution of Europe’s Vega family of rockets, Vega-C can launch 2.3 metric tons into low-Earth orbit. “Preparing and launching two satellites together is no easy task,” ESA’s director of Earth observation programs, Simonetta Cheli, said. “My thanks go to the many experts who have contributed throughout both satellites’ development, testing, and preparation for launch, and who have worked tirelessly to ensure that both satellites have reached orbit safely.”
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
French company test-fires new rocket engine. French launch startup Sirius Space Services has successfully test-fired a complete prototype of its STAR-1 rocket engine for the first time, European Spaceflight reports. The company announced the milestone on Sunday, stating that it had conducted the first hot-fire tests of the complete STAR-1 engine at Airborne Engineering’s propulsion test facility in southern England.
Playing a starring role … According to the company, the testing included multiple successful ignitions. These tests marked the first time that all of the engine’s critical subsystems had operated together. These included the turbopumps, combustion chamber, injector plate, avionics, and software. The liquid oxygen and methane-fueled STAR-1 is designed to produce 55 kN of thrust. The engine will be used across the company’s planned family of launch vehicles, which will use a common core stage featuring nine STAR-1 engines.
China launches four rockets in two days. China carried out four launches in quick succession, starting Tuesday, using its Jiuquan and Hainan spaceports and a maritime mission from the East China Sea, Space News reports. The rockets were: LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E; Orienspace’s Gravity-1; the Chinese space agency’s Long March 12; and ExPace’s Kuaizhou-11. The launches occurred within 44 hours of one another.
A maturing commercial industry … Notably, three of the four launches were from commercial or quasi-commercial entities distinct from the Chinese government. This highlights the growth of the country’s commercial space industry and suggests that the buildout of constellations in China will no longer depend on the country’s traditional fleet of Long March rockets. The industry, as well, is moving rapidly from rocket test flights to operational missions.
SpaceX hits Falcon 9 milestone. SpaceX launched a trio of satellites for its oldest commercial customer, SES, on a Falcon 9 rocket flying Sunday afternoon from Florida. Notably, this was SpaceX’s 700th Falcon rocket launch to date, split between 687 Falcon 9 rockets and 13 Falcon Heavy rockets, Spaceflight Now reports.
A lot of missions for a single rocket … SpaceX launched the mPOWER-F mission using the Falcon 9 first stage booster with the tail number B1080. This was its 29th flight after launching four missions to the International Space Station, the European Space Agency’s Euclid observatory, SES’ Astra 1P, and 22 batches of Starlink satellites. This was also the 400th orbital launch to take flight from Space Launch Complex-40, of which SpaceX was responsible for launching 345.
Two launch companies spar over Mars mission. NASA finally reached a decision earlier this month on the development of a “Mars Telecommunications Network” spacecraft, selecting Blue Origin to develop, launch, and operate a $700 million spacecraft at Mars, Ars reports. However, the other main competitor for the award, Rocket Lab, was not happy—at all. The company filed a protest of NASA’s decision with the US Government Accountability Office.
A war of words … “The agency’s punitive review of Rocket Lab’s technical volume was inconsistent, making incorrect assertions and conclusions,” Rocket Lab said as part of the protest. In response, Blue Origin said the protest could potentially delay the mission’s goal of launching in 2028. “We remain confident in the strength of our proposal, in NASA’s rigorous selection process, and in Congress’s clear intent to support competition for the Mars Telecommunications Network program,” Blue Origin replied.
SpaceX set for first Starship orbital flight. Pending regulatory approval, SpaceX said this week it intends to launch its 14th Starship mission as early as September 22, Ars reports. The company set a target liftoff time of 7:15 am local in Texas (12:15 UTC), with a 75-minute launch window. (Note on Thursday, new notices to mariners indicated the launch target had slipped to September 28.) This flight is notable, as it will be the first time that SpaceX attempts to launch the experimental vehicle into orbit.
Delivering a long-promised capability … The super heavy lift rocket will be carrying 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites into an orbit 275 km above the Earth. SpaceX said the Starship upper stage will seek to complete six orbits around the Earth before completing its mission after about 10 hours. Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in the company’s Starship development campaign, which conducted its first test flight on April 20, 2023, and has since made progress in fits and starts.
What does the future hold for United Launch Alliance? Pretty much every rocket company in the United States, save one, has embraced two fundamental tenets: reusability and diversification. The exception? United Launch Alliance, which was founded in 2006 during an era when the US government was the dominant force in the domestic launch market. But 20 years later, with the rise of SpaceX and a host of new startups building medium-lift and large rockets, the time of ULA’s dominance is long past. In a new feature, Ars explores where the company may go from here.
Getting back to flying … The rollout of the company’s new Vulcan rocket has been dogged by problems with the vehicle’s solid rocket boosters. But soon, perhaps by the end of this month, Vulcan could return to flight with a commercial launch of satellites for Amazon. This comes amid worsening finances for the company, co-owned by Boeing and Lockheed, which has been seeking to raise additional funding. A new owner willing to invest in new technology could be the company’s only long-term hope.
Chinese space company reveals Raptor 3-like engine design. The Chinese launch startup Space Pioneer, which has raised nearly $1 billion, showcased a new design for its Tianhuo-21 methane-liquid oxygen engine this week, which was subsequently shared on social media. From outward appearances, the engine looks strikingly similar to SpaceX’s Raptor 3 engine. Its thrust, 2,450 kN at sea level, is also virtually identical to that of the Raptor 3.
Would it be difficult to replicate? … In response to Space Pioneer’s engine design, SpaceX founder Elon Musk said copying Raptor 3 would not be easy. “I would recommend against a new company trying to make Raptor 3,” he said on X. “While it appears simple on the outside (necessary to survive extreme heat without a heat shield), the inside has very complex geometry that can only be manufactured using highly modified 3D metal printing.”
Falcon Heavy nailed Roman telescope’s launch. NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft’s fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, Ars reports. The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension.
That was a conservative estimate … “As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said. The Roman telescope launched August 30 from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, kicking off a mission to widen our view of the Universe.
Blue Origin studying full-flow staged combustion. Blue Origin and the Rocket and Space Propulsion Division of the Air Force Research Laboratory at Edwards Air Force Base have announced an expanded private-public partnership to develop new rocket propulsion technologies, the company said this week. The new agreement comes as “we work to develop next-generation rocket propulsion technologies,” said Nicholas Robertson, senior vice president of engines at Blue Origin. “Studying these historic and technical artifacts grounds our engineering models in real government research.”
Also working on lunar-lander engine … The Blue Origin news release notes that the Air Force lab has done pioneering work in oxygen-rich and full-flow staged combustion technologies. The company said it would also continue to collaborate on testing and maturing the BE-7 lunar lander rocket engine with the Air Force at the Area 1-42 High Altitude Rocket Test Facility at Edwards.

Trump’s Attacks on the Media Are Self-Defeating
When the president asserts that all negative coverage is false, he seals his party off from necessary criticism.
Donald Trump is presiding over a failing presidency and lashing out at the news media—most recently by banning CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from the White House. There might seem to be a connection between these two things, but the causal link is not that Trump is punishing the press because he is failing; rather, it’s the opposite. His inability to govern is in part a consequence of his hatred for the news media.
Trump has been bullying and manipulating the news media since before he entered politics. And though it may be tempting to believe that his efforts to strangle independent reporting result from his current political travails, he has been pursuing that project throughout his current term. Trump attempted to ban the Associated Press from the White House during his first days in office, when his popularity was at its short-lived apogee. Trump’s most dangerous moves against the media came in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s assassination, when some conservatives perceived that the tragedy handed them a window to discredit their critics. In fair weather and foul, Trump simply cannot tolerate critical news coverage.
His belief that the mainstream news media is profoundly biased against him and his party is an article of faith on the political right, although he has pushed much further in response to that belief than any of his predecessors ever dared. More than 50 years ago, conservative distrust of the media was already so deeply entrenched that the Nixon administration could hinge its defense of the Watergate scandal largely on attacking the credibility of reporters uncovering its misconduct.
Many mainstream news outlets really are staffed by reporters and editors whose political views, on average, run to the left of the American public, and their efforts to prevent these predilections from tilting their coverage have not always succeeded. Yet conservatives generally fail to acknowledge that mainstream news organizations are at least trying to report objectively, and that their own relentless lobbying has sometimes prodded the media to overcorrect in their favor.
Instead, the right has treated liberal media bias as one of the fixed truths of its worldview. “There are certain facts of life so long obvious they would seem beyond dispute,” argued a Wall Street Journal editorial more than 20 years ago. “One of these—that there is a liberal tilt in the media that shapes news coverage and dictates, all too often, what can and can’t be said on the air or in print—continues to provoke hot denials and even rage.”
Because they consider this bias so pervasive, conservatives rarely make an effort to test it. Bernard Goldberg’s celebrated 2002 book, Bias, which was toted in public by President George W. Bush and reviewed respectfully in mainstream news outlets, suffered from “the epistemological trap of interpreting every news story that jibes with your ideology as obviously true and every story that doesn’t as evidence of media bias,” as I wrote at the time.
That trap has swallowed the Republican Party. Its leaders have long since decided that negative news coverage of any kind merely reflects innate hostility, and they accordingly trained themselves to ignore it.
In Trump’s version, the news media’s unfairness is a kind of syllogism. Any story that reflects poorly upon him is definitionally fake, a hoax, the product of “Trump Derangement Syndrome.” His supporters have largely accepted this formulation. The Fox News media critic Howard Kurtz wrote a 2018 book, Media Madness: Donald Trump, the Press, and the War Over the Truth, that revolves around the premise that critical stories about Trump inherently reflect media bias, rather than the reality that Trump tends to lie or commit scandals at a higher rate than traditional presidents.
Trump has made little effort to disguise his view that all news coverage can be categorized as either positive or fake. Speaking with reporters after his ban Friday, he said, “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories.”
The First Amendment fortunately prevents Trump from operationalizing his premise that negative stories about his administration should not be legal. (The courts will almost certainly reverse his ban on Politico, CNN, and MS NOW, just as they did his earlier ban on the AP.)
But the Constitution does not prevent the GOP from acting as if negative coverage is inherently illegitimate. Reinforcing that belief, in fact, may be part of Trump’s motivation. He has turned his party into a personality cult that disregards all evidence of failure. This project requires constant reminders that the hated press cannot be trusted, and that Trump himself is the source of all truth.
A healthy political party would long ago have rebelled against Trump’s haphazard protectionism, his ill-thought lurch into a quagmire with Iran, his untrammeled corruption, and his embarrassing obsession with building extravagant monuments to himself. While Trump’s war on the media may be an effort to tamp down criticism of the Republican Party, that criticism has only intensified. The most profound effect of his attacks has been to seal off many Republican minds from the fresh air of critique and correction. But the GOP’s efforts to discredit the media, rather than protecting the party from its own governing failures, have only made those failures worse.

Japan air chief General Takehiro Morita flies Tejas, calls it 'a truly invaluable experience' | Watch
The two air chiefs undertook the sortie as part of the ongoing exercise, which is being conducted at Air Force Station Jodhpur.
Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) Chief of Staff General Takehiro Morita on Sunday flew a Tejas aircraft during the ongoing India-Japan bilateral air exercise Veer Guardian in Rajasthan's Jodhpur, describing the sortie as “a truly invaluable experience”.
Morita flew the Tejas alongside an Indian Air Force pilot, while IAF Chief Air Chief Marshal Amar Preet Singh flew a separate Tejas fighter jet during the formation sortie at Air Force Station Jodhpur.

Air chiefs fly Tejas in formation
In the video, Air Chief Marshal Singh and General Morita can be seen taking off in the two Tejas jets as part of the formation sortie. The formation sortie lasted around 20-25 minutes.
The formation flew over the airfield before carrying out a peel-off manoeuvre for landing, an official said.
Morita praises Tejas Fighter
“As an aircraft born from indigenous defence capabilities, Tejas stands as a symbol of India's technological innovation and embodies the Make in India initiative,” Morita said.
Morita said flying the Tejas gave him a first-hand appreciation of the efforts of the many people, both in the military and industry, who had contributed to the aircraft's development.
He also said the experience allowed him to appreciate the training environment available to the Indian Air Force and understand the value of Exercise Veer Guardian for the JASDF.
Morita said he would remember the sortie not only as an invaluable experience but also as a symbol of the trust, confidence and friendship built between the two air forces over the years.
“Veer Guardian is the second bilateral fighter exercise between our services. More importantly, it marks the first-ever deployment of Kōkū Jieitai fighters to India,” he said.
The JASDF chief said India and Japan had steadily expanded their defence cooperation and military exercises over the years. He recalled Shinyuu Maitri, the first bilateral exercise between the two air forces, which was held in India in 2018.
Morita said the deployment of Japanese fighters to India had been a long-standing aspiration, particularly after the historic first visit of Indian Air Force fighters to Japan three years ago.
‘Symbol of trust, confidence and friendship’
He said advanced training exercises help deepen mutual understanding, strengthen trust and enhance practical cooperation between the two air forces.
“It was with this belief in mind that we finally made it a reality together, bringing our defence cooperation to a new stage,” Morita said.
The two air chiefs later addressed the media, highlighting the role of such exercises in building interoperability and strengthening the defence partnership between India and Japan. India's Tejas and Japan's F-2A fighter aircraft, parked on the runway, formed the backdrop.
The IAF is participating with a mix of frontline combat aircraft, including indigenous Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) Tejas, Su-30 MKI and Rafale, while the JASDF is taking part with its F-2A fighter aircraft.
This is the first time JASDF fighter aircraft are operating from Indian soil as part of a bilateral exercise.

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.
Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.
A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.
The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.
Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.
Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.
Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.
They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.
JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.
The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.
Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.
That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.
In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.
And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.
The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

Trump cuts weekend trip at Camp David after Middle East warning and heads back to DC – with two top golfers at his side
President flies home with Gary Player and Bryson DeChambeau as State Department warns Yemeni conflict is ramping up
Donald Trump flew home to D.C. late Saturday evening, cutting short his trip to Camp David as the State Department warned Americans abroad that the conflict between Saudi forces and Yemen’s Houthi rebels was rapidly escalating.
But the president was focused on other issues Sunday as he took an early morning ride to his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, after he was spotted with golfers Gary Player and Bryson DeChambeau – along with DeChambeau’s model girlfriend Mikayla Demaiter – on his helicopter ride back to the White House. Rain and clouds rolled through the D.C. area over the weekend, which typically cause changes to the president’s schedule when he’s flying back from Camp David.
The Independent reached out to the White House for a reason why Trump cut short his trip to the presidential retreat in Maryland, after White House officials declined to give an explanation to pool reporters tailing him. On Sunday morning, Trump left for his Sterling, Virginia club — a short drive from the White House — just before 9 a.m.
Meanwhile, the conflict in the Middle East appears to be deteriorating with no sign of a negotiated settlement to end hostilities on the cards for the near future. Territorial gains by Houthi militants in Yemen and further clashes with Saudi forces have caused fears to rise of even tighter restrictions or greater danger to civilian energy traffic passing through the Strait of Hormuz and the surrounding waterways.
The conflict poses a significant political risk for the president’s party, which is defending twin congressional majorities in the midterm elections. The midterms, on November 3, are set to be held under a cloud of gas prices which are now well north of $4 a gallon nationally and climbing even higher as energy supply shortages on the global market continue.
A State Department notice was issued Saturday evening, warning that the Yemeni conflict had the potential for further unforeseen escalation and that Americans traveling around the region were at risk of being targeted by Iranian-backed groups. The same day, Houthi forces struck Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, using ballistic missiles and drones. No injuries or deaths were reported by Saudi officials, but major flight disruptions occurred around the region.
“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation. Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions. Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports,” read the State Department notice.
“This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly.”
It’s largely understood by D.C. political analysts that the president does not see his party’s success in the midterms as tied to his own political brand, however. Trump has up until recently been hesitant to disburse funds from his massive campaign war chest, which was largely sitting unused as the president cannot run again in 2028. He has also made only sporadic campaign appearances this cycle, compared to strategically-timed rallies he has hosted in key battleground states in past election years.
U.S. officials met with Houthi leaders in Oman one week ago. The meeting, which ended with U.S. officials affirming that America had no plans to get involved in the Yemeni conflict, also resulted in Houthi officials agreeing to hold to the terms of a 2025 ceasefire — sparing civilian merchant ships, with the exception of Saudi vessels, from attacks.
Tracking services indicate that hundreds of vessels are still waiting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which remains open only to small amounts of traffic per day. Tankers and other ships passing through the strait continue to face a serios risk of attack, with the latest Iranian attack occurring less than a week ago.

A non-public Russian government document shows Moscow was working to build a broad economic and strategic partnership with Iran, including alternative financial channels that could help the two countries reduce their exposure to Western sanctions.
The 44-page Russian-language document, titled “Plan for Cooperation Between the Russian Federation and the Islamic Republic of Iran for 2024-2026,” was approved by Russia on September 2, 2024. Marked “For official use,” it assigns Russian ministries, agencies and state companies specific responsibilities and deadlines for projects running through the end of 2026, according to a Fox News Digital report.
The plan also covers alternative payment systems, nuclear cooperation, oil and gas projects, aircraft-component production in Iran, new rail and shipping links, technology cooperation and coordination through international organizations such as Brics.
The roadmap was drawn up more than a year before the current war involving Iran and the United States. It therefore does not show which projects remain active or how the conflict changed Moscow’s plans. However, a review of the document and later public reporting shows that several initiatives included in the plan subsequently moved forward.
“The roadmap is not revelatory: people paying close attention to the relationship between Russia and Iran will see many collaborations between the two countries that have been public for years,” Fox News Digital quoted Keti Korkiya, a research analyst with the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Russia program, saying.
“What is more revealing is the architecture of the relationship Moscow is trying to build,” she said, pointing to financial mechanisms, transportation routes, energy investment and aviation cooperation as different ways of reducing vulnerabilities created by sanctions and Western economic pressure.
Building financial system outside the West
Some of the most significant provisions deal with how Russia and Iran planned to move money between the two countries.
The roadmap sought to increase the share of bilateral trade conducted in Russian and Iranian national currencies from 68% in 2024 to 71% by 2026. It also called for expanding correspondent banking accounts denominated in national currencies.
The plan went further, directing the Bank of Russia and the Central Bank of Iran to develop the use of central bank digital currencies for cross-border payments.
Another provision called for “ensuring the use of independent systems for transmitting financial messages,” including connections between financial institutions using independent channels to exchange financial information.
The document does not specifically name SWIFT or explicitly say that the systems were intended to bypass US financial controls. Instead, it calls for greater use of national currencies, independent financial infrastructure and measures against what Moscow calls “unilateral restrictive measures.”
A European intelligence source who reviewed the document told Fox News Digital that the plan covers areas including nuclear programs, energy and financial transactions that “aim to evade the US sanctions.”
In February 2025, Russian deputy PM Alexei Overchuk said Russia and Iran had “practically completely” shifted bilateral settlements into national currencies using their own financial and banking messaging systems.
Iran’s ambassador to Russia said around the same time that the two countries no longer needed SWIFT for their bilateral banking relationship and were using confidential systems of their own. He also said the first phase of connecting Iran’s Shetab payment network with Russia’s Mir system had begun the previous year.
Korkiya described the strategy as an effort to create redundancy in the relationship.
“Individually, none of these initiatives is transformative,” she wrote. “Collectively, however, they amount to an attempt to remove single points of vulnerability and build redundancy into the Russia-Iran economic relationship.”
Nuclear cooperation at Bushehr
Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom was assigned responsibility for continued cooperation at Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, including fuel and maintenance support for Unit 1 and construction work involving Units 2 and 3.
Some of that cooperation existed before the roadmap. The document incorporated the Bushehr projects into its wider framework rather than creating them from scratch.
The cooperation has continued.
On Sept 2, 2026, Rosatom said Russian specialists had begun returning to Bushehr. The company said Unit 1 was preparing for scheduled maintenance and partial fuel replacement and that nuclear fuel had already been delivered to the facility.
Rosatom also said work was continuing at the plant and that additional Russian specialists were expected to arrive.
Russian aircraft parts could be produced in Iran
The document calls for Russia to help establish production in Iran of individual parts and assemblies for Russian aircraft.
Russian authorities were instructed to identify aircraft parts that could be repaired or manufactured in Iran, find Iranian companies capable of producing them and have selected facilities certified by Russia’s aviation regulator, Rosaviatsiya.
The roadmap set March 31, 2026, as a deadline for an agreement on localized production and Dec. 31, 2026, as the target for beginning prototype production.
There is public evidence that aviation cooperation between the countries expanded, although the more ambitious aircraft-parts provision has not been independently confirmed as implemented.
In February 2025, Rosaviatsiya’s chief said three Iranian companies had been approved to perform maintenance and airworthiness work on Russian-operated aircraft. The move followed maintenance of an Aeroflot Airbus A330 in Tehran.
Russian officials also discussed broader aviation cooperation with Iran, including aircraft manufacturing and joint work on passenger-aircraft engines.
Oil, gas and hidden financing
The roadmap names three Iranian oil and gas projects where Russia sought a role: Shadegan, Kish and North Pars.
Russia’s Energy Ministry and unspecified Russian companies were assigned responsibility for advancing the projects.
In several cases, the document lists financing as “confidential.”
At least one of the projects later showed signs of progress. Interfax reported in February 2026 that Russian state-owned ZN-Vostok was developing Iran’s Shadegan oil field. Iranian officials also said Tehran wanted to expand Russian investment in additional oil and gas projects.
The document set deadlines for work on Shadegan through 2025, while projects involving Kish and North Pars extended into 2026.
A new trade route to the Persian Gulf
Russia and Iran also planned to expand their transportation links.
The document calls for work on a proposed railway using Russia’s 1,520-millimeter track gauge that would run from Iran’s border with Azerbaijan toward ports on the Persian Gulf.
Another major project is the Rasht-Astara railway, a roughly 162-kilometer missing section of the International North-South Transport Corridor.
Russia and Iran launched engineering surveys for that railway in May 2025, according to Russia’s Transport Ministry.
The project had not reached full construction by late summer 2026, with the two governments still working on implementation and construction arrangements.
The roadmap also called for Iranian investment in port infrastructure in Astrakhan, Russia, including a terminal, warehouses, a logistics park and facilities for grain and vegetable oil.
Cooperation extends to media and technology
The plan reaches beyond finance, energy and transportation.
It calls for Russian and Iranian media organizations to exchange content, train journalists and produce joint media projects.
The document also seeks Russian technology contracts in Iran covering information and communications technology, “information security,” telecommunications and the video-game industry.
The two countries were also expected to coordinate through Brics and other international institutions in opposition to what Moscow describes as “unilateral trade restrictions.”
Korkiya said the strategy was not limited to finding ways around sanctions.
“Especially interesting is that the roadmap also goes beyond practical sanctions workarounds and includes an effort to build an intellectual and diplomatic campaign against sanctions themselves,” she wrote, citing plans for expert communities, discussion platforms and an international forum focused on unilateral restrictions.
The document itself does not establish that every project was completed or remains active. But its detailed assignments, deadlines and financial provisions show that Moscow was seeking to make its relationship with Tehran broader and more resilient well before the current US-Iran war.

First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.
The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.
Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.
The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.
It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.
Rightwing political figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he would seek new laws to strip citizenship from people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.
Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.
An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretz warned that their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as did international press freedom organisations.
The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.
The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.
Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.
Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.
“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”
The rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.
By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.
“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”
At points, the threats of violence have been realised.
On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.
“The discussion about NAZA has been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.
“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”
The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towards dissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.
As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry found Israel continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.
Israel’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.
Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.
The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.
The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.
The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz, wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”
And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.
“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” he wrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”

Hello there and welcome to a new week. STAT reporter Andrew Joseph here in London filling in for Mr. Pharmalot for the day. Before we get to the headlines, an extra dose of encouragement to check out all the great pieces that STAT has to offer today, from Reed Jobs opining on the NIH budget to our new trust-in-science reporter Nick Florko outlining his own experience grappling with, as he puts it, “how frustrating it is to realize that modern medicine does not have all the answers.” Now to those headlines. …
Novo Nordisk is seeking to assure investors that it can regain its momentum in the coming years, outlining plans to expand its pipeline and find new products that it could sell more like consumer goods than traditional medicines, building off what’s occurring with its obesity treatments, STAT shares. At the company’s capital markets day in London, CEO Mike Doustdar said Novo would launch at least five multi-blockbusters by 2030 and deliver revenue growth on par with other major pharma firms. He also presented a strategy that involved investing more in disease areas outside diabetes and obesity and said the company “will be more active within business development,” an acknowledgment of investors’ concerns that Novo was too reliant on its landmark GLP-1 drugs and needed to develop other products.
Drugs called orexin agonists have been hailed for their ability to treat rare sleep disorders, but with new data, Alkermes is showing for the first time that the new class of therapies may benefit people with ADHD, STAT writes. In a randomized Phase 1 study, the company’s new drug, called ALKS 7290, was well tolerated and showed a signal of efficacy. Participants in the study started with a median score of 39 on a diagnostic known as the Adult ADHD Investigator Symptom Rating Scale, indicating that they had moderate to severe symptoms. After two weeks, those taking a high dose of 50 milligrams of ALKS 7290 experienced a 19-point reduction on the scale, indicating that their symptoms had become mild.

China gets closer to Jupiter mission by bringing Nasa’s StarNAV concept to life
The tech uses subtle shifts in starlight to track speed and position, allowing spacecraft to navigate deep space alone
Known as stellar aberration navigation, the approach uses tiny shifts in the relative position of stars to work out how fast a probe is moving and in what direction, allowing autonomous real-time navigation without constantly relying on tracking and commands from Earth.
In a low-Earth-orbit experiment in January, the Tianhui-7 satellite used this method to determine its position to within about 5km (3.1 miles), a performance comparable to Nasa’s antenna-based Deep Space Network.
Jupiter can be up to 900 million km from Earth, with radio signals taking more than 50 minutes to travel one way. That made it impossible for ground controllers to intervene in real time, wrote researchers from the China Academy of Space Technology – the country’s main spacecraft manufacturer – in a paper that will be published in the Journal of Deep Space Exploration.
