After a feast of points in week one, defences hit back in week two of the NFL.
The Chicago Bears came crashing back down to earth after a flying start - and they suffered one of the two worrying injuries to two of the league's top young quarterbacks.
The Kansas City Chiefs were back doing what they do best but the Baltimore Ravens were surprisingly beaten, while two games were settled in overtime and one decided with just nine seconds on the clock.
Here's our pick from Sunday's week two action.
- Allen stars as Bills open new stadium in style 
  - Published2 days ago
Superstar quarterbacks suffer serious injuries
The Chicago Bears scored 59 points last week but just three this time in an ugly 9-3 home loss to the Vikings, as Minnesota won their seventh straight game at Soldier Field.
The 56-point drop-off is the second most in NFL history as the Bears saw two touchdowns lost with a dropped catch and a fumble, had a field goal blocked but worst of all lost their star quarterback Caleb Williams.
The first pick of the 2024 draft was carried off the field in the fourth quarter looking in serious pain, but initial reports are that his hamstring injury may not be as serious as first feared.
Jayden Daniels was the second pick of that 2024 draft behind Williams and he left Washington's defeat at Dallas with a serious injury to the same elbow he dislocated last season.
Daniels, who seems certain to be out for some time, would still have struggled to keep up with Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott who threw four touchdowns in their 37-20 victory.
Prescott surpassed Tony Romo's team record of 248 touchdown passes by taking his tally to 249.
Classic Kansas City Chiefs win in overtime
The Kansas City Chiefs gave another ominous sign that they were back in business with a 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts.
Winning tight games was a hallmark of the Patrick Mahomes dynasty during three recent Super Bowl wins, so there was a familiar feeling when Harrison Butker kicked the winning field goal right at the death.
Mahomes threw three touchdowns and his 382 passing yards was his most for three years. Travis Kelce had 101 yards and a touchdown and summer signing Kenneth Walker had another huge game.
The Super Bowl MVP had 178 total yards and was crucial in overtime to help overcome a strong challenge from Daniel Jones and the Colts - who may have lost their first two games but look to have plenty to build on.
The Green Bay Packers also triumphed in overtime by erasing a 10-point deficit in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets to win 20-17 - and snap a six-game losing streak.
Which team is the best at 2-0?
Super Bowl champions Seattle look the real deal again after beating the Arizona Cardinals 31-7 for a 12th straight win.
Drew Lock showed he is no ordinary back-up quarterback with three touchdown passes to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, including an 82 yarder that is the longest of the talented receiver's career.
The Seahawks lost Walker to the Chiefs but have retained a remarkable 17 of 22 starters and 44 of their 53-man roster from last season's title win.
That consistency should see them go close again, but they'll face a rejuvenated San Francisco 49ers in their division, who are also 2-0 after beating the Miami Dolphins 35-15.
Showing no signs of jet leg from their victory over the Los Angeles Rams in Australia, the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five possessions to blow Miami away - Christian McCaffrey scored twice, George Kittle also found the end zone and Brock Purdy accounted for three scores.
With the 49ers having their defensive stars back from injury Kyle Shanahan's squad look the total package once again.
The Cincinnati Bengals also look more well rounded this season after winning a 20-6 battle in Houston, thanks to an early touchdown of the season contender catch from Ja'Marr Chase.
We expect fireworks from Chase and Joe Burrow, but having a defence capable of keeping CJ Stroud out of the end zone, and sacking him four times in a road game is the biggest reason for optimism among Bengals fans.
The Philadelphia Eagles were on the ropes against the Tennessee Titans until Jalen Hurts threw the winning touchdown pass to Darius Cooper with just nine seconds left in the game.
Although not as impressive overall as other 2-0 sides, that ability to win games at the death is a familiar trait with Philly - and will make them dangerous all season again.
Saints shock Lamar Jackson's Ravens
The New Orleans Saints just fell short after a monster comeback in Detroit last week, but went one better this week by upsetting Lamar Jackson's Baltimore Ravens 24-17 in their home opener.
Tyler Shough bundled over in a big crowd for a slightly controversial touchdown given the ball was largely unsighted, before two-time MVP Jackson then threw a late interception when trying to salvage the game.
The Saints may just surprise a few more teams this season.
Raiders riding high as Falcons falter
Surprising everyone right now are the Las Vegas Raiders, who sit on 2-0 after winning 26-14 at the hapless Chargers.
The Chargers have lost by double digits to two of last season's biggest strugglers and with away games at Buffalo and Seattle, things look likely to get much worse.
DeShaun Watson threw a fourth quarter touchdown as the Cleveland Browns also sprung an upset win on the road in Tampa Bay, with a weather delay meaning they had to wait an extra two hours to seal the deal.
Perhaps the biggest surprise so far though is just how bad the Atlanta Falcons are. They were beaten 34-3 by the Carolina Panthers to become just the fourth team since 1978 to fail to get into an opponents red zone in their first two games.
The quarterback mess has played a part - and what summed them up nicely was undrafted rookie Jack Strand replacing a struggling Cooper Rush, and duly threw a pick six.
Atlanta could already be eyeing the first draft pick next year if this continues.

Trump to meet with Mayor Mamdani in New York City ahead of UN General Assembly
While confirming the meeting, the White House declined to provide additional details
President Donald Trump is set to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during his upcoming visit to the city for the U.N. General Assembly.
The encounter is scheduled for Monday at Gracie Mansion, the official mayoral residence, according to Anna Bahr, Mamdani’s communications director.
Bahr noted that the two will discuss key matters affecting the city and New Yorkers.
While confirming the meeting, the White House declined to provide additional details.
Mamdani, a democratic socialist who defeated former Gov. Andrew Cuomo in the Democratic primary before winning the general election in November, has frequently served as a political foil for Republicans.
Surprisingly, Trump has often displayed warmth toward Mamdani, appearing charmed by the young mayor.
Their initial meeting following Mamdani’s election was notably cordial, with Trump stating at the White House that the then-mayor-elect would "surprise some conservative people."
This came despite the Republican president branding Mamdani a "100% Communist Lunatic" throughout the 2025 campaign.
In a February sit-down, Mamdani presented Trump with a mock New York Daily News front page reading "Trump to City: Let’s Build."
The gesture referenced the famous 1975 headline, " FORD TO CITY: DROP DEAD," regarding President Gerald Ford’s vow to veto financial assistance to the city.
Mamdani’s aides explained the gift was intended to demonstrate the positive reception that new federal housing investments could inspire across the city.

What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta?
Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals.
An estimated 60,000 people from Morocco are believed to have crossed into the North African enclave that has long been a focal point for migrant attempting to reach Europe.
Dozens of people died while trying to make the crossing.
On Friday evening, Spanish officials confirmed that more than 48,000 of the migrants had voluntarily returned to Morocco.
BBC's Sarah Rainsford explains what may have triggered the surge in crossings and what happens next.

What to consider when buying an Ethernet switch for your home network
The right Ethernet switch can add ports without slowing your network or saddling you with features you don't need.
If you're running out of Ethernet ports, that doesn't mean you need another router. If your Wi-Fi coverage is already working well, an Ethernet switch is the simpler option to connect additional PCs, game consoles, TVs, network-attached storage and other wired devices.
However, shopping for an Ethernet switch gets complicated quickly. There are five-port and eight-port models, Gigabit and multi-gig options, and managed switches with settings that most people will never use. Buying the one with the most numbers on the box doesn't mean it will be the best for you. The best approach is picking a switch that will accommodate your existing network and leave room for future devices.
Start with the number of Ethernet ports and their speed
The port count is the simple part, though there is a catch. Typically, you'll use one port to connect the switch to your router, leaving four ports for other devices on a five-port switch. If you need four more ports right now, an eight-port switch (with room for seven devices) gives more breathing room for future devices.
Speed takes a little more thought. If your internet connection, router and wired devices all max out at Gigabit speeds, then a 1GbE switch is perfectly reasonable. If you have multi-gig internet, a newer PC with 2.5GbE or a fast NAS with multi-gig networking, then a 2.5GbE switch makes more sense. It also avoids jumping up to pricier 10GbE hardware if you don't really need that.
What's vital is that the switch shouldn't become the bottleneck. If the router has a 2.5Gbps port and the switch is limited to 1GbE, the traffic between the router and switch will be limited to 1GbE. The same applies at the other end: plugging a device with a 1GbE port into a 2.5GbE switch doesn't magically make it faster.
Internet speed isn't the whole story, either. Two 10GbE-capable devices connected to the same 10GbE switch can move files across your local network much faster than your internet plan allows, which can matter for large NAS backups or video files. And 2.5GBASE-T can run over existing Cat5e cabling, so moving beyond Gigabit doesn't necessarily mean rewiring the house.
Most homes don't need a fully managed switch
For a lot of homes, an unmanaged switch is all you need. These add more ports without requiring any configuration. Just plug one into your router, hook up your devices and get on with your life. You can even use methods to wire in more devices without Ethernet.
Managed and smart switches typically cost more and provide you with greater control. Features can include virtual LANs (VLANs), traffic monitoring, quality-of-service controls and other device separation or management tools. These can be useful if you're creating a complex home network. But if you don't need these features, there's no reason to pay extra for a settings page you never visit.
Another feature to consider is Power over Ethernet (PoE). PoE can transmit power and data over the same Ethernet cable, which is especially helpful for security cameras and Wi-Fi access points. But you have to do more than only counting the PoE ports. Switches have an overall PoE power budget, meaning that a model with multiple PoE ports may not have sufficient wattage to operate all devices at their maximum power simultaneously. Check what your devices need, what each port can provide and the total budget available across the switch.
The boring physical details matter as well. A small fanless switch will blend in next to a TV or on a desk, while larger models with active cooling make more sense tucked away with the rest of your networking gear.

Spacetech At A Crossroads The Indian spacetech ecosystem is facing its biggest test yet. Despite record funding, regulatory push and new technical milestones, the sector’s commercial viability remains uncertain. So, can Indian spacetech startups turn technical triumphs into long-term businesses? Capital Meets Capability: The sector has already raised $253 Mn this year so far, nearly double of last year’s total. Skyroot recently turned unicorn, while Pixxel grabbed headlines when it raised $100 Mn, the largest round in Indian spacetech. This momentum has been bolstered by engineering and launch milestones as well particularly for Skyroot. The Investor Thesis: VCs see opportunity across the space value chain: launch infrastructure, payloads, and the downstream applications layer. While some investors are betting that the downstream level offers the most attractive economics, others underline the nascent earth observation as a large market. But have potential and promise taken investors too far? The Hype-Demand Gap: Rapid capital inflows are raising concerns about frothy valuations. Critics also warn of FOMO-driven pricing in a market where launch capacity, satellite longevity data and predictable revenues are still developing. On top of this, hardware risks remain significant. As many startups target similar problems, VCs expect consolidation as stronger players integrate vertically. Who Will Win? Investors are now focusing on precise use cases, defensible differentiation and clear buyers. Backers now also want tangible metrics, and are repricing portfolio companies as startups move towards commercial deployment. That said, the funding pool remains limited for capex-heavy businesses. As a result, many see spacetech startups tapping into the public markets for liquidity once they achieve scale and recurring revenue. So, after a decade of building capabilities, can Indian spacetech startups finally turn breakthroughs into bankable business models? Snapdeal-parent AceVector Ltd has filed its red herring prospectus (RHP) with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), nearly a year after receiving the markets regulator's observations on its confidential IPO filing. The company has cut the fresh issue by ₹13 Cr to ₹287 Cr from the ₹300 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP) filed in December 2025. Important to highlight that the cut came at the behest of AceVector raising a pre-IPO placement round aggregating to ₹ 13 Cr. The offer-for-sale (OFS) component has also been reduced by 34.9% to 4.16 Cr shares from 6.39 Cr shares proposed in the UDRHP. SoftBank's selling entity Starfish I Pte Ltd has cut its OFS by 34.8% to 2.76 Cr shares from 4.23 Cr shares earlier. The three Nexus-affiliated selling entities — Nexus India Direct Investments II, Nexus Opportunity Fund Ltd and Nexus Ventures III Ltd — will collectively sell 86.96 lakh shares, down from 1.33 Cr shares proposed in the UDRHP. Meanwhile, individual investor Priyanka Shreevar Kheruka, who had proposed to sell 19.37 lakh shares in the UDRHP, is not participating in the OFS in the RHP. Other selling shareholders include Jason Ashok Kothari (11.11 lakh shares), Rupen Investment and Industries (2.69 lakh shares) and Centaurus Trading and Investments (2.69 lakh shares), among others. AceVector's IPO will open for public subscription on Friday, September 25, following anchor bidding on September 24, and will close on Tuesday, September 29. (The story will be updated shortly)

Barely four months after making its stock market debut, digital lending platform Kissht is back in the public markets for more funds. Kissht’s parent OnEMI Technology Solutions has received shareholder approval to raise up to ₹832 Cr through a preferential issue of equity shares. The proposed fundraise comes after the company raised around ₹926 Cr through its IPO, including a fresh issue of shares. Kissht intends to utilise 75% of the new proceeds to fund its lending arm Si Creva, with the money expected to support its loan-book growth. The rest for general corporate purposes. The preferential issue a few months after listing has raised some eyebrows among market observers. But Kissht is not the only one going back to the capital markets after going public. Over the past couple of years, several tech companies have returned to the equity markets after going public. While most opted for Qualified Institutional Placements (QIPs), others have used preferential issues or rights issues. Thus far, new-age listed companies have not gone for a follow-on public offer or FPO. Swiggy raised ₹10,000 Cr through a QIP around a year after its listing. Ather Energy raised ₹1,300 Cr through a QIP roughly 14 months after its IPO, while Ola Electric raised ₹780 Cr less than two years after listing, also through a QIP. Zaggle, RateGain, Nazara have also tapped institutional investors through QIPs. Travel tech company ixigo raised around $146 Mn through a preferential issue roughly 16 months after its listing. For companies that spent years raising successive private rounds, the public market is now emerging as another source of follow-on capital. Analysts also point to the relatively high OFS component in some new-age IPOs, where existing investors got an exit while the businesses themselves raised a relatively low amount of fresh capital. Even where fresh capital was raised, a lot of it went towards debt servicing. Now, the short gap between IPO and another equity raise is raising questions around capital requirements, dilution and how companies are deploying money raised from public investors. Is the need for funding that was a prominent hallmark of Indian startups before their IPOs now trickling into their post-listing lives? Why Are Startups Raising So Soon After IPOs? Avinash Gorakshakar, a senior market analyst observing the market over a decade, said, new-age companies are still working on innovation and expanding their user bases, while debt brings servicing requirements and leverage restrictions, which demand free cash flow. But the preference for equity does not necessarily point to weak cash flows or an inability to borrow. For growth-stage companies, raising debt comes with commitments around interest payments and repayment obligations, while raising funds through a preferential issue or QIP adds to the permanent capital base. This is particularly relevant for companies that are still investing heavily in growth and may take longer to generate cash from those investments. Look at the companies raising through QIPs or preferential issues. The likes of Ather, Ola Electric, Swiggy, Nazara, ixigo operate in sectors and segments that may need fresh capital to upgrade manufacturing, the technology base, expand into new product areas and for market share expansion. These are companies that would have typically turned to debt for such capital if their cash flow situation was more predictable and consistent. Sandeep Gogia, managing director and co-head investment banking at Equirus Capital said equity can provide companies the capital foundation without obligations, allowing them to fund opportunities where cash generation may take longer or be less predictable. For Kissht, this distinction is particularly relevant because fresh equity can strengthen its lending business, while it scales up its other verticals such as its payments vertical. With MDR now coming in, Kissht has all the incentive to leverage growth in the NBFC business to fuel its other segments. The timing of the raise can also be influenced by the fintech company’s stock price. Kissht is raising ₹832 Cr at ₹314.11 per share, against its IPO price of ₹171. Shares have risen sharply since listing, so now the company can raise capital by issuing fewer shares. “The attraction of equity over debt arises when the startup’s valuation is strong. In this case the stock has almost doubled in the last 4-5 months since listing and a higher share price means it can raise the given amount with less dilution,” Gogia added. The valuation logic can apply to most of the other new-age companies when business growth outpaces the assumptions made during the IPO. Gorakshakar said companies often pare down their initial IPO fundraising targets to improve the chances of successful listing. If growth accelerates after listing, the money raised during the IPO can get absorbed faster than management had planned, leading to an earlier return to the market. So while the casual observation might be that a company going back to the market for new capital did not plan its IPO well, that may not be true. In fact, the opposite may apply. The utilisation of IPO proceeds can change based on business plans which are often determined by market conditions, even after a company becomes public. If a company wants to push for faster growth, because of a new policy or a new market opportunity, it needs to be agile enough to reallocate the funds to meet these needs. However, analysts also see a second possibility. A company that uses its IPO proceeds faster than expected because of poor financial modelling or cost overruns may have to return to investors out of necessity rather than choice, said Rahul Sharma, head of research at Equity99. Getting this distinction right becomes more important for investors and institutions when assessing preferential issues or QIPs that come shortly after the IPO. Fresh Equity Brings The Dilution Question Every fresh issue changes the ownership structure of a company. If the additional capital generates enough growth in earnings and business value, the dilution can be justified. But if earnings do not rise in line with increase in the share count, existing investors can see their earnings per share come under pressure. “Raising a massive chunk of the company’s market cap too soon can penalise existing EPS (earnings per share) unless the new capital deploys into high return projects immediately,” Equity99’s Sharma said. This makes the intended use of funds an important part of the analysis for any investor or outside observer. Kissht says most of the ₹832 Cr will go towards its lending business. For a company expanding its loan book, investors will need to track whether the additional capital leads to higher book value and earnings without a comparable deterioration in asset quality or returns. Ather, meanwhile, raised ₹1,300 Cr through QIP in July 2026, almost 14 months after its public listing for repayment or prepayment of borrowings, research and development and marketing. Swiggy’s ₹10,000 Cr QIP was primarily aimed at expanding its quick commerce businesses and potential acquisitions. Bhavish Aggarwal’s Ola Electric is looking to raise up to ₹1,500 Cr, three months after the company had already raised ₹780 Cr through a QIP soon after listing. This is expected to accelerate debt repayment and increase the cash runway, especially when the company is investing heavily in manufacturing and battery technology. For any investor evaluating new-age tech stocks, per-share growth metrics will become more important to track. Investors should track revenue, EBITDA, earnings and free cash flow on a per share basis, along with the incremental return on invested capital compared with the cost of equity. The time taken for the fresh capital to become earnings accretive is another key measure of an investible stock. This is a broader test of whether the fresh capital is translating into higher earnings and value per share, rather than simply increasing the company’s absolute revenue or user base. “A company may report rapid absolute growth while existing shareholders experience limited value creation because the share count has increased just as quickly,” Gogia added. As in an IPO, pricing also matters. For QIPs, investors typically assess the issue price against the prevailing market price and recent trading averages. A discount can help attract institutional investors, but a large discount can also increase dilution borne by existing shareholders. The profile of incoming investors provides another data point. Long-only mutual funds, pension funds, insurers and sovereign institutions taking large positions can indicate a willingness to hold the stock for several years, But institutional participation by itself does not determine whether a fundraise creates value. What’s In It For Institutional Funds? Despite the concerns around dilution, institutional demand for new age companies remains strong, Several recent QIPs have been oversubscribed, pointing to continued appetite for companies. But a proposed QIP does not always make it to the finish line. PB FIntech’s experience earlier this year showed that investors can push back when they believe the proposed use of capital or potential dilution does not justify another equity raise. In February 2026, PB Fintech board had said it would consider a QIP to fund inorganic expansion in international markets. The announcement triggered a sell-off in the company’s shares, with analysts questioning the need for fresh capital when PB Fintech was already sitting on more than ₹5,000 Cr of cash and warning about potential dilution. The company subsequently cancelled the proposed QIP. Access to public market capital cannot be taken for granted. Investors are looking at what the money will be used for, how much dilution a transaction could create and whether the proposed investment can generate returns above the company’s cost of capital. Compare this to another recent QIP bid. Ather’s ₹1,300 Cr QIP attracted bids worth more than ₹10,000 Cr, PB Fintech’s proposed raise faced an immediate negative reaction and had to be shelved. Part of this demand comes from better visibility into these businesses after listing. Companies that were once private now have to disclose quarterly financials, material impact, operating metrics and management commentary. This allows institutional funds to build meaningful positions if they may have missed their desired allocation during the IPO. Naturally, high-growth companies tending towards profitability will gain some organic interest too. But QIP discounts, strong share price performance, limited free float and the possibility of future index inclusion can all share an issue attractive to institutional investors. “There is huge liquidity available for investors in QIPs. Also if the quality of the franchise is good and growth prospects look strong over the next 2-3 years ahead, then QIP investors are ready to invest," Sharma said. But oversubscription should not be read as a blanket endorsement of a company’s business or trajectory. Some QIP order books can be inflated because investors expect to receive only part of what they bid for. Stronger evidence of conviction would be broad participation from long-term investors, disciplined pricing and investors continuing to hold their positions after the issue. The bigger change is in how routinely new-age companies are approaching public markets. Their confidence in markets is similar to their confidence in routinely raising VC rounds previously. They are more than familiar with approaching private investors every few years for a Series C, D or E round. That is a key difference in the mindset of the new-age tech stock promoter class compared to traditional businesses which approached the markets more tentatively. “This represents a maturing public capital ecosystem. Listing is no longer necessarily viewed as the final fundraising event. It can become the beginning of ongoing access to a larger and more liquid institutional capital pool,” Gogia said. All of this makes financial sense if a company has attractive opportunities to deploy the money. Concerns will arise and red flags will be raised when funds remain undeployed, or if promoters and management hesitate in using them for growth, or if companies simply fail with regards to performance and targets. At some point investors will call out a company that is simply accumulating capital for a rainy-day reserve. That’s always a risk for companies routinely raising from public markets, especially after a high-profile IPO. A document circulating on social media, purportedly issued by the Ministry of Finance, claims that the Central Government has notified a scheme for the merger of nine Public Sector Banks into three entities. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Notification issued by the Union Ministry of Finance to merge nine Public Sector Banks into three.
Fact: This is a fake notification. The Ministry of Finance has not made any such announcement, and no official notification was issued in the Gazette of India. PIB Fact Check also has confirmed the document is fabricated. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
An internet search using relevant keywords did not yield any announcements made by the government regarding such a merger. Furthermore, no such notification has been published by the Finance Ministry on the official Gazette of India website.
Moreover, PIB Fact Check has clarified (archive) that the Ministry of Finance has not issued any such notification, declaring the circulated document to be entirely fake. Earlier in June 2026, when a post went viral claiming that Punjab National Bank, Canara Bank, and State Bank of India were merging into one entity, PIB flagged it as fabricated and clarified that the government had not approved any such proposal.
To sum it up, the viral document claiming the merger of nine public sector banks is fake.

Prime Video looks to have another hit on its hands with Neagley, a new spinoff series set in the same universe as the streaming platform’s critically acclaimed Reacher, now in its fourth season. Both shows are solidly addictive escapist fare, and while Neagley has some uneven elements, it mostly sticks to the successful formula while exploring new ground to give a very different main character her due.

Not much has changed about the Apple Watch Ultra since its debut in 2022. The company’s heavy-duty smartwatch is still massive, titanium-clad, and equipped with enough emergency features to make one feel slightly more prepared for an apocalypse than the average Joe. Each generation has brought incremental improvements, but the Ultra has largely stuck to the formula, and this year’s release isn’t any different.
After testing both the Ultra 4 and the new Series 12, I noticed how little separates the two Apple Watches. The gap between them seems to shrink a little further every year, leaving fewer reasons to pay $799 for the beefier version. The Series 12 now shares many of the Ultra 4’s health and safety capabilities, and the Ultra’s biggest differentiators—its multiday battery, dedicated Action button, and satellite messaging—are more tailored to people who actually spend time off the grid.
This makes the Ultra 4 a more specialized smartwatch than ever, but also a tougher sell. Its benefits are clear for trail runners, divers, or anyone who regularly ventures outside cellular coverage. However, if your main goal is tracking health, workouts, and daily tasks, the Series 12 offers the same core experience for $400 less. And for current Ultra owners, the Ultra 4 serves as a reason to appreciate—and stick with—the generation you already have. Fortunately, there are no price changes, but there are no new finishes either.
Ready, Set, and Recover
The Ultra 4 gets the same new Health Sensing System as the Series 12, powered by Apple’s faster S11 chip and improved optical and electrical heart rate sensors. The system now tracks heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, and it measures heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, which is up to 24 times more frequently than its predecessor. It also logs two HRV variants: Recovery HRV, which is intended to identify daily stressors, and overall HRV, which provides broader cardiovascular context.
While both of the new Apple Watches benefit from the higher-frequency tracking, it’s probably a more meaningful upgrade for people considering the Ultra as a fitness tracker. The Ultra 4 can now provide a more comprehensive picture of how your body is recovering and responding to stress throughout the day. Overnight Vitals now compares Recovery HRV against your personal baseline, and a new daytime view lets you look through differences between your day and overnight metrics.

A year ago, President Trump pledged to lower Medicaid drug prices. Has that happened?
What's the latest with the Trump admin's promise on lower drug prices in Medicaid?
When President Trump talks about accomplishments of his second term, he often mentions the deals he's struck with pharmaceutical companies to lower drug prices.
"We went from the highest prescription drug prices, by far, anywhere in the world, to the lowest prescription drug prices anywhere in the world," Trump said during his remarks at the midterm Republican National Convention in Dallas on Sept 10. "And that alone should get us a big victory in our midterms that are coming up."
Last year on Sept. 30, the president and his health officials gathered in the Oval Office to announce a major agreement with Pfizer — the first of what he said would be a series of deals with pharmaceutical companies. Eventually, the White House said 26 companies signed agreements, but they have not been made public.
Trump refers to these agreements as "most favored nation" deals, meant to bring U.S. drug prices in line with what other wealthy countries pay for drugs.
The most buzzed-about part of the first announcement was the creation of TrumpRx, a website for consumers to find discounts on some drugs if they choose not to use their health insurance. But, as NPR has reported, the drugs available are limited, and most consumers will get a better price if they just use their insurance and pay the copay.
But Trump's announcement also included another promise, for the low-income and disabled Americans who are covered by Medicaid:
"Today Pfizer is committing to offer all of their prescription medications to Medicaid," he said on Sept. 30, 2025. "And it will be at the most favored nation prices. It's gonna have a huge impact on bringing Medicaid costs down like nothing else."
And Trump said he expected other drug companies would do the same.
Medicaid covers 66 million Americans, and its net spending on prescription drugs grew by 46% between 2019 and 2024, costing taxpayers $46 billion dollars that year, according to the nonpartisan health policy research group KFF.
But turning Trump's promises into an operational program has been difficult. A year later, that effort has been plagued by uncertainties, delays and a general lack of transparency.
The pilot program relies on voluntary participation, by both drug companies and individual states, which means the number of drugs that will be discounted, and the number of patients who will have access to those prices, could be lower than what Trump originally promised.
Companies might not offer all of their drugs
Because the administration has refused to release the actual pharmaceutical agreements, it's not clear if participating companies have to offer Medicaid most-favored nation discounts for all their drugs.
NPR reached out to Pfizer and 16 other major drug companies that struck pricing deals with the Trump Administration over the past year. None would confirm to NPR that all of their drugs would be discounted in Medicaid, or say exactly which ones would be discounted.
Gilead told NPR it is working with states to make "selected covered products available," including drugs that treat hepatitis C, hepatitis B and HIV.
Sanofi said it would make the discounted pricing available for "certain wholly owned medicines that treat diabetes, cardiovascular and neurological conditions, and cancer."
Eli Lilly said it didn't have a final list but expected "many" of its medicines to be part of the pilot program at a discount. It said "any" of its "eligible covered outpatient drugs " could be selected — except for its GLP-1 medicines that are part of another pilot program in Medicare.
Genentech would only say that "certain medicines" would be a part of the Medicaid program.
Two companies told NPR the terms of the Medicaid agreements were confidential.
The federal regulatory agency, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, wouldn't tell NPR how many of each company's drugs would get Medicaid discounts either.
This fact that companies aren't discounting all of their drugs as part of this pilot program is worrisome, said Dr. Thomas Hwang of Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston. It makes it easier for companies to game the system, he said
"Companies have every incentive to cherry-pick [for this program] the products for which they already give Medicaid the best discounts and for which the international price may not be that much lower," Hwang said. In other words, the companies might publicly get credit for discounts that are actually negligible.
"So there would be an incentive for companies to try to limit their liability and pay less to Medicaid," Hwang explained. "That gaming is what worries me about this backsliding over the past months — from the initial messaging that all drugs will be offered from participating manufacturers, and now to maybe only certain drugs will be offered."
The discounts won't reach all states
Even if pharmaceutical companies do end up offering lower prices on a wide range of products, those new prices won't simply take effect nationwide. Instead, the discount program is being set up as a voluntary pilot. That means every state has to decide whether to opt-in, and then agree to certain conditions.
The pilot is called the Generous model. And the ramp-up has been slow. Deadlines for drug companies and states to sign up were originally set for the spring and summer, but they've been pushed back.
"It's always a bad sign when you keep pushing back your deadline," said Ameet Sarpatwari, a professor of population medicine at Harvard, and a drug policy researcher.
Why states might hesitate to commit
Even though the aim of the Generous pilot program is lower drug prices, a state that signs up could be exposing itself to some financial risks.
The federal government splits the cost of Medicaid with the states. In most states, Medicaid is the biggest part of the state budget, after education.
But unlike the federal government, states have to balance their budgets every year, according to Jack Rollins, who directs federal policy at the National Association of Medicaid Directors.
Even if a prescription drug is expected to save money on projected health care costs over many years, a state Medicaid program might not have enough budgeted to pay for every patient who needs the drug in a given year.
"Everything in Medicaid is going to be a trade-off," he said. "There's no silver bullet to the drug costs that we're navigating."
State budget managers already try to control Medicaid costs using various coverage rules for drugs with high price tags.
For example, some drugs might require a doctor to submit a "prior authorization" request to the state Medicaid program. Another rule is to require patients to try cheaper drugs first, to manage their condition, before trying a more expensive brand.
But in the Generous pilot program, states would have to toss out their own coverage criteria and accept a standardized system, if they want the negotiated price.
That would mean states that previously had some coverage limitations on certain drugs might be forced to offer unfettered access, says Sarpatwari.
"Then all of a sudden your state Medicaid plans might be spending a whole lot more because a whole lot more people might be getting the drugs," he says.
The deadline for states to apply was Sept. 10, and a few states like Massachusetts said publicly that they would opt-in. California officials said they would apply, but as a means to see more details before committing. States have until September 30 to finalize and sign binding agreements.

Poison suspected in deaths of ten lions in game reserve in Tanzania
Ten lions found dead in a wildlife reserve in Tanzania are suspected to have been poisoned, according to wildlife officials. The animals were discovered on Friday in the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, home to pastoral tribal communities that raise cattle. It is also one of the most visited tourist destinations in the country.
"Preliminary findings suggest the animals may have died after ingesting poison," a statement from The Ngorongoro Conservation Area Authority said, adding the authority has launched a full investigation "to determine the cause of the incident and identify those responsible."
Large animals are under threat across East Africa, in places where they frequently come into conflict with humans. An investigation is underway in neighboring Kenya, where over the summer, 18 elephants died from suspected poisoning. Police have arrested four people.
According to Kenya's Wildlife Service, preliminary tests showed the elephants may have ingested cyanide. Tomato farmers in the Amboseli region are known to use banned pesticides on their crops. But growers deny using cyanide.
Tanzania is home to Africa's largest lion population, about half the world's wild lions. But they are listed as a vulnerable population by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Lions are under threat from shrinking habitat and poaching.
The Ngorongoro Conservation Area in Tanzania is a UNESCO World Heritage Site protected under international law. It is the location of the Ngorongoro Crater and home to the Big Five game animals -–the elephant, lion, leopard, buffalo and rhino.

Major super PACs associated with AI labs and investors have poured close to $1 million into incumbent Republican Mike Rounds’s South Dakota senate race, seeking to shape the outcome of a noncompetitive race amid a critical national debate over AI regulation.
Rounds has been the beneficiary this cycle of around $600,000 in spending by outside groups, with the vast majority of that figure coming from the super PAC Defend American Jobs, which receives funding from a super PAC financed by the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.
He has also received roughly $215,000 directly from the employees and super PACs affiliated with AI labs, most notably Anthropic, as well as a constellation of other tech companies including Google and Microsoft, according to FEC filings.
With fewer than 50 days until the midterm elections in November, recent polls show Rounds ahead of the independent candidate Brian Beng after the Democratic candidate Julian Beaudion dropped out last month.
Rounds has so far raised more from tech groups than from donors in South Dakota, and this spending reflects a new effort by AI labs to deploy vast war chests to shape thorny issues on AI and the data centers that power it. Rounds has been viewed by AI executives as a top supporter of the industry, which could prove crucial in the next Congress when AI regulation is expected to become a top priority, according to congressional aides familiar with the matter.
It also appears to reflect how AI labs have become focused on keeping allies, which have been in short supply on Capitol Hill as lawmakers spring up a raft of bills as they react to public anxiety around AI safety concerns.
A spokesperson for Rounds did not respond to a request for comment.
On Thursday, Leading the Future, the super PAC funded in part by OpenAI president Greg Brockman, along with investors Ben Horowitz and Marc Andreesen, announced that it would put $2 million towards a raft of Senate Republicans that have been supportive of the AI or crypto industry. The list included Rounds.
In South Dakota, AI regulation is already a live issue after the state legislature passed a bill earlier this year forcing hyperscalers to bear a larger share of the water and energy costs associated with powering data centers.
Data centers have been the subject of a bitter fight among Republicans in the state legislature, which voted against giving tax breaks for equipment and software purchases required by data centers earlier this year, stalling construction of a planned development by Applied Digital, a company that builds and designs data centers.
Rounds also ultimately endorsed adding restrictions on data centers, although his senior aide and former chief of staff, Robert Skjonsberg, is a registered lobbyist for Meta for matters before the South Dakota legislature. (Meta operates a network of data centers, though there isn’t currently a Meta-affiliated center in South Dakota.) Rounds’ office told Politico that their general counsel consulted with the Senate ethics committee about the unusual arrangement and was told there was no conflict of interest.
Concerns about data centers have been bipartisan across the country: A recent Gallup poll for instance found that seven out of 10 Americans are opposed to data center development, given their outsized draw upon water and energy resources that local communities often end up subsidizing.

With cases of mumps being reported from various parts of Thrissur district in Keralam, the District Medical Officer (DMO) has urged the public to remain vigilant.
Mumps is a viral infection that spreads through air, particularly through droplets from coughing and sneezing, nasal secretions and close contact with infected persons. The disease is most contagious from about two days before the onset of swelling to four to six days after the swelling appears.
Children between five and 15 years are commonly affected, although adults can also contract the infection. The disease can be more severe in adults.
Symptoms
The most prominent symptom is swelling on the sides of the cheeks, below the ears. The swelling may affect one or both sides of the face. Mild fever and headache are among the early symptoms, followed by difficulty in opening the mouth, chewing and swallowing. Loss of appetite and fatigue may also occur.
The DMO has advised patients to seek treatment for fever and pain, drink plenty of fluids and take adequate rest. If proper precautions are not taken, the infection can, in some cases, affect the brain, testicles, ovaries, pancreas and prostate. Complications such as encephalitis may occur if the infection spreads to the brain. In adults, complications involving the reproductive organs can, in some cases, affect fertility.
Avoid contact
Teachers should immediately inform parents and health workers if children develop symptoms. Infected persons should remain at home until they have recovered. They should avoid close contact with others. Children with mumps should not be sent to school.
Disinfecting items used by infected persons, wearing masks, maintaining physical distance and washing hands with soap are among the measures recommended to prevent the spread of the infection. The illness usually subsides within one to two weeks.
MMR vaccine
The DMO has advised parents to ensure that children receive the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine at 16-24 months of age, as it provides protection against the three infections.
Anyone developing symptoms has been advised to consult a doctor promptly and seek appropriate treatment.

Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband reveals why he forgave her for killing their children in first interview since mistrial
Patrick Clancy spoke to 60 Minutes alongside his new wife Rachel Denis, with the couple revealing they were starting a family
Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband has revealed why he forgave her for killing their three children, in his first interview since her mistrial.
Patrick Clancy spoke to 60 Minutes Sunday, two weeks after a jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the high-profile case.
During the trial, Clancy’s defense team did not deny she killed her three children at their Duxbury, Massachusetts home in 2023, but argued that she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis.
Her former partner, interviewed alongside his new wife Rachel Danis, explained he did not know how to handle the condition.
“I could piece together what it was like to be really, really anxious or depressed, but I didn’t know how to manage a postpartum illness,” he said. “I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive. So I’m sure there are things that I didn’t see.”
He went on to address the perception of his ex-wife in the media and social media, revealing he decided to forgive Clancy.
“I saw headlines that said, you know, ‘Killer Mom,’ and ‘Baby Murderer,’ ‘Monster.’ And none of them were accurate,” he continued.
“I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that. So I shared those words. And I think when it comes to forgiveness, I also felt that if I didn't get there, I would be eaten up inside forever.”
He also revealed that he and Danis, an infertility specialist, are starting a family and planned on sharing the memories of his lost children with their future brothers or sisters.
The grieving father testified during the trial, describing the postpartum mental health battle that led to the killing of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight month-old Callan.
During the trial, 11 of 12 jurors had been ready to clear Clancy of criminal responsibility due to her suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. However, one juror sided with the prosecution, leading to a deadlock that resulted in the declaration of mistrial.
During the 60 Minutes interview, Patrick Clancy said his ex-wife had made repeated emergency room visits after the birth of their third child. Clancy admitted herself to a program for patients with postpartum depression, but was discharged after just a day of treatment.
“December was... it was a big struggle for her,” he said, referring to December 2022. “Just a huge lack of sleep; deep, deep depression; intrusive thoughts. And, at the end of that month, she went to hospital.”
Weeks after being discharged, Clancy would kill their three children. Their father said Callan, the youngest, survived for several days after the deaths of his siblings.
“I remember just thinking: ‘Just give me one. Just give me one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister,’” he said. Callan died in his arms at the hospital.
Clancy’s ex-husband became the target of much speculation on social media during the trial, with some even suggesting that the father was responsible, in some way, for the killing of his three children.
Speaking on 60 Minutes, he hit out at the speculation.
“It’s deeply harmful to the legacy of my children,” he said. “It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health.”

Guatemala’s Democracy Dilemma
A reformist president weighs the pressure to move fast against the imperative to restore institutions his people can trust.
Just over three years ago in Guatemala, a coalition of young and Indigenous voters helped propel Bernardo Arévalo, a reformer who campaigned against corruption, to an astounding presidential win. Guatemala had not only refused the global trend toward populist authoritarianism; it had also defied what its citizens called “the pact of the corrupt,” a loose alliance of politicians, judges, criminal networks, and crony capitalists that had gained control of the country’s institutions.
Today the mood in Guatemala is less hopeful. Some of Arévalo’s former allies, and many of those who voted for him, are dejected, convinced that the president missed a once-in-a-generation opportunity to transform the country. When I met with Arévalo in Guatemala City in May, he defended the pace of his administration’s progress and suggested that the alternative would have been to abuse the powers of a government he was elected to reform.
In Latin America, “we never truly got used to understanding that the rule of law is fundamental,” he told me. “Rule of law is not the same as rule by law. Rule of law is when we all accept that we are subject to the law and we operate within that framework to solve problems. Rule by law is when I use the law that’s at my disposal as part of my political arsenal.”
Had he crossed that line, Arévalo insisted, he would have risked being ousted by his opponents and replaced by someone willing to do much worse. His critics disagree.
Arévalo’s personal integrity is undisputed. But some of the reformers who helped elect him now argue that he may be too scrupulously rules-respecting to deal effectively with the “pact of the corrupt” and the institutions it captured—too much of a liberal democrat to save democracy. When he leaves office in 2028, they fear that the pact will quickly retake control of the few institutions it has lost, or that voters will choose an autocrat who promises to crush crime without concern for legality.
Guatemala’s predicament points to a more universal problem. Can liberal reformers unwind authoritarian state capture without, themselves, engaging in at least a little bit of illiberalism? The dilemma is not Guatemala’s alone. Move too aggressively, and you risk being branded an autocrat, or even becoming one. Move too cautiously, and you risk obstruction, sabotage, and ineffectuality. South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa chose a gradualist approach to reversing Jacob Zuma’s state capture and disappointed many of his supporters. Placing the opposite bet, Poland’s Donald Tusk bent rules to try to undo the damage done by the right-populist Law and Justice party—and stood accused of undermining the rule of law. Hungary’s post-Orbán leader, Péter Magyar, seems to be following Tusk’s example.
In a way, both Arévalo and his critics are right. Guatemala has avoided a democratic breakdown. But the president’s rules-bound approach has also left many Guatemalans feeling that he has not fought for them forcefully enough. The question now is whether Arévalo has preserved democracy as an ideal that Guatemalans believe in and, if necessary, will defend.
In Guatemala City, I watched as hundreds of people gathered outside the country’s public prosecutor’s office, a bunker-like building ringed by a huge black-steel fence put up three years before, allegedly to shield the occupants from nonviolent democracy protesters. The crowd had come to celebrate the long-awaited end to the term of María Consuelo Porras, the country’s attorney general and, to many citizens, the personification of the pact of the corrupt.
For the past eight years, Porras had been a figure of fear. She used the power of her position to investigate and jail critics of state corruption. When Arévalo was elected in 2023, her office tried to overturn the results, alleging irregularities that international observers found baseless. That effort looked likely to succeed—until indigenous Maya communities organized peaceful demonstrations that lasted 106 days and drew the participation of nearly 2 million Guatemalans. Arévalo was inaugurated.
That he did not take extralegal action to remove Porras from her post has given rise to some of the fiercest criticism against him. She opened an investigation into Arévalo’s party, the Seed Movement, for relatively minor party-registration irregularities. Although the probe did not produce formal charges, it led to the party’s dissolution and thus thwarted any hope of its controlling Congress. Porras also brought more than 75 legal cases or complaints against the president and his supporters, including the arrests of two of the Indigenous leaders behind the 2023 protests, and even a cabinet minister. Now Porras was finally leaving, and a new attorney general was taking over.
The Guatemalans gathered outside the office had waited for this moment. What they had not anticipated was how long Porras’s departure would take, and how few people would come out to celebrate it. Thousands had massed in the same street just a few years before.
When I met Arévalo a few days later, he justified the delay by explaining that his government had arrived “with an enormous level of public legitimacy, but without control of the Congress, and with the justice system positioned against us.”
Legally, he had no authority to simply eject the attorney general. He sent a bill to Congress to grant him that power, but the opposition blocked it. “If, in that scenario, I make a political miscalculation, the result isn’t that I go with a hundred people to pull Consuelo Porras out of that building and that this is sustainable and produces results,” he said. It was that “I go to prison or into exile, and someone else comes in, one of them, to take power.”
Like much else in Guatemala, the colossal, mint-green presidential palace where Arévalo sat down with me is a holdover from a bygone era of authoritarianism. It was built by Guatemala’s Hitler-admiring, yet U.S.-backed dictator, Jorge Ubico, who rose to power in 1931 and was forced to resign amid mass protests in 1944.
Arévalo, before winning the presidency, was best known as the son of the man who succeeded Ubico, in Guatemala’s first truly free elections. Juan José Arévalo, an educator and a social democrat, returned to Guatemala from exile in 1944 to run for president against the ex-dictator’s favored candidate. As his son would later, he won by a landslide, and Guatemala’s “democratic spring” began, a time of expanded rights and education. But after his freely and fairly elected successor, Jacobo Arbenz, went further, carrying out a land reform that threatened the interests of wealthy families and the powerful U.S.-based United Fruit Company, the United States organized a coup that put the military in power in 1954. Nine years later, a guerrilla leader asked Arévalo to help spearhead armed resistance to the regime, and the former president refused, saying that confronting the military head-on would turn Guatemala “into a lake of blood.”
He was right. In the name of crushing the greatly outnumbered guerrillas, the military and its allies killed or disappeared more than 100,000 Guatemalans over the next three decades. It massacred leftists, labor leaders, and residents of more than 400 Maya villages suspected of supporting insurgents. Guatemalan courts eventually deemed the latter crime a genocide.
Bernardo Arévalo, born in exile in Uruguay, returned with his family in the middle of the dictatorship period, and he began a career as a diplomat at its tail end, as the country formally returned to elections and civilian rule in 1985. He later left the diplomatic service, earned a Ph.D., and worked in international peace-building.
The wood-paneled presidential office where we met was decorated only with two portraits: his father’s, in black-and-white, and his own, beside it, in color. Arévalo’s demeanor was professorial.
“We are in a process of recovery,” he said. “Democracy doesn’t develop in a linear, unidirectional way; it has leaps and twists, not only here, but everywhere in the world.” For much of the 1990s and 2000s, Guatemala had been twisting its way toward democracy, but corruption networks and drug traffickers had insinuated themselves into the country’s institutions. “Part of what we set out to do is to recognize the serious damage this had caused the country—this corrosion, this penetration of political-criminal networks” that served no “ideological interest,” Arévalo said, but rather “the highest bidder: whoever could pay for impunity.”
Dislodging these forces from the machinery of the state has been neither swift nor straightforward, and even those most anxious for change are hard-pressed to offer practical solutions. The president told me that some supporters had asked him to use the military to remove Porras. He found the suggestion unsettling: “Are you really asking us to go back to the years of military dictatorships of the 1970s, when armies were the only solution?”
I asked Arévalo about the Indigenous protest leaders, Luis Pacheco and Hector Chaclán, who had then been imprisoned for more than a year while under investigation on terrorism charges. “I would like the people who say ‘But the government could have done something else’ to tell me what,” Arévalo replied, exasperated. “What they’re venting is the frustration we all feel.”
He assured me that the pact of the corrupt was weakening incrementally as its networks lost access to the state: first the executive branch, then the public-works contracting system, now the prosecutor’s office. “Without tools, they aren’t powerful. And our task is to keep removing those tools from them.”
Arévalo can point to some successes. Young lawyers have worked to clean up corruption in the judicial selection process. Appointed in March, the new bench of the Constitutional Court, which rules on the constitutionality of laws and policies, is more favorable to reformers than the one it replaced, as is the new electoral tribunal, which oversees elections. I spoke with the new attorney general a few days after he assumed his post: He was so busy firing Porras’s apparatchiks and preparing for the institution to resume serious criminal investigations that he was sleeping only four or five hours a night. An anti-corruption commission that Arévalo formed early on has already filed more than 200 criminal complaints against former officials.
Arévalo was tasked with not only freeing a state captured by kleptocrats, but also strengthening one that was fundamentally weak. The bureaucracy he inherited had little capacity to provide public services, reduce poverty, or fight organized crime. In this, too, his administration has made some progress. It has hired more than 15,000 new teachers, and built or refurbished more than 150 rural-health clinics (his predecessor built just six in four years, Arévalo said). The government has also replaced dirt floors with cement in more than 75,000 households in the country’s poorest rural municipalities, and has distributed water filters and cleaner-burning stoves.
Still, much else that Guatemalans had hoped for has failed to materialize. Congress, which remains dominated by the old-guard pact forces, has blocked or stalled bills aimed at curbing corruption—for example, bills to modernize public-works contracting, require shell companies to disclose who owns them, and protect whistleblowers. Partly because the contracting system remains dysfunctional, the government has made little visible progress toward repairing the country’s crumbling highways. And, unwilling to buy votes in Congress outright, as his predecessors did, Arévalo has resorted to pork-barrel spending and raising congressional salaries to win legislative support. Such tactics are deeply unpopular with the public.
Another limiting factor has been the Trump administration. Although Arévalo’s cooperation on crime and drugs has kept the relationship cordial, his opponents have courted President Trump to try to tip the scales against reformers. In April, the U.S. ambassador to Guatemala personally called reluctant Guatemalan lawmakers to pressure them to approve a Constitutional Court judge favored by pact elites and conservatives, a top lawmaker, Luis Aguirre, told me. This tied the court between reformers and their opponents, leaving Arévalo without a reliable majority.
The young reformers who campaigned with Arévalo knew that he would face constraints, but some wish that he had more often tested those limits.
Samuel Pérez, 34, is a member of Congress; he was also the head of the Seed Movement bloc in Congress before it was dissolved. I went to see him in a building plastered with missing-persons flyers for those who were disappeared during the military dictatorship decades ago. The flyers are a common sight in Guatemala City, posted and reposted by the victims’ families.
Pérez told me that Arévalo was elected not only “to overthrow the regime, but also to construct something new, and that isn’t happening.” Now Pérez was creating a party, called Raíces, to which most of the lawmakers formerly associated with the Seed Movement had defected. They would still support Arévalo, but they would advocate for a more confrontational approach. “The president interprets power and good government as doing things a little better and a little more than what already existed. For me, no. You don’t use power to administrate what’s already there, but to transform what isn’t working,” Pérez explained.
I’d last seen Pérez during Arévalo’s presidential campaign in 2023. He’d told me then that if the Seed Movement won, the government’s greatest difficulty would be managing popular expectations. But he hadn’t predicted that he himself would be among the disappointed. Arévalo should have rallied the public to pressure Congress to pass the law removing Porras, Pérez said. He should have conceded less to business elites, and done more to free Pacheco and Chaclán. Pérez was particularly upset that the police had come to arrest the two men in a white van with tinted windows—a symbol of the dictatorship, which used such vehicles to disappear its victims—and that the government had not stopped this.
Several young Guatemalans in the reform movement suggested to me that the political caution of their parents’ generation was a product of the fear instilled in them during the years of military rule and internal armed conflict. Some speculated that Arévalo’s aversion to escalation emanates from that experience, too, given his youth in exile and the persecution of many of his father’s supporters in the years after the 1954 coup. “I think he is a son of his circumstances,” said Andrea Reyes, a young lawmaker helping Raíces organize.
Arévalo readily locates his most formative influences in that era—as a source not of fear, but of strengthened conviction. He spoke to me of his father’s refusal to abandon democratic principles: “Even when the world began to change around him, he kept his convictions, which today we see were the correct convictions, after all, 80 years later.”
Arévalo, too, has found his convictions under pressure—not only from former allies who worry that his reforms have gone too slowly, but also from constituents and conservative politicians who want a government that will ignore constitutional limits in cracking down on crime. In this they compare him unfavorably with the autocrat next door: Many Guatemalans who live in daily fear of extortion and kidnapping see gangs, not illiberal state capture, as the biggest threat to their basic freedoms, and they see President Nayib Bukele’s El Salvador as a beacon of safety.
Bukele, first elected in 2019, took an almost opposite approach from Arévalo’s to governing. He purged institutions of his political rivals, packed them with loyalists, and then cut secret deals with gang leaders before cracking down on their followers. His mass roundups virtually eliminated violent crime in his country, by jailing more than 90,000 people suspected of gang ties, many without due process. Arévalo is unwilling to pursue such methods. He has, however, seized record quantities of cocaine, extradited crime bosses, hired thousands of new police officers, and begun building the country’s first new maximum-security prison in 40 years. But murder and extortion rates have proved stubborn, and many are now demanding more-radical methods.
“Guatemalans are searching for their Bukele,” said Alvaro Arzú Escobar, a conservative lawmaker sanctioned by the Biden administration for allegedly trying to undermine Arévalo’s inauguration. Arévalo “isn’t radical in his ideas or his actions,” Arzú told me. But, he added, “the country’s biggest problem right now is a lack of authority. As president, he doesn’t exercise the power he holds. There is a lot of rhetoric, but little action.”
The Mariscal Zavala military prison sits on a pine-covered ridge on the outskirts of Guatemala City. A former army base, it houses the state’s highest-profile prisoners. I went there to meet Pacheco and Chaclán, the Indigenous leaders who’d played such an instrumental role in safeguarding the 2023 presidential election. Both had been on the board of the 48 Cantones of Totonicapán—one of the country’s oldest Indigenous self-governing bodies, in rural western Guatemala—when the attorney general’s office had moved to annul the vote. Pacheco and Chaclán canvassed rural villages on foot, helping gather some 50,000 signatures calling for Porras’s resignation. Later they helped organize protests in the capital.
“The 48 Cantones is also a democracy, with elected leaders and term limits,” Chaclán told me. “For us, democracy is sacred, and although Guatemala often doesn’t reflect it much, we must respect it.”
In April 2025, Porras ordered him and Pacheco into pretrial detention. After that, their court hearings were repeatedly delayed, seemingly intentionally, and when I met them in May, they had no idea when the next one would be.
I asked them whether they believed Arévalo should have rallied protesters or found some other tool to remove Porras, and thus to free them. Pacheco responded, “I would have liked it at first, but later I realized it would have only changed the person, not the form of doing justice.” Chaclán added, “This is nothing simple, and surely he is doing what is best for the country. We have faith we have already passed the majority of our time here.”
Chaclán was right. On August 5, a judge released Pacheco and Chaclán to house arrest, reuniting them with their families. Around the same time, the prison-like, black-steel fence was taken down from around the public prosecutor’s office.
Guatemala’s next presidential election is just nine months away. Right-wing candidates are beginning to emerge, some imitating Bukele, and many sure to court the White House, in the hope that Trump will try to tip the scales. Arévalo’s and Pérez’s reformists claim that they will join forces behind a unity candidate, but such a figure has not yet surfaced. Democracy is twisting its way forward, in Arévalo’s words. No one thinks it is leaping.
But the passage of time may provide a different perspective. On one of my last days in Guatemala City, I walked by a cathedral I had passed dozens of times before. I had never previously noticed the tiny engraved names of more than 13,000 victims of the internal armed conflict, so small as to be illegible from even a short distance, on its stone columns.
For much of the 20th century, Guatemalans who advocated for self-government, equality before the law, and the welfare of the majority—that is, social democrats—knew that the state might try to kill them. Today, social democrats govern. Reformers may disagree as to whether Bernardo Arévalo made the most of the opportunity he was given. But that such an opportunity could ever arise is more than many members of his father’s generation likely thought possible.
