Head of European Investment Bank eyes Canada opportunities as Carney pushes EU ties
Nadia Calviño says 'the time is ripe' as the bank explores financing Canadian projects
The president of the European Union's investment bank says "the time is ripe" to deepen its co-operation with Canada by exploring how to finance Canadian projects — comments that come as Prime Minister Mark Carney pushes for more EU ties.
"We haven't been very active in Canada until now," said Nadia Calviño, the president of the European Investment Bank (EIB) in an exclusive interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday morning.
But Calviño, who is visiting Canada to meet with various federal ministers, said her trip "clearly shows that in Europe, we put our money where our mouth is."
Calviño said the first area where there's a shared interest between the two parties is critical minerals. She also said the EIB is exploring how to get a framework agreement that would enable the bank to invest in critical minerals "and beyond."
"I think the key idea is one that Prime Minister Carney is sharing, which is strategic alliance and strategic co-operation," Calviño told host Rosemary Barton. "We speak the same language, we share the same values."
Asked whether the EIB could invest in future oil and liquid natural gas pipelines, Calviño said the bank has "consolidated its role as the climate bank" and is "much more interested in new technologies" and green energy generation.
Calviño's comments come on the heels of Carney's Canada Investment Summit, which the federal government says attracted nearly $500 billion in new investment into Canadian businesses and infrastructure.
Plus, Carney is pushing Canada to deepen its ties to the European Union, though exact details of his vision are unclear.
- What we know about the proposed partnership between Canada and the EU
- Canada won't pay directly into EU budget under Carney's plan: ambassador-designate
On Thursday, Carney addressed the European Parliament and outlined a goal to secure "seamless, digital" trade in non-agricultural goods and services, co-operation on computing capacity and AI safety protocols, and exploring an integrated market for financial services.
However, opposition parties have been questioning whether Canada will need to make concessions, particularly after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Canada could become an EU "associate member" — a term that is not a legal designation.
Calviño said she wouldn't waste any time on "the process, the procedures, the names [and] the headlines" and said the EIB is "a very practical organization."
"We do investments. We put money. We support projects. We make things happen. And I think that's the approach of Canada, which very much resonates with the way we look at things," Calviño said. "I would say the sky's the limit."
In an interview with CBC's The House this week, Canada's ambassador-designate to the EU, Jonathan Wilkinson, ruled out Canada paying directly into the 27-nation bloc's budget.
"It's a number of specific areas that the prime minister has described as strategic capabilities — those areas where countries really need to have access to certain things that enable them to actually make sovereign decisions," said Wilkinson, who will be sworn in to his new role in the coming weeks.
Latvian MEP weighs in
Rihards Kols, a Latvian member of the European Parliament, told Barton in a separate interview that Carney's EU push is a "geopolitical necessity in these times that we live in."
"Democracies around the world, for the past two decades, are in decline. We're a minority, I would say. We need to stick together," Kols said.
But Kols does have questions about what other Canadian politicians think of the idea, and where they think the Canada-EU relationship is headed.
"We generally understand this is a natural partnership, and we should not delay any of these co-operation elements to bring the EU closer with Canada across the front," Kols said.
Other European politicians who've spoken to CBC News over the past few days have expressed support for Carney's idea, but some worry a formal arrangement will create protracted talks that amount to little progress.
Instead, those European politicians argue the focus should be doing the work of deepening ties — in areas like diplomacy, culture and academic research — rather than debating a formal process.
There's also the question of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has called the Canada-EU idea "laughable." He's also threatened new tariffs if he deems the arrangement to be a "hostile act."
In his speech, Carney said Canada is not "proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power — only with better manners."
"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."
Calviño said it's difficult to say whether Canada and the EU would be pushing for closer ties if Trump's trade war had not occurred, but today there's a strong determination from global partners to move forward.
"Everybody's looking at Europe and wants to join forces with Europe because we want to continue to build a world based on mutual respect, on win-win partnerships," Calviño said.
"We are very strong, the European Union is strong, Canada is strong. But we are stronger together."

A shopkeeper’s alleged murder in West Bengal’s Titagarh on September 11 has triggered a controversy after Barrackpore BJP MLA Koustav Bagchi attempted to give it a communal spin by describing the victim as a ‘Sanatani’ murdered by ‘jihadis’.
In a 33-secong-long video that has now gone viral for over a week, the MLA’s claim was challenged on camera by the victim’s son, who interrupted Bagchi to say that there was nothing communal or political about his father’s murder.
The victim, Ramji Shaw, used to run a small corner shop from a portion of his home in the GC road area of Ward 18 of Barrackpore Municipality. He was allegedly killed after he refused to sell cigarettes on credit.
According to the locals, on September 11 afternoon, Shaw was trying to protect his son, who was allegedly being assaulted by three young men who were demanding to buy cigarettes from the shop without paying money on spot. As Shaw declined to sell cigarettes on credit, the men allegedly began attacking him and his son.
In the physical altercation, Shaw was pushed and heckled and lost consciousness. His family members rushed him to Barrackpore B N Bose sub-divisional hospital, where he succumbed to his injuries. According to locals, the three accused have been identified as Banti Ghosh, Sk. Sahil and Md. Nasir. Shaw’s wife had told Bengali news channel ABP Ananda that the accused had assaulted their son in the past.
Deceased’s Son Corrects MLA
As news of the alleged murder spread in the locality, Bagchi visited the deceased’s family the same day. Speaking to news channels while at Shaw’s home, he attempted to present the murder as communally motivated, specifically targeting the identity of the two accused who belong to the Muslim community.
In the viral clip, Bagchi can be heard saying (translated from Bengali), “This incident is not just related to an altercation over payment. Three Jihadis have killed a Sanatani. They wouldn’t have killed someone from their own religion.” However, even before Bagchi could finish his sentence, the deceased’s son corrected him, (translated from Bengali), “Sir, there is nothing related to religion in this case. The accused had come to my shop, looking to buy things on credit. When my father objected, they beat him up.”
The BJP MLA, seeming baffled by the interruption, responded: “I am speaking! Why are you not letting me speak!”. A few moments later, a person in purple shirt can be seen escorting the son to another room. While leaving the scene, the son stated, “This is not a matter of party politics.”
‘Politicians Inciting Locals for Electoral Gains’
Alt News visited the locality to independently verify the claims surrounding the murder and Bagchi’s allegation of a communal motive. While the bereaved wife and son both declined to speak, Shaw’s daughter Rikita confirmed to Alt News that it was indeed her brother who was seen correcting Bagchi in the viral video.
Sheikh Afroz (Ripon), who is Shaw’s immediate neighbour, said that the people in the area lived in communal harmony, as Hindus and Muslims co-existed there for generations. He added that politicians were, in fact, attempting to incite hostility between the communities. He also confirmed that Shaw’s son was seen in the video. “After the tragic incident, locals started to protest against the ‘gundagardi’ culture, and police officers had to come and pacify the situation. As the area is predominantly occupied by Muslims, most of the protesters were also Muslim. Does this not prove that this was not a communal incident?” asked Afroz.
A few metres from Shaw’s house, Md Mansoor, who runs a mobile repairing shop, said that Shaw’s shop used to have ‘ittar’ (perfume) and ‘surma’ (kohl) which were not found anywhere else in the area. “Every Eid, people from the Muslim community thronged to his shop to buy these products. Given that this was the reality which we saw every day, we don’t understand where this communal angle is coming from,” he said.
According to Mansoor, the accused youths were “known troublemakers”. “It is unfair to malign the name of an entire area and community for the wrongdoings of a select few. One of the accused is a Hindu, but the MLA still went on to claim that Shaw was murdered by Jihadis. Most of the shops in the neighbourhood, which is a predominantly Muslim area, were all shut in protest of Shaw’s murder for a few days after, only because there is no feeling of communal tension in this area,” Mansoor added.
No Communal Motive: Police
Alt News spoke to Titagrah officer-in-charge (OC) Atanu Chakraborty. The police station is located 1 km away from the crime scene. The officer confirmed that three people had been arrested in connection with the case. He said police did not find any communal motive behind the incident. The accused had pushed and beaten Shaw, following which Shaw suffered a stroke and died, he added.
“The accused are Sk Sahil, Md Nasir and Banti Ghosh. We have primarily booked them under sections pertaining to murder and further investigation is on. We couldn’t find any communal angle behind the crime,” he said, adding, the accused have been involved in public nuisance in the area in the past.
The police account, therefore, refutes Bagchi’s claims of a communal motive behind the alleged murder.
My Comments Twisted, Victim’s Son Apologised later, Claims MLA
Speaking to Alt News, Bagchi alleged, “There is no confusion. Some people are trying to do mischief with my quote. If I wanted, I could have done a lot of things over this issue, but I restrained myself considering the situation of the family. The area where this family lives are surrounded by Muslims — 90 out of 100 people living here are Muslims. The Hindu’s are constantly under a lot of pressure. So, whatever they said that day is due to fear.”
“I have a video of Ramji Shaw’s son. He had made a video and had sent it to me, clarifying their position. He also called me and apologised. Since my comments are being twisted, now I feel I have to publish the video that I have. I told his son that I can understand his emotions, his pain and fear. In the video, he also said that Hindus in that area are very few in number compared to the Muslims. However, they haven’t yet realised that the TMC government is gone and they [Hindus] are safe. I told him to be fearless,” Bagchi claimed, adding, “There definitely is a communal angle to this incident. The Muslims have kept the Hindus in that are terrorised.”
When asked about the one Hindu accused and how he could confidently claim that Shaw was murdered by ‘jihadis’, Bagchi said, “Banti Ghosh is a rowdy element and he mixes with them [the other two accused]. However, the main culprits are the two Muslims men. They have continued this for long, and you won’t find them attacking any Muslim.”
Alt News’ interactions with the locals and an observation of how they live, however, contradict Bagchi’s ‘fear of Muslims’ narrative. Shaw’s house is 550 metres from the Titagarh railway station. About 200 metres from the station, beside G C Road, stands a Muslim shrine (mazar), and next to it, a Ganesh Puja pandal has been erected. The two structures are separated only by a food stall.
A search on Google Maps of the area brought up an image from two years ago, in which a Durga Puja pandal was erected right next to the same Muslim shrine.
Further down the road, opposite to Mansoor’s shop, is Hasanjan Sporting Club, and a Hindu temple stands right next to it.
Pointing towards the narrow path beside the club, Mansoor said, “Ten families live there. Six are Muslim and four are Hindu.”

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.
In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.
Keeping his options open, Trump reportedly told a Fox News reporter “very big things are going to be happening in the not-so-distant future” and that the options he was considering were “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal”.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps warned that if an attack does take place, “all US bases and interests in the region will become targets of continuous, effective and painful attacks without any limitations or considerations”.
Iran’s leaders also pledged some of the reprisals could extend as far as US naval forces in the Indian Ocean, and accused some Gulf leaders of “double dealing” by allegedly giving a green light to the US attacks.
The outburst of sabre rattling appears to have been prompted by attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh by Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels. The barrage on Saturday marked the first time the capital’s Aramco oil facilities had been subject to such a sustained attack since the Saudi Houthi ceasefire broke down in June. Riyadh insisted it had intercepted the missiles, but local photographs show smoke pouring from the Aramco facility. The port of Yanbu, vital for Saudi oil exports, was also targeted.
The US largely regards the Houthis as a proxy Iranian force and argues that the group’s attacks on Riyadh would not happen without Tehran’s approval, a claim Iran denies.
Trump last week provoked profound questions about the level of US commitment to its Middle East allies when he spurned a call by the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman asking the US to come to Saudi’s direct military help.
The Saudis wanted US aid after the Houthis suddenly captured strategic ports along Yemen’s west coast overlooking the Red Sea, giving the Houthis control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway that takes commercial shipping through the Red Sea towards Asia.
On the other side of the Arabian peninsular, the strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman is already effectively closed to western traffic and the pressure on European energy supplies is growing by the day, leading states such as France to take emergency measures to prevent fuel shortages.
In a bid to keep the US out of its war with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis had given commitments to US officials that it would only target Saudi-related shipping in the Red Sea, an undertaking that Trump appeared to regard as sufficient to ensure essential US interests would be protected and that the US need not become involved militarily.
Pressure on the Pentagon budget and dwindling munitions supplies due to the Iran conflict have also made the US reluctant to broaden the theatre of war. Successive bombing campaigns have not dislodged the Houthis, whose lighting advance to the Red Sea coast took the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces by surprise.
Trump appeared to disregard the wider security threat by telling Fox News “The US is in constant contact with the Houthis and they have agreed not to go to war with the US.”
The Houthi government said 318 ships passed through the strait from 10-18 September.
Trump is due to meet the six member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council when he attends the UN general assembly in New York, in a meeting that is likely to cover Iran, Yemen, Gaza and the future of the US security guarantee.
Trump said he was also open to a meeting with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York, an encounter that would probably be rejected by the Iranians, who refuse to negotiate directly with the US, operating instead largely through mediators.
Pezeshkian is one of many world leaders due to address a general assembly that is likely to be dominated, on the sidelines at least, by Trump’s Middle East crisis.
In the first sign of a potential change of White House thinking about renewing US military action, the state department issued a security alert on Saturday to US citizens across the region warning “the security environment remains complex with potential for unforeseen escalation. American citizens in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance.”
Hizam al-Assad, a member of the Houthi political bureau, said the attacks on Riyadh are a response to “hundreds of airstrikes that Riyadh had carried out against the people of Yemen”.
In a lengthy statement to parliament on Sunday, Mohammad Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator, insisted that Iran was not interested in waging a forever war with the US. But the new secretary of the supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei, a hardliner, told Al Jazeera that Iran’s seven preconditions for peace – which include the US lifting its blockade of Iran oil ports, the restoration of its frozen assets and the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil exports – remained.
Rezaei also expressed his anger with the Gulf states, saying they had been invited to a meeting in Salahah in Oman last week to approve the agreed Oman-Iran plan for a new authorised shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, but Saudi Arabia rejected attendance.
He said: “We invited them to the Salahah meeting and they reciprocated with a secret meeting in Germany with US Central Command and Israel.”
Despite the Houthi victories last week, forces allied to the UN-recognised government of Yemen claimed to be pushing back against the Houthis across the country with 75 Houthi soldiers killed on Saturday alone.

Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial
- Published
Many things about Russia are hard to predict.
The result of this election wasn't one of them.
In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia –had been widely expected to remain the largest in parliament by a large margin.
There were no upsets. No surprises. No other party came close.
Preliminary results suggest that United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma - with even bigger numbers than last time round.
And that's after more than four-and-half years of war on Ukraine, which have resulted in massive battlefield losses for the Russian army, economic difficulties and, most recently, widespread petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities.
Those parties trailing far behind, but which have cleared the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma, featured in the previous parliament, too: a Duma that was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation.
One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko.
Yabloko had been the only anti-war political party permitted to take part in the election - permission that was short-lived.
Just twelve days after being registered for the vote it was removed from the ballot (the party list) by the Supreme Court, an indication of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public.
The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as pro-Kremlin as the previous one.
"What other result can there be if there were ten parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me.
"I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did."
Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around a hundred of its candidates remained in individual constituency races. According to preliminary results, none have won seats. The party claims it has come under sustained pressure.
"Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says.
Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. Three people were killed in Moscow Region, while in the capital the city's oil refinery was hit.
At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack.
There was no sense of surprise. More a quiet resignation. With Russia's war on Ukraine now in its fifth year, Muscovites have grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line.
"People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," a voter called Viktor told me.
"And they just get on with their lives."
The outcome of this election was predictable. What happens next is less clear.
The Kremlin is likely to use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the course of the war.
The key question: what will those decisions be?
President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation.
"There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared.
Not today, then. But what about tomorrow?
Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety about the possibility of a new round of mobilisation.
At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a 'mandate from the people' to continue the war.

My dream was to be a doctor, now it could come to zero
- Published
Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.
It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis.
"He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this."
"That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help."
She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government.
Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue.
Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies.
The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility".
The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year, external directs colleges to ensure that students are registered.
The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study.
For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course.
"I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream."
So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name.
"We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us."
Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position.
"I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says.
Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education.
Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution.
"It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says.
Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one.
While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry.
Similar comments were made the previous week, but the students say they have not seen any change to their situation.
With the outcome of her studies still uncertain, Nooria has been trying not to think about what returning to Afghanistan could mean.
"My family counted on me. These five years I have sacrificed everything that would be zero, multiplied by zero. And then I would become a poor and helpless Afghan female, facing this destiny. I cannot imagine this."

GB reach Davis Cup Finals as Patten and Skupski win
- Published
Great Britain will play in November's Davis Cup Finals as Henry Patten and Neal Skuspki won their doubles match to give the nation an unassailable 3-0 lead in their qualifying tie against Ecuador.
Toby Samuel and Arthur Fery both triumphed in their singles matches at a sold-out Copper Box Arena in London on Saturday to get Britain off to a winning start in the best-of-five tie.
Patten and Skupski then took to the court on Sunday and booked Britain's ticket to the 'Final 8' event in Bologna at the earliest opportunity with a 6-3 6-4 win over Gonzalo Escobar and Diego Hidalgo.
It is the first time that Great Britain have reached the knockout stage of the competition since 2023.
"Three years - it feels like quite a long time," Britain's captain Leon Smith told BBC Sport.
"To do it in three straight rubbers is really good and I'm actually delighted for the guys to look forward to something at the end of the year."
Even against underdogs Ecuador, whose singles players were both ranked outside of the world's top 200, there were doubts if Smith could lead Britain back to the knockout stages given his inexperienced team in London.
Jack Draper ended his difficult season early, while Jan Choinski and Jacob Fearnley were both unavailable through injury.
Smith was then dealt a late blow when British number two Cameron Norrie pulled out on Friday after feeling pain in his arm during a practice session.
However, Samuel - after a breakthrough season that has seen him rise from outside the world's top 250 to 95th in the rankings - stepped up on his Davis Cup debut.
Just weeks after winning his first Grand Slam match at the US Open, the 24-year-old overcame nerves and fought back from a set down to beat Andres Andrade 4-6 6-4 6-1.
Fery, meanwhile, was making just his second Davis Cup appearance as the British number one claimed an assured 7-5 6-0 win over Alvaro Guillen Meza.
And with world number one Patten and new US Open champion Skupski to call upon for Sunday's doubles rubber, victory seemed to be well within Britain's grasp.
The pair, despite not playing together on the ATP Tour, combined effortlessly and did not face a single break point against the Ecuadorians.
"We are good friends off the court, which I think always helps, and we spend time with each other when we are on the tour anyway," Patten told BBC Sport.
"[LTA coach] Louis Cayer has created the British system so it's quite easy for Brits to play together - we both have a good idea of what the other player is going to do, where they are going to hit it, where they are going to move to."
The last time Britain made it to the quarter-finals in 2023, they fell to a 2-0 defeat by Novak Djokovic's Serbia, with Norrie and Draper both losing their singles matches.
"When you get to the Final 8 and you play one of the seeded teams, they are extremely strong," Smith said.
"[Italy's Jannik] Sinner could be back playing, [Spain's Carlos] Alcaraz has talked about his commitment to it at the end of the year, but you've got a chance. You try and steal one of the singles, and it goes to the doubles and you've got a good doubles team.
"There's a lot of excitement about it, it brings the team together again."
Who else has made the Finals?
Three-time defending champions Italy qualified automatically as hosts for the Finals, which will take place in in Bologna from 24 to 29 November.
But the United States, who have won a record 32 Davis Cup titles, will be absent from the quarter-finals for a second successive year after they fell to a 3-2 defeat by the Czech Republic.
Christian Harrison and Austin Krajicek won their doubles match to give the Americans a 2-1 lead, but US Open runner-up Ben Shelton lost to Jakub Mensik before Jiri Lehecka sealed the tie for the Czechs with victory over Learner Tien.
South Korea advanced to the knockout stage for the first time on Saturday after beating India 3-1, while Austria joined them with a win over Belgium.
Canada, the 2022 champions, are also through after a 3-1 victory against France, while US Open champion Alexander Zverev won both his singles matches to help Germany to a 3-1 win over Croatia.
Spain are 2-0 up against Chile, with their qualifying tie resuming at 15:00 BST on Sunday.

Iraola left Bournemouth for Anfield after three seasons with the Cherries, capped off by leading the club to a maiden European berth last season.
Liverpool had enjoyed two more days of rest than the hosts, who beat Real Sociedad in San Sebastian on Thursday to open its Europa League campaign with a victory.
But it struggled to impose itself for long periods of Iraola’s home-coming before Isak made the breakthrough in the 57th minute.
Cody Gakpo’s cross was intended for Florian Wirtz, who could not connect under pressure, but Bournemouth failed to deal with the cross and Isak pounced to sweep home.
“I was disappointed with the first 20, 25 minutes. I think we didn’t start the game with the intensity it requires,” Iraola said.
“To win here is very difficult, I know it very well. Normally Bournemouth starts really strong, and it took us this 20, 25 minutes until we matched a little bit this level.
“From there I think at the end of the first half and the second half we played better. Better situations with the ball, and we could win the game.”

The Centre has told the Delhi High Court that an adult can nominate a partner, including one in a non-heterosexual relationship, to make medical decisions if they become incapacitated, potentially opening the way for same-sex partners to act for each other despite existing rules not clearly recognising such arrangements.
The submission comes in a case filed by Arshiya Takkar, who has been in a relationship with her partner since 2015 and married her in New Zealand in 2023. Her plea highlighted that in the event of a medical emergency, she could be left without any legal mechanism to make critical decisions for her partner, despite the couple having lived together in Delhi since 2018.
Responding to her plea, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Medical Commission said that allowing a competent adult to nominate a partner, including one in a same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions in the event of incapacity was “substantially capable of being accommodated within the existing legal and ethical framework”.
“Permitting a competent adult to nominate his/her partner, including a partner in a non-heterosexual/same-sex relationship, to take medical decisions on his/her behalf in the event of incapacity would constitute a logical and tailored extension of the same principle,” the affidavit said. It added that such a nomination could be subject to appropriate safeguards and the applicable law.
The Centre said decisions concerning an adult patient who is unable to make or communicate a decision must be considered in light of the nature of the treatment, the circumstances requiring the decision, the patient’s own wishes, and the legal framework governing such representation.
It further submitted that where a competent adult has nominated or otherwise authorised their partner to act on their behalf in the event of incapacity, “there appears to be no medical or ethical rationale for excluding such person merely on account of the sex, gender or sexual orientation of the partners or because their union does not fall within the conventional understanding of marriage...”.
The Centre also said it recognised and respected the constitutional guarantees of dignity, privacy, autonomy, equality and individual choice available to all persons, including members of the LGBTQIA+ community.
The petition is likely to come up for hearing on Thursday (September 17, 2026).
Ms. Takkar, in her petition filed last year through advocates Manjira Dasgupta and Bhargav Ravindran Thali, highlighted the lack of a clear legal framework or common law recognising “partners in a union”, making it difficult to provide consent during medical treatment or emergencies.
The plea stated that the existing regulation, Clause 7.16 of the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette, and Ethics) Regulations, 2002, mandates consent for medical procedures or treatment from a “husband or wife, parent or guardian in the case of a minor, or the patient himself”.
“This lack of explicit recognition of partners in a union renders the petitioner effectively powerless to make critical medical decisions for her partner, or vice versa, a right readily available to heterosexual partners under the current regulations,” it stated.
The petition contended that despite the Supreme Court directive for a high-powered committee to address entitlements of LGBTQIA+ couples, including their recognition as “family” for medical decision-making, the authorities have failed to take expeditious measures.
“This inaction leaves the petitioner and other same-sex couples vulnerable and unable to exercise the fundamental right to care for each other in medical emergencies,” the plea said.

Fiji has declared an HIV national emergency after data showed one in 60 people in the South Pacific island nation is now estimated to have the bloodborne virus.
The country says it is boosting testing and treatment efforts to fight a surge in new infections, which have increased 12-fold over the last 15 years, according to the Joint United Nations Program on HIV and Aids (UNAIDS).
Latest figures showed there was about 9,000 people living with HIV in 2025 in a country which has less than a million people, according to the UN agency. It said only 39 per cent of patients knew their HIV status and just 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.
Fiji said that one in every 60 adults in the country has HIV, compared with one in 167 five years ago.
"This means HIV is now a national crisis and the government is treating it like one. No more business as usual," Fiji's Health Minister Antonio Lalabalavu said in a video statement on Facebook. “More people in Fiji are living with HIV than ever before.” The government said it was finding more cases because its testing efforts are reaching more people. It will provide more free testing, clean needles for drug users and free treatment for people who test positive.

Clans can have a major effect on how your character performs in Slayers 2, especially once you start building around a specific Breathing Style, Demon Art, or weapon. Some clans give you useful bonuses across almost every build, while others are much more valuable when paired with the right setup. Here is the complete Slayers 2 clan tier list, where we rank them so you know which ones to reroll when the time comes.
Full Slayers 2 Clan Tier List
Clans are more than a way to boost your stats, as their skills and passives can change how your character plays. A good clan can improve your damage, survivability, mobility, progression, or even complement a specific Breathing Style or Demon Art. So before you spend the spins from Slayers 2 codes on a random clan, we suggest you check the rankings.
| Tier | Clans | 
|---|---|
| S | Kamado, Rengoku, Uzui, Soyama, Shinazugawa, Himejima | 
| A | Agatsuma, Douma, Shabana, Tomioka, Urokodaki, Iguro, Tamayo, Kocho, Sabito | 
| B | Ubuyashiki, Makomo, Yahaba, Susamaru, Kaneki, Yamagiri, Kurotsume, Aoshima, Aori | 
| C | Yukimori, Kanzaki, Mori, Kurosaki, Hozumi, Aokawa, Saito, Tsukino, Ando, Suzuki, Kuroaki, Fujiwara, Sakurai, Hagiwara, Kazetani, Fukukoshi, Toka | 
| D | None | 
For this tier list, we look at a clan’s overall combat value, useful passives, unique skills, stats, survivability, progression benefits, and how well it works across different builds. We also consider specialist clans when their bonuses can significantly improve a particular playstyle, rather than judging them purely by rarity.
Slayers 2 Tier List for All Clans Explained
The current placements in our Slayers 2 clan tier list are based on the latest post-balance change rankings, with the strongest clans separated by how broadly useful their bonuses are and how well their specialist effects translate into actual combat. With that being said, here is a detailed breakdown:
- Kamado (S Tier): Gives you excellent damage, survivability, crowd control, sustain, and Demon utility. Great for almost any build, especially Demons and PvP, but its value is less specialized than some clan and style combinations.
- Rengoku (S Tier): Built around huge offensive pressure, Flame synergy, Burn damage, and strong stats. Excellent for Flame Breathing and aggressive Katana builds, while its defensive bonuses stop it from being purely offensive.
- Uzui (S Tier): Combines strong damage boosts with defensive tools, stamina utility, counters, and useful progression bonuses. Great for PvP, general progression, and technical builds, although some of its strongest abilities require good timing.
- Soyama (S Tier): Focuses heavily on counters, crowd control, damage conversion, and punishing opponents. Excellent for PvP and players who know when to counter, but missing its defensive tools can leave you vulnerable.
- Shinazugawa (S Tier): Gives Wind builds a strong collection of damage, movement, stamina, regeneration, and weapon bonuses. Great for aggressive players and Wind Breathing users, while its value is less universal than Kamado or Rengoku.
- Himejima (S Tier): Combines damage amplification with strong defensive tools, Block Points, regeneration, and M1 pressure. Excellent for melee builds, PvP, and bosses, although some of its value comes from surviving and responding to incoming attacks.
- Agatsuma (A Tier): A strong Thunder specialist with damage boosts, movement, cooldown reduction, stamina regeneration, and low health bonuses. Excellent with Thunder Breathing, but much less impressive if you are not using Thunder.
- Douma (A Tier): Gives you multiple defensive tools, including auto dodges, a clone escape, and resistance to troublesome damage types. Great for PvP and defensive Demon builds, but it lacks the raw offensive package of the S Tier clans.
- Shabana (A Tier): Provides excellent team utility, damage bonuses, survivability, and Poison effects. Great for Demon builds, bosses, and coordinated parties, but its value drops when playing completely solo.
- Tomioka (A Tier): Focuses on Water Breathing, cooldown resets, damage, stamina, and longer fights. Great if Water is your main style, but its specialization limits its value compared with more universal clans.
- Urokodaki (A Tier): Gives Water users strong damage, stamina efficiency, mastery, EXP benefits, and extra defense while wearing a mask. Excellent for Water Breathing and progression, but much less useful for builds that do not use Water.
- Iguro (A Tier): Provides strong mobility, Poison synergy, Serpent bonuses, Katana progression, and percentage health damage. Great for Serpent, Poison, and mobile PvP builds, but its specialist nature keeps it below the most universal clans.
- Tamayo (A Tier): A support focused clan with healing, cooldown resets, control, and useful debuffs. Great for parties, PvE, and boss fights, but its lower personal stats make it less appealing for solo players.
- Kocho (A Tier): One of the strongest choices for Poison and Insect builds, with Poison boosts, debuffs, and aerial sword bonuses. Great when paired with Insect Breathing, but its specialized kit loses value outside Poison focused builds.
- Sabito (A Tier): Gives Water and Katana users useful movement, sword damage, mastery, and party bonuses. Great for focused Water builds and progression, but it lacks the broader combat package of higher tier clans.
- Ubuyashiki (B Tier): Focuses on EXP, farming, drops, defensive resistances, and utility rather than raw combat power. Great for progression and PvE farming, but its negative offensive stats make it a poor choice for serious damage builds.
- Makomo (B Tier): Offers Water and Katana bonuses alongside Block Regen, Block Points, and movement. Good for defensive Water builds, but its party dependent bonuses and lower stats limit its long term value.
- Yahaba (B Tier): Works well with Arrow Evil Art and Demon party setups while providing disruption and stamina utility. Great when paired with the right Demon build, but its usefulness drops outside that setup.
- Susumaru (B Tier): Built around Tamari and Evil Art, giving you extra stamina and damage when landing abilities. Good for Tamari users and Demon parties, but too specialized to compete with the stronger general purpose clans.
- Kaneki (B Tier): Provides a simple combination of Health, movement, and Additional Damage Factor. Good for general early game builds, but it does not have the specialized skills needed for endgame builds.
- Yamagiri (B Tier): Focuses on Max Stamina and Stamina Regeneration. Good for stamina hungry builds and leveling, but it gives you less direct damage and combat utility than other options.
- Kurotsume (B Tier): Provides movement and Additional Damage Factor that work with almost any build. Good as a general purpose clan while progressing, but its simple bonuses are quickly outclassed.
- Aoshima (B Tier): Gives you Health, movement, and universal damage bonuses. Good for early game characters that have not settled on a build, but there is little reason to keep it once stronger clans appear.
- Aori (B Tier): Provides Health, movement, and Additional Damage Factor without locking you into a specific setup. Good for general progression, but its bonuses are too small to make it a long term endgame choice.
- Yukimori (C Tier): Gives you a noticeable Additional Damage bonus for a Common clan. Good for basic offensive leveling, but it lacks the skills, passives, and scaling of stronger clans.
- Kanzaki (C Tier): Provides a straightforward Additional Damage bonus that works for any build. Good for early offensive progression, but there is little reason to keep it once better clans become available.
- Mori (C Tier): Gives you Damage Reduction for a simple defensive boost. Good for surviving early fights, but the lack of additional abilities makes it weak later on.
- Kurosaki (C Tier): Improves Block Regen for players who rely on guarding. Good while learning the combat system, but stronger defensive clans offer much more than a single blocking bonus.
- Hozumi (C Tier): Adds Block Points, giving you more room before your guard breaks. Good for early defensive builds, but it does not offer enough utility to remain competitive later.
- Aokawa (C Tier): Provides universal Additional Damage Factor that works with almost every build. Good for early offense, but the small boost is quickly surpassed by higher rarity clans.
- Saito (C Tier): Gives you a small Additional Damage Factor bonus with no build requirements. Good for generic early offense, but Aokawa provides a stronger version of the same idea.
- Tsukino (C Tier): Adds Max Health for a simple survivability boost. Good for early quests and PvE, but the small increase cannot compete with stronger Health focused clans.
- Ando (C Tier): Gives you a small amount of Max Health without any requirements. Good for basic survivability, but it offers little reason to keep it once better options appear.
- Suzuki (C Tier): Provides a small Damage Reduction Factor bonus that works for every build. Good defensively during early progression, but the effect is too small to define a build.
- Kuroaki (C Tier): Adds Max Health for a basic survivability boost. Good for leveling, but other Common clans provide stronger versions of similar bonuses.
- Fujiwara (C Tier): Gives you extra Max Stamina for slightly better resource management. Good for early stamina hungry builds, but the bonus is too small for long term use.
- Sakurai (C Tier): Provides a small Max Stamina increase that can help during early progression. Good for basic stamina management, but it offers very little beyond that.
- Hagiwara (C Tier): Improves Health Regen Speed for a little extra sustain. Good for repeated PvE encounters, but the effect is too small to compete with clans that combine regeneration with stronger stats and abilities.
- Kazetani (C Tier): Gives you a small Stamina Regen Speed increase. Good for early builds that frequently spend stamina, but the bonus is not large enough to make the clan worth keeping.
- Fukukoshi (C Tier): Provides a small Movement Speed Factor boost. Good for making early movement slightly smoother, but it lacks the stronger mobility tools found on clans such as Iguro.
- Toka (C Tier): Gives you the same basic Movement Speed Factor role as Fukukoshi. Good for early progression, but there are no additional combat skills or specialist bonuses to make it worth keeping.
That completes our full Slayers 2 clan tier list. Which clans are you combining with the weapons and breathing styles? Let us know in the comments.
What is the best Clan in Slayers 2?
Kamado is one of the most versatile Clans, with high damage, survivability, crowd control, sustain, and Demon bonuses. Rengoku, Uzui, Soyama, Shinazugawa, and Himejima are also in S Tier and offer strong options for different builds.
Should I reroll my Clan in Slayers 2?
You should consider rerolling if you have a lower tier Clan and enough spins available. If you already have a strong Clan that works well with your Breathing Style, Demon Art, or weapon, it can be worth keeping rather than chasing a specific roll.
Does Clan rarity matter in Slayers 2?
Rarity can give you an idea of how difficult a Clan is to obtain, but it does not automatically determine how useful it is. Some lower rarity Clans have strong bonuses for specific builds, while certain high rarity Clans may be less useful if their abilities do not match your setup.

Salt, as an essential electrolyte, sits at the centre of human well-being, but being most prone to overuse and misuse, the condiment remains at the heart of illness as well. When Tamil Nadu Health Minister K.G. Arunraj took salt to the floor of the Assembly, he dragged it willy-nilly into public discourse. He announced plans to launch a multi-pronged mission to reduce salt intake, turning attention to the right quantities and forms that must be consumed. The Minister’s speech made it clear that the government’s plans were not merely about a dietary tweak, but instead, a recalibration of how wellbeing is perceived.
Salt, in the right proportions, facilitates hydration, nerve signalling, muscle function, and digestion and also has a role to play in stress physiology. However, in excess, or in ultra-processed foods, it can have a deleterious impact on health, increasing the risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney strain over time. On the other hand, very low salt intake can contribute to hypotension, fatigue, dizziness and brain fog, as well.
The health difference comes from the quantity of salt consumed and the overall diet patterns, undergoing rapid changes in favour of ultra-processed, packaged foods, and fast foods, that tend to be high in salt. The Indian diet itself, with its pickles and spicy curries, lends itself to tilting the salt cellar over a little too often. Surveys by the Indian Council of Medical Research show that in India, men consume an average of 8.9 gms daily, while women consume about 7.1 gms. Urban areas tend to consume higher amounts of salt, averaging around 9.2 gms a day. The WHO, which recommends keeping the intake under 5 gms of salt per day, released a set of guidelines in January 2025, recommending the use of lower-sodium salt substitutes, essentially including potassium chloride, and reducing the percentage of sodium chloride in table salt.
In Tamil Nadu, hypertension is a major public health concern. A 2024 study by Selvavinayagam T.S. et al., published in PLOS 1, showed adult prevalence of hypertension hovering around 33.9%, much above the national average of 28.5%. There is a direct link between consuming excess salt and hypertension — eating too much salt causes the body to retain extra water, which increases blood volume and puts higher pressure on the artery walls, leading to clinical hypertension.
Action plan
The Tamil Nadu government’s plan is appropriately comprehensive. For the first time, a statewide survey using urine samples will scientifically measure salt consumption. Salt will be gradually reduced in government-run kitchens, including the Nutritious Meal Programme, ICDS centres, government hospitals and hostels. The feasibility of introducing a low-sodium salt substitute will be examined.
This will be backed by a state-wide awareness campaign on how to read labels on packages, tasting before adding salt and using natural flavour enhancers. Researchers of a randomised, double-blind, controlled trial reported in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, in 2021, wrote that the replacement of salt with a reduced-sodium, added-potassium salt substitute is an acceptable and effective dietary intervention for lowering systolic blood pressure in persons with hypertension in rural India.
The State also intends to step up its hypertension control activities through its community health outreach programme ‘Makkalai Thedi Maruthuvam’ and other public health care institutions. People diagnosed with hypertension will receive systematic counselling and anti-hypertension drugs. There is evidence that such closely-monitored health interventions succeed. A study published recently in Nature, Archana Ramalingam et al., studying the cascade of care between 2019-20 and 2023-24 in Tamil Nadu, showed that overall, hypertension care in Tamil Nadu improved, with increased use of public health facilities for treatment.
The Sapiens Health Foundation has welcomed the new salt reduction campaign of the Tamil Nadu government. Founder Rajan Ravichandran says: “This is a wonderful surprise; we have been knocking at many doors to bring in awareness of salt reduction in the public health sector. It can be very powerful in changing the way people consume salt. We just have to go back to 2005, when the campaign initiated by Graham MacGregor of the World Action on Salt, Sugar and Health resulted in a reported 30% reduction of salt in bread in the United Kingdom,” Dr. Rajan adds.
G. Sengottuvelu, senior interventional cardiologist, Apollo Hospitals, explains further: “Excess salt is one of the most important and preventable contributors to high blood pressure, heart attack and stroke.” His argument is that Indians’ preference for salty food is largely an acquired habit, often beginning in childhood, and the palate can adapt when salt is gradually reduced. Cutting down salt is a simple change that can make a major difference to cardiovascular health — less salt today can mean lower blood pressure, fewer heart attacks and fewer strokes tomorrow.
Incidentally, the regulator Food Safety and Standards Association of India’s submission of guidelines for ingredient labelling on packaged food has grabbed eyeballs. While experts point to lacunae within the labelling guidelines, it does seem that momentum is growing towards building a society that is aware of the importance of salt and regulating it, and reclaiming the kitchen staple as a transformative touchstone for improved public health. As Tamil Nadu rolls out its programme, hopefully with scientific vigour and cultural sensitivity, other States will do well to watch and emulate. If it is possible to cut down hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and kidney disease with adjusting the size of a single pinch, then, the question is why not?

BepiColombo has been on a bit of an Odyssey. The space probe—named after an acclaimed Italian scientist who developed the “gravity assist” trick that enables interplanetary journeys today—was originally scheduled to arrive at Mercury last year. However, after a malfunction with the propulsion, the probe was forced to change course so it could reach Mercury at reduced power. As a result, the arrival date was pushed back by nearly a year, and now after eight years in space, BepiColombo is beginning its descent to low orbit around Mercury.
On September 3, ground control confirmed that the propulsion module had successfully separated from the rest of the craft, marking the final phase of the joint mission between the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). After a bumpy journey—reaching more than 200 million kilometers from Earth—transmissions from the probe indicated all went smoothly.
Mercury has only been explored twice before, both times by NASA probes. Because even without propulsion mishaps, Mercury is especially challenging to reach due to it’s position as the closest planet to our sun. When traveling towards the center of our solar system, a spacecraft is essentially “falling” from Earth towards the much greater gravity of the sun. That’s the easy part. The hard part is to not keep falling. Getting to Mercury therefore requires a lot of fuel not to travel there but to engage rockets to put on the breaks.
Spacecraft can also use the gravity of other planets as a means of slowing down, but that involves taking a more convoluted path, looping between celestial objects. To-date, BepiColombo has traveled approximately 6 billion miles (9.9 billion kilometers), swinging around Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times for a total of nine gravity assist maneuvers to control its velocity.
Furthermore, being so close to the Sun, Mercury’s surface can be intensely hot—over 800 degrees Fahrenheit or about 430 degrees Celsius. And because the small planet has essentially no atmosphere, temperatures drop to -290 degrees Fahrenheit (-180 Celsius) at night. BepiColombo therefore needs to survive not just these extremes, but the daily swings between them.
Once in position, BepiColombo will break into two separate spacecraft: the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which will study Mercury’s surface and internal structure, and the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (dubbed “Mio”), which will investigate the planet’s magnetic field and tenuous atmosphere. This is the first time multiple probes will orbit Mercury simultaneously, with the goal of gaining a more comprehensive picture than any single probe could capture on its own.
Mio will enter a higher elliptical orbit oriented to circle across the poles. MPO will then lower its altitude further and is scheduled to reach its final orbit in March of 2027. Even after the probes take their positions, full-scale observations will not begin immediately. The probes must go through a series of procedures—such as the deployment of Mio’s essential sunshield—before conducting scientific observations, which are scheduled to begin in April 2027.
The two probes will attempt to uncover answers to much that remains unknown about the swift planet. Some key questions include why Mercury has an extremely large iron core relative to its size; why ice exists in permanently shadowed craters at the poles despite the scorching heat; why it’s the only rocky planet other than Earth to possess its own magnetic field; and the true nature of the mysterious depressions known as “hollows” that dot its surface.
Answers to into these questions are expected to provide crucial clues for how terrestrial planets—including Earth—formed and evolved within the solar system. Astrophysicists also plan to use precise orbital data from the mission to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity, because—due to its proximity to the sun—Mercury is an ideal testing ground for verifying the gravitational distortion of spacetime.

Patrick Clancy gives first TV interview after Lindsay Clancy mistrial
Lindsay Clancy's former husband spoke with 60 Minutes in a Sunday episode on CBS
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.
Lindsay Clancy's former husband said he forgave her for killing their three young children in his first televised interview Sunday on CBS News' 60 Minutes since a jury deadlocked in her trial for the children's deaths.
Patrick Clancy talked about his grief, saying he battled suicidal thoughts after the killings and experienced a panic attack while testifying at Lindsay Clancy's trial when attorneys played to jurors his 911 call to report the children's deaths.
At trial, the anguished 911 call included Patrick howling and crying after he discovered the bodies of his children in the family's basement as a confused dispatcher repeatedly asked what happened.
Earlier this month, 11 of 12 jurors were ready to clear Lindsay Clancy of criminal responsibility, with the majority feeling that the Massachusetts mom was in the grip of a rare condition called postpartum psychosis when she strangled her kids in 2023.
But a lone juror sided with prosecutors, who had argued that Clancy knew what she was doing. The deadlock forced a judge to declare a mistrial on Sept. 4.
Clancy says son died in his arms
Patrick Clancy also said his youngest son, Callan, didn't die immediately that fatal day on Jan. 24, 2023, but lived four more days before dying in his arms.
While holding his 8-month-old son, he said he typed with one hand tributes to his other children, Cora, 5, and Dawson, 2, and also forgave his wife.
"I saw headlines that say 'killer mom' and 'baby murderer monster' and none of them were accurate," he said. "I believed that it was her mental illness that caused that."
Calls conspiracy theories a 'distraction'
Clancy said stress from the murders and trial took a toll.
"There was a time I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday, and I was completely fine with it," he said.
He also addressed social media conspiracy theories surrounding the case, which have included unfounded claims he was connected to the death of his children.
- Lindsay Clancy holdout juror breaks silence, says he didn't have 'any doubts' of her guilt
- Will Lindsay Clancy face a new trial? What's next after mistrial declared
"It's deeply harmful to the legacy of my children," Patrick Clancy said. "It is a huge distraction from what really matters here, which is perinatal mental health."
His new wife, Dr. Rachel Danis, joined him in the interview, describing Patrick Clancy as the "most selfless and supportive partner."
"I don't understand how the story has been so twisted," she said. "I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday. And I don't think there's anything wrong with that."
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:
- Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
- Provincial and territorial mental health support.
- Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
- This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

The Union Health Ministry has proposed making CCTV surveillance mandatory at licensed premises selling prescription drugs, as part of proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945.
The draft notification, G.S.R. 791(E), issued on September 8, proposes inserting a new provision in Rule 65 requiring the supply of drugs on the prescription of a registered medical practitioner, other than through wholesale dealing, to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the licensed premises. The recordings would have to be preserved for at least three months.
The proposal follows deliberations by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequent consideration by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). The DCC had earlier recommended that CCTV cameras be made mandatory at medical stores and that they be positioned so that drug sales could be verified.
The move is aimed at strengthening oversight of the sale of prescription medicines and providing a mechanism to verify transactions in cases of suspected unauthorised sale. Under the existing Drugs Rules, medicines covered by Schedules H, H1 and X cannot be sold at retail without a prescription from a registered medical practitioner, with additional record-keeping requirements for certain drugs.
The draft, however, is not yet a final rule. The Ministry has invited objections and suggestions from affected persons and other stakeholders for 30 days from the date the Gazette was made available. The proposed rules will be considered after the expiry of this period.
The Ministry has said submissions may be sent to the Under Secretary (Drugs), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, U-6, Work Hall-C Wing, First Floor, Kartavya Bhawan-1, New Delhi, or emailed to drugsdiv-mohfw@gov.in.
“The draft does not merely propose CCTV for Schedule H, H1 and X medicines by name. Its wording is broader — it covers any drug supplied on a registered medical practitioner’s prescription, except wholesale transactions,” said a senior health official.

Reading for pleasure is linked to better mental health, greater empathy and a lower risk of dementia, Cambridge University scientists said on Tuesday.
As part of a National Year of Reading tie-up with the Queen's Reading Room, a charity founded by Queen Camilla to highlight the benefits of reading for pleasure at any age, the scientists argue that it doesn't matter what or how we read.
In a review published in 'Psychological Medicine', Professor Barbara Sahakian and Christelle Langley said reading for enjoyment can bring huge benefits and reading with others, whether it's as part of a book club or a parent reading with their children, can bring even greater rewards.
"Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our wellbeing. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age,” said Sahakian.
Some of the strongest evidence of the benefits of reading for pleasure comes from a study by Sahakian, Langley and colleagues of more than 10,000 young people, which found that children who began reading for pleasure in life showed benefits including: better attention, memory, and executive functioning, greater academic achievement, fewer mental health problems, and healthier lifestyles, including more sleep and less screen time. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.
"The important thing is to find something they really enjoy – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”
In ‘Reading and associations with brain health, cognition, well-being, and mental health’ published this week, the experts draw on subjective surveys and objective studies using longitudinal, neuroimaging, and behavioural methods to highlight converging findings that link reading engagement with improved brain and mental health, better cognitive performance, and reduced risk of cognitive decline.
"Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia,” said Sahakian.
“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy,” she added.

Ferrari’s two-seat sports cars might be the brand’s identity, but the Italian automaker has always catered to customers who want to bring more than one passenger along for the ride. It started building cars with back seats in the 1960s with the 250 GT 2+2; as the name suggests, the second row was more for occasional use, something that was true all the way through to the 612 in the early 2000s. Ferrari followed with its first true four-seater, the all-wheel drive FF, which adopted “Breadvan” styling. Its first hatchback was still a three-door, though, and slightly more practical for carrying cargo rather than humans in the rear. That was true for the GTC4 that followed, too. But with the Purosangue, the rear passengers have been given something of an upgrade.
For one thing, there is an extra pair of doors, rear-hinged ones that provide direct access to the pair of rear bucket seats. There’s still a rear hatch, so this is technically a five-door. But there’s an immovable firewall between the cargo area and the passenger cabin, and the rear seats do not fold flat. So unlike the 21st century breadvans we have previously reviewed, a Costco run in the Purosangue might be possible, but you’re probably going to want a roof rack if you plan to go skiing, cycling, or anything else that requires bulky equipment. It’s also probably accurate that Ferrari says the Purosangue is not an SUV but an FUV—a Ferrari Utility Vehicle.
Underneath that long hood lives a 6.5 L naturally aspirated V12, but mounted back in the chassis such that this is technically a front-mid engined layout. That contributes to the 49:51 front-to-rear weight ratio, as does the use of a transaxle gearbox for the rear wheels (an eight-speed, dual-clutch box); a separate power transfer unit at the front of the engine drives the front wheels, for this is an all-wheel drive Ferrari. But make no mistake, it’s a substantial one, too, befitting that massive 715 hp (533 kW), 528 lb-ft (716 Nm) engine: 195.8 inches (4,973 mm) long, 79.8 inches (2,028 mm) wide, 62.6 inches (1,589 mm) tall, with a 118.1-inch (3,018 mm) wheelbase and a 4,784 lbs (2,170 kg) curb weight.

Despite that size, it doesn’t take very long for the car to shrink around the driver; earlier this summer, I spent a couple of hours driving another Purosangue around Rome on the eve of Ferrari’s Luce reveal, where it coped quite ably with millennia-old streets. It’s an easy car to drive slowly or in traffic despite its size and power output. The stop-start system works even from cold and is unobtrusive, and your speed is easy to modulate thanks to plenty of pedal travel for the throttle and an engine with sufficient torque that you’ll rarely see more than 2,000 rpm on the digital tachometer if you’re in Comfort mode and letting the eight-speed transmission shift for itself.
Which is something, considering the fact that the engine doesn’t redline until 8,250 rpm. You’ll probably want to be in Sport to experience that; it’s the most extreme of the Purosangue’s settings, for you won’t find a Race mode on the steering wheel-mounted manettino dial that toggles through drive modes, although you will find one for Ice instead. Regardless of the mode, you can choose to change gears for yourself using the large and tactile paddle shifters, either to temporarily override the auto function or in true manual mode, selectable via a switch on the center console, where you’ll also find reverse.
The steering is heavier than something like a 296 but still feels very direct, with good feedback of the road conditions as the front wheels are experiencing them. In Sport, you can feel the chassis control systems and the electronic differentials doing their thing to tighten your line if you’re steering and adding power at the same time. And because there are four seats, you can share the experience with three passengers: The squeals of delight from happy young neighbors getting their first ride in a Ferrari were a real high point of our time with the car.

At least the multifunction steering wheel uses actual physical buttons for most of its controls rather than the near-unusable capacitive touch version that we experienced in the 296. Real buttons that you can use without taking your eyes off the road make it possible to do things like control Apple CarPlay while on the move—this appears in the main instrument display directly in front of the driver, and in doing so replaces the digital Ferrari dash with its central tach. Things get more complicated when you want to adjust the seats or the climate, though.

While there isn’t a central infotainment display, there is a full screen for the front-seat passenger. Painted in lustrous Rosso Portofino paint that glittered in the August sun, the Purosangue was something of a head-turner; certainly more striking than the yellowy-green metallic example I drove briefly around Rome earlier this summer. But this is a Ferrari, and between the standard colors and various customization programs, like Atelier and Tailor Made, the sky (and your ability to pay) is the limit when it comes to exterior and interior finishes. It’s certainly a Ferrari you could daily-drive, although at 12 mpg combined (19.6 L/100 km) that is perhaps a better task for the battery-electric Luce. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) on Friday said it has initiated legal action against Nestle India Ltd for alleged non-compliance with food safety norms in three infant nutrition products.
According to FSSAI, it examined NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, Lactogen Pro 1, and a follow-up formula along with their promotional material available on e-commerce platforms.
In NAN Excella Pro Stage 1, the regulator flagged claims relating to "5HMOs" and "Whey Protein," while in Lactogen Pro 1, it observed a claim describing "Whey Protein" as easy to digest, the regulator said in a social media post.
FSSAI said it had sought clarifications from Nestle India on these claims.
Both the products were found to be in contravention of Regulation 4(2) of the Food Safety and Standards (Foods for Infant Nutrition) Regulations, 2020, which restrict promotional claims or material aimed at increasing the saleability of infant foods, as well as Section 3 of the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles and Infant Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, which bars the advertisement or promotion of such products.
Separately, a sample of a follow-up formula manufactured by Nestle India was found sub-standard for Biotin content during laboratory analysis. The sample was sent for re-analysis, and the referral laboratory also found it non-conforming with the Biotin requirement prescribed under the 2020 regulations.
In light of these findings, FSSAI has filed three separate adjudication cases against Nestle India in respect of the three products, it added.
At 1.10 p.m., shares of Nestle India were down nearly 2% at ₹1,345.45 on the BSE.
