At the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the documentary NAZA received a 25-minute standing ovation. In Israel, it’s all anyone’s talking about, even though few have actually seen it.
An Israeli documentary about Gaza is sweeping the world – and Israelis are furious
Almost no one has seen NAZA yet, but almost everyone has something to say about it.
Made by two Israeli filmmakers, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, the movie takes place on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, where 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence agents and soldiers discuss things that they did in Gaza and how they did them.
As Bilge Ebiri writes in his Vulture review of NAZA, “One officer recalls blowing up a building with 500 people in it to go after one target. They admit to knowingly wiping out entire neighborhoods, fully aware of the catastrophic human toll.”Another interviewee agrees that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza.
Since its reception in Venice, the film has faced harsh criticism from the Israeli government — with at least one politician issuing a call to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship.
Shany Littman is a journalist for Haaretz in Israel and has been reporting on the film’s reception. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the conversation around the movie in Israel.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Have you seen the documentary NAZA?
I haven’t. I asked the PR person of the movie to send me a link and it’s not possible. I mean, considering the huge storm that came out, they’re probably rethinking how to handle the distribution of the film.
What I hear you saying is it’s safe to assume most people in Israel have not actually been able to see the movie. Is that right?
Yes, that’s correct.
But they are aware of what is in it. Let’s talk about the conversation around this movie in Israel. What’s the reaction been like?
You can find many different types of criticism from all sides of a political range. It’s not only right-wing people or people who are supporting the war. The claims are first that maybe the film itself is not verified. They have witnesses that are anonymous that they didn’t verify well enough. But I think most people — they just feel that this is an opportunity for all the pro-Palestinian, anti-Israeli, and [antisemitic] people in the world to attack Israel. Israelis from all sides are afraid of the way the world is seeing us at the moment.
Is anybody in Israel saying, “Hey, we’re glad that they did it. We’re glad that they made this movie”?
Yes. There are people who are supporting Yuval and Rachel, the filmmakers, supporting their right to criticize, to investigate. As a liberal country, we should be able to investigate ourselves, to criticize ourselves. They are doing their work as journalists.
There has also been a reaction from the Israeli government at a more official level. What has the Israeli government said about this film?
“There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers. But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now. This is really frightening.”
The first person to react was the minister of culture. He said that the nationality of Yuval and the filmmakers should be revoked. That they should not be Israeli citizens anymore. There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers. But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now. This is really frightening. I’m completely horrified by this.
I already saw some clips on social media by people who were filming themselves where…you could see a house [in the background] and someone was saying, “You can all come here. This is the house of Rachel Szor’s parents. They live here and you can come and do whatever you want. I invite you all to come here and take revenge.” And there were several clips with the same message.
I’m guessing they’re not coming back to Israel at the moment. I think it has become really dangerous for them to be here, and it’s a new level. I published an article about this. I didn’t do the movie. I just published an article supporting them in Haaretz and my mother is afraid that someone will attack me. The echoes of this event, they’re going very far now.
Are you frightened for the filmmakers if they choose to return? Do you fear for their safety?
Yes, absolutely. Especially because the elections are coming in a month. Many Israelis see this day as like the red line or the moment where we will be able to know if we can still live in Israel as a democracy, as a liberal democracy, or that the country has changed in a way that many [civil] rights and liberties that we think we have are gone. And that this country is not a democracy anymore. And so I think this is also why the blood is boiling.
This is a very, very tense and fragile moment. And for them I assume it is even more crucial and I hope they will not do anything that will put them in danger.

What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.

It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity. We want justice. An atmosphere should be created in the capitals of India… pic.twitter.com/QmHjnTkk3W
— ANI (@ANI) September 9, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

Celtic can't sack manager O'Neill, says Lambert
- Published
Martin O'Neill leaving Celtic would not surprise Paul Lambert, but the former club captain would be "shocked and disappointed" if the manager was to be sacked.
The 74-year-old said he would use the international break to take stock following back-to-back defeats by Rangers.
Those Old Firm setbacks came either side of a home loss to Ferencvaros in the Europa League, while there was a shock Champions League collapse to LASK in August, with a 4-0 aggregate lead surrendered.
"I will reflect on the games," said O'Neill, who was made permanent manager for a second time in the summer after two stints as interim boss last season resulted in a league and Scottish Cup double.
O'Neill, who won another seven trophies with Celtic from 2000-05, when Lambert was playing, added: "I'm not immune from criticism. Absolutely and utterly far from it.
"I think there's every reason to ask 'can you turn this round? Can you change the whole thing?' I have to kind of look at the bigger picture at this minute."
Lambert insists O'Neill is Celtic's best manager since the great Jock Stein, but the 57-year-old added: "It wouldn't surprise me if he left. I don't think he needs it.
"I'd be shocked and disappointed if Celtic sacked him.
"I think they give him the option, if that's what's on his mind, if he did want to walk away.
"He's got enough credit in the bank. It wasn't that long ago people were shouting for a statue for him, so I don't think you can go from one extreme to the other.
"If he wants to go, then he goes himself."

Tea shortage warning as climate crisis sees production plummet and prices soar
Local farmers face increasingly unpredictable weather patterns, lower crop yields and quality, alongside escalating operational expenses over recent years
Kenyan growers who produce black tea for British supermarket shelves have warned that climate impacts are damaging crop harvests and further diminishing their already "scarce" household incomes.
The East African nation currently provides half of all black tea consumed across Britain, but local farmers face increasingly unpredictable weather patterns, lower crop yields and quality, alongside escalating operational expenses over recent years.
These compounding issues have driven up global tea costs, leaving supermarket shoppers in the UK paying noticeably higher prices for their favourite beverage.
Yet impoverished farmers at the start of the supply chain see little financial gain from higher market prices. Harvesting smaller crops while spending more to maintain them, growers watch as intermediaries, brokers and large corporate firms continue absorbing the vast majority of total profits.
Across the western Kenyan regions of Kericho and Bomet, many local agricultural workers say they cannot cover basic family living expenses, let alone invest in essential protective measures to build future climate resilience on their farms.
These areas are experiencing severe weather volatility this year, including heavy rainfall during usually dry January periods, unseasonal heat in July, intense storm activity and prolonged drought conditions.
Nelson Ngeno, manager of Fintea, a union of tea farming cooperatives based in Kericho, said farmers are “really scared” as their livelihoods are “cut short” by the changing conditions.
Production across Fintea’s five cooperatives fell by 30% in May and June this year compared to what their farmers usually harvest during those months, he said.
“Climate is really affecting our farmers,” Mr Ngeno said. “There has been a complete change as far as the weather is concerned.
“It is very serious.”
In January, an unprecendented hail storm damaged thousands of tea plants in the district of Kabartegan, with Fintea estimating losses of 20,000 to 30,000kg daily over four months as the plants recovered.
Lilian Mutai Levin Langot, from the village of Kesebet, was among some 500 tea farmers who lost significant earnings when the storm wiped out her farm.
The 48-year-old smallholder farmer told the Press Association: “It was scary. The hailstones hit everything. On the tea plants, only the stems remained.
“I could not pick anything. It meant there was no income. There was nothing. We just had to survive.”
While she normally earns around 120,000 Kenyan Shillings (Kes) annually (£692), this will likely drop to no more than 90,000 Kes (£520) in 2026.
Ms Langot said she has taken out a loan to get through the year but has still struggled to pay for healthcare fees, school fees for her son and the upkeep of her infant granddaughter.
And having bought a cow and calf to diversify her income, the farmer said she was unable to buy enough feed, so the cow stopped producing milk, and both eventually died.
“It was so hard,” she said, adding that she is “very worried” about such a storm happening again.
“It will be so bad on us,” she said. “When we see the rain, we are just hoping: ‘Don’t let it be the hailstones. Let it just be the rain’.”
Meanwhile, Paul Kipsigei Koech, 50, who lives in nearby Chepchabas, told PA that he is earning so little from his tea farm that he can only provide one meal of mushed-up maize each day for his seven children, wife and elderly father.
Extreme weather events are now happening “once a year”, he said. “You can’t predict like we usually do in the previous (years).”
This, alongside the rising cost of living, is putting further pressure on his ability to make ends meet, with his current income sitting at around 3,000 to 4,000 Kes (£17 to £23) a month, equivalent to less than £1 a day.
“The income is really low to support the entire family,” he said, adding that he is also 80,000 Kes (£462) in debt.
“It is not enough. It is very scarce,” he said. “There is no breakfast. No lunch.”
Asked what he would spend the money on if he received a higher price for his produce, Mr Koech said he would pay the fees so his children – the youngest of which is six – could go to school and eventually help to support the family.
“I do not want them to come back to pick tea. I want them to go forward and even get different jobs than what I do,” he said.
Meanwhile, Gladys Maiywa, 50, also from Chepchabas, also earns around 3,000 Kes (£17) a month to support her eight children and sometimes less depending on the weather.
She similarly has sunk 19,000 Kes (£109) in debt to pay for school fees and has an overdraft in the bank of 3,000 Kes.
“It’s very difficult,” she said. “If we get droughts for one, two or three months, we don’t get money. We can’t harvest anything.”
Ms Maiywa said she would spend additional income on her children, their education and build a new home to replace the basic hut they all currently live in.
“I want to see an increase to the rate of pay for our tea,” she added.
And Philip Kitur, a 66-year-old farmer based near Kericho Town, said he has produced 50 per cent less tea than usual for July as climate change and unfair trade practices hit his income.
He said: “A long time ago, the weather was very, very reliable but now the weather patterns have changed.”
His income “just covers the production costs right now”, he said, adding that he has to look for other means of earning money to cover his household’s needs.
“I expect to see less profit this year because of the dry period. We don’t know what’s to come,” he said. “It is very painful.”
Their stories come against a wider backdrop of Fintea seeing a drop in the amount of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms from around 5 per cent five years ago to less than 1 per cent today.
This means its farming cooperatives receive less money from “premium payments”, which they can use to invest in climate resilience measures or social impact projects.
Supermarket Lidl last week announced it would be sourcing more tea from Fintea on Fairtrade terms and pay additional money to boost farmers’ incomes, for a new tea called “Way To Go!”, which will hit shelves on Tuesday.
Fintea said the commitment means the percentage of tea it sells on Fairtrade terms may increase to around 2.6 per cent in the coming years.
But Fairtrade is urging more businesses to source tea on Fairtrade terms as the organisation marks the start of its annual “Fairtrade Fortnight” campaign on Monday.
Kerrina Thorogood, partnerships director at the Fairtrade Foundation, said: “Today, just one in five tea farmers in Kenya earns enough income each month to support their families with the essentials.
“As a result, many struggle to invest in their farms, adapt to climate change, and plan for the future.
“Addressing this challenge requires businesses to take responsibility for the prices they pay.”

Google to report child abuse content directly to Indian authorities
The direct reporting arrangement breaks from a global practice under which such reports are first routed through a US non-profit.
BENGALURU: Google said on Monday (Sep 21) it has agreed to report content flagged as child sexual abuse material to Indian authorities, breaking from a global practice under which such reports are first routed through a US non-profit.
The decision follows a similar announcement by Meta last week. It comes after two Indian government sources told Reuters they had in recent weeks pressed tech companies like Google and Microsoft to report child abuse content concerning India directly, given concerns that the existing system delays reports significantly.
A Google spokesperson said the company "invests significantly to detect, deter, remove, and report child sexual abuse material", and described the proposal as part of the company's "ongoing discussions with the government of India".
India is the largest market by users for both Meta's Facebook and Google's YouTube, and Meta's own shift followed weeks of friction with the Indian government, including an apology last month by CEO Mark Zuckerberg over the spread of child sexual abuse material on the company's platforms.
Meta and Alphabet's Google have for years made such reports to the US-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, which then relays reports to law enforcement in the country involved.
Indian officials had argued to tech platforms that the arrangement costs precious time in cases where a child may be in active danger, since reports pass through that intermediary before reaching domestic police who can act on the ground, according to two sources.
Child sexual abuse material remains a vast and growing global problem. The CyberTipline, run by that same nonprofit, received more than 21.3 million reports from around the world of suspected child sexual exploitation in 2025.
Technology and law enforcement officials in the United States, the European Union and elsewhere have pushed platforms to speed up detection and reporting, though most countries continue to route reports through the US nonprofit as the primary international clearing house.

In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.
As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.
Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.
Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.
What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.
In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.
Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!
In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.
A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.
That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?
One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.
Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”
But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.

Srinagar, Sep 21:The National Institute of Technology (NIT) here is set to become the country's first NIT to have a dedicated campus-based observatory equipped with a high-performance 14-inch aplanatic Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope, officials said on Monday.
The telescope provides aberration-free flat-field images for advanced astrophotography and planetary observation. The Observatory for Astronomy and Astrophysics (NSOAA) will be inaugurated on Tuesday, marking a significant milestone in science education and research, they said.
"The facility will bring advanced observational astronomy to the campus and create a new platform for students, researchers and the wider community to engage directly with the night sky," an NIT-Srinagar spokesperson said.
The centrepiece of the observatory is a 14-inch Celestron C14 EdgeHD Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope, equipped with a computerised equatorial mount and supported by specialised astronomical imaging equipment, he said.
According to the spokesperson, the system includes planetary and cooled deep-sky cameras, LRGB filters, a 2.5x Barlow lens and high-speed imaging capabilities, allowing observations ranging from the Moon and planets to nebulae, star clusters and distant galaxies.
The facility is being developed with scientific guidance and collaboration involving the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, one of India's premier institutions dedicated to astronomy and astrophysics, he said.
Dr Niruj Mohan Ramanujam, Scientist F and Head of the Science Communication, Public Outreach and Education (SCOPE) Section at IIA, is associated with the initiative as an advisor and collaborator, he said.
His expertise in astronomy education and large-scale public outreach adds an important dimension to the observatory's vision, the spokesperson said.
"With the establishment of NSOAA, NIT-Srinagar will become the first National Institute of Technology to establish a dedicated campus-based observatory of this kind, providing students with access to advanced observational astronomy and astronomical imaging facilities," the spokesperson said.
Speaking about the initiative, Professor and Head of the Department of Physics, NIT-Srinagar, Prince Ahmad Ganai, who is leading the project, said the observatory for Astronomy and Astrophysics is an effort to bring the excitement of observing and exploring the universe closer to our students.
"Our aim is to create a space where students can move beyond theoretical learning and engage directly with astronomical observations, data and scientific inquiry. We hope NSOAA will inspire curiosity, encourage research and help develop a stronger culture of astronomy and astrophysics in Jammu and Kashmir," he said.
Beyond being a telescope facility, NSOAA is envisioned as a centre for experiential science education, astrophotography, observational projects, student training and astronomy outreach, he added.
Ganai said the observatory can provide students with an opportunity to move beyond learning astronomy from books and simulations to actually acquiring and analysing astronomical data.
Its potential impact extends well beyond the NIT-Srinagar campus. The observatory could become a regional hub connecting schools, colleges, universities and science enthusiasts across Jammu and Kashmir with modern astronomy, Ganai said.
Regular sky-observation programmes, student workshops, teacher-training activities and public viewing sessions could help bring astronomy closer to young learners and encourage them to pursue physics, space science and astrophysics, he said.
Ganai said NIT-Srinagar is mulling to start its hands-on course on Astronomy and Astrophysics in the coming months, where special sessions will be allotted to schools, colleges and universities in the valley as part of its outreach programme.
The facility also places NIT-Srinagar among a relatively small number of Indian technical institutions with substantial campus-based astronomical observatories.
IIT-Kanpur, for example, operates a 14-inch Schmidt-Cassegrain astronomical observatory with CCD imaging and remote-operation capabilities, the NIT spokesperson said.

Kenya's Brigid Kosgei achieved a convincing victory in the women's race at the Great North Run after Great Britain's Eilish McColgan withdrew with injury.
McColgan, 35, was continuing her return to racing after recovering from a broken toe, but she suffered a foot injury early in the half-marathon and limped off.
Kosgei, an Olympic silver medallist and former London marathon winner, eased to the win in one hour, six minutes and 15 seconds.
Despite that being slower than the course record of 1:04:28 she set seven years ago, Kosgei, 32, dominated from the start and ran much of the 13.1-mile race solo.
She crossed the line over two minutes quicker than compatriot and last year's winner Sheila Chepkirui in second place.
Amy-Eloise Neale was the first British athlete to finish, coming fifth overall.
McColgan, who finished third in last year's Great North Run, suffered the toe injury during the London Marathon in April where she was the first British athlete to finish, taking seventh place.
The Scot had blood seeping through her shoe as she crossed the line and subsequently had to miss the Commonwealth Games in July.
She made her comeback in last week's Big Half in London and won that race in 1:10:54, but McColgan admitted afterwards that she was still concerned about the injury and her fitness.

The pair were running side by side for most of the course before 31-year-old Talbi surged ahead in the closing stages and held on to win in 59:47.
He narrowly missed out on beating his personal best of 59:41.
Mutiso finished 14 seconds behind Talbi in 1:00:01.

Britain's David Weir won his 10th Great North Run title in the men's wheelchair race as he finished in 43:06, while Melanie Woods was the women's winner in 50:19.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort

The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s new press ban
The president wants to keep CNN, MS NOW, and Politico out of the White House.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is escalating his fight with the media.
What happened? Trump announced he was banning three media organizations — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, “effective immediately.”
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump wrote that the ban was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and that other outlets would follow.
Why is Trump doing this now? We don’t know, and other than his blanket statement alleging “FAKE NEWS,” it seems like Trump doesn’t either. In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said that “it’s really just cumulative stories of the last two years. You get sick of it.”
That complaint — “fake news” — is a long-running Trump attack that generally refers to unfavorable but true stories about him and his administration.
Can he do this? Probably not, though it might take a while for journalists to get their access back. The ban sure looks like a First Amendment violation, and also like the White House’s attempt to ban the Associated Press last year as part of a dustup over the Gulf of Mexico, which a judge ultimately blocked.
At the time, US District Court Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump appointee, ruled that “Under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists — be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere — it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints.”
What’s the big picture? Trump has been flinging around “fake news” accusations for a long time now, but his attacks on the press and other media — like late-night shows — have grown more serious in his second term.
The Pentagon, under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, banned press from its press office earlier this year and has tried to force reporters covering the building to sign a restrictive new press policy (that move was struck down in March).
Trump has also repeatedly threatened broadcast licenses for networks like ABC and NBC; last month, ABC sued over an FCC review of its licenses.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

I've spent decades testing, reviewing, and (most importantly) using different to-do list applications. It's a career, yes, but it's also a bit of an obsession.
And I think we can all admit that most of these apps are way too complicated. A to-do list is just a list. Humans have been making lists for thousands of years, long before computers existed. Paper works well, but so does a stone slate if that's what you've got handy.
It's possible that you, a modern human, absolutely need a to-do list application with bells and whistles—due dates, recurring tasks, sharing features, and maybe even an AI integration. But there's a good chance all you need is the digital equivalent of a piece of paper: A simple list of things that need to get done.
And that's what Tasks.txt, a totally free Mac app, offers. From Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi, this tool is based on the todo.txt system developed by Gina Trapani. It's a complete alternative to a to-do list app that is based on a single text file.
The important thing here, though, is that it offers more than just a text file. This is a well-executed app. Open Tasks.txt and you'll see a simple list broken down into three categories: Done, Next, and Backlog.
The general idea is to use "Next" for the tasks you want to accomplish today and "Backlog" for the things you want to do later. The "Done" section is populated as you check things off, then cleared out at the beginning of every day.
It's possible to use this application using only the keyboard, which I love. Open the window and you can just start typing tasks—your cursor is already active in the text box at the bottom. Hit Enter and your task will be added either to Backlog or Next, depending on what you choose in the drop-down menu to the right of your text box. Press the Tab key to switch from the text box to your task list. You can use the arrows to change which task is currently selected. Pressing the Enter key adds a note below the name of a task, and Cmd+Enter marks a task complete. You can also move tasks up and down the list using Cmd+Up/Down.
There are no unnecessary controls or interface elements in your way. You can open this application, decide what you need to do, then get to it. And you aren’t stuck using keyboard shortcuts—using the mouse is just as intuitive, if that's what you prefer.
The to-do list is the heart of the app, but there's also an Archive and Scratchpad tab. The Archive includes every task you’ve completed in the past—everything from the Done section is moved here at the end of each day. The Scratchpad is just a blank text document you can use for keeping notes.
All of this, notably, is stored in a couple of text documents. You can find these documents in the app’s settings and open them with any text editor. It's pretty easy to look at the document and figure out what's going on.
Your task list isn't in some database in the cloud—it's on your computer, in an open, human-readable format. This simplicity means you can easily grab your tasks to use in some other application later, if that's what you want.
And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private. "There is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting," the website states. "There are no servers. Nothing leaves your machine." This is a rarity in the modern age, where every piece of software is trying to hold your data hostage to sell a subscription. This alone makes this an app worth considering.
Mostly, though, I just think it's a well-implemented app that gets the basics extremely right. It won't work for everyone, sure, but it might work perfectly for you.

The US narrowly avoided boarding a Chinese ship based on an “entirely false” US intelligence report generated with the help of AI tools, according to a CNN report.
That erroneous intelligence, submitted by a US Special Operations Command analyst, suggested the Chinese ship was transporting nuclear arms program components through the Middle East, according to “four sources familiar with the episode” cited by CNN. The US military was preparing to intercept and board the ship, with air support, before officials discovered a chatbot used in generating the report had “inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.”
One source told CNN the AI-powered fiasco “almost started a war.”
What’s the worst that can happen?
CNN’s report said the analyst in question used a chatbot to analyze intelligence reports regarding the Chinese ship’s manifest, leading to the near-disastrous result. That chatbot “fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings,” and that information was packaged into an intelligence report that almost set off a disastrous chain of events, according to CNN.
The near-miss is one of the more potent and consequential instances of a hallucinating AI ruining the reliability of a professional report. Since “hallucinating” became the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year in 2023, we’ve seen prominent examples of non-fiction authors, journalists, academic researchers, judges, doctors, police departments, corporate call centers, and more getting taken in by AI tools that simply make something up when their training data doesn’t provide sufficient context. And despite some adorable attempts at “do not hallucinate” prompts, some researchers suggest that it may be impossible to prevent LLMs from hallucinating altogether.
One would hope the US military would be aware of these kinds of problems when relying on AI for analysis of intelligence reports. But the Department of Defense in January rolled out an “AI acceleration strategy” that sought to “make all appropriate data available across federated IT systems for AI exploitation, including mission systems across every service and component.”

Cargo ship slams into Chinese fishing boat in Singapore Strait
Dramatic footage shows the moment a Panama-flagged bulk carrier collided with a Chinese trawler in one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes
Footage of a cargo ship ploughing into a Chinese fishing boat in the Singapore Strait, sending seawater surging across the smaller vessel’s deck as its crew scrambled to hold on, has circulated widely online.
The 229-metre-long (750-foot) bulk carrier First Margaux struck the Luqing Yuanyu 108, a 49-metre (160-foot) Chinese fishing vessel, at around 5pm on Thursday last week, according to ship-tracking data cited by The Maritime Executive.
Video that surfaced over the weekend, filmed from aboard the fishing boat, shows the cargo ship bearing down on the smaller vessel from behind before ploughing into its side.

Ports remain the same. Two forward-facing USB-C 3 ports (up to 10 gigabytes per second), as well as a headphone jack and a power indicator light. On the back, there are three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI 2.1, an Ethernet jack, and the power adapter port. Using the available USB-C ports and HDMI on the back, you can connect up to two 5K 120-Hz external displays (such as the Studio Display XDR or BenQ 5K MA270S) or three 4K displays.
One controversial design is that the power button is still hidden underneath the back left corner of the computer. If you know where it is, just tilt the Mac Mini to the side and reach your finger back—easy. If you don't know (or keep forgetting, as I do), it means having to flip the thing over entirely, with all your cables attached. It remains a silly design decision in my view, but it's nowhere near as egregious as the Magic Mouse it pairs with (sold separately), which still infamously charges from the bottom. But I digress.
I still wish it had an SD card slot (forward-facing, like the Mac Studio) though. Plenty of photographers and videographers would be well suited for the Mac Mini, and yet they'll need to buy an additional dock or adapter. And yes, some color options, like the iMac, would be nice. But from the outside, it's the same well-built, compact mini PC it's always been. It's the performance under the hood where you'll need to dig in to see the extra value in this latest generation.
AI Gains
Right off the bat, I was eager to test a couple of new components in the M6 Mac Mini. First, there are the advances in the M6 chip itself. This is our first glimpse of the next generation of Apple Silicon, and the first built on a 2-nm process node. It represents a significant step up in transistor count on the die—46 billion in this case. That's around a 35 percent increase in transistor density, which translates to higher efficiency and more performance. In theory.
The M6 Mac Mini also adds two more CPU cores than the M4 model, for a total of 12. That's a 21 percent increase in single-thread performance and a 36 percent improvement in a multi-threaded run. Those numbers sound impressive, but compared to the M5 in the MacBook Air, they're not as substantial. It's only around 10 percent faster than the M5 Pro chip in the MacBook Pro in single-threaded performance (and unsurprisingly, much further behind in multi-threaded). Those two extra CPU cores, though, do prop up the multi-threaded performance, even compared to the base M5 chip. It's hard to do apples-to-apples comparisons to only a laptop.
Like previous Mac Minis, it has a fan inside. And when you get to work on something heavy, you'll definitely hear it start to make some noise. It's not terrible, but if you're coming from a MacBook, you'll definitely notice. That active cooling ensures you get stronger performance from that M6 chip than you would in a MacBook Air (though I won't be able to do a side-by-side comparison until the M6 MacBook Air comes out, presumably in 2027).

Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.
Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.
Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely.
In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period.

Kamala Harris wades into 2026 midterms with a visit to Michigan as 2028 decision looms
Harris’ campaigning could serve to solidify or undermine her status as a potential Democratic front-runner for the 2028 presidential election
As Kamala Harris considers whether to seek the presidency once again, she is immersing herself in the midterms by campaigning alongside fellow Democrats, beginning with a Tuesday trip to Michigan on behalf of Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
The stop is a particularly significant choice for the former vice president. Michigan was among seven battleground states she lost to Donald Trump two years ago, and it now stands as one of six states that will initiate the next presidential nominating process for Democrats. Harris also has upcoming rallies set for Nevada and Georgia, two other vital stops on the political landscape.
Her campaign appearances could either solidify or weaken her standing as a prospective Democratic front-runner. Although she remains one of the nation's most recognizable politicians and a pathbreaking figure, others in the party are eager for a fresh chapter after she failed to defeat Trump when she replaced President Joe Biden at the top of the ticket.
"I think she’s run her course," said Barry Goodman, a Michigan Democratic National Committee member who raised funds for Biden and later Harris. "I just don’t think her running again would be the right thing for America moving forward."
A number of Democratic candidates, particularly in regions Donald Trump carried easily, have flatly rejected the prospect of appearing with Harris. "No thanks," Iowa gubernatorial nominee Rob Sand told Politico. "Let’s move on. We need some new leadership."
Yet many Democrats, including influential Black women who helped persuade Biden to choose Harris as his running mate in 2020, contend she has earned the right to deliberate over her options without being pushed aside or criticized. Emphasizing her distinct position, California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently told CNN he would not enter the contest if Harris runs.
"Kamala isn’t under any deadline to run for anything," said Donna Brazile, a former Democratic National Committee chair who managed Al Gore’s 2000 presidential bid. Calling it a "waste of time" to dwell on Harris’s shortened 2024 campaign, she suggested other White House contenders "should follow Kamala’s lead and get out there" to assist midterm candidates.
Harris has not announced visits to South Carolina, where Democrats will hold their opening primary. Antjuan Seawright, a political consultant based there, said she could present a compelling case, though a future campaign would need to look and sound different.
"She’s going to have to admit that she was wrong about some things," he said.
Michigan presents risk and opportunity
Harris shares a complicated history in the state, where prominent Arab American communities grew angry over Biden's support for Israeli military actions in Gaza and were disappointed when Harris did not separate her stance from his after becoming the nominee.
El-Sayed, by contrast, is a prominent critic of Israel who has called the war a genocide against Palestinians, a description Israel rejects. He has faced concern from some Jewish voters, which he has tried to navigate by apologizing for past controversial statements.
El-Sayed noted to MSNOW that "there were some hurt feelings" in Michigan following the 2024 election, with some Black voters feeling Arab Americans did not offer enough support to Harris.
With the former vice president visiting, he sees an opportunity "to bring communities together that have often been torn apart by recent events."
The joint appearance will draw intense focus for other reasons as well. Harris maintains a complicated relationship with the party's progressive wing, which includes El-Sayed, while El-Sayed aims to secure establishment backing in his contest against Republican nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman.
"We can build together on the areas of agreement, and we can come to understand each other far better on the areas where we might have seen eye to eye, and I think her coming into town will help us to do that," El-Sayed said.
Harris' travel schedule remains light compared to other prospective candidates like Pete Buttigieg, who ran in 2020 before serving as Biden’s transportation secretary. Buttigieg recently visited South Carolina and has been actively campaigning for midterm Democrats.
Harris visited South Carolina in the spring for smaller party functions, and recently joined an organizing call aimed at registering and mobilizing 1 million Black voters.
"There’s value in doing a lot of stuff behind the scenes instead of being front and center, especially for her," said Bre Maxwell, a Democratic National Committee member from South Carolina. She noted little reason for Harris to step into media cycles knowing "she’s still a target of Donald Trump right now."
Jaime Harrison, a South Carolinian who served as national party chair under the Biden-Harris administration, said her standing gives her a timing advantage other potential candidates lack.
"Many of these folks who do get in quickly would love to have that type of name ID, would love to have that type of network, to have that type of email list," Harrison said.
Harris has stated repeatedly, including in an Associated Press interview last year, that she feels no pressure to decide her plans. "Right now – midterms, midterms, midterms," she told Megan Rapinoe on a recent podcast. Spokesman Eduardo Negrón declined to comment regarding her timeline.
Her other upcoming campaign appearances include events for Nevada’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Aaron Ford, and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is sparking 2028 speculation of his own while running for reelection.
"She is certainly being strategic," said Seawright, the South Carolina consultant.
He pointed out that her book tour for her campaign memoir, "107 Days," visited nearly every major Southern city in states where Black voters carry heavy influence in early primary contests.
Meanwhile, Goodman said he sees no sign that Harris is engaging top party donors, and Harrison noted he has not spoken with her since last December.
Past campaigns offer Harris lessons
Harris first ran for president in the 2020 cycle as a U.S. senator from California, but exited in late 2019 before any votes were cast.
Some progressives viewed the former prosecutor as part of a system that disproportionately imprisons Black men, while some moderates saw her as a typical San Francisco liberal.
Biden selected her as his running mate, making her the first woman and Black person to serve as vice president.
When Biden ended his reelection effort after a poor debate performance, Harris energized voters, generating crowds matching or exceeding Trump’s. Her convention address and debate performance drew praise from many analysts.
However, she struggled to distance herself from Biden on inflation and immigration, famously telling interviewers on "The View" she could not think of anything she would have done differently. Trump targeted her in advertisements focusing on her support for transgender rights, declaring: "Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you."
If she runs again, Seawright said she must stress moderate positions and "be willing to say, you know, ‘I’ve rethought some things.’" Voters, he added, "reward that kind of authenticity and humility."
Harrison observed that presenting her own platform would be easier than when "she was a sitting vice president, somebody else’s No. 2." But he warned she must shed the formal trappings of the vice presidency.
"You can’t act like a sitting vice president, standing up on that stage," he said. "I’d tell her she has to run hard, just as hard as everybody else, working every rope line, taking every selfie."
Unlike 2024, Harrison warned, "This is going to be the wild, wild west."
