Despite Yemen's plea for US military support, president 
Donald Trump
 stopped short of committing American forces to counter the Houthis during a call with Yemeni president Rashad al-Alimi on Sunday.
Alimi had sought Washington’s backing for his Saudi-backed government after the Iran-aligned Houthis rapidly seized key areas along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, particularly around the strategically vital Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
According to sources cited by Reuters, Trump made no direct pledge of military assistance during the call.
Earlier, US officials had reportedly met Houthi representatives at the US embassy in Muscat, organised by the longtime regional mediator, Oman. The Houthis had affirmed their commitment to the 2025 ceasefire, saying no commercial ships would be targeted in the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, except the Saudis. Reuters reported.
Nearly seven-month-old Iran conflict has already kept US forces in deep waters, with the Mandeb strait acting as an alternative to Hormuz. In such a case, a US military campaign in the now Houthi dominated waters could prove disastrous for the regional allies and overall global trade.
U-turn at the last moment
According to The New York Times, Trump administration had prepared to launch airstrikes against the Houthis on Sunday, following fresh pleas from the Saudi crown prince. However, the newspaper reported that Trump called off the strikes at the last minute.
Two people briefed on the operation said Trump pulled back from, or at least delayed, striking Houthi targets even as commanders had approved target lists and troops were loading bombs onto US warplanes chosen for the missions, with the wave of attacks about to begin.
Trump had reportedly met with advisers the previous day and told them he was not in favour of the strikes.
The Houthis have fought against the Saudi-led coalition for more than a decade. Tensions reignited in July when the group declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as a response to the Saudi blockade of Yemen's ports.
According to Reuters, Saudi forces have launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the highlands.
The 
United Nations
 has reported that nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up in fighting, with nearly 130,000 Yemenis displaced within the country and more than 3,000 fleeing by boat across the Red Sea to Africa.
On Sunday, Trump said he remained in “deciding mode” over the Middle East situation, this includes whether to protect its long term regional ally, or maintain truce with the Iran-backed group.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that Iranian airlines will be shut down globally by 23 September while he threatened countries that allow Iranian aircraft to land or use any of their facilities with secondary sanctions.
In an interview with CNBC, Bessent said, "On September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world." He warned that any airport that services Iranian aircraft could face consequences from the US.
"If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he said.
The comments were made after Bessent concluded his talks on Sunday night with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Bessent also said that Washington was having productive discussions with Beijing's financial authorities, which includes the People's Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, on compliance with its sanctions on Iran.
He also said that Chinese officers were "very engaged" in the economic pressure that the US has been putting on Iran.
US sanctioned 27 Iranian airlines earlier this month
Earlier in September, the United States' Department of the Treasury placed 27 Iranian airlines on its Specially Designated Nationals List, which targetted all commercial carriers in the country as part of its pressure campaign.
In a press statement, the department had then claimed, "Iran's commercial airlines have long supported the Iranian regime's destabilising activities."
It also added that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps IRGC) has been routinely using private airlines to procure and transfer weapons as well as ferry personnel.
The measure was also aimed at "covert front companies, foreign intermediaries, and deceptive transhipment routes that Iran relies on to obtain US-origin aircraft and sensitive technology," the Treasury release noted.
The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated four entities based out of Türkiye, Malaysia, and Kazakhstan for operating as cargo service providers and general sales agents for Mahan Air.
The OAFC also suspended authorisations that earlier allowed overflights and also let non-US airlines to operate US-origin or controlled commercial flights to Iran.

Why Cardiff is set to win race to host Fury-Joshua
- Published
The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday, 11 December.
While BBC Sport understands final details are still being hammered out between Netflix, Saudi Arabian organisers Sela and both fighters' camps, Cardiff has firmly emerged as the frontrunner, with an official announcement expected this week.
It marks another dramatic twist in a saga that, only weeks ago, appeared destined for New York. A date at Madison Square Garden was so close to completion that plans were already being drawn up for a Manhattan news conference.
Instead, after Joshua and promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil, the Welsh capital has taken centre stage.
BBC Sport takes a look at how Cardiff became the leading candidate to host what would arguably be the biggest event in British boxing in the 21st Century.
Joshua and Matchroom stood firm on Britain
Wembley Stadium was long assumed to be the natural home for a meeting between the two defining British heavyweights of their generation. However, the path to making the fight was complicated by Joshua and Fury having signed separate agreements with Sela rather than a joint contract.
Joshua's deal explicitly stipulated that the bout must take place in the United Kingdom, whereas Fury's contained no such restriction.
That distinction proved critical when organisers and broadcast partner Netflix began lobbying to move the show to the United States.
Hearn acknowledged that virtually every other party involved preferred New York, with Matchroom even exploring what compensation would be required to waive the UK clause.
For a moment, that stand-off threatened to scupper the entire event. Fury publicly accused Joshua of stalling and briefly floated the prospect of a trilogy fight with Oleksandr Usyk.
But once Fury relented, organisers needed to find a British venue capable of satisfying the broadcast demands without leaving fans exposed to the British winter.
Cardiff, almost by process of elimination, became the answer.
The roof solves the December problem
The fight had initially been discussed for November but, with negotiations over the venue dragging on, it now looks set for December.
Staging an open-air stadium fight in the UK at that time carries immense risk.
While Wembley offers unmatched prestige, exposing tens of thousands of fans and a massive international broadcast operation to potentially freezing temperatures, wind and rain was deemed unacceptable.
Moving the event indoors to an arena like London's O2 would eliminate weather risks, but at the cost of sacrificing tens of thousands of ticket sales.
The Principality Stadium's retractable roof allows organisers to capture the immense scale, atmosphere and gate revenue of a stadium show while offering full protection from the elements.
The venue's official seated capacity is just under 74,000, but boxing configurations allow for even larger crowds.
Joshua has already proven he can sell out the venue, having defended his WBA and IBF titles there against Carlos Takam in front of nearly 80,000 fans in 2017 before adding the WBO belt against Joseph Parker five months later.

A US-friendly start time is easier to accommodate
Perhaps the most difficult hurdle has been aligning the event with Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime-time hours in the United States.
A projected UK ring walk of about 01:00 GMT - 20:00 on the US east coast - created a logistical headache for London. Wembley operates under a strict 23:00 event curfew.
While Mayor of London Sadiq Khan offered his support and Wembley officials were open to discussions, securing the necessary approvals from Brent Council and local safety advisory groups for a 01:00 start presented an administrative hurdle.
Cardiff offers a far smoother path. The Welsh Rugby Union, which owns and operates the Principality Stadium, previously indicated it would be delighted to host the fight and confirmed a late-night finish would not be a dealbreaker.
While early-hours finishes still require extensive coordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a clear precedent for late-night boxing. In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy American television network Showtime.
Delivering a true stadium super-fight
For all the delays and frustrations that have plagued this rivalry over the past decade, Fury against Joshua remains the pinnacle of domestic boxing. Downgrading to an indoor arena would diminish the magnitude of the occasion.
Crucially, taking the fight to America would have deprived domestic fans of a generational spectacle. British supporters have driven the commercial value of this rivalry for years, filling stadiums for both fighters' respective careers and following every collapsed negotiation.
Staging the bout on home soil serves as a long-overdue reward for that loyalty, even if both men are now former world heavyweight champions.
A stadium fight of this magnitude dominates the national conversation in a way a 04:00 New York or Las Vegas broadcast simply cannot, and local amateur boxing clubs could see a surge in interest when the country's biggest stars compete on home soil.
Wales also has history of staging a huge fight between two British heavyweights: In 1993, Lennox Lewis defended his WBC title against Frank Bruno at Cardiff Arms Park - the venue that the Principality Stadium replaced.
When the demands surrounding the event are broken down, Cardiff's emergence becomes easier to understand.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire on Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. The man was hospitalized in life-threatening condition.
The Canadian province’s special investigations unit said the exchange of gunfire happened near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, about 110 miles (160km) east of Toronto. Belleville police said the officer encountered the man at about 7.10pm and that both were taken to a hospital.
Police have not said what led to the shooting or whether the synagogue or Jewish community was targeted. They said there was no risk to public safety and asked people to avoid the area while officers investigated.
The special investigations unit, the civilian agency that investigates serious incidents involving police, said it sent investigators to the scene.
Belleville police said they would not provide further information while the investigation was under way.
Doug Ford, Ontario’s premier, said the shooting took place outside the synagogue as people gathered for Yom Kippur.
“I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford said in a post on social media.
Ford said Jewish people “have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear” and called for those responsible to be arrested and prosecuted.
“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones,” Ford said.
York regional police said there was no known threat in the region but residents should expect increased patrols at places of worship.
Sunday’s shooting comes months after Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, warned that the country was failing its Jewish community amid a surge in antisemitism.
Carney cited shootings at Jewish schools, firebombings of synagogues, and attacks on community centers and Jewish-owned businesses. His government announced millions in additional funding to help faith-based institutions pay for security infrastructure, training and personnel.
Synagogues in the Toronto area have also previously been targeted by gunfire. In March, shots damaged the entrances of synagogues in Vaughan and Toronto. No one was injured. Police later arrested three suspects in connection with those shootings.

Can an AI chatbot save lives by answering texts about pregnancy?
It started with an accident.
A network of clinics for pregnant women in Kenya set up an automated text messaging service to send out appointment reminders. But when the moms received the texts, they started to write back.
Some asked if it's safe to eat avocados during pregnancy (you can!). Others asked if certain symptoms they were experiencing, like swelling or headaches, are normal during pregnancy.
"At the time I joined I think we were getting less than 100 questions a day," recalls Jay Patel, director of technology for Jacaranda Health. "Now it's 15,000."
At first, Jacaranda hired nurses to answer questions one by one. But over the years since 2020, developers have created a program that uses artificial intelligence to understand patient's questions, prioritize them and flag when a user may need immediate medical care. It's called PROMPTS — and is used by patients visiting public clinics in 24 Kenyan counties.
For women without a smartphone, cell reception, or easy access to the internet, a text to PROMPTS may be the fastest way to get a question answered. Other times, it's a reliable way to determine if a long trip to a hospital is necessary.
"If a mom in a rural part of Kenya starts bleeding at 2 a.m., she can't just Google it," Patel says. "But this service runs completely over SMS. It's completely free to the user, and it's accessible to anyone who has a basic phone."
About 7% of messages are flagged by the system as potentially urgent. These are routed directly to a nurse.
"It bypasses all AI functionality and gets straight to the help desk, into a special queue," Patel says. "They can pick it up immediately, look at the mom's question history and call her."
That kind of quick response is critical in Kenya, where about 6,000 women die each year from childbirth or pregnancy-related causes. That's 16 women a day. Almost a third of those deaths are believed to be related to delays in seeking care.
Lisa Mushega, a policy expert for HENNET, a Kenyan coalition of health care providers, says PROMPTS helps prevent these delays by giving women a direct line to a health professional. (Jacaranda Health is a member of the coalition).
"It's a referral," Mushega says. "[PROMPTS] is data driven and can improve the quality of care — informed by the voices of mothers themselves."
Mushega says she has met women who used PROMPTS to correctly identify signs of pre-eclampsia, a life-threatening condition that can start with swollen legs. Another new mother used the system when her newborn seemed sick, and she wasn't sure how to calm him.
"She was told to go to the nearest health facility, because her baby was actually having jaundice," Mushega says. "It really comes in handy."
At a time when the use of artificial intelligence is drawing existential concerns and calls for regulation, a program like PROMPTS demonstrates its potential value, says Smisha Agarwal, director of global digital health at Johns Hopkins University.
The AI Edge
Historically, most public health messaging is one-sided: Public service advertisements, billboards or automated messages written by health authorities and disseminated to the public.
"That conversation is really bounded by what a health system decides a mother should know," Agarwal says. Artificial intelligence sets a different course: "What the LLM really changes is the direction of conversation. Because now we can center it on what the mother actually wants to know, and in a private space on her own phone. There is a fundamental change in power."
In Kenya, PROMPTS understands messages in English, Swahili and Sheng — a popular dialect in Nairobi that is a mix of the two languages. Jacaranda has also expanded to parts of Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, building versions for speakers of Twi and Hausa.
"There's local context," Patel says. "If there's a question about nutrition in Kenya, and you give the same answer from a question about nutrition in Nigeria, you're going to get laughed out of the room."
Jacaranda Health is also using PROMPTS to help doctors identify areas of need, based on anonymous feedback from some of the estimated 700,000 users each year.
"Lots of mothers are reporting that they're getting blood pressure checks, but very few report getting breast exams," says spokesperson Laura Down. "It gives mums more agency in the health system — as well as a better understanding of their pregnancy history."
In other cases, Down says the questions mothers are asking can help doctors understand what's happening in their own community.
"So for example, we're starting to see correlations between a spike in extreme heat and a spike in mothers reporting issues like headaches or swelling or dehydration," Down says.
Any potential drawbacks?
But there are limits. These interventions work best in places that already have functional healthcare systems, Agarwal says. There's very little margin for error when human medical needs are processed by a machine. The way the system is trained to do a rapid handoff to a human nurse in an emergency becomes a key factor.
"The first thing I want to know is, what happens when the system gets a message wrong?" says Javaid Iqbal Sofi, a researcher focusing on AI policy and governance at Virginian Tech University. "Suppose a woman describes something urgent, but the system treats it as routine. Would someone catch that? How quickly?"
Patient privacy issues and missed opportunities for care are common concerns, as AI platforms are adopted in medical contexts worldwide. Last month, the use of platforms developed by Palantir to automate staff schedules in hospitals in the United States drew protests by a national nursing union. The use of AI by insurance companies to process and deny medical claims — even without a human reviewing them — has led to outrage and calls for regulation.
In contrast, PROMPTS operates as a limited-use program, trained on a relatively narrow set of issues and concerns. Its developers say the human element of the system is the most important part. A team of 18 nurses are employed to monitor, audit, and respond to PROMPTS questions around the clock.
"Humans are responsible for ensuring the quality of messages going out, and we audit the quality of the answers," says Javan Waita, Jacaranda Health's director of programs in Kenya.
Maintaining a significant human component of the program improves accuracy but raises the cost. Right now, it costs about $2 per user to maintain PROMPTS, which is absorbed by the nonprofit. That gets a mom through pregnancy, and stays with her for a year after birth.
Waita says this is an important backstop, especially when mothers might not have an alternative.
"The sooner a mother is able to access care, the sooner doctors will be able to understand the problem," Waita says. "If PROMPTS isn't there, it means more complications for mothers, more complications for newborns."

TOI correspondent from Washington: Everything is supposed to be bigger in Texas, a state where cats are the size of dogs, dogs are the size of European cars, where you can fit two Germanys and 20 Belgiums – or 158 of the world’s smaller countries – into it.
But apparently, Texas’s Christian conservatives are not capacious enough to accommodate a large – very large – statue of Hanuman.
Amid an uprush of "Hanumania" in India following a Hanuman Ansh movie documenting the life of the mystic Neem Karoli Baba, the largest state in contiguous America has been witnessing a blazing row over a 90-foot Hanuman statue towering over the Sri Ashtalakshmi Temple in Sugar Land outside Houston.
Conceived as a monument to strength, devotion, and unity by local Hindu groups, and officially called the Statue of the Union, the icon has become an unlikely lightning rod in Texas’ increasingly heated argument over immigration, religion, identity and what counts as “American.”
The 90-foot, 90-ton figure was officially unveiled in August 2024 after a three-day consecration ceremony and is counted as the fourth-tallest statue in the US, behind the Birth of the New World, the Statue of Liberty, and Florida’s Pegasus and Dragon.
But no sooner was it installed, it attracted controversy, with members of a local church calling it a “false god” and local politicians jumping on the issue to assert that it has no place in a “Christian nation” – which, constitutionally, the US is not.
Since then, arguments for and against the statue have surfaced frequently in an increasingly toxic atmosphere in a once-capacious state that has seen a large influx of Indian-origin residents, particularly in and around Dallas and Houston.
Indian-American community leaders maintain that the statue is not an assertion that Texas has suddenly become India, but rather that Hindu Americans are part of Texas.
“There’s nothing that’s un-American about it,” says Dr Vijay Sreenarasimhaiah, a former temple board member, arguing that the statue’s message of bringing people together reflected constitutional values.
Temple members also say the structure is fully legal and they followed all due permitting processes.
Engineers designed the structure to withstand hurricane-force winds exceeding 180 mph that the area is sometimes subjected to.
The statue was constructed by traditional Indian sthapatis, or temple sculptors, shipped to Texas in pieces and assembled on site. The project cost about $8 million and was financed through donations from Hindus in Houston and elsewhere in the US.
((The idea for the statue came from Sri Chinna Jeeyar Swami, the Indian spiritual leader who also conceived Hyderabad’s Statue of Equality. He envisioned Hanuman as a “builder of bridges” and a symbol of unity, and named it the Statue of Union because Hanuman, in the 
Ramayana
, helps reunite Rama and Sita.))
The irony is that Hanuman is hardly a recent immigrant to America. At the Mount Madonna Centre in California, the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple grew out of the devotion of American followers of Neem Karoli Baba, venerated by a legion of celebrities in Silicon Valley, Hollywood, and Bollywood – from the late 
Steve Jobs
 and 
Mark Zuckerberg
 to Julia Roberts and Virat Kohli.
After Baba’s death in 1973, American devotees commissioned a Hanuman murti; the temple was consecrated in 2003.
In New Mexico, the Neem Karoli Baba Ashram likewise traces its Hanuman devotion to American followers from the late 1970s.
In Texas itself, the Karya Siddhi Hanuman temple in Frisco developed from a satsang group formed in 1999; its stone shrine was carved in Bengaluru and assembled by a team of 29 sculptors in 2015.
And the cultural reach of Hanuman extends far beyond Hindu immigrants. Barack Obama, hardly the image of an Indian religious traditionalist, disclosed in a 2016 interview that among the small objects he carried in his pocket as personal reminders and good-luck charms was a miniature Hanuman figurine given to him by a woman.
The National Archives confirms the existence of a Hanuman figurine in the Obama presidential collection.
The backlash, however, has migrated from theology into politics amid increasing race-baiting and xenophobia in the MAGA universe. In February this year, Carlos Turcios, a Texas conservative activist, released a social-media video of the statue, describing it as evidence that “third world aliens” were taking over Texas and America.
And last month, conservative commentator Kaylee Campbell pushed ahead with the fear-mongering with the question: “How is anyone supposed to take Texas seriously when we have a 90-foot ‘monkey god’ statue?”
Texas politicians themselves have sent mixed signals. Governor Greg Abbott, while not specifically commenting on the statue, has publicly courted Texas’ Indian-American community, saying at a Diwali celebration, “As long as I am governor of this great state, Texas will be a land for the Indian community.” But the fireworks just won’t stop.

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

‘Doesn't seem like suicide’: Surendra Koli’s brother files complaint, seeks high-level probe into 'suspicious' death
Surendra's brother Chandan told police that the circumstances surrounding the death raised doubts about the possibility of suicide.
Chandan Koli, brother of deceased Surendra Koli, submitted a complaint at the Saptarishi police outpost in Haridwar on Sunday, seeking a high-level probe into his brother’s death, which he alleged occurred under suspicious circumstances.
Chandan told police that the circumstances surrounding the death raised doubts about the possibility of suicide. He said family members who saw Surendra Koli’s body on Saturday noticed blood coming from the body, along with blood stains around the mouth and nose. He also pointed to a rope tied around the neck.
Speaking to HT on Sunday, Chandan said these circumstances had led the family to suspect that his brother may not have died by suicide. He demanded a detailed investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the death and ensure that legal action is taken if anyone is found responsible.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

You can find anything on Amazon—plus hundreds or thousands of versions of that thing. If its virtual shelves were translated into a brick-and-mortar storefront, it would probably be the most overstimulating space in the world. Take power banks, for example. Search “power bank” on Amazon and you’ll get more than 50,000 results, ranging from well-known brands like Anker and Jackery to obscure brand names with zero product reviews. There are hundreds and hundreds of companies and sellers to sift through, with varying capacities, port options, and charging speeds on offer.
So how do you know which brands are high-quality? Which listings are legitimate? What’s a good price to pay? Are any of these power banks actually on sale and worth buying, or are the discounts fake?
It’s remarkably easy to sell products on Amazon (as evidenced by its millions of sellers). That means there are plenty of subpar product listings that come from sketchy sellers—often with gibberish names or multiple sellers that are using the same photos and claiming to sell the same product. While many items on Amazon are safe and legitimate, you do need to be aware of the risks when you’re shopping. The site has problems with fake reviews and counterfeit items. Amazon has fairly good return policies, including an A-to-Z guarantee for items sold by third parties, but ideally you want to avoid having to deal with a return in the first place.
We can help. Below are a few tips for shopping at the Everything Store, especially ahead of Prime Big Deal Days on October 6 and 7, to make it more likely everything will arrive as advertised.
Updated September 2026: I’ve refreshed this story with current tips and information.
Buy Direct
When possible, you should buy items directly from Amazon. Amazon keeps a better eye on its own inventory than it does on items sold by third-party sellers. Items it sells directly are more likely to arrive as advertised and qualify for free two-day Prime shipping. Because Amazon manages everything, returns are usually painless. Sometimes you can even get refunds for defective items without having to return them at all.
If you’re already checking out a product on Amazon, like our favorite iPad, always make sure the seller info says "Ships from and sold by Amazon.com." This information is typically in one of two places. Either it’s under the red price (and green "In Stock" text) or under the yellow Add to Cart and orange Buy Now buttons on the right rail. It’s also under those buttons on the Amazon app.
If you’re browsing through Amazon listings, filter the site’s search results to only show items sold by Amazon.com. Buying an item sold and shipped by Amazon generally makes delivery and customer-service inquiries more straightforward. However, it does not guarantee that the product is high-quality or authentic, so you should still investigate the brand and listing. I’ll use the Google Pixel 10a as an example of a product you might search for. It is our pick for the best affordable phone, after all.
Step 1: Search for a particular item in Amazon’s search box with the category set to “All.” In this case, I searched for "Pixel 10a."
Step 2: Amazon’s search should select the right department automatically, but if needed, you can navigate to the menu on the left and click on a department that fits.
Step 3: Once the page refreshes, scroll to the bottom of the left rail and choose "Amazon.com" as your seller.
Step 4: Now you will only see "Pixel 10a" products sold directly by Amazon.com.
If you still don’t see "Amazon.com" as a seller, try hitting the See More button. It will bring up a dense but readable alphabetical list of sellers. If Amazon is one of those sellers, it will show up in the list. You can use CTRL+F (or Command+F on Mac) to search for the phrase "Amazon.com." Sometimes you’ll see Amazon Resale, which only sells used and refurbished items, listed as well.
One thing to note about trusted third-party sellers: In some instances, a product manufacturer might be the seller fulfilling the order. This is the case, for example, with many Anker products. This is OK; Anker is a widely known and trusted seller. But if it’s a seller or manufacturer you haven’t heard of before, you may want to think twice (or dig in deeper, as we’ll show you how below).
Avoid Fake Discounts
Seeing a product we want on sale can trigger a wave of excitement. Instead of thinking about how much we’re spending, we start to think about how much we’re saving. Coupons and discounts exist because they create a sense of urgency, leading us to buy things we normally wouldn’t. Some sellers abuse that pricing power. There are a lot of products on Amazon that are endlessly "on sale," and this makes it difficult to know whether you’re getting an actual bargain.
There’s an easy way to check. Just copy the URL or ASIN and paste it into CamelCamelCamel. You’ll get a page with a graph on it showing every price fluctuation in the past year. A lot of products have deceptive list prices, to varying degrees. Knowing the actual going rate for a product puts you in charge.
Alternatively, the Keepa extension for Chrome will add a similar box right onto Amazon pages for you—though it does try to get you to register, and it can slow your browsing down. You can also click the “Check Price History” button or ask Amazon’s Alexa chatbot, but we’ve noticed inaccurate information checking this way, so take it with a grain of salt. You can add something to your cart and check back later to see how the price has changed, too.
Tools like Keepa and CamelCamelCamel may also help you determine the best time to buy an item. Amazon’s Fire TV Stick 4K Max, for instance, consistently fluctuates between its normal $60 price and $40 (and in fact may skyrocket up to an $85 sticker price). As of press time, it has sold for less than $40 only a couple of times, meaning that if you see it on sale for $40, you (probably) don’t need to wait to get a better deal—unless you care a lot about the $7 difference and you’re willing to hold off for as long as it takes for that rock-bottom price to come around again. But that context can also help you realize that $40 isn’t that big of a discount. The tools can help you spot similar trends in other products, like televisions, which tend to get a lot cheaper around Christmas or the Super Bowl.
Don’t Trust Every Review
Amazon’s five-star review system is supposed to make it easier to choose between products, but it’s easily manipulated. If you’re looking at an expensive product from a company you’ve never heard of, or if there are hundreds or thousands of very positive reviews, do a little sleuthing. Many sellers try to use fake reviews to get their products listed more prominently on Amazon (or to make you more likely to purchase them).
There aren’t a ton of reliable ways to double-check for fake reviews anymore, but it’s helpful to trust your gut and pay attention to middling reviews rather than overwhelmingly positive or critical ones.
You can also browse the reviews yourself. Click on the link to reviews under the product name on a page and you’ll end up on a dedicated reviews section. To start, browse through the customer questions. You can use the search box above them to scan questions and reviews for keywords that may indicate issues with a product, like "break,” “bad,” “defective,” “customer service,” or "return." Amazon has also implemented an AI-generated summary of reviews on most product pages, but take these with a grain of salt. For example, this blender’s AI-generated summary says that customers have mixed opinions on everything from the durability of the blender to how loud it gets. That’s not very useful information—you’re better off reading the reviews on your own.
I don’t give much credence to one- or five-star reviews. They’re often filled with too much elation or anger to be useful. You can usually learn more by reading two-, three-, and four-star reviews. These reviewers tend to have a more balanced perspective and may elaborate on the good and bad aspects of a product. Verified buyers are also more trustworthy than non-verified, but they could still be receiving compensation for purchasing and reviewing a product. You also want to be alert for reviews that sound alike, reviews that repeat key marketing phrases, or any that seem overly happy and wordy. (This can be hard to do in the era of generative AI, but I believe in you.)
And finally, I’m biased, but trusted, in-depth reviews from professionals—such as those we publish on WIRED—can help you narrow down worthwhile products.
Examine the Basic Stuff Too
Most third-party sellers won’t try to scam you or sell you fraudulent goods, but it’s good to be extra vigilant when you’re buying from a seller other than Amazon.com. Amazon doesn’t do a great job policing third-party sellers and doesn’t require them to follow the same return policies.
Here are a few tips to help you know if a product listing or seller is trustworthy.
- Check the manufacturer and product: Make sure there’s nothing suspicious about the company name, product name, description, or images. Do they look like real high-resolution, clear photos taken of a real product? Do they look professional? If not, that’s an immediate red flag. Have you heard of the manufacturer before? It doesn’t hurt to click on the manufacturer’s name on Amazon (it should be a link) to see what else it’s selling. You can make sure it has a real website and its products are sold in US stores by Googling the manufacturer’s name or plugging the product name into a tool like Google Shopping. Third-party manufacturers sometimes use names that are very similar to legitimate companies, so check the spelling closely if you’re in doubt.
- Check for the “frequently returned” flag: Sometimes a product page will show a flag that says it’s a “frequently returned item.” The reasons for this aren’t usually listed, so it’s up to you to read through the reviews. Sometimes an item is frequently returned because it’s available in several confusing options; sometimes it’s a seller issue; sometimes the product breaks easily. A “frequently returned” flag isn’t an immediate reason for dismissal, but if you see it, check out the critical and most recent reviews carefully.
- Click the seller’s name: Read the seller’s page to make sure there are thousands of positive reviews (which at least tells you it’s been in business for a while), and check its refund policy to make sure it matches Amazon’s. AnkerDirect is an example of a professional third-party seller. Anker makes its own products and has more than a million reviews. You can also Google it and see that it has a valid website and is a real business with a Wikipedia page. If a seller only has a few reviews, your risk increases.
- Is the product “fulfilled by Amazon"? Even if you’re buying from a third-party seller, make sure the product page still says, “Fulfilled by Amazon.” This means that the manufacturer warehouses its items at Amazon’s distribution centers. Amazon fulfillment won’t prevent all issues, but it does help ensure smoother delivery and that Amazon will be your contact for customer service issues. You can see who fulfills the order right next to the "Sold by [Company]" text on a product page, under the Buy Now button or selling price. If a third-party seller is fulfilling the order itself, shipping and returns are more of an unknown. You might get slapped with additional shipping charges or delayed shipping. Returns may also be more difficult. Check the seller’s return policy (it’s in the Returns & Refunds tab of the seller page), which could be different from Amazon’s.
- Check the full list of sellers: Amazon algorithmically suggests a seller for every product. The steps above will help you determine if the seller is trustworthy, but there are usually multiple seller options for every product. To view a list of other sellers offering a product, click the Used & New link in the "Other Sellers on Amazon" box. This page will let you buy or filter out used and refurbished versions, or eliminate sellers that don’t offer free or Prime shipping. It also lets you see how many reviews each seller has, when they will deliver by, and any extra fees or taxes they charge.
- Ensure you’re looking at the right product: At this point, if anything looks fishy or unprofessional, hit Back on your browser and look through your search results again (and don’t forget to filter for Amazon.com as your seller if that’s an option). Amazon search results are a mess of text and images, many of which look remarkably similar and have confusing overlays such as “Amazon’s Choice" or “Overall Pick.” Sometimes different sellers even use the same images—discerning whether that’s because they’re the same company trying to game Amazon’s system or two different companies both selling the same drop-shipped item is often difficult or impossible. Read the titles of the products thoroughly and check to make sure you clicked on the right product. Sellers will also often list different colors, refurbished (sometimes called Renewed), international, or other variations of an item as a separate product. This kind of thing happens in all sorts of categories on Amazon. It’s often just the result of the messy way Amazon lets sellers list products in its database, but third-party sellers may find a way to create a duplicate-like product that’s different in some small way to get better visibility for their listing.
A Few Final Tips
There are a few other quick tips to help you avoid outright scams. You should never be asked to leave Amazon.com to complete a purchase. That indicates that something is majorly wrong. Amazon also won’t ever ask for your social security number or anything incredibly sensitive like that, so alarm bells should start ringing in your brain if that ever happens.
Watch out for fake emails as well. Since Amazon is the most popular retailer online, a lot of phishing attack emails pretend they are from Amazon. A good rule of thumb is to not click links in an email unless you know Amazon sent it. You can find Amazon’s messages to you in its notification center. If an email is legitimate or important, it should be here. Be sure to report any suspicious emails to Amazon.
For help with returns or other issues, check Amazon’s support site. Your recent orders should show up on this page if you want to initiate a return.

Pavlo Bazilinskyy still can’t believe he was on PornHub for work. He’s an assistant professor at the Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands, and has spent more than a decade researching AI-driven interactions between humans and robots. But he found himself typing “public transport” into the search bar of a very specific website’s “amateur section.” 297 hits.
“People are hard to predict,” Bazilinskyy says. It’s why he researches what he does. So his prurient pursuit had a point. Robotaxis without cabbies behind the wheel have started picking up passengers in a handful of countries, including the US. Meanwhile, there’s a long history of people getting up to antisocial behavior inside the quasi-private or straight-up public spaces of trains, planes, and automobiles—think the prom night limo, the “Mile High Club,” Tom Cruise in slow motion aboard the Chicago L in Risky Business, the stuff he found on PornHub.
What might riders do when there’s no authority figure inside a vehicle to say, “Hey, stop that!”? What do they do? Can people be convinced to stop before they start?
This week, Bazilinskyy and academic colleagues with backgrounds in systems engineering, computer science, psychology, and tourism studies are hosting an industry workshop asking participants to brainstorm along those very lines: How do you stop people from doing it in self-driving cars? Thinking about sex in autonomous vehicles, they theorize, can let anyone who cares about the future of mobility “stress-test” the role the vehicles might eventually play as communal spaces, where social norms get acted out every day.
The event focuses on prevention not just because these academics are no fun (though Alexandros Rouchitsas, an engineering psychologist who is also hosting the event, admits they are “taking the side of the parents, the elderly—we are not the cool people here”). They don’t want people to have sex in self-driving cars because they’re worried it will give a potentially positive technology a really bad rep.
“We want to see automated mobility solutions accepted, trusted by the general public,” Rouchitsas says. Self-driving could have huge upsides for the elderly, children, and people with disabilities, who have a harder time getting around places where driving is quicker and sometimes necessary. The tech might eventually move beyond private taxis and into public transit, where all sorts of people should be able to travel safely and comfortably. “We want automated mobility solutions to be seen as something that is equitable, serious, societally minded,” he says.
Rouchitsas’ biggest fear is that self-driving gets co-opted by the partiers, the drug users, the sort of hedonistic folk who have descended on some islands of his native Greece. “You know ‘Bang Bus’?” he says. “We don’t want that.”
The four-hour workshop—rise and shine, it starts at 8:30 am—is part of an industry conference in Gothenburg, Sweden, focusing on how people interact with vehicles and larger mobility systems. The organizers expect participants from academia but also the wider industry. (Gothenburg is home to Volvo Cars and the tech supplier SmartEye; BMW and Google are conference sponsors.) Those who show up will be prompted to come up with physical and design interventions that encourage people to not do that. The workshop will focus on preventing consensual interactions, its organizers say.
Rouchitsas, who studies human-machine interactions, says he hopes participants will get creative with their anti-action designs. But just off the top of his head: Maybe the vehicles could be transparent? Maybe a light begins to blink if the technology senses behavior it disapproves of? The organizers intend to publish a paper based on the workshop’s results.
Sex is the fun, eye-catching part here, made all the more alluring because it’s “the elephant in the room” for those thinking about how humans might interact with machines in the future, says Bazilinskyy—very under-studied. But the results of this sort of inquiry could help designers, companies, and lawmakers figure out how to compel people to safely share communal spaces like public self-driving buses in the future.
Prevent sex and maybe you’ll also prevent robbery, bullying, and homicide. “It could be helpful for the industry and academics to use this example to design other things,” he says.

Following the recent reports of a Houthi drone being intercepted south of Mecca (here, here), a video showing a missile intercepting in the night sky is being widely shared on social media with the claim that it shows Saudi Arabia’s air defences intercepting a Houthi drone near Mecca in September 2026 (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The viral video shows Saudi Arabia intercepting a Houthi drone that attempted to enter Mecca’s airspace.
Fact: The viral video does not show the recent alleged Houthi attack on Mecca. The video is from September 2025 and shows Saudi forces intercepting a missile fired by Yemen’s Houthis towards Israel near the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina. Recently, Saudi Arabia claimed that its forces destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca on 15 September 2026. However, the Houthis denied targeting Mecca. Hence, the claim is MISLEADING.
According to reports, Saudi Arabia said its air defence forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca on 15 September 2026, before it entered the restricted airspace over the holy city. The Houthis denied targeting Mecca (here, here, here, here).
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to several older posts carrying the same visuals. We found that the video was shared as early as September 2025, nearly a year before the current incident. Greater Kashmir published the video on 13 September 2025 with a caption claiming that it showed an alleged Houthi missile being intercepted over Medina, near the Prophet’s Mosque. We also found that The Times of India had published the same visuals on 12 September 2025, reporting on an alleged missile interception near the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina.
The Yemeni news outlet Belqees TV had posted these visuals on 12 September 2025, with a caption stating that a missile had been intercepted over Medina while Saudi authorities remained silent. More reports related to this can be seen here, here.
To sum up, an old video is being shared as recent visuals of a Houthi drone attack near Mecca.

A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”.
The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean.
The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further.
In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”.
He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.”
The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks.
US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”.
As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking.
Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”.
The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US.
“Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added.
The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment.
Although Trump recently claimed the bombings had stopped 97% of all illegal drugs entering the US by sea, according to available data, the attacks have had no impact on the volume of cocaine entering the US.
Journalists and human rights groups have managed to identify some of the victims, who in many cases were innocent or, when suspected of involvement in criminal activity, were at best low-ranked participants in trafficking networks.

U.S. health regulators will review the scientific evidence on testosterone use in menopausal women on Thursday, including its benefits, risks, dosing and role in female health, as well as perspectives from doctors and patients.
The public meeting, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said could help guide future research and drug development, comes as a growing number of women are turning to testosterone to manage menopause symptoms.
There is no FDA-approved testosterone therapy for women, despite years of off-label use to treat low sexual desire, known as hypoactive sexual desire disorder, or HSDD.
Last year, the FDA removed the boxed warning about increased cardiovascular risk from testosterone products for men after reviewing post-marketing studies, though the products still carry warnings about increased blood pressure.
Physicians who prescribe testosterone to women typically rely on low doses of products approved for men, often dividing existing products such as AbbVie's AndroGel and Keenova Therapeutics' Testim, or on compounded formulations.
The lack of a female-specific product creates practical challenges for clinicians, said Diana Tordoff, an instructor in obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, noting that an approved product could provide standardised dosing, labeling and safety-monitoring guidance and potentially improve insurance coverage.
Still, some experts say key questions remain unresolved. More long-term safety data are needed, said Stephanie Faubion, director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Women's Health.
The United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa have approved or licensed testosterone products specifically for women.
The FDA's request for public comments ahead of the meeting attracted hundreds of submissions, many from women describing improved libido, energy and quality of life while using testosterone.
Evidence and safety gaps
Interest in testosterone among menopausal women has grown alongside claims on social media that it can improve energy, muscle mass, bone health and cognition, though specialists say the evidence is strongest for HSDD.
"We do not have any evidence in women that it will improve muscle mass or bone density or mood or well-being or really any other metric," Faubion said.
Karen Adams, director of Stanford Medicine's Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging, said testosterone has been reviewed by the FDA four times for use in women but has never been approved because of a lack of long-term safety data and concerns about cardiovascular and breast cancer risks.
The FDA has approved non-testosterone options like Sprout Pharmaceuticals' Addyi and Cosette Pharmaceuticals' Vyleesi for certain patients with HSDD.
Testosterone is generally not recommended for women with a history of breast cancer because it can be converted to estrogen in the body that can drive some cancers.
Excessive testosterone exposure can cause acne and increased hair growth, physicians said, while rarer effects such as voice deepening and hair loss may be irreversible.
Studies show that testosterone therapy is generally considered safe for men with medically diagnosed low levels of the hormone when prescribed and monitored by a doctor.
Tordoff and Adams are leading Stanford's MIX-T pilot study examining how low-dose testosterone affects vaginal health and the vaginal microbiome in postmenopausal women. Results are expected within the next two years.
