In Summary
- New Apple CEO, John Ternus, announced a range of products at the Surprise and Shine event.
- While most of the focus was on the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable phone, there was much more to the event than just devices and a CEO debut.
- We bring you eight takeaways that were buried in the buzz around the new devices, which might have escaped your attention.
It might not have surprised too many people – the leaks messed that up – but Apple did a fair bit of shining at its recent Surprise and Shine event. The event, which also marked John Ternus’ debut as Apple CEO at a launch, went on expected lines, with Apple revealing new AirPods, Apple Watches, new iPhone Pros and, of course, the iPhone Duo, which has grabbed the most attention. There was, however, much more to the event than just the launches. Here are our eight biggest takeaways from the day on which the world saw Apple’s new foldable and the CEO on stage:
Table of Contents
New Era? Presentation-wise, Apple is still Cook-ing (Pun intended)
Yes, it was John Ternus who held the reins at Surprise and Shine. But in terms of presentation style, the template that was followed was still from the menu of the preceding chef, Tim Cook. We had multiple speakers, elaborate backdrops, and a similar race through a number of products, leaving the most time for the star of the show (it was the Air last time around, the Duo this time). Yes, in terms of presentation style, Apple remains well ahead of the competition, although we miss the wit and humor of the past; this launch was more from the Cook manual than the Ternus one.
No surprises (Sigh)…
It’s been a while since Apple surprised the Dickens out of us at a launch, but in recent years, the brand’s product announcements have often been leaked out well in advance. And that was pretty much true this time around. From the iPhone Duo to the shades of Burgundy to the fact that there would be no suffix-less iPhone at the event, the leak community got a lot of things right, which, as we have said in the past, takes some of the mystique and surprise out of the event. Mind you, Apple did pull one rabbit out of its hat.
…except for the AirPods 5
There were no suffix-less iPhones at Surprise and Shine, but there sure were suffix-less AirPods. And while most of the noise was about Apple’s first foldable, the AirPods 5 might have emerged as the silent, value-for-money heroes of the show. While most people had been expecting new AirPods Pro with perhaps a camera built into them, Apple brought in a new version of the classic AirPods, complete with better ANC and battery life, even while retaining the “open” fit and, surprise, surprise, the same price tag as its predecessors. Not too many noticed…until the price of the Duo was announced, and suddenly a device with no price increase became the belle of the tech ball.
Hooray, we will now have TWO iPhone launches every year
Surprise and Shine marked the beginning of a new iPhone era, in which Apple will release its iPhones in two tranches over a twelve-month period. While Apple has released iPhones at two different times of the year in the past, the second launch has generally been a relatively low-profile and soft one (of the SE and ‘e’ mainly). That is set to change now. Even if Apple does a soft launch for the iPhone 18, the iPhone Air 2 and the iPhone 18e, rather than a full-fledged event, the fact is that close to half of the iPhone portfolio will be launched in the second half of the year, and the remainder in the first half of the next year. The iPhone schedules just got tweaked.
Apple is getting REALLY serious about AI (no, really, this time)
Two years ago, Apple launched the iPhone 16 series, saying it had been designed from the ground up for Apple’s avatar of AI, Apple Intelligence. However, AI is one area where the Cupertino brand has been found trailing the competition. So it was not surprising that the brand was clearly out to write a new chapter at Surprise and Shine. Every device it announced – iPhones, Apple Watches, AirPods – had a strong element of AI, which different presenters stressed would work wonderfully well, even while preserving the users’ security. Well, we have heard that a few times in the past, but never in such a comprehensive manner. Is Apple finally going to crack the AI puzzle? Based on what we saw, it would be no Surprise if it went on to Shine in that department in the coming months.
Whoop, Whoop, the Apple Watch is now a full-fledged fitness and health device, and is targeting Whoop
It started out trying to be a computer on your wrist, complete with apps, notifications and alerts, but the Apple Watch has of late graduated (or been demoted, depending on your perspective) to being mainly a health and fitness tracking device. And Surprise and Shine saw this trend continuing, with most of the talk about the Apple Watch 4 Ultra and Apple Watch Series 12 revolving around better sensors and measurement. The highlighting of features like Readiness Scores and Health Age seems to indicate that the Cupertino brand now has the screenless Whoop, which popularised these features, in its sights.
The narrative is unmatched, but is now very hardware-driven!
Processors, camera apertures, health sensors, ANC, battery life…these formed the major part of the narrative around Surprise and Shine, showing how Apple’s has shifted from storytelling to specs at its launches in recent times. This might be fine for some, but we do miss the time when an announcer would walk us through nuances of design and amazing (or they called amazing, and often, unbelievable) features on devices.
Yes, Apple remains the lord, master, and commander of product launches, but we prefer tales to tech, and a live presenter on stage to edited videos, no matter how sleekly edited. The fact that the Duo section stood out from the others because of its stress on design and UI only reinforces our belief that Apple might perhaps reconsider going back to its storytelling roots, and leave the specs on the spec sheet, rather than on the speech notes. Everyone else talks specs anyway.
Cosmic orange is out of the Apple cosmos… and Black is back!
This was so typically Apple. After making orange the color of the last twelve months, courtesy of the Cosmic Orange variant of the iPhone 17 Pro series, and making a number of brands come out with orange phones and other devices (JBL even had a pair of headphones in orange), the Cupertino giant pushed the shade out of its color palette. It also brought back the one color that everyone had missed in the Pro series – Black. Henry “Any Color As Long As It Is Black” Ford and AC/DC would approve of the return of the color, and so do we. We are not shedding any tears for orange, although we suspect those orange Pros are going to have great antique value some day.
And one more thing…
Craig Federighi’s hair looks as awesome as ever!

Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. So far, three deaths have been recorded and many areas are still flooded, with numerous villages affected, along with the region of Bhutni. Erosion from the flooding, reported from Khaskol, led to a disruption in river flow which led to a more severe impact in Bhutni. More than 100 boats have been sent out for evacuation.
At East Basudevpur, a 20ft (6-metre) embankment collapsed, reducing the channel from 550ft to under 150ft, which could lead to further flooding unless repaired. This flooding resulted after the Ganges River rose about 75cm above its “extreme danger” level owing to heavy rainfall.
A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.
After the hottest summer on record for the US, the above average temperatures are expected to continue this week as a heatwave grips many central states. A persistent area of high pressure and a very warm surface after recent heat will help to drive the daytime temperatures widely into the high 30s celsius or up to 40C across Oklahoma, Kansas and nearby states. Models keep the heat locked in through much of the remainder of the month, increasing the risk of wildfires, with other parts of the country already under red flag warnings.

US President Donald Trump on Monday defended the move to ban top US media from White House calling it an "assault on fake news". This comes after MS NOW, CNN and Politico said that they would sue the Trump administration to protect their First Amendment rights.
"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
"It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!" he added.
Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW, two White House reporters from the two cable networks, went live to report that when they arrived for their positions at the White House, they were turned away and had their press badges revoked.
Soon after, Politico reported that Cheyenne Haslett, its White House reporter, was also refused admission and had her badge taken away.
The measures were the most recent test of First Amendment rights in the US and a blatant escalation of Trump's long-running attempts to limit news coverage by journalists he considers offensive, both through administrative action and in court. Trump had announced on Friday that he would ban all three outlets due to news coverage he didn't like.

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

Super League: Wakefield prop Emre Guler set to miss rest of play-offs after being given two-match ban for punching
Wakefield will be without prop Emre Guler for Saturday's semi-final against Wigan; The Super League play-offs continue live on Sky Sports as Leeds host Warrington at 8pm on Friday before Wigan host Wakefield at 5.30pm on Saturday
Monday 21 September 2026 15:27, UK
Wakefield prop Emre Guler is set to miss the rest of the Super League play-offs after being handed a two-match ban for punching.
The forward was sent off following a clash with Leigh's Owen Trout during Trinity's 26-16 victory over the Leopards in their eliminator last Friday.
The punishment was confirmed following a meeting of the Rugby Football League's match review panel on Monday.
Barring a successful appeal against the grade E offence, Guler will now miss Wakefield's semi-final against Wigan on Saturday and the Grand Final, if Trinity reach it.
Guler only joined Wakefield last month having brought forward his planned arrival from St George Illawarra Dragons from the start of the 2027 season.
Team-mate Mike McMeeken will be free to play after being fined following a grade B charge of dangerous contact against Leigh's David Armstrong in the same game.
Warrington's James Harrison was also fined following a grade C charge of head contact in the Wolves' win over Hull KR, which set up a semi-final at Leeds. Team-mate Luke Yates will face no further action over a grade A dangerous throw.
Hull KR centre Peta Hiku has also been banned for two matches for punching Warrington's George Williams but, with Rovers now out of the play-offs, his suspension will be served next season.

Premium flexible workspace operator Innov8 Workspaces sharply improved its profitability in the fiscal year FY26 while rapidly expanding the network of centres it operates across the country. Innov8's net profit surged nearly 11.8X to ₹13.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹1.2 Cr in FY25, as per its annual report. Important to highlight that the startup's profitability took a 97% hit in FY25 from ₹37.7 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 76% to ₹201.3 Cr from ₹114.5 Cr, while EBITDA net of lease increased 64.6% to ₹49.4 Cr from ₹30 Cr. The company had projected its FY26 I-GAAP EBITDA to double to ₹60 Cr back in September 2025. The sharp improvement in the bottom line was also aided by a notable uptick in non-operating revenue. Innov8 reported ₹38.9 Cr in other income during FY26, more than 12X the ₹3.1 Cr recorded in the previous year. A substantial portion of this came from a ₹36.7 Cr gain on termination of lease contracts. Including other income of ₹38.9 Cr, the total income stood at ₹240.2 Cr in FY26, a 104.4% increase from ₹117.5 Cr in the previous year. Revenue Nearly Doubles In Two Years Innov8's growth has accelerated considerably over the past two years. Operating revenue increased from ₹52.7 Cr in FY24 to ₹114.5 Cr in FY25 and further to ₹201.3 Cr in FY26. In this, rental income remained the company's primary source of revenue, contributing ₹173.6 Cr, or around 86% of operating revenue, in FY26. This was up 59.3% from ₹108.9 Cr in FY25. The company also generated ₹27.6 Cr from other operational income, while revenue from the sale of food and beverages stood at ₹15.5 Lakh. Other operational income rose sharply from ₹5.4 Cr in FY25, indicating that ancillary services are becoming a larger part of the company's revenue mix. The annual report says the growth was driven by expansion of the portfolio, higher occupancy, improved pricing and the scaling of its managed workspace business. Innov8 follows a landlord-led capex model in which landlords fund the fit-outs while Innov8 provides the brand, demand generation, design and operations. This model allows the company to expand without taking on the entire fit-out burden for new centres. Innov8 said this asset-light structure has allowed it to open a new centre roughly every three weeks over the past 15 months. Innov8 ended FY26 with 58 operational centres, adding 16 centres during the year. The expansion continued after the end of the fiscal year. The company added another 14 centres in the three months following March 31, 2026, taking its network to 72 centres as of July 2026. It has set a target of reaching 101 centres during FY27. Importantly, the company plans to expand to 22 cities during FY27, with Kochi, Coimbatore, Kolkata and Jaipur among the cities identified for expansion. It continues to focus on business districts and commercial clusters in cities including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Chennai. Its stated strategy is to prioritise high-density commercial locations rather than pursue suburban volume. Vatika Acquisition Adds Enterprise Business One of the biggest developments after the close of FY26 was Innov8's acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited. The company entered into a share purchase agreement on June 8, 2026, to acquire the entire share capital of Vatika Business Centres for ₹27 Cr. The transaction closed on June 18, with 80% of the consideration payable at closing and the remaining 20% due three months later. Innov8 paid ₹10.2 Cr at closing, according to the annual report. The acquisition gives Innov8 an established managed-office platform and is expected to strengthen its enterprise workspace business. The company said Vatika brings marquee enterprise clients on long-term commitments and provides further room for expansion in the managed-office segment. "Our ambition has always been to build premium workspaces that combine thoughtful design, vibrant community, enterprise-grade infrastructure and fully managed services, while giving businesses the flexibility to adapt as their needs evolve... A customer can begin with five seats and grow to five hundred without ever leaving the Innov8 network. Our expansion into managed workspaces, including through the acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited, completes that ladder," said Rakesh Kumar, director and CFO, Innov8. Breaking Down Innov8’s Expenses The company’s total expenses increased to ₹226.2 Cr in FY26, an uptick of 86% from ₹121.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Here is a closer look at the areas where Innov8 spent the most: Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Constituting 42.7% of the overall expenditure, spending under this head rose 2.3X to ₹96.7 Cr in the year under review, from ₹42.4 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Expenses towards interest on lease liabilities, interest on borrowing and bank charges came up to ₹70 Cr in FY26, marking 127.8% increase from ₹30.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. Finance costs contributed to 30.9% of the total expenses. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, including salaries, wages, bonus, gratuity expense and contribution to PF and other funds rose 75.3% to ₹6.8 Cr in the reported year, from ₹3.9 Cr in FY25.

Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the UN, ending a bid that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the same determination as always, my international work.”
The two-time Chilean president and former UN human rights chief had positioned her campaign around defending multilateralism and international law at a time when she said both were under sustained pressure.
Bachelet’s exit leaves seven candidates in the race to succeed the secretary general, António Guterres, who will conclude his second five-year term on 31 December. It is still possible for more candidates to enter the contest.
Her withdrawal comes after a third informal straw poll, held on Friday, showed her support had all but collapsed. That same poll put Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan in the lead.
The UN security council will formally recommend a single candidate to the 193-member general assembly for election. The assembly’s approval has long been seen as a formality once the council reaches consensus.

In late August, the Food and Drug Administration approved a new therapeutic for pancreatic cancer, daraxonrasib, developed by Revolution Medicines. This drug is for previously treated patients and represents a revolutionary new therapeutic to target KRAS inside pancreatic cancers, the most commonly mutated oncogene found in the disease. Having this mutation is a very bad sign for a pancreatic cancer patient, often indicating that their case is terminal.
Medicine has known about KRAS for decades, but because of its physical shape, it’s been nearly impossible to treat. Until daraxonrasib proved for the first time that KRAS could be treated, bound, and stopped.
While pancreatic cancer remains a devastating diagnosis, this therapy nearly doubled the survival rate in a clinical trial — an incredible result for those patients and their families. Time is priceless.

As a personal stylist for corporate clients, I believe that picking out an outfit shouldn't be the hardest part of someone's morning — it should be the easiest.
After four years of helping professionals build wardrobes that suit their lifestyles and boost their confidence in the office, I've learned what works — and what doesn't — when dressing for the workplace.
These are five of the most common mistakes I always tell clients to avoid.
Relying on an all-black outfit eliminates any personality.
One of the biggest mistakes I see people make is what I call the "all-black blob."
Because wearing black feels easy, professional, and safe, people tend to use this same formula every day: a black ballet flat, black straight-leg trousers, a black tee, and a black blazer.
There's nothing necessarily wrong with that attire, but when everything is the same, I think it starts to eliminate any sense of personality or interest in the outfit.
Instead, I recommend simply adding one thing to give the look some dimension, like mixing cotton with wool, cashmere, leather, or suede. That way, even though everything is black, the outfit doesn't feel flat.
Another way to elevate an all-black outfit is to incorporate an interesting pair of shoes. I love snakeskin as a way to add a little pattern to an otherwise simple ensemble. I also recommend trying a loafer in a deep brown or navy, or grabbing a suede pair to add even more texture.
The same goes for shirts and ties. I wouldn't necessarily wear a black button-down with a black blazer. Instead, I recommend breaking it up with a different color, texture, or accessory.
Wearing a suit is not the only way to look professional.
Of course, if someone's job or corporate event requires a suit, then they should absolutely wear one. But in any other case, looking professional doesn't always mean reaching for a blazer.
Instead, I recommend that women look for a lady jacket — a collarless outerwear that hits nicely at the waist — which gives a more relaxed feel while still looking polished.
For men, I suggest classic trousers paired with a shorter dress shirt that can be worn untucked.
Skipping accessories leaves outfits feeling unfinished.
I find that a lot of clients tend to stay away from accessorizing at work. But embellishments to an outfit don't have to be loud to make an impact.
Even something as simple as a few dainty layered necklaces, small studs, a great ring, or a delicate bracelet can add interest to otherwise simple work attire.
And if a workplace allows for a little more fun, I recommend wearing a statement earring, necklace, or belt to bring even more personality to the look.
Thinking that a work bag can't be both chic and practical is a big mistake.
A work bag absolutely needs to be functional, as it carries a myriad of things, such as a laptop, folders, a water bottle, lunch, and maybe even an extra pair of shoes. However, that doesn't mean it needs to be boring.
I think people sometimes assume that if a bag is practical, it can't also be chic, but I don't think that's true.
I've found many bags that not only provide space and functionality, but also look more elevated and make a statement — specifically those with hardware elements, textured leather, or pebbled finishes.
There's no need to have separate work and personal-life wardrobes.
I hear this all the time: "Well, it's just for work. I'd rather spend my money on the clothes I wear in my actual life."
However, the reality is that if someone is going into an office five days a week, their work clothes are a huge part of their actual life. So if someone spends hours and hours in these clothes every single week, why wouldn't they invest in them?
Investing doesn't just mean buying something expensive. It means selecting breathable fabrics, choosing pieces that feel good against the skin, and paying attention to clothes that actually make sense for the season.
Before purchasing a whole new wardrobe for the office, I always recommend clients look through their own closets first. Many work-appropriate pieces can also transition outside the 9-to-5, including heels, ballet flats, and bags.

From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary
- Published
It is Thursday, 9 November, 2023. Brighton manager Roberto de Zerbi is addressing his players in the Amsterdam Arena before their Europa League tie with Ajax.
"There's 3,000 Brighton fans in this stadium tonight," said the Italian. "But there's more than twice that number in the city who have travelled over. Remember that when you go on to that pitch."
A long-standing senior Brighton official was in the dressing room that day. A fan first and foremost, but someone who has spent almost three decades working for the club.
"It made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up," he said.
For some clubs, an encounter with Ajax is commonplace. Not Brighton.
"The royalty of European football," says the official. "From where we've come from, to be in that environment. It was a pinch-me moment."
Brighton won 2-0. It was the high point of the first European campaign in the club's history.
Ask Paul Samrah for his single most memorable moment as a Brighton fan and a very different answer comes back, which goes to the heart of why, as they celebrate their 125th birthday around the visit of Arsenal, the Seagulls are almost unique among English clubs.
August 2007. "After the years of campaigning, the days and nights I spent fighting for regime change and then for the stadium, the moment I heard we'd actually got planning permission, that our objectors had decided not to continue their fruitless efforts to stop the stadium," he explained.
"We'd won our battle."
The two stories highlight the before and after reality of Brighton & Hove Albion.
Formed in 1901, Brighton were a Southern League club for almost two decades before they were voted into the Football League. They had experienced only seven seasons in Division Two when they were promoted to the top flight for the first time in 1979.
For years, they were known outside Sussex chiefly for "And Smith must score..." - the BBC radio commentary, delivered by the late Peter Jones, at a critical point during the 1983 FA Cup final, late in extra time. It was the moment when Gordon Smith, clear on goal with a chance to earn Brighton their first major trophy, saw his shot saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Gary Bailey. United won the replay.
But in 1995, chairman Bill Archer sold Brighton's Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, because of escalating debts that there was no obvious way of paying. Fans were not consulted and no alternative stadium was put in place.
Brighton did not leave until 1997, although their final season at the Goldstone was only confirmed by the property company who owned the stadium, after the final game of the 1995-96 campaign, which had to be abandoned as thousands of furious fans spilled on to the pitch to demonstrate against the ownership. Both crossbars were snapped amid the tumult.
After two seasons playing 70 miles away at Gillingham, and with the idea of a new stadium in the Toad's Hole Valley area of Brighton a non-starter, the club returned to the city in 1999 and started playing at Withdean Stadium, most famous for being the home athletics track of Olympic middle distance gold medallist Steve Ovett.
That brings us back to De Zerbi's pre-match team-talk at Ajax.
Brighton had more than 7,000 fans in Amsterdam that night. When they moved into the Withdean, its capacity was only 6,000. The modern Brighton really is a totally different club to the one that existed before.
"After the 1983 FA Cup final, players were sold, there was no investment, the Goldstone was decaying and the crowds were dipping," said Samrah. "There was no communication between board and fans, directors came and went. There was no continuity, no leadership, no direction. We were just rudderless."
There are some notable figures in the Brighton story.
Former Football Association executive director David Davies got involved, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott overturned a rejected planning application for Brighton's current stadium in Falmer. Former chairman Dick Knight stabilised a club that in 1997 came within 27 minutes of being relegated out of the Football League.
Without that trio, and many more, it is quite possible Brighton would not exist.
The contemporary Brighton are different.
They began their second European campaign in the Norwegian city of Tromso last month, knowing the Conference League offers the chance of that elusive first trophy.
They play in a magnificent stadium, a short train journey from the city centre, with its new corporate areas, and, generally, inclusive family atmosphere. Their recruitment model, buying players in and selling them on for vast profits, is envied. The new Brighton just beat Manchester United at Old Trafford for the fifth time in six visits. Four games into their 10th consecutive Premier League campaign, they sit fifth.
The contemporary Brighton exist the way they do largely because of the vision and investment of Tony Bloom.
Born in Brighton, Bloom is a lifelong fan. His connection to the club is through his grandfather Harry, a former vice-chairman, and uncle Ray, a director.
Bloom, 56, is an entrepreneur. He made his money in finance and gambling, largely through the use of data. He became chairman in 2009, and masterminded the rise from League One and move into the American Express Stadium. Last season, Brighton's average attendance was more than 31,000.
In their 125-year history, Brighton have never had it so good.
"Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.
"The club has been on an unbelievable journey. We've got staff members and many fans who have done that journey. For those of us who weren't here 15 years ago, our responsibility is to ensure what's to come - and I think there's lots - is better than what's happened in the recent or long-distance past."
As for Bloom himself, he has reflected on Brighton's 125th birthday in the programme for the Arsenal game.
"Since 1901, this football club has been part of the fabric of our city and the broader county of Sussex," he said.
"It has connected generations of families and communities. Grandparents have brought their children and grandchildren to matches. Lifelong friendships have been forged on terraces, in stands and on away trips.
"Through good times and bad, Brighton & Hove Albion has provided so many of us with some of the most memorable moments of our lives.
"This club is in my blood. Some of my earliest and most cherished memories are wrapped up in the sights and sounds of the Goldstone.
"When I had the privilege of becoming owner and chairman, it was like being entrusted with something precious to safeguard and help develop for the future.
"Many of you reading these words will remember those difficult years. The loss of the Goldstone. The long journeys to Gillingham. The challenges of the Withdean era.
"What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear. This anniversary belongs as much to those supporters as anyone. Quite simply, without them, we would not be here today."
Whether they beat Arsenal or not, Brighton stands tall, for those who fought to preserve something they felt was special, and a man who had a vision - and finance - to build something better.

Trump’s Monumental Obsession
The president fantasizes about a capital city full of memorials—to himself.
Donald Trump is facing multiple challenges. The United States is losing to one of its worst enemies in a war that has left the American economy mired in the sludge of growing inflation and rising energy prices. His popularity is now hovering around second-term George W. Bush levels, and may even be headed for end-stage Richard Nixon numbers. His party faces the prospect of a crushing defeat in midterm elections that are only six weeks away. (In some places, early voting has already begun.) The country, and the 47th president’s administration, are in trouble on every front.
Despite all this military, economic, and political chaos, Trump has stayed true to a handful of projects: Renaming the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, demolishing the East Wing of the White House and replacing it with a ballroom that even the French kings might have thought over the top, and building a triumphal arch in front of the bridge to Arlington Cemetery whose design looks like it was found in the bottom of Albert Speer’s desk drawer.
 The president is very concerned about these undertakings. He is, as they say in Washington, laser-focused on them. Ordinary folks might say “obsessed,” because at times he seems unable to talk about anything else, even when asked about matters of national importance, including America’s slow-motion defeat in the Middle East.
Perhaps this world of troubles is why Trump is taking refuge in plans of marble and gilt. Even an emotionally healthier man might want an occasional break from the travails of a presidency in crisis: Harry Truman would retire to the White House balcony with a bourbon, Dwight Eisenhower played a lot of golf, Kennedy and George H.W. Bush loved sailing, Ronald Reagan watched hundreds of movies in the mansion theater and at Camp David.
But Donald Trump is not an emotionally healthy man, and his obsession with monuments is not a mere diversion from the pressures of the job. His most recent tirade—posted at 7:34 this morning on his Truth Social site, some six hours after his last post the night before—suggests a president who is now lost in a fantasy city in his mind, a capital where the buildings are festooned with his name, drenched in glitz, and bristling with weapons.
As is often the case with Trump’s more unhinged posts, it is necessary to read his actual words to get a sense of how alarmingly strange they are:
At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.
Trump goes on to complain that Washington is the only capital city that does not have a “triumphal arch,” and vows that it will now have “the greatest of them all!”
Trump’s pivot from a memorial to a gilded turret is at least in part a legal strategy. When Trump’s ballroom plans faced legal challenges, the president went to the Supreme Court and argued that he had the right to continue with its construction because the bunker beneath it was a matter of national security. (Other presidents have on occasion tried to circumvent checks on their power by invoking national security, but Trump has made it a routine ploy.) The Court agreed, and Trump may now be trying to squash opposition to the arch on the same grounds.
This militarization of Washington ballrooms and memorials, however, is more than politics. Trump’s imaginings of castle-like defenses on the Potomac move beyond mere bad taste to a place of genuine weirdness. He does not merely imagine the new ballroom, for example, as the cap over a new, more secure presidential bunker; he imagines a space meant for parties and celebrations as a fort where he and his guests can celebrate beneath a drone port crewed by military and security personnel, including snipers.
The ballroom, however, almost seems like a rational investment compared to the arch Trump wants to build in front of America’s most hallowed ground. The entrance to the resting place of thousands of the nation’s war dead would be a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch”—whatever that means. (Perhaps it should include a portcullis and a drawbridge.) It would also be a permanent storage facility for a lot of ammunition.
What could go wrong? A space open to the public would also be a continuously operating military installation. Just imagine the sense of peace visitors, tourists, and schoolchildren would feel standing atop an ammo dump full of ordnance. But at least it might stop Chinese paratroopers or Al-Qaeda frogmen from seizing Washington with a daring raid after they’d subdued suburban Virginia.
None of this makes sense as a matter of national security. Yes, the White House is one of the most important centers of command and control in the United States, but it already has an array of defenses—including snipers on the roof when the Secret Service determines they might be needed. Other memorials and tourist attractions in D.C. are likewise guarded by layers of security and law enforcement. Trump, however, is imagining permanent military installations, including one on the roof of a White House annex, all because the current president apparently wants his successors to wake up every morning, see a ginormous eyesore, and remember that Donald Trump once lived there.
Militarizing an arch in front of the Memorial Bridge is an even more dangerous and stupid idea than turning a ballroom into a bastion. Motorists crossing the river would have to drive around the structure, potentially creating the kind of traffic jams terrorists could more easily exploit in a city already full of choke-points. (I lived in Arlington and commuted to the District; it’s a messy trip even now.) The arch would also stand close to the approaches to Reagan National Airport, as if that overburdened facility needed more safety and security challenges. And stuffing the arch with weapons would not only contradict the notion of honoring those who have died in battle, it would increase the possibility of a mistake or a malfunction.
The most important reason not to build the arch, of course, is that it is ugly and un-American. It is fascistic bombast, a militaristic yawp in front of a cemetery that is meant to be a place of respect and rest for the dead and quiet reflection for the living. It will loom over the cemetery, insisting that instead of thinking of the honored dead Americans think only of Donald Trump.
The president has never understood why Washington does not look like other capitals. America does not have a “triumphal arch” because Americans are not the kind of people who generally build such things. They do not ask their fellow citizens to swan about in uniform to celebrate foreign conquests. Napoleon broke ground for the Arc de Triomphe in Paris in 1806 to welcome his troops home after their victory at the battle of Austerlitz. It would take another 30 years to complete it, by which time Napoleon had long since returned in defeat from Moscow and then died in exile.
Speaking of Moscow, most of the institutions of the Russian government are surrounded by walls and parapets. The word “Kremlin” comes from the Russian word for “fortress,” and while it is imposing and even beautiful in its way, it is a symbol of centuries of autocracy and paranoia. And yet Trump wants to turn the White House and an outpost on the Potomac into similar citadels, with little regard for why America’s capital city was named for one of its greatest examples of unadorned republican virtue.
Trump clearly cares nothing for such symbolism. His ego wants what it wants. He lives in a city that he evidently hates and which, for the most part, hates him back. But Trump’s obsession with these vulgar memorials to his own vanity is a reminder of the darkness around him, of his hostility to democracy, his loathing of honor, and his disordered mind.
Perhaps the president is looking ahead to the day he is no longer the most powerful man in the world, and it pains him to think that he would be reviled—or worse, forgotten. If so, he seems determined to leave his mark on America’s capital even if it requires scarring it with militarized obscenities.

Quick Answer
AI prescription readers can help decode hard-to-read prescriptions, medicine names, doses, and doctor notes. Tools like August AI, Prescription Reader AI, Docus AI, AI Prescription Reader, and Google Lens/Gemini can simplify medical text, but results should always be verified with a doctor or pharmacist.
I am sure you have been in a situation where you walk out of the clinic, look down at the prescription slip the doctor handed to you, only to find that you cannot understand a single word written on it. It looks less like English and more like something scribbled by a 1-year-old. For decades, deciphering a doctor’s handwriting was a superpower reserved for experienced pharmacists. But that is no longer the case. Thanks to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), the power now rests in your pockets. Here are five AI tools that you can use to your advantage to break down medical jargon and medicine names easily without needing to revisit the doctor.
Table of Contents
Best AI Prescription Readers
August AI Prescription Reader
If you are looking for something that is more than just a simple text translator for your prescriptions, then August AI is the digital health companion that you need to use. Instead of just scanning the document and showing you the raw text, August behaves like a virtual health assistant that you can actually converse with regarding the document that you have uploaded. It has a fully chat-like interface. You take a photo of your prescription (either handwritten or typed) and upload it to the chat. The AI engine then extracts the medication names, dosages, and instructions. But wait, there is more to it.
Instead of spitting raw text, it rewrites those instructions into plain, everyday language. You can then type back your questions to the virtual assistant, like “Can I take this tablet on an empty stomach?” etc., and get personalized answers. Additionally, August AI strips out medically complex jargon and also tells you what the drug will do to your body when taken. Since health data is highly sensitive, August AI uses advanced encryption to ensure medical records aren’t uploaded anywhere. The good thing is that you get this AI tool for free, and it is available for Android and iOS.
Prescription Reader AI: Meds
Another dedicated app that can help you understand what the doctor has written on your prescription is the Prescription Reader AI: Meds app, which is available on Android. This app is built by MS Productions and is arguably the most feature-packed app designed for this purpose. You open the app, point your camera at the prescription, the app takes a scan, and its smart medication recognition engine instantly detects the drug names and formatting. It converts your prescription into readable text, so that you can make informed decisions. Once the app detects a medicine, you don’t have to manually Google its uses, as the Prescription Reader AI app itself shows you the drug’s uses, precautions, and side effects.
Everything that you have searched for remains in your history, so that you can access it quickly. There is a pill reminder and alarm as well, so that you don’t miss your doses. Not only English; it supports multiple languages, supports light and dark modes, and you can also share or save the readable prescription in PDF format. The Prescription Reader AI: Meds app is available for free, but only available on Android.
Download: Android
Docus AI
While you can still apply some workarounds as mentioned above, to read prescriptions, lab reports are still the worst. A blood test report gives you a wall of numbers, acronyms, and reference ranges that are guaranteed to induce anxiety. Some numbers might look too high, while some may look too low, making a normal person confused. Docus AI helps to solve this specific problem. It is built for heavy-duty medical document analysis. You need to upload a PDF, screenshot, or photo of your lab test (blood, urine, swab, etc.). Using Docus AI’s “AI Doctor,” the app will then compare the specific numbers against standard medical guidelines to figure out exactly what is going on inside your body.
Docus AI breaks down hundreds of biomarkers like cholesterol, cortisol, or thyroid levels and lets you understand if the numbers are high or low. It goes a step further and also explains what these numbers actually mean for your health. This way, you can make necessary decisions in your lifestyle. Based on your results, this AI tool may suggest dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, or prompt you to consult a human specialist immediately. The free version lets you access features like an AI doctor and lab test interpretation, but you can unlock full potential by paying a fee.
AI Prescription Reader
The name says it all. The AI Prescription Reader is a web tool that is good for those who don’t want an AI companion and don’t want to install an app. The AI Prescription Reader is for people who want a fast, free, no-nonsense tool that gets the job done in five seconds. The good thing about this tool is that, apart from being web-based, it is dead simple. All you need to do is upload a document, or you can take a picture with your camera and hit the Analyze button. The AI runs its OCR magic and gives you a clean, formatted text box with the detected medicine, strength, and frequency.
There is a built-in prescription dictionary as well that you can go through to understand the medical terms that doctors have mentioned in the note. You can also export the deciphered text into a PDF and send it to anyone who needs it. The best part about this tool is that it doesn’t ask you to sign up or sign in using any account. You can use it straight away by visiting its website.
Google Lens/Gemini
This list would be incomplete if we do not appreciate the powers Google Lens and now Gemini have brought to our phones. Google Lens wasn’t specifically built for medical prescriptions, but its world-class text recognition engine makes it one of the powerful tools out there. Recently, I also needed some help, and with the help of Google Lens, I was able to decipher what was written in the prescription, get it checked by the doctor, and it was 100% correct. Though this may not be the case with everyone. It is available for Android and iOS, and you probably already have the Google app on your phone.
It pulls out the medical details about the medicine it has detected and shares them with you, such as what the drug looks like, common uses, and side effects. If an elderly member of your household is using it, they can tap the Listen feature so Google Lens reads the prescription aloud.
Be cautious
Yes, AI is advanced, and things are going in the right direction, but it is to be taken with a quick dose of reality. AI is smart, but it is not 100% accurate. A smudge on the paper or rushed handwriting can still cause the AI to incorrectly determine the wrong medicine. It is easy to confuse 10mg with 70mg for two similarly named drugs. It is always important that you get it verified by experienced medical personnel or the doctor themselves and get the right medicine.

Why is there a waitlist for Siri AI in iOS 27?
Siri AI is the headline feature of iOS 27, but you can't use it right away.
After months of testing, Apple's iOS 27 and other updates are now available to the general public. On iPhone and iPad, the latest updates bring a litany of performance improvements, such as faster app launching and AirDrop transfers, but the headlining feature is undeniably the new Siri AI.
Siri AI is a comprehensive overhaul of Apple's virtual assistant that's capable of conversational input, similar to modern chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini. In fact, the new Siri shares many of Gemini's underpinnings as Apple partnered with Google to build its own semi-custom AI models. Apple has gone a few steps further to integrate Siri into the OS, giving it access to your emails, messages and other on-device content.
With Siri AI getting such a drastic overhaul, you might expect it to be available as soon as you update to iOS 27. However, that's not the case — you need to manually enable the feature and join a waitlist for now. Here's how you can do that and why Apple has gated the much-anticipated Siri overhaul behind a waitlist.
How to enable Siri AI and join the waitlist on iOS 27
Siri AI requires iOS 27 or iPadOS 27, so your first order of business is to check for pending software updates to make sure you're on the latest version. Open the Settings app and navigate to General > Software Update to check, then install as needed.
Once that's done, head back into Settings and tap Siri > Try Siri AI (Beta). If you don't see the option, try changing your language to English (United States) within the same Siri menu if it's not already. Be sure you have United Stated selected under Settings > General > Language & Region > Region, as well. Support for French, Spanish, Portuguese, Japanese and Korean is expected to arrive in October 2026.
Even though iOS 27 is available on iPhone models back to the iPhone 11 series, not all of them support the new Siri AI. Just like the general Apple Intelligence cutoff, devices older than the iPhone 15 Pro series (including the non-Pro iPhone 15 models) don't get the new Siri AI. For Siri AI on your iPad, you'll need either the seventh-gen iPad mini (A17 Pro) or an iPad with an M1 processor or later.
You won't be able to sign up for the Siri AI waitlist if your Apple Account region is set to China or a country in the European Union. The European Commission has required Apple to give rival AI companies equal access to the same underlying system data Siri AI has, citing the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA). However, the iPhone maker pushed back, arguing that opening up access to third parties could pose a threat to user privacy. Apple says that its Private Cloud Compute system used for Siri AI is specifically designed to prevent eavesdropping and data collection.
While the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 16 series and newer support Apple Intelligence and Siri AI, you'll need the iPhone 17 Pro or newer for the most advanced features. Specifically, Apple has restricted Siri's Expressive Voices and Advanced Dictation features to these newer models, since they require more powerful hardware.
Why does Siri AI have a waitlist?
Several aspects of Siri AI rely on advanced models. The digital assistant can now access personal context from apps on your device, read on-screen content and pull information from the web. Some Siri AI tasks are handled by the on-device Neural Engine, but more complex tasks rely on the processing power of powerful servers in the cloud.
Millions of iPhone users updating to iOS 27 and enabling Siri AI at once could strain Apple's cloud infrastructure before it has a chance to ramp up. Limiting access through a waitlist allows the company to balance demand against available computational load and prevent slowdowns for those who already have access. If the new Siri were enabled by default for everyone, resources would be wasted by people who didn't care to upgrade anyway.
As for how long you'll have to wait, there's good news. Some folks have reported gaining access to Siri AI within a day of joining the waitlist, although others have had to wait longer. Your iPhone or iPad may also say it's "Optimizing Search and Siri" while you wait, which means it's building the personal context database for Siri AI to draw from later on. This process runs in the background when your device is charging, and works most efficiently while your phone is locked and on Wi-Fi.
During the iPhone 18 Pro keynote, Apple said it will offer expanded AI usage limits with paid iCloud+ plans in the future, although it didn't provide any further details. For now, the company says to expect daily usage limits depending on server load, request complexity and other factors.

Goa elderly sisters found dead at home, leave cash for last rites: Police
It is unclear when and how the two elderly women died. Police said only an autopsy would indicate the cause of death.
Two elderly sisters were found dead at their residence in South Goa’s Canacona area in a suspected case of suicide, police said.
The women, aged 70 and 73, lived together in the coastal district of Canacona. Neighbours told investigators that the sisters, who were unmarried and lived alone in the house, had recently said they had no desire to keep living.
Their elder brother had visited the two earlier this month. Neighbours initially called him about the foul smell from the house; he called the police.
Deputy superintendent of police Canacona Division Nilesh Rane, said a handwritten note with some money was found in the house. The note said the money was to take care of their last rites.
It is unclear when and how the two women died. Police said only an autopsy would indicate the cause of death.
Rane said both bodies were found in an advanced stage of decomposition.
“During the initial scene investigation, police confirmed that nothing inside the house appeared disturbed, suggesting no immediate signs of forced entry or ransacking,” he added.
“The bodies of both deceased women have been shifted to and preserved at the South Goa District Hospital Morgue in Margao for required medico-legal procedures and post-mortem examination to determine the cause of death,” he added.
