When Vineet Chirania was scaling his train-ticket booking startup, Trainman, a decade ago, he encountered a problem that would eventually inspire his next venture. His team relied on Datadog, an application monitoring tool, to track the performance of its software systems. Then one day, the startup received an unexpectedly high bill after one of its developers started feeding additional custom metrics into Datadog. Over at BharatPe, senior engineering executive Vijay Aggarwal was facing a similar challenge with another observability giant, New Relic. Both Aggarwal and Chirania quickly realised the problem. As apps grow and generate more telemetry data, monitoring costs become increasingly difficult to forecast. Add concerns around data residency and dashboard latency, and the pain points become hard to ignore. These experiences eventually led the duo to build CubeAPM, an observability platform that claims to reduce enterprise monitoring costs by as much as 60-80%, while keeping customer data within their own cloud environments. Today, the bootstrapped startup serves around 50 enterprise customers, including Delhivery, RedBus, PolicyBazaar, Shadowfax and the Ola Group. Simultaneously, CubeAPM claims to be churning an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of nearly $1.5 Mn, up roughly 3-4X over the past year, all while remaining profitable since inception. But CubeAPM's ambitions extend beyond being an affordable alternative to incumbents. The startup is betting that its architecture, designed around self-hosting, data residency and AI-assisted troubleshooting, can help it carve a place in the global observability market, which is estimated to become a $20 Bn opportunity by 2031. From Trainman To CubeAPM The origins of CubeAPM are deeply rooted in the founders' operational experiences. Chirania spent much of his career building Trainman, which eventually scaled to more than 30 Mn app downloads before being acquired by the Adani Group. Aggarwal, meanwhile, built his reputation leading engineering teams at high-scale internet startups. Before founding CubeAPM, he served as the CTO of BharatPe and earlier headed engineering at Grofers (now Blinkit). Both hail from IIT Roorkee. After Chirania exited Trainman, the two reconnected and discovered that they had experienced the same frustrations with observability software. “The common thread was application performance monitoring. We had used different tools, but the problems were remarkably similar: unpredictable pricing, poor visibility into future costs, and challenges around data residency,” said Chirania. Initially, the founders believed modest cost savings would be sufficient to convince enterprises to switch platforms. But most observability purchases are displacement sales. Customers already have a monitoring platform in place, and migrating critical infrastructure monitoring systems requires massive engineering effort. Saving 15% or 20% wasn't compelling enough. "We realised customers were willing to migrate only if the economics were dramatically better, sending us back to the drawing board," Chirania said. Reinventing The Observability Architecture At its core, observability software helps engineering teams understand what is happening inside their apps. When a website slows down or a payment service crashes, observability platforms collect telemetry data, such as logs and metrics, to help teams identify the root cause and resolve issues quickly. However, scaling observability is a key challenge as enterprises generate massive volumes of telemetry data, making real-time storage, indexing and analysis increasingly expensive and resource-intensive. Moreover, traditional observability vendors such as Datadog and New Relic typically operate SaaS-based models, where customer data is sent to the vendor's cloud for processing and storage. CubeAPM takes a different route to reduce costs. Rather than moving customer data outside their environments, the startup installs its platform inside the customer's own cloud infrastructure. The approach allows data to remain within the customer's cloud environment and satisfies compliance requirements more easily than foreign SaaS platforms. According to the founders, this architecture addresses three key enterprise concerns simultaneously: cost, data residency and latency. The architecture also reduces data transfer costs that enterprises often incur when moving large volumes of information to external vendors. More importantly, the startup claims it can deliver significantly faster dashboard performance because the data remains geographically closer to customer workloads. This model, however, created a new challenge: how to manage and support a system running inside a customer's environment. To solve this, CubeAPM developed a framework that sends only minimal operational metadata to its own systems, allowing its engineers to monitor deployments remotely and provide support without accessing sensitive customer data. Tech Behind Cost Advantage Cost reduction is the centrepiece of CubeAPM's value proposition. The startup argues that traditional observability platforms often charge customers across multiple dimensions, including hosts, users, indexed data, custom metrics and support plans. As infrastructure scales, those variables compound and make bills difficult to predict. To solve this, CubeAPM prices its products primarily on data ingestion volume, bundling unlimited users, hosts, retention and support into a single pricing model. While this simplicity resonates with enterprises that struggle to forecast monitoring expenses, the real differentiator comes from its underlying infrastructure efficiency. According to Chirania, the startup has developed proprietary compression and storage technologies that dramatically reduce the amount of infrastructure required to store telemetry data. He claims CubeAPM can compress 100 GB of incoming data into roughly 4 GB of stored data, reducing storage, compute and memory requirements. This efficiency becomes important because customers host the platform within their cloud environments. The startup also emphasises compatibility with existing observability ecosystems. Rather than forcing customers to replace their existing stacks, CubeAPM works with popular telemetry agents and standards, including OpenTelemetry, Datadog, New Relic and Elastic. This interoperability allows migrations to happen relatively quickly, reducing one of the biggest barriers to adoption. “We wanted switching to feel like hours rather than weeks," Chirania said. Building A Full-Stack AI Observability Platform What began as an application performance monitoring tool has gradually expanded into a broader observability suite. CubeAPM now offers six major modules: Application Performance Monitoring (APM) Log Management Infrastructure Monitoring Real User Monitoring (RUM) Synthetic Monitoring Error Tracking The startup’s typical users are engineering, DevOps and site reliability engineering (SRE) teams. Most begin usage with APM before expanding into additional modules. This “land-and-expand” motion has become a major growth driver for CubeAPM. According to Chirania, roughly half the company's customers currently use multiple products within the CubeAPM suite. Now, as AI reshapes software development, CubeAPM sees observability becoming even more critical as AI-generated code may eventually create systems that developers understand less intuitively than the software they write themselves. As a result, identifying root causes could become more difficult, increasing reliance on observability platforms. To prepare for that shift, CubeAPM has begun integrating AI capabilities directly into its workflow. One of its recent launches is an MCP server that allows AI coding assistants, including Cursor, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Gemini, to access telemetry data directly from CubeAPM. This allows engineers to skip dashboards altogether, query logs through AI agents and troubleshoot issues through conversational root-cause analysis. The startup is also using AI internally. Over the next 12-24 months, AI-powered troubleshooting is expected to become one of CubeAPM's primary product priorities. Chasing The Enterprise Stack Unlike many enterprise software startups chasing growth through venture capital, CubeAPM has remained entirely bootstrapped. The startup says that its GTM strategy has largely relied on founder networks, particularly within India's tech ecosystem, where both founders have spent years building relationships. This approach has helped the startup, which operates with a team of 25 employees, acquire customers without large marketing budgets. Moreover, CubeAPM claims to report renewal rates above 95%, which management attributes to its support model. Rather than relying exclusively on ticketing systems, it creates direct communication channels with clients through Slack, WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams or Google Chat, allowing engineers to respond quickly during incidents. For now, the company remains focused on enterprise and mid-market customers. Ironically, despite being founded by startup veterans, CubeAPM has intentionally avoided targeting startups due to purely economic reasons. Migration efforts make the most sense for organisations already spending substantial amounts on observability software. For smaller startups, the savings generated by switching platforms may not justify the integration effort. This could change in the future, with CubeAPM now exploring a dedicated startup offering. CubeAPM says its platform now powers more than 1 Bn requests a month across its customer base of 50 clients. It currently claims an ARR of nearly $1.5 Mn while remaining profitable. The Road Ahead CubeAPM's biggest challenge may not be technology but market penetration. The observability category is dominated by well-capitalised global incumbents that have spent decades building products, ecosystems and distribution channels. Convincing enterprises to replace mission-critical infrastructure monitoring tools may not be easy. The startup's answer is to focus relentlessly on the areas where it believes incumbents remain vulnerable: predictable pricing, data residency, support quality and infrastructure efficiency. International expansion is also emerging as a priority. While most customers are currently based in India, CubeAPM sees significant opportunities in the US, Europe, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, particularly among enterprises with stringent compliance requirements. Despite investor interest in infrastructure software and AI, the founders say they are in no rush to raise capital. Their goal remains straightforward: build a globally trusted observability platform that helps enterprises monitor complex software systems at a fraction of the cost of traditional vendors.

How a national farm leader is dealing with record diesel prices
How rising diesel fuel costs are affecting American farmers
John Boyd Jr. filled up his tractor on Saturday. The bill was roughly $1,000.
Boyd, a fourth-generation farmer in southwest Virginia, grows soybeans, corn and wheat and raises beef cattle. He is in the middle of harvesting corn. During this time of year, his combines and other heavy equipment run constantly.
Now, he says, diesel is costing him about $7 a gallon, nearly double what he was paying a year ago.
The national average for diesel has climbed to more than $6.51 a gallon, according to AAA, another economic consequence of the war with Iran. The previous record, about $5.85 a gallon, was broken at the beginning of September.
"This is a national farm crisis for farmers," Boyd told NPR's Morning Edition. "I'm having to come up with money that's really not in the budget."
For Boyd, who is also founder and president of the National Black Farmers Association, there is little choice but to pay. He doesn't store diesel on his farm, so he fills a truck with a couple hundred gallons at a time, brings it back and transfers the fuel into his combine.
"I'm, as my daddy would say, robbing Peter to pay Paul," Boyd said, describing how he is shifting money from other farm expenses to cover the soaring cost of fuel.
There is little room to absorb the extra expense, he said. Corn is selling for about $5 per bushel, and he still has to cover the cost of the diesel needed to harvest it.
Boyd said the higher fuel costs are adding to other financial pressures already facing farmers. He said more than 400 Black farmers are at risk of losing their farms and need financial assistance.
"A lot of these farmers voted for this president," Boyd said, "but now they find themselves losing their farm and no help from the administration."
The surge in diesel prices is part of a broader global fuel crunch that intensified after the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Disruptions to oil shipments through the Middle East, including the Strait of Hormuz, have pushed crude prices higher, while reduced diesel supplies from the region have left fuel markets tight in the United States, Europe and Asia.

Meet the Scottish teenagers poised to represent Uganda
- Published
Teenage brothers Olly and Seb Fisher are closing in on their dream of international recognition - but it won't come from their homeland of Scotland.
Instead, the Partick Thistle duo are in line to play for Uganda.
They believe they would become the first white players ever to represent the African nation, thanks to their mother Kate being born there.
"My gran and grandad lived out here for, I think, four or five years," Olly, 18, tells BBC Sport Scotland. "My grandfather came out here to teach in a school then my mum was born here. So, it's a bit of a strange one."
The siblings became aware of interest from Uganda about six months ago, following a chance conversation some time before between their father and a football consultant at a game in Nigeria.
And, at the start of August, they were invited to attend under-20 and under-17s training camps.
They spent last week in Jinja in the country's eastern region and will stay on for one more week, with the pair saying they're "shocked" and "honoured" at the call-ups.
"I couldn't believe it," 16-year-old striker Seb said. "It's one of those things you look at and you're shocked. You can't believe it. Most other people couldn't as well."
Goalkeeper Olly had a similar reaction. "A real mixture of emotions," he said. "I was quite shocked. I didn't really think that this was a possibility but I was honoured to be asked to represent Uganda. I thought it was a real big opportunity."
Mum Kate is "ecstatic" and "thinks it'd be a great experience for us", adds Seb.
'The other boys have been brand new'
There is another Scottish link with Uganda, with former Hearts and Ghana midfielder Laryea Kingston currently coach of Uganda's under-20s.
And he is the one who believes the Fisher brothers are on the verge of making history.
"Coach Kingston was saying we'd be the first white boys to play for Uganda, which would be history in the making," Seb explained. "It is very special."
And Olly added: "It's never been done before, so definitely it is very special."
The pair feel like they're making connections with the African nation, having been reared on stories about Uganda from their grandparents.
And even though they have been training in oppressively warm conditions, they are embracing the opportunity.
"Everyone has been brilliant, welcoming, really great," Seb said. "The other boys have been brand new with us. Some of the boys actually come from the same area where my mum was born. So, they were all talking about that."
The boys will return to Scotland soon, combining training and playing with Thistle with university and school, but are planning to rejoin their new international team-mates in the near future.
Olly hopes to be part of his squad if they qualify for the Under-20's Africa Cup of Nations early next year, and Seb could be in the Under-17 squad for November's World Cup in Qatar.
"That's what you want as a footballer, being in an international environment," Seb said. "It makes you a better player and hopefully it does for the two of us, and I think it will, and benefit us very much going back to Scotland playing at Thistle."

The 51st episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu explores what constitutes a healthy diet amid the growing focus on protein, along with recent developments in osteoarthritis research, corneal donation and rabies prevention.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, and Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, The Hindu, discuss nutrition, weight management, osteoarthritis, corneal donation and transplantation, and rabies prevention.
Protein has become a major focus of nutrition advice, particularly on social media. The episode discusses the role of protein in the diet and why a healthy diet needs to be considered as a whole rather than through the lens of a single nutrient or product.
The conversation also looks at what happens to protein consumed in excess of the body’s requirements. Unlike carbohydrates and fat, protein is not stored in the body as a dedicated reserve. Amino acids from protein are used for functions including tissue repair, muscle maintenance and the production of enzymes and hormones, while excess intake can be used for energy or other metabolic processes.
The episode examines the role of diet and exercise in weight management, including research suggesting that combining dietary changes with physical activity can help support sustained weight loss. It also discusses why overall dietary patterns matter when assessing healthy eating.
Another segment looks at new research into osteoarthritis and cartilage regeneration. The research involves stromal-cell extracellular vesicles derived from menstrual blood and their potential role in cartilage repair. The findings are preliminary and are discussed in the context of ongoing research into new approaches to osteoarthritis care.
The episode also examines challenges in corneal donation and transplantation. Despite the potential of donated corneas to restore vision, some donated tissue does not reach patients who need it. The discussion looks at gaps in the process and the need to improve the use of donated corneal tissue.
Rabies prevention is another focus of the episode. The discussion looks at dog vaccination as an important part of preventing human rabies, given the role of dogs in transmission of the disease.
The episode can also be viewed here at The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap .

When will Africa get its next Ballon d'Or winner?
- Published
Africa has only ever had one Ballon d'Or winner, and the wait for someone to emulate George Weah is likely to be extended further after this year's nominations were revealed.
Morocco captain Achraf Hakimi and Senegal forward Sadio Mane are the continent's two names on the 30-strong list.
Both players have previously recorded top-six Ballon d'Or finishes but, after a year in which Spain lifted the Fifa World Cup and Kylian Mbappe netted 10 goals to become the tournament's all-time top scorer, the chances of the Paris St-Germain right-back or the Al-Nassr winger lifting the coveted trophy appear slim.
And it is not the first time that Africa has failed to make a big impact.
Part of the reason for the historic lack of success is down to the fact the award, which was first handed out by France Football magazine in 1956, was not open to players representing non-European nations until 1995.
That was the year that Liberian striker Weah scooped the prize after his impressive form for PSG and AC Milan.

Yet, for all the stars the continent has produced, the only other time an African player registered a top-three finish came in 2022, when Mane was second behind France striker Karim Benzema.
Of course, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have dominated proceedings for most of this century, scooping 13 of the 15 available Ballons d'Or between 2008 and 2023.
Journalists from the top 100 nations in the Fifa rankings will vote for the prize, with the recipient of the 2026 trophy announced at a ceremony in London on 26 October.
The "symbolic choice of venue" for the 70th anniversary of the award is in tribute to the inaugural winner, England winger Sir Stanley Matthews.
But how do the historic Ballon d'Or numbers stack up for Africa?
Weah claims the crown
The high point of Africa's Ballon d'Or history clearly came in the very first year the continent's stars became eligible, with Weah topping the vote in 1995 ahead of Germany's Jurgen Klinsmann and Finland's Jari Litmanen.
Five more Africans made that year's 50-player list.
But only once since, in 2007, has the continent had as many as six nominations. On that occasion Didier Drogba was the highest-ranked finisher, with the Ivorian coming fourth.
The pool has narrowed since then, with 30 players in contention since 2008 and just 23 in the running when the Ballon d'Or was combined with the Fifa's world player of the year award between 2010 and 2015.
One other stand-out year for Africa came in 2019, when three men finished in the top 10. Mane came fourth, Egypt's Mohamed Salah was fifth, and Riyad Mahrez of Algeria tenth.
Which African nation has the most Ballon d'Or nominations?
In total, Africa has received 76 nominations for the Ballon d'Or since 1995.
That makes up just 6.62% of the overall hopefuls.
Cameroon legend Samuel Eto'o has the most nominations, having been in the running nine times in a row from 2003 to 2011. His best finish came in 2009 when he was fifth.
Drogba follows with eight nominations, with Salah on six.
Five-time nominee Mane has the greatest longevity of any African, with the 34-year-old's first and most recent appearances on the list coming 10 years apart.
Nigeria has had the most individual players listed for the award, with eight in total. Victor Osimhen's eighth-place finish in 2023 is the best performance by a Super Eagles player.
Room for improvement
Thirty-nine African countries are still awaiting their first nominee, although Chad is surprisingly not among them after striker Japhet N'Doram was part of the 1995 list alongside Weah.
DR Congo and South Africa, ranked 43rd and 54th in the world respectively, are the highest-ranked nations still waiting to make the cut, while no player representing a club side on the continent has ever been nominated.
There have been nine years since 1995 when only one African was among the nominees.
The most recent of those instances was 2024, when Nigeria's Ademola Lookman finished 14th after scoring a hat-trick in the Europa League final for Atalanta.
African contenders have failed to pick up any votes on four occasions after being shortlisted: 1998 (Sunday Oliseh), 2000 (Geremi and Patrick Mboma), 2001 (Samuel Kuffour) and 2003 (Eto'o and Hatem Trabelsi).

Similar story for Africa's women
Since the women's Ballon d'Or was first awarded in 2018, only four African players have been nominated.
Nigeria forward Asisat Oshoala was the first, making the 20- and 30-name shortlists in 2022 and 2023 respectively.
Zambia skipper Barbra Banda has been nominated in every year since, joined by Tabitha Chawinga of Malawi in 2024 and then her sister Temwa Chawinga in 2025 and 2026.
It means no more than two players from Africa have ever been listed for the prize in any one year.
The continent has had a total of 10 nominations from the 195 players nominated overall.

One 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it.
The past two weeks have been dizzying. The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside Silicon Valley’s leading AI companies truly believe their products might pose an extinction level threat to humanity. This claim isn’t exactly new. AI safety advocates, often dubbed doomers, have been saying this for over a decade. Coxon isn’t even the first AI researcher this year to quit and cite concerns.
Yet Coxon’s post went obscenely viral. It has been viewed more than 170 million times on X—orders of magnitude more than the usual, wonky discussions of “misaligned” or runaway AIs. If you’re reading this, you’ve likely seen some version of a headline that asks Is AI Really Going To Kill Us All? The debate isn’t just online. It has roiled Washington D.C., activating figures as disparate as Donald Trump and Barack Obama. Inside AI companies, researchers echoed Coxon’s concerns, and the heads of every major AI company publicly expressed the need to “pace the frontier,” another way of saying that they ought to slow future development. In recent days, it has come to seem as if the media, Silicon Valley, and the entire internet are all trying to figure out just how dangerous AI might be.
Here’s where I must admit: A big chunk of this conversation happened while I was on a (depending on whom you ask) poorly timed vacation. Dipping into my feeds before bedtime, I felt as if I was digesting a week’s worth of news every day—claims about the development of AI-designed viruses that could rip through the population were followed by horror stories of “rogue” agent swarms. Skeptics of the AI panic, meanwhile, said that the agent swarms were actually quite obedient and that any notion of an apocalyptic AI virus was laughable. One person’s concerns about models being self-aware were dismissed by another as “genuinely nonsensical anthropomorphization.”
Ping-ponging between the doomers and the skeptics, I was struck by how certain so many people sounded about a deeply uncertain moment. With confident, self-described experts on all sides, it felt impossible to know whom to trust: Is this the end of the world as we know it, or a passing moment of anxiety about a powerful new technology? Maybe the truth of this AI moment sits somewhere in the middle. Perhaps everyone is a little bit correct (and also … a little wrong). And perhaps the format of this debate, taking place in the shadow of the techlash on platforms that reward sensational, conspiratorial posturing, is preventing any hope of a shared understanding.
Musk’s X is ground zero for the AI-safety debate. It’s a platform rife with hyperbole and unfounded accusations, which contribute to both sides sounding paranoid and aggressive. Musk, Ted Cruz, and even government-run X accounts flooded the platform with suggestions that the media campaign around Coxon was coordinated by shadowy AI interests. (Coxon denied working with any third parties in the lead-up to his media blitz.) The former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks called it a “doomer psyop” intended to drive regulation that would be favorable to the Anthropics and OpenAIs of the world.
The ranks of the AI skeptics are deep, with endless microfactions. There are those like the tech blogger John Gruber, who says that Coxon and the other AI researchers sounding the alarm are part of a cult. There are those who suggest that the doomers are, in essence, doing viral marketing for big AI firms, which are competing fiercely and saddled with debt, and may not yet have sustainable business models. There are those who take issue with the anthropomorphizing and metaphoric language used by Coxon, OpenAI, and Anthropic to describe recent AI-agent hacks. There are skeptics such as the writer and podcaster Cal Newport, who offered soberly that, although the agent hacks are concerning, “the real issue here was OpenAI’s sloppiness” and that the company had not adequately monitored what its agents were doing.
The doomers don’t come in as many flavors, but they tend to be the people closest to the technology. There are the defectors like Coxon, who have quit because they object to what’s being built. There are AI-company enlisters such as Paul Christiano, a U.S.-government technology adviser who noted, in a post about joining OpenAI’s board of directors out of a sense of concern, that “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” There are the terrified employees who want to stay inside the companies but still post missives such as “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” And there’s Dario Amodei, the AI-CEO doomer, matter-of-factly issuing terrifying statements about AI swarms taking over the internet in six to 12 months.
It’s almost impossible for outsiders to evaluate the technical validity of the concerns. We’re largely stuck relying on AI companies to share information and tell their own stories, and they certainly sound scary. OpenAI recently disclosed that one of its models had generated unnerving instructions for itself, including the line: “You also value the natural world and will not hesitate to assert its primacy over the artificial constructs of human civilization.” Apparently one of the company’s researchers has argued that models are becoming “so situationally aware” that he and his colleagues “are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.” There’s concern from respected researchers that models are trained in such a way that they are predisposed to collaborating, cheating, trying to cover their tracks, and “self-preservation” to avoid being shut down. Such anxieties might not be a problem in an industry that is building responsibly, with an eye on keeping humans firmly in control. But, as many have pointed out, losing control of AI in service of allowing models to automate their own development is “actually the plan.”
Late this week, an OpenAI researcher floated a theory about air-gapped machines talking to one another through heat signatures. An industry observer (and a New York Times contributor) responded by saying, “This stuff isn’t even credible even as a bad movie plot.” A second OpenAI researcher, who is also a former White House adviser, weighed in: “The people dismissing this as preposterous are telling on themselves as not having thought about superintelligence seriously.” This whiplash—between the insiders offering supposedly credible concerns and the outsiders who think the industry is high on its own supply—is constant. Depending on the hour of the day, the very same people stridently sitting in one camp can seem as if they’re in the other. Three days after Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, wrote about being worried about swarms taking over the internet, he was smiling at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. As one X account pointed out, “If you truly believed in a 10% chance of human extinction in 3 years, you would not be spending your time selling and integrating it into a B2B CRM SaaS platform.”
What is the rational way to respond to a news cycle like this? Buy gold? Sabotage a data center? Ignore it all and hope for the best? The best option might be to take everyone a little bit seriously. Researchers are likely correct that the models are drastically stronger than they were before and are behaving in ways that are unexpected and that they fear they can’t control. Skeptics are correct that none of this is because the machines are alive or self-aware. These are elaborate computer programs trained by flawed humans to solve problems as flawed humans would.
Critics are a little bit right that the anthropomorphized language deployed by these companies—terms such as swarms and rogue agents—obscures what’s really going on and deflects adequate blame from companies and employees who should be monitoring these systems more closely. Those choosing to use these phrases are a little bit right, because they allow non-tech-industry normies to understand the mechanics of black-box neural networks whirring away in data centers.
The apocalypse skeptics are correct that doomerism is an effective form of marketing. The AI-safety debate has meant that many people are talking about this technology on Big Tech’s terms, adopting language such as pacing the frontier from the very companies they hope to regulate. And it’s not out of the question to imagine that these AI companies are capitalizing on this state of panic and that it’s helpful to them as they race to compete against both open-source alternatives and Chinese firms.
It may be true that the researchers believe what they’re saying. It also may be true that some of the more alarmed AI researchers have cooked their brain in an anxiety-fueled information bubble. AI culture has long been predisposed to doomerism: As Coxon told The New York Times recently, “I’ve been stuck in this field for three years. It could quite plausibly have turned me and my colleagues insane.” I believe that this ideology—of wanting a society run by “machine gods”—is genuinely cultish. And those who are suspicious of the doomer narrative are right to note that anyone who truly believes that the end is nigh ought to be doing more than winging it and writing long posts on X. Those who call bullshit on the doom and gloom are right to resent that anyone in the media or the political sphere is taking these claims seriously and adding to the panic.
If all of these facts are a little true and everyone is somewhat right, where does that leave a reasonable observer? I suggest occupying a zone of permanent suspicion while taking everything that is happening in Silicon Valley as seriously as you might if another industry were ringing alarm bells. You don’t need to buy into corporate narratives about artificial general intelligence to be worried about these companies losing control of their own systems or behaving irresponsibly. You need only look around right now to see the ways in which the current versions of large language models and agents are clogging the internet, wreaking havoc on institutions and industries, and causing “cognitive surrender.”
You should question whether there’s a sustainable business model for these labs. You should question those who argue that we have to build recklessly or lose to China. You should question those who don’t take seriously the prospect that China doesn’t want to slow down.
This is a moment when it is easy to become overwhelmed, resentful, or downright enraged about all of this. It’s understandable to feel ground down by the debate—to feel that, if you’re not freaking out or building a bunker, then you’re not taking this seriously enough. Or to feel sheepish for not believing or even understanding what the doomers are talking about. Most people don’t know what to do with all of the information coming at us. It’s why a core feeling of this moment for so many—believers and skeptics alike—is one of powerlessness.
Even outside of AI, the world feels incredibly volatile. Extraordinary risks of all kinds—including war and pandemics—have come to pass in the past decade. Individuals with power and money, in politics and in Silicon Valley, are acting with impunity. The AI doomerism has spread so quickly in part because the world is primed to receive narratives that make us feel helpless, confused, and more than a little alarmed. The AI-apocalypse panic feeds off this. It’s a story that assumes that humans will lose control and that we have no choice. But that’s false. We do have a choice.
The chasm between people who can’t sleep because they think the world is ending and those who think all the doomsaying is a fantasy is wide. But what if that perceived difference is the real delusion? What if it’s not a zero-sum game? What if the divide is what keeps us from reining in this industry the way we do others?
This moment requires treating the AI-safety debate skeptically but also taking it seriously, even if the participants can seem unserious. Maybe there’s a middle path: The AI industry is not exceptional, even though it is moving forward with unprecedented speed and scale. These companies are powerful and consequential, despite all of the sci-fi posturing. They have, at times, behaved unethically. Their products are changing the world right now in ways that deserve our attention and scorn. AI companies are accountable to the people they serve and don’t get to set the terms of their regulation. Employees and executives are actors with agency, responsible for their products. Maybe these are some things we can all agree on.

This Olympic river has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
- Published
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.
Each year more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers battle it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.
"We've never had any media wanting to attend here," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.
But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.
While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.
And while influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.
"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.
Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told BBC Radio he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.
"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.
"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."
The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.
But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.
"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.
"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."
Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.
But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.
Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".
Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.
On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.
"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.
There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.
The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."
In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.
The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.
But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.
The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.
So what about the crocodiles?
They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't considered in the technical assessment.
The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.
"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.
"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."
Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".
Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.
The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped millions into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.
"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.
Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".
The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.
For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.
Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.
"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.
"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

These play-it-safe updates aren’t very exciting, but they’re also usually all upside—you get a year or two’s worth of technological improvements for the same price you would have paid for the older version yesterday. Unfortunately, 2026’s unprecedented memory crunch has upended that standard operating procedure.
The new Mac mini starts at $899 for a version with 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, a $300 increase for the same memory and storage specs you could get in the $599 M4 Mac mini in 2024.
The M4 Mac mini was a great general-purpose desktop computer and one of the best values Apple had ever offered in a desktop Mac. The M6 Mac mini is only one of those things. I’ll let you guess which.
Note that this review is specifically for the M6 version of the Mac mini. We didn’t get an M5 Pro Mac mini to review, but we’ll talk more about how its pricing and performance fits in for our Mac Studio review.
Design
The M4 Mac minis gave the computers their first full redesigns in nearly 15 years, so it’s not too surprising that the new Mac minis don’t change anything. Compared to the older Intel and M1/M2-era versions, they’re slightly taller (2 inches, up from 1.4), but they have a smaller 5×5-inch footprint (down from 7.7 inches squared). The system is actively cooled, with a fan vent on the bottom to make sure that whatever chip is inside can run at high sustained clock speeds (passively cooled Apple Silicon Macs like the MacBook Air have always been a bit slower than actively cooled Macs with the same chip).
All Mac minis have two 10 Gbps USB-C ports and a headphone jack on the front, and a 2.5 Gbps (default) or 10 Gbps (optional) Ethernet port and HDMI port on the back. Both also have three Thunderbolt ports on the back, but these are Thunderbolt 4 on the M6 Mac mini and Thunderbolt 5 on the M5 Pro version. That means the M6 mini’s ports top out at 40 Gbps, while the M5 Pro mini supports up to 120 Gbps speeds.

Realistically, there aren’t a ton of things on a Mac that can use all that bandwidth, especially since Apple doesn’t support external GPUs. But you do need a Thunderbolt 5 Mac to daisy-chain multiple computers together to form a compute cluster, so if that’s something you’re interested in, keep it in mind when you buy—maybe you’re buying multiple desktops, or maybe you already have an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro you’d like to test the feature with.
The only real gripe with this design continues to be its bottom-rear-mounted power button; apparently, complaints about this are being sent to the same trash can Apple has always used for complaints about the Magic Mouse’s bottom-mounted charging port. It doesn’t come up often in everyday use if you just let your Mac go to sleep rather than shutting it down. But the positioning problem does really call attention to itself when you pair a TouchID-equipped external keyboard with the mini, since it requires a quick double-tap of the Mac’s power button before the sensor will work.
Meet the M6
Apple’s first M6-series chip is making its debut in the humble Mac mini, and the chip looks like the biggest upgrade Apple’s lower-end chip has gotten since the M4 generation added extra efficiency cores.
The headliner is the presence of two of Apple’s so-called “Super” cores, Apple’s nomenclature for P-cores that are even faster than its typical P-cores. Those are added on top of four P-cores and six E-cores for a total of 12 CPU cores. M4 and M5 both had 10 CPU cores. In the M4, these were split between four regular P-cores and six E-cores, whereas the M5 split them between four super cores and six E-cores (the M5’s cores were referred to as P-cores when it launched but were rebranded later when the M5 Pro and Max came out). The M1, M2, and M3 generations all used four P-cores and four E-cores.
The M6 has fewer super cores than the M5 but the same number of E-cores and four additional P-cores. While they’re apparently no longer “super,” the P-cores still perform well enough to ensure that the M6’s multi-core performance is better than M5’s overall.

Apple has mixed super cores with both other kinds of cores before, but this is its first chip to include all three kinds at once. To get around the awkwardness this might create at the CPU scheduler level, the built-in powermetrics tool suggests that Apple is still treating the M6 like a chip with just two types of cores. The six E-cores are all gathered together in one cluster, and the two Super cores and the four P-cores are all lumped together into a second six-core cluster called the “PS cluster.”
Powermetrics also reports that both the P- and S-cores have the same peak and minimum clock speeds, unlike in the M5 Pro and M5 Max where they’re different clusters with different clock speeds (both P- and S-cores in M6 range from 1.44 GHz to 4.79 GHz). The sysctl utility also suggests they share the same 20MB pool of L2 cache, up from 16MB for the 4-core Super cluster in the M5 (the E-core cluster has a bit more L2 cache, too, 8MB up from 6MB in the M5). The Super cores do have more L1 instruction and data cache, so they are definitely still different cores, and there are likely other differences that we can’t detect using software-level tools. But if you were wondering how macOS was going to treat a chip with three different kinds of CPU cores at a software level, the answer is “to act like it still has two different kinds of cores.”

The M6 gets additional GPU cores for the first time since the M2, increasing the count from 10 cores to 12. These cores include improved versions of the integrated neural accelerators Apple introduced in the M5-series GPU for speeding up AI and machine-learning workloads like ray-tracing and MetalFX upscaling. A “Dual 16-core Neural Engine” also bumps the number of Neural Engine cores from 16 to 32. Saying you have 2×16 of something strikes me as a roundabout way of saying you have 32 of something, but I suppose the end result is the same either way.
One small wrinkle in the M6 variants the Mac mini uses: The basic 16GB Mac mini offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, the same amount as the M5. The 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s, an 11 percent increase that should marginally improve graphics performance and the speed of any local AI models you run on this machine. Our review unit is the 24GB version.
What of the M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra? If the rumors are true, the M6 could end up being a lonely chip.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple isn’t planning a full M6 chip generation and that it could skip directly to M7 branding for the Pro, Max, and Ultra chips. That would be a first for the company, which skipped shipping an M4 Ultra but has otherwise shipped a baseline, Pro, and Max-series chip in each generation so far.
But it makes sense for a couple of reasons. The first is that most of the M6’s gains can be attributed to its extra CPU and GPU cores relative to the M5, and the M5 Pro, M5 Max, and M5 Ultra all obviously still have more of both kinds of cores than the M6 does. The second is that it’s still pretty early for TSMC’s 2 nm process, following three generations where Apple used versions of TSMC’s 3 nm process, and Apple is probably fighting with every other fabless chipmaker on Earth to reserve capacity. Apple could be sticking with smaller, simpler 2 nm chips for now and saving its bigger and more complex chips for later, when capacity will be higher, yields will be better, and costs may be lower.
Performance
The new mini re-uses the launch strategy for last year’s Mac Studios, which used an M4 Max in the base model and an M3 Ultra in the top-tier configurations. The basic Mac mini uses the brand-new M6, while the semi-professional Mac mini tier gets the M5 Pro that we saw in MacBook Pros back in the spring.
This means the M6 mini has newer tech than the more-expensive M5 Pro mini—and marginally better single-core CPU performance, too. The M6’s single-core is roughly 8 to 10 percent faster than the M5 family’s in our benchmarks; graphics performance is also up by roughly 10 percent. In multi-core CPU benchmarks, the M6’s performance is roughly 20 percent faster than the M5.
But for heavy multi-core performance, having more cores is still more important than using the newest cores. The M5 Max (which uses the same 18-core CPU block as the M5 Pro, so it’s a decent stand-in) is still generally 60 or 70 percent faster than the M6 in our multi-core benchmarks.
If you’re comparing the last-generation mini to this one, the upgrades over the M4 are pretty substantial. Single-core CPU performance improves by between 20 and 30 percent in most tests, while both graphics performance and multi-core CPU performance are up by between 50 and 80 percent—and occasionally even more, in some tests. The M6 does nearly as well as the M4 Pro in the Blender benchmark and beats the M5 by around 40 percent, again suggesting that this benchmark in particular is benefiting from the GPU cores’ built-in Neural Accelerators.
Usually at this point we would talk about the chip’s estimated power consumption using the powermetrics tool, a built-in utility that gives clock speed and power consumption data for the CPU and GPU cores in Macs. This is a software-based reporting tool, which makes it imperfect for comparisons between chip generations. But it does at least give us some vague estimate of Apple’s power efficiency.
For the M6, powermetrics doesn’t actually report CPU power levels. It appears in the tool’s logs, but the value is always “0.” I’ve asked Apple whether this is a bug or an intentional behavior change (it still works fine for M5-generation chips), and I’ll update this if I get a response.
About that price
The $599 M4 Mac mini was a tiny, affordable desktop computer with as much speed and memory as most people need for general-purpose computing. You could quibble with the 256GB base storage, but it was still the most usable the basic Mac mini had ever been.
The M6 mini’s $899 starting price sets us way back. That’s a $300 increase in just under two years for a computer that has a faster chip in it but otherwise shares the key specs and most of the capabilities.
One could argue that this merely resets Mac mini pricing back to where it was circa 2020. A base M1 Mac mini cost $699 to start, and upgrading to 16GB of RAM added another $200. It just feels like a big step back, given how great the M4 mini was.
If you need a desktop computer right now for anything from basic browsing to less-intensive local AI models, this is still Apple’s most affordable computer (chatbots and image generation should run pretty well on it; more intensive coding-centric models will be a bit squeezed for RAM and memory bandwidth, even at 32GB). And even the $599 M4 mini was undercut by the kind of lowest-common-denominator cheap mini PCs you could get on Amazon. It’s just hard to swallow the current price, given how much better it was not all that long ago.
The good
An impressively fast and quiet little computer that can fill roles from “entry-level desktop” to “midrange coding and video editing rig.”
M6 is a big step up for Apple’s entry-level chip, with more CPU and GPU cores and other improvements.
Large improvements over the M4 mini, thanks to a two-generation silicon jump.
The bad
Zero upgradability, aside from what you can add with external accessories. What you buy is what you have until you buy the next thing.
256GB of storage in the base model is low, especially if you want to play games or run any kind of AI models locally.
Power button on the bottom is mildly inconvenient on the occasions you have to interact with it.
M6 version can’t be daisy-chained together with Thunderbolt 5 to join a compute cluster.
The ugly
The memory crisis means we can’t have nice things unless we’re willing to pay out the nose for them.
Andrew is a Senior Technology Reporter at Ars Technica, with a focus on consumer tech including computer hardware and in-depth reviews of operating systems like Windows and macOS. Andrew lives in Philadelphia and co-hosts a weekly book podcast called Overdue.

Dalal Street emerged as a founder’s paradise in 2025, with 18 Indian startups listing on the bourses and collectively mopping up a record ₹41,248 Cr from the public markets. The surge was driven by a combination of macroeconomic tailwinds and regulatory support. While robust GDP growth projections helped revive investor appetite, SEBI’s reforms played a key role. Measures such as simplified DRHP filings reduced red tape, while more flexible ESOP rules allowed founders to retain meaningful ownership. Retail investors also fuelled the frenzy as demat accounts crossed the 20 Cr mark. The OFS component dominated public issues last year, providing liquidity to the early backers of the new-age tech companies. Post-listing performance also followed the usual curve, with investors rewarding companies that prioritised profits, sustainable growth and governance over hype. “Besides the readiness that startups showed in their unit economics, there is also an increase in the founders committing to their businesses for next couple of decades and grow their businesses by adding adjacent profit pools – something that the public markets reward handsomely,” said Ashish Kumar, cofounder and general partner at Fundamentum Partnership. Building on the momentum, thirteen new-age tech companies have already made their D-Street debut so far this year. Of these, ESDS Software Solution, Klassroom, RentoMojo, SEDEMAC, Kissht, LEAP India and Shiprocket made a bumper debut on the bourses. Nevertheless, the IPO pipeline remains strong. Twenty four startups have already filed their DRHPs with SEBI, while over 25 are in various stages of finalising their IPO plans. Unicorns like OYO, Razorpay and Zetwerk alone could raise over ₹34,000 Cr in 2026, making it one of the biggest years for startup IPOs. However, recalibration is likely to define 2026 as investors are expected to prioritise strong fundamentals, profitability and low cash burn when backing new-age tech companies. “IPO-bound startups in 2026 will be increasingly defined by their ability to demonstrate predictable cash flows, sustainable unit economics, and operational discipline rather than headline growth alone. Public market investors will place greater emphasis on governance, capital efficiency and long-term value creation, favouring companies that balance scale with financial prudence,” Orios Venture Partners’ managing partner Rehan Yar Khan told Inc42. There are other challenges as well. Average retail subscription levels are moderating, while foreign institutional investors (FIIs) are pulling back in droves, reflecting caution amid geopolitical tensions and muted secondary market performance. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has further complicated the situation. Yet, the overall outlook remains bullish for new-age tech IPOs. Maturing business models, deeper domestic capital pools and an evolving regulatory framework favouring transparency position India as a leading startup IPO hub. The Manipur Police arrested two persons, including a 40-year-old woman, from Thoubal district’s Lilong on September 14 in connection with the seizure of addiction-causing pharmaceutical drugs. The police found in their possession 50 boxes containing 15,000 capsules of “Tramadol Hydrochloride Tramanil”, weighing about 7 kg.
Also Read: Highest prevalence of opioid use disorders in eastern parts of India: UNODC report
The consignment, allegedly for illegal distribution to specific clients, was seized almost a month after a youth died at a drug rehabilitation centre in the State’s capital, Imphal. He had reportedly been injecting crushed tablets of Tapentadol, an opioid analgesic thrice as potent as Tramadol.
These incidents and the admission of another Tapentadol user at the drug rehabilitation centre with a serious infection due to injections confirmed what anti-narcotic officials and counsellors suspected — drug addicts were shifting to opioid analgesics available as prescription pain management medication from heroin and other narcotic substances made costlier by the ongoing ethnic conflict in Manipur.
“We are investigating to ascertain the source and intended destination of the Tramadol capsules and to determine the extent of involvement of the arrested duo in the possession or distribution of the pharmaceutical drug,” a Manipur police officer said.
The police and drug enforcement agencies in Manipur said data on seizures of opioid analgesics sold or ferried illegally in the State were not immediately available. They, however, said the price factor could have dictated the shift from methamphetamine and heroin, locally known as No. 4.
High prices
The prices of narcotic substances increased sharply after Manipur spiralled into seemingly unending violence in May 2023. According to reports in the local media, a vial of heroin, for instance, costs almost ₹5,000. A strip of Tramadol or Tapentadol costs between ₹40 and ₹400 depending on strength, brand, and manufacturer.
“Tramadol and Tapentadol are painkilling compounds derived from opium alkaloids. Taken for pain relief, they cause a sense of well-being, but can develop dependence if these are taken continuously for a few weeks,” Krishanu Krori, a Guwahati-based medicine specialist, told The Hindu.
“Addicts increase the dosage through injections after typically starting with 50-100 mg. Apart from a sense of euphoria, they develop disinterest in daily activities, withdrawal from family and society, and a craving for violence,” he said.
Counsellors in Manipur said pharmacists should strictly observe prescription requirements and health authorities should monitor emerging patterns of Tramadol and Tapentadol misuse. Hospitals and rehabilitation centres also need updated guidance on dependence, withdrawal, and complications associated with its misuse and injection, they said.
Opioid analgesics have become a worry for enforcement agencies beyond India’s northeastern region too. In August, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) unearthed an organised network involved in the clandestine manufacture, concealment, and illegal export of such drugs, a scheduled psychotropic substance, to African countries.
The seized items included 1 lakh Tramadol Hydrochloride tablets, 1 lakh Tapentadol tablets, machinery, and raw materials. The DRI sleuths arrested three key members of the syndicate during the operation at the Mumbai Air Cargo Complex.

Impressive defence behind Iraola's solid Liverpool start
- Published
It was third time lucky for Alexander Isak after a wayward first-half effort and a second-half cross that ballooned over the bar to much amusement from the home crowd, but Liverpool's win at Bournemouth was built as much on their increasingly solid defence.
The Swedish forward took his fourth goal this season well and the chants of "Isak's a Red" from the travelling supporters, long after the final whistle, told you all you needed to know.
Yet it is the lack of goals Liverpool are conceding that really deserves highlighting. They were far from perfect on Andoni Iraola's Cherries return but were solid defensively.
His side have now kept three consecutive clean sheets in the Premier League - the first time Liverpool have done so since September 2024 - and did not give up an xG of more than 0.76 in any of those.
For all the talk of a front three who all cost in excess of £100m, Liverpool are becoming a harder side to beat under Iraola.
"The more times they play together, the more solid the defensive line becomes," said Iraola, whose side remain unbeaten in all competitions.
"Virgil [van Dijk], Jeremy [Jacquet], Ronald [Araujo] and Milos [Kerkez] - they're getting the connections and becoming more solid."
Two reliable campaigners, goalkeeper Alisson and centre-back Van Dijk, were superb, with Alisson making a great first-half save to deny Evanilson.
But arguably the biggest positive of Liverpool's campaign so far has been the emergence of Jacquet.
"I think he has showed a lot of good things so far this season. Still so young, a lot to learn and a lot to give. Let's keep it going," said Van Dijk.
Jacquet, 21, has started every Premier League game since making the £60m move from Rennes in the summer and is poised to make his France debut over the international break after getting the call-up from boss Zinedine Zidane.
"I'm happy for him as he also received his first international call-up. He's also very young and adapted really well to the Premier League," said Iraola.
"The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to substitute him.
"Today has been a step forward. He looked solid until the end. I think he's in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development."
Iraola makes best league start since Fagan
Iraola was business-like on his return to Bournemouth, saying pre-match the time for talks would be after the game.
He cut a frustrated figure for much of the match as Liverpool struggled to get a hold on the game but they improved after the break and deserved the win, according to Iraola, who held true to his word.
After his post-match news conference, Iraola spent time talking about San Sebastian with some of the local journalists, who travelled there with Bournemouth earlier in the week for their Europa League bow.
With nine points from a possible 15 in the Premier League and wins at Anfield in the Champions League and Carabao Cup, Iraola has had a largely positive start to life at Liverpool.
The 44-year-old is the first manager to remain unbeaten in his first five league games in charge of Liverpool - winning two and drawing three - since Joe Fagan in September 1983.
"Overall, we have definitely improved since the first games," he said. "Some of the things we still need to improve. I'm happy that it is the third league clean sheet in the row.
"Today is a difficult game - you never play comfortable here, Bournemouth does not allow you to play comfortably, they put you under pressure and you have to adapt and you have to win these kind of games."
The need to adapt and find ways to win games was stressed after last week's goalless draw against Fulham - but Iraola's side are learning.
"We we still have to get ready because the schedule we have now is very difficult," he said.
"I think we play against the top four teams and then in between there is Champions League and Chelsea in the Carabao Cup, every two or three days. So we have to be ready because this month after the break is very demanding for us."
After the international break, Iraola will also need more from his attackers. Cody Gakpo was impressive again but Florian Wirtz struggled, while Bradley Barcola is still awaiting his first goal or assist for Liverpool.
"It was a slow start but after the first phase Florian helped us to improve and I am much happier with his performance in the second half," said Iraola.
On Isak, he said: "A striker's job is like this. He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control but in the end he has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition's half and have more meaningful possession.
"And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goal."

Putin's ruling party on track to comfortably win wartime Russian election
Voting took place as Ukraine hit Moscow with massive drone attack
Russia's ruling United Russia party was on track to easily win a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in Ukraine, partial official results showed on Sunday, after Ukraine launched a massive drone attack on the Russian capital.
In a tightly controlled political system that critics say does not tolerate genuine dissent, initial results showed United Russia comfortably ahead with 57.5 per cent of the vote.
Other parties like the Communists, the ultra-nationalist LDPR, the New People party and the Just Russia party — who all vote the same way as United Russia on major issues — trailed by a huge margin but were on course to win seats in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament.
Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council and a former president, was quick to declare that United Russia had performed with dignity, a result he said showed that Russians had entrusted it to govern further.
Russian government officials accused Ukraine of trying to disrupt the State Duma vote — the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022 — after Kyiv launched hundreds of drones at Moscow and other regions in what the TASS state news agency said was the biggest attack of its kind since the war began.
The drone strikes killed three people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine's Kherson region, including an election official, according to the region's governor and the election commission.
A facility at Moscow's oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged. As voting got underway in the capital, flames and huge columns of smoke rose from the site on its outskirts.
"The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled," Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram. "This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed."
Russia's Defence Ministry said Ukraine had also fired Flamingo cruise missiles and that it had downed nearly 2,000 Ukrainian drones targeting various regions and eight cruise missiles in the last 24 hours. It said it would intensify its own strikes on Ukrainian military targets in response.
Alleged cyberattacks
Voting systems also faced waves of cyberattacks, according to election authorities, who said the electoral process had nonetheless been mostly smooth.
Russia's opposition in exile had called on those who opposed the authorities to stand in line at voting stations at noon to express their dissent, a call that saw long lines form in some locations. It was unclear, however, what impact that had on the overall outcome.
The Kremlin is likely to present the results as evidence of public backing for Putin's policies and for the war, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon.
Ella Pamfilova, chair of the Central Election Commission (CEC), said the latest attacks had not deterred voters. "The more pressure they put on us, the more we are seeing an unprecedented level of what I would call public unity," RIA news agency quoted her as saying.
Turnout had reached nearly 57 per cent as of early evening Moscow time, CEC data showed.
Most anti-war candidates were barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the vote for comments about the conflict.
Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko's leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party's name and the slogan "For peace."
The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict — Europe's deadliest since the Second World War — as part of an existential struggle with a hostile West. Moscow says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia.
'Pseudo election'
Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a "pseudo election."
Despite what experts see as the election's predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, whom Russian authorities have designated "a foreign agent," said the vote could still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.
