When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
- Published
Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.
But this year, one tree was visibly suffering.
"Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.
The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.
A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?
The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym.
"Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die.
"How heartbreaking would that be?"
So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.
Who is killing 'Grandpa Ginkgo'?
Tucked between two mountains, Buam-dong is recommended by travellers and locals for its picturesque views, art galleries and cosy cafes - an escape from Seoul's bustle.
Because of its proximity to the Blue House, the president's official residence, urban development has been restricted, allowing the neighbourhood to retain its quaint charm.
In a place where you usually find ginkgo trees in private gardens or untamed forests, this one is special, Jung says, because it flourished on the side of the road. To her, it's "Grandpa Ginkgo".
"I pass this tree whenever I come home. I would say, 'Grandpa, I'm home.' Or 'Grandpa, I'm heading out now'."
Jung only moved here four years ago, but the grand old tree was the first thing she noticed, and she grew to love it.
"It was the only tree in the neighbourhood that belongs to everyone."
To Park Jeon-hee, who has lived here for nearly all his 74 years, the ginkgo is his "oldest friend".
It's the same for 10-year-old Kim On, who walks past it everyday on his way to school. It has stood since before he was born, Kim says, and "thinking it might fall down makes me sad".
So it wasn't surprising that Jung found ready allies in the community who had also noticed the ginkgo's withering leaves.
They soon became suspicious of 10 white plastic funnels peeping out from behind the trunk. Jung had initially assumed they were providing nutrients, but then began to wonder if something more sinister was at play.
She and her neighbours sieved through security camera footage from a nearby house, until they found something odd: one morning in late April, the camera had recorded two men wearing white gloves and crouching over the base of the tree with a drill.
Were these men installing the funnels? Jung and the others couldn't exactly tell from the footage.
But then they remembered something the local council had told them: a museum had previously asked landowners in the area for permission to remove the tree.
The Whanki Museum had apparently claimed that its outer brick wall, which sits inches from the ginkgo, was under strain from the tree's roots.
The residents soon suspected the funnels contained some kind of herbicide that was slowly killing the tree - a suspicion also shared by arborists who came to examine it. And they believed the Whanki Museum was behind it all.
On the very day they saw the footage, a group of Buam-dong residents stormed into the museum, accompanied by four police officers. When confronted, an employee "basically admitted" the museum had done something to the tree, Jung and her neighbour alleged.
"Once they had said it, there was really no taking it back," the neighbour told the BBC.
The museum has neither publicly confirmed nor denied injecting herbicide into the tree, and has not responded to the BBC's questions.
But it did publish a statement in May, saying the wall of its compound was "collapsing because of the ginkgo's roots". It said it had sent letters to more than 40 property owners "requesting a solution".
There was no response, the museum said, so its staff "attempted to resolve the situation". It did not explain what they had done.
A local council representative told the BBC that an inspection last year found "no meaningful connection" between the ginkgo tree and damage to the museum wall. If there had been an issue, "we would have taken appropriate action and informed the relevant parties," the official added.
The residents, who still believe the Whanki Museum had the funnels installed, want them to reveal what was in them, so experts can treat the ginkgo. They have filed a police report against the museum's director. Officials say police are investigating the case, but police declined to share more information when contacted by the BBC.
'In the hands of heaven'
Opened in 1992, the museum is dedicated to the late Kim Whanki, a celebrated painter and abstract artist, known by many as the "Picasso of Korea".
On the museum website, architect Woo Kyusung explains he wanted to create a space for Kim's works "that would complement the elements of the nature - the moon, mountains, clouds, rocks and trees - that were so important to his art".
In fact, Kim wrote essays under the pen name Su-wha, which translates to "conversation with trees".
The irony is not lost on Buam-dong's indignant residents. Decades after Kim's death, the museum built in his honour is accused of trying to snuff out a tree. A ginkgo, no less, which is precious in Korea, where it symbolises longevity and resilience.
"Treating life that way is ignorance and there was never any apology," Jung says.
The residents have co-opted Kim's poetic nom de plume "Su-wha" for their moribund tree. They have also roped in an environmental activist group, which has launched a petition calling for citizens to be authorised as guardians of urban trees.
"When I first heard that a tree next to a museum had been poisoned with herbicide and was dying, I simply couldn't believe it," says activist Choi Jin-woo.
But when he saw the ginkgo shrivelling, he "realised something this horrific could actually happen in our society".
If there's a silver lining to be found in the ginkgo's troubles, it's that the campaign to keep it alive has brought the people of Buam-dong closer together.
While spending her days garnering support, Jung would return to find home-cooked meals from her neighbours left by her door. She, in turn, made vegetable soup for neighbours she'd never met before.
As summer went by, they all watched the ginkgo's branches increasingly go bare and brown. An arborist who inspected it said it was "90% of the way toward death", Choi says.
The fate of the tree is now "in the hands of heaven", says a resigned Jung. "Perhaps all I can do is stay beside it and pray."
For weeks, around 20 residents regularly gathered in front of the tree to pray for its recovery. Some recited Whanki's essays, while a local shaman performed a "healing ritual".
Notes of well wishes fluttered against the trunk as music rang out, and the group joined hands and swayed in unison for an "elm dance", which some nature lovers and activists believe helps trees heal.
"If someone had truly understood this tree was deeply loved, they probably would not have made the decision to inject herbicide," says Kim Min-joo, who has lived in Buam-dong for more than a decade.
It recently occurred to Jung that all the days that she spent scrambling to save the ginkgo were the most active she had been since she fell ill last winter.
She had struggled to walk much and would often observe the tree from home. On better days, she strolled up to it, even hugging its jagged trunk and inhaling the earthy scent to lift her spirits.
"I felt so depressed and hopeless but those feelings disappeared. I entered a tree-like state."
She still can't walk very much, she adds, but "the tree helped bring me back out into life again. Ironically, it was because the tree became sick."
"Although it has been heartbreaking, there were also incredibly moving moments," Jung says, on reflection. "The neighbourhood came together, cared for one another, looked after each other."
As Seoul transforms into various shades of yellow with the arrival of autumn, the leaves on Buam-dong's once-prized ginkgo are a crispy brown.
The neighbourhood is still hoping for a miracle.
Because they cannot imagine an autumn in which they don't pause to admire the ginkgo at its finest, swathed in a feathery coat of gold.

What could a 'super' El Niño mean for the Prairies?
Developing El Niño could be one of the strongest ever recorded
The much-talked-about El Niño continues to heat up in the Pacific Ocean.
"Every indicator has shown that this [El Niño-Southern Oscillation] is continuing to strengthen," said Lindsey Long, a meteorologist with the ENSO team at the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) in the U.S.
"We're getting [sea surface temperature] anomalies of up to 11 C, so those are extremely warm waters that are helping to fuel this."
El Niño is part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) , which is a fluctuation between warmer sea surface temperature anomalies — El Niño — and colder anomalies — La Niña — in the equatorial region of the Pacific Ocean.
These fluctuations happen in periods of two to seven years.
During normal conditions, west-blowing trade winds push warm sea surface temperatures from South America toward Asia. However, those winds can break down or reverse direction, allowing that warm water to instead pool near South America.
What does this mean for the Prairies?
This disrupts weather patterns around the world, including a stronger Pacific jet stream and an amplified polar jet stream over western Canada.
As of Sept. 14, a very strong El Niño was being observed in what's called the El Niño 3.4 region in the eastern equatorial Pacific, where average sea surface temperatures were 2 C warmer than normal.
Experts predict the current El Niño to peak during the late fall and winter months.
The last El Niño classified as very strong occurred during the 2015-16 winter. The Prairies also experienced a moderate El Niño during the 2023-24 season. Both brought warmer than normal temperatures to the Prairies.
Research scientist Bill Merryfield with Environment and Climate Change Canada says that could also be the case this winter.
"The odds are certainly tilted in that direction of having a relatively mild winter, possibly by a large margin," he said.
"Some of those temperature differences from normal during past very strong El Niños have been in the range of 5 or 6 degrees averaged over the winter, which is quite substantial.”
Both Long and Merryfield say that El Niño events typically lead to less snowfall in the Rocky Mountains, and that warmer temperatures could mean less snow in the Prairies, but that trends for precipitation are not as strong as with temperature.
Research aims to correlate ENSO, precipitation
With a correlation between precipitation and ENSO on the Prairies unclear, researchers are diving deeper into it.
David Sauchyn, director of the Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative at the University of Regina, says a proxy of soil data across the Prairies has been collected to see years where soil and trees received more or less moisture in a given year.
The research is looking into whether drier or wetter periods might correlate with El Niño or La Niña events.
"We can't say exactly if a dry year was an El Niño year, but we get this cycle — this cycle of every two to eight years it's either quite wet or quite dry," he said.
"It's not the direct measurement of sea surface temperature, but we have a proxy record of soil moisture on the Prairies going back 1,000 years."
Cold snaps, snowstorms still likely this winter
The current projection from the CPC has the El Niño continuing into next spring with a 55 per cent chance of a return to neutral conditions in the April-May-June timeframe.
Merryfield is concerned that less snow than normal or a reduced snowpack could create problems with streamflow, drought and wildfires next spring.
"We might expect vegetation to be drier than usual, which could be conducive to drought and wildfire risk if there's not a good amount of rainfall in late spring and summer to offset that," he said.
But Long notes that a warmer or drier winter does not mean classic Prairie cold snaps and blizzards won't appear at all this season.
"Just because overall you might be warmer, you can still have big snow events, big cold snaps, things like that," she said.

In mid-August, along the Bengaluru-Mysuru expressway, an agricultural labourer in C.K. Tandya village in South Bengaluru district (formerly known as Ramanagara) noticed something unusual on a strip of farmland: a heap of medical waste.
This wasn’t the first time that the villagers in South Bengaluru had noticed suspicious objects or activity around the area which contained a farmhouse, say the police. They had seen men frequently moving in and out of it on a scooter without a number plate. They had also seen courier and e-commerce delivery vehicles making regular trips to the secluded location.
Spanning nearly eight acres and fenced by a compound wall, the farmland is situated on the outskirts of the village. According to the police, the owners, who live in Bengaluru, seldom visited the place.
The villagers would whisper among themselves about what they suspected — until the day the labourer decided to report the dumped medical waste to the local beat police.
The officers at Taverekere police station put the farmhouse and the movements around it under surveillance, while also making inquiries about the property and its occupants. The people they spoke to did not seem to know anything substantial.
According to an officer, the police learned that the farmhouse had been rented about a year earlier. But what was happening inside the compound remained unclear.
Days later, the police and Karnataka’s health department, in a joint operation, decided to enter the premises. What they saw there — labels, medicine boxes, drugs, and other items associated with the preparation and packaging of medicines — changed the nature of the investigation. They alerted senior officers, who joined hands with officers from the State Drugs Control Department and conducted a raid on August 18.
The police took four people into custody. They discovered that the secluded farmhouse was being used as a counterfeit drug repackaging and re-labelling facility. What began as a local’s suspicion had opened the door to a much larger pharmaceutical investigation.
According to investigators, the operation involved the procurement of low-cost, substandard, or expired pharmaceutical formulations from other States, which were then transferred into fresh vials and given counterfeit labels and packaging. “The aim was to make the medicines appear as genuine products of established pharmaceutical companies and introduce them into the pharmaceutical supply chain,” says a police official familiar with the investigation.
During the seizure, the police recovered more than 5,600 vials of counterfeit antibiotic injections used in treating serious bacterial infections. The total seizure was estimated at ₹4.91 crore.
They also seized ledgers, invoices, mobile phones, and other records, which provided them with details of the supply chain.
From a farmhouse to the big city
The police then moved their investigation beyond C.K. Tandya. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted.
The trail led to Bengaluru and to Krupa Healthcare, a wholesale pharmaceutical distributor located on a busy commercial street in the city. According to the police, the operators in the farmhouse supplied medicines to Krupa Healthcare, which distributed them.
The police found that the counterfeit medicines were not limited to antibiotics, but also included critical-care injections and cancer medicines. They say some of the medicines were offered to hospitals at “discounts of up to 50%”.
Krupa Healthcare owner Veeresh Kumar Jain, who was arrested by the SIT, allegedly employed more than 15 medical representatives to promote the medicines and offered commissions to push the discounted stocks to private hospitals and medical centres.
The police then found that the alleged racket was not confined to Karnataka. A joint force subsequently carried out simultaneous searches across Karnataka, Himachal Pradesh, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and Telangana. The police are currently on the hunt for Bengaluru resident R. Prashant, who they believe is a key figure in the network. He is currently in Azerbaijan, and is Jain’s partner, say the police.
Unanswered questions
The families of patients are shocked and angry at these revelations. On his WhatsApp profile picture, Maheshprasad Upadhya, 30, poses with his mother. A cervical cancer patient, she passed away in 2024. After hearing the news, Upadhya, a native of Odisha, cannot help second-guessing the events before his mother’s death.
She was diagnosed with cancer in 2022, he says. For a year, she underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy in Mumbai. The doctors then suggested immunotherapy. As treatment in Mumbai was expensive and there were also logistical difficulties in travelling to the city, the family decided to shift treatment to Bhubaneswar.
“The doctor we consulted referred a Bengaluru-based pharmaceutical distributor to us. I bought a medicine from them. It cost ₹1,65,990 per vial. My mother needed two vials. The distributor said if we purchase one, we would get another free,” recalls Upadhya.
He searched online and found that the manufacturer did offer such a programme. He decided to go ahead with it.
Upadhya spent about ₹20 lakh on the overall treatment. “But we saw no improvement in her condition,” he says. “When she was diagnosed with cancer, the doctor had said she would live up to five years. My mother passed away in one and a half years.”
Upadhya sounds calm, but he admits within him a tumult of emotions — anger, suspicion, and helplessness. “One person who had got his father treated at the Bhubaneswar hospital had advised us against buying this medicine from this particular distributor,” he says. “But we didn’t listen since the doctor himself had advised it. After my mother passed away, I started suspecting something, perhaps a nexus, but I was in no state of mind to think about it. Now I’m questioning everything.”
He confesses that there are times when he considers migrating abroad “after seeing how the corrupt try to profit from the desperation of the most vulnerable.”
Parth Sharma, a resident of Gurugram, returned to India in 2017 to care for his ageing parents and mother-in-law, after spending 37 years abroad. “The people I came here for are no more,” he says.
In October 2020, Sharma’s mother was diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome, a condition where the bone marrow doesn’t make enough healthy blood cells. The doctors informed the family that the disease was not curable. Given the patient’s age — she was in her 70s — a bone marrow transplant was also not an option, they said. Nevertheless, treatment, including chemotherapy injections and blood transfusions, was started at a private hospital in December.
Sharma remembers that some of the expensive medicines were not available in India. “The doctor gave us the phone number of a person and said he would help get it imported. When you are desperate, you simply trust everyone. So, we contacted him,” he says.
Sharma’s mother’s condition never improved. With her body too weak to fight the disease, she passed away in May 2021.
“After the report on the counterfeit drug racket came out, I started wondering more deeply about something I had suspected all along: were the medicines even working? We had spent a lot of money and given her the prescribed medicines. At that point, we trusted the system and did not even suspect the possibility of fake medicines,” he says. He still has some of the tablets, which cost him around ₹80,000.
Living in uncertainty
The police say the suspect medicines have so far reached more than 90 hospitals and clinics in Karnataka and other States. While the State government has published a list of antibiotics seized during the Bidadi raid, it has not yet disclosed the names of oncology drugs or the hospitals and clinics that may have received the medicines, or the names and batch numbers of counterfeit medicines reportedly linked to serious illnesses such as cancer. There is pressure on the government to disclose this information.
According to the Karnataka Minister for Health and Family Welfare, U.T. Khader, the full list of spurious and counterfeit drugs has been communicated to the Union government and all State governments. “The SIT has taken charge of the investigation now. Once the report is finalised, we will reveal everything. We have got the list of hospitals. But when the SIT is there, it is not right on my part to disclose anything,” he says.
As the SIT continues with its investigation, Upadhya wonders what patients must be going through with the information they have. “Imagine their state of mind. Would they want to continue or discontinue treatment when they have no way of knowing whether the medicine they are taking is genuine or counterfeit,” he asks.
Dr. B.S Ajaikumar, radiation and medical oncologist and Founder and Chairman at HealthCare Global (HCG) Enterprises, says counterfeit drugs are a major problem in India today.
“I have been sounding the alarm on this for several years,” he says. “Whenever somebody — say insurance companies — wants to bring drugs from outside, I don’t allow it at HCG because I’m concerned it could be spurious. Any drug we purchase should come directly from the manufacturer. The authorities should also lay down stringent guidelines and ensure they are enforced. They should consult major users of oncology drugs like us, collaborate with us to develop a plan, and ensure spurious drugs don’t enter the system.”
Noting that cancer treatment often depends on the right drug, at the right dose, given at the right time, Dr. Nitish Ranjan Acharya, Surgical Oncologist at Manipal Hospital, Bhubaneswar, points out that any compromise in the authenticity or quality of a medicine can directly affect a patient’s treatment.
“If a patient receives a counterfeit, substandard, or expired medicine, the drug may not work as intended. This can delay disease control, allow the cancer to progress and, in some cases, affect the chances of achieving a good treatment response. The impact may be particularly difficult to identify because a lack of response can sometimes be mistaken for the cancer becoming resistant to treatment,” he explains.
Dr. Acharya adds that there are more risks when the contents of the counterfeit drugs are unknown. “A drug could contain an incorrect dose, inactive ingredients, contaminants, or substances that may cause unexpected side effects. These risks can be especially serious for patients already receiving multiple cancer medicines,” he notes. He also stresses the importance of appropriate storage and handling to maintain quality.
The question of accountability
The alleged racket also raises questions about what hospitals should do when patients may have already been exposed to counterfeit medicines. As S.V. Joga Rao, a lawyer who specialises in healthcare law and ethics, says, “Given the circumstances in India, a detailed investigation may take time. By that time, the spurious drugs may have found their way to patients.”
According to him, hospitals need to work with investigating agencies to identify the medicines in question and their batch numbers. “If there is some kind of leeway in terms of information, the hospital has an ethical duty to inform potentially affected patients,” he says.
Noting that regulatory authorities need to be mindful of Section 17B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, which defines a spurious drug, and Section 18, which prohibits their manufacture, sale, stocking, distribution and other related activities, Rao also points to the legal duty of hospitals to procure responsibly, verify authenticity, and detect sophisticated counterfeiting. “If there are warning signs, they need to respond to that. The duties of the hospitals and regulators operate concurrently, although they are different in nature. It is a shared responsibility,” he says.
Dr. Gopal Dabade, president of Drug Action Forum, Karnataka, says, “Drug inspectors are the first line of foot soldiers, but they are not adequately equipped. Punishment for wrongdoing is also not stringent enough.” He is a part of the All India Drug Action Network, a group of non-profits working to “increase access and improve the rational use of essential medicines”.
Another reality is the high cost of medicines, particularly cancer drugs, which can create a parallel market for cheaper counterfeit versions. “Better access to good quality and affordable treatment is the crux of the issue,” Dabade says.
Sylvia Karpagam, a public health doctor and researcher, says people must demand an accountable public health system as part of the election mandate. She also points to the responsibility of doctors, and questions the role they play in ensuring accountability within the healthcare system. “Doctors who harp about ‘evidence-based practice’ in allopathy go mum when such incidents occur. Other than for their own pay cheques and to oppose any form of regulation, one barely sees doctors protesting on behalf of patients,” she says.
She also stresses the importance of adequate budgets, trained and sufficient staff, and regular public scrutiny. “Unless the government has an ongoing system to prevent drug rackets, and makes it known to the public through ongoing reports, these kinds of incidents will continue — some get picked up, and many don’t.”
SIT head C. Vamshikrishna says he cannot comment on the case while the investigation is on. Repeated phone calls and messages to reach Srinivas K. Commissioner of the Food Safety and Drug Administration, Karnataka, have not elicited any response.

Senior Advocate Abhishek Manu Singhvi has emerged as one of the key legal figures in the escalating dispute between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons.
Neol Tata-led Tata Trusts has appointed Singhvi to represent it in opposing the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons and the proposed listing of the Tata group holding company.
The Trusts, which hold about 66% of Tata Sons, have challenged the validity of the September 17 board resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran for another five-year term.
Quick answers to key questions
Abhishek Manu Singhvi has been appointed to represent Tata Trusts in their legal challenge against the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as chairman of Tata Sons, opposing the legitimacy of the board resolution from September 17.
Tata Trusts argue that the board resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran was invalid since it did not receive the necessary support from both Trust-nominated directors, as required by Tata Sons’ Articles of Association.
Singhvi's previous role on the Tata side during the Cyrus Mistry case lends significant weight to his current representation of Tata Trusts as it showcases his deep understanding of the governance issues at stake.
The legal dispute may lead to judicial intervention to either uphold or annul Chandrasekaran's reappointment, which could significantly impact corporate governance and shareholder rights within the Tata group.
The decision to list Tata Sons publicly remains contentious; Tata Trusts assert that existing governance structures should be respected, while Tata Sons view listing as crucial to enhance corporate governance.
Singhvi said he entered the dispute with “sadness and regret”, citing his association with the late Ratan Tata.
His appointment is also notable because he was part of the Tata side’s legal team during the earlier Tata Sons-Cyrus Mistry dispute. He now represents Tata Trusts in a fresh battle over the governance and control of the group.
Singhvi is a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court and a senior Congress politician. He is a Rajya Sabha member representing Telangana and has held several prominent parliamentary and organisational positions within the Congress.
Singhvi became the youngest Additional Solicitor General of India in 1997, at the age of 37, and served in the position from 1997 to 1998.
His father, Laxmi Mall Singhvi, was a noted jurist, diplomat and parliamentarian who served as India’s High Commissioner to the UK and was also a member of the Rajya Sabha.
Singhvi studied at St Columba’s School and St Stephen’s College, Delhi, where he completed a BA (Hons) in Economics. He later pursued postgraduate studies at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he obtained an MA and PhD.
He also attended a summer programme in Public International Law at Harvard University.
Singhvi’s current role in the Tata dispute is particularly notable because of his earlier involvement in the Tata Sons-Cyrus Mistry case.
He was part of the legal team representing the Tata side after Mistry was removed as chairman of Tata Sons. The dispute eventually reached the Supreme Court, which in 2021 upheld the Tata Sons board’s decision to remove Mistry and examined the role and rights of the Tata Trusts under Tata Sons’ Articles of Association.
Singhvi has represented senior Congress leaders, including Sonia Gandhi, in proceedings connected with the National Herald case involving Associated Journals Ltd (AJL) and Young Indian.
The case has involved proceedings by investigative agencies and legal challenges concerning the affairs of AJL and Young Indian, making Singhvi one of Congress’s prominent legal representatives in the matter.
Singhvi has also been associated with the long-running DK Basu litigation concerning custodial violence and human rights.
In subsequent proceedings in the case, the Supreme Court appointed Singhvi as amicus curiae. He made submissions seeking further directions and measures to strengthen safeguards against custodial abuse and improve the implementation of human rights protections.
The original DK Basu judgment remains a landmark ruling on safeguards against custodial torture and illegal detention.
Singhvi has represented the Animal Welfare Board of India in litigation concerning Jallikattu in 2017.
The Supreme Court proceedings involved questions around animal cruelty, the legality of the practice and subsequent legislation seeking to permit or regulate it.
Another notable case associated with Singhvi is Union of India v. Naveen Jindal, concerning citizens' right to fly the national flag.
Singhvi appeared for Naveen Jindal before the Supreme Court. The court held that flying the national flag is protected as an aspect of freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions.
Singhvi was also associated with some of India’s biggest telecom companies and major disputes that shaped the sector. Over the years, he represented companies including Bharti Airtel, Vodafone and Idea Cellular in litigation involving issues such as spectrum charges, revenue-sharing arrangements, 3G intra-circle roaming agreements, licence renewals and the broader legal fallout from the 2G spectrum controversy.
Singhvi has also been a defence lawyer for Aam Aadmi Party leaders in the Delhi excise policy case.
He represented former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and former Delhi Deputy Chief Minister Manish Sisodia in their challenge to the CBI's arrest and their bail plea before the Supreme Court.
Singhvi represented Congress leader Rahul Gandhi in the criminal defamation case that led to his conviction and subsequent disqualification from the Lok Sabha in 2023.
The Supreme Court subsequently stayed Gandhi’s conviction, paving the way for the restoration of his parliamentary membership.
Singhvi has also been involved in major legal challenges concerning the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and its stringent bail provisions.
He has argued against the stringent “twin conditions” for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA and has challenged the law's enforcement powers in major Supreme Court proceedings, including Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India.

The Jehovah’s Witnesses have partly eased their long-standing prohibition on the medical use of donated blood, allowing members to receive products derived from blood but maintaining a ban on transfusions of whole blood.
The policy, announced Friday, is the second revision this year in what has long been one of the most controversial and distinctive teachings of the religious organization.
The new policy says that individuals can receive products derived from blood donated by other people. It says they can receive medical treatments that involve the use of the four main components of whole blood: plasma, platelets, and red and white blood cells.
“Each Christian must make his own personal decision about the use of these four primary components in all medical and surgical care,” said Geoffrey W. Jackson, a member of the Governing Body of the organization, based in New York State.
The new announcement also allows members to decide as a matter of individual conscience whether to donate blood to be used for blood products for the medical treatment of others.
But the organization continues to oppose members receiving transfusions of whole blood or donating blood for that purpose.
In March, the Governing Body also announced a revised policy, authorizing members to have their blood stored for their own future medical treatment, but not for others’.
Critics have faulted the organization for prohibiting the use of a proven treatment that can be lifesaving in replenishing blood lost in surgeries, accidents, or violence. Critics, including former church members, say that the teaching has led to deaths that could have been prevented.
The Jehovah’s Witnesses’ longtime opposition to blood transfusions derives from their interpretation of Bible passages requiring believers to “abstain” from blood. While Jewish and other Christian religious traditions have interpreted this as a dietary law, Jehovah’s Witnesses have extended that prohibition to transfusions.
Blood components are often used for specific treatments.
Plasma, the liquid component of blood, is often used for those suffering from trauma or certain diseases, according to the American Red Cross. Red cells can be used to treat conditions such as anemia and white cells to treat certain infections. Platelets are used in some cancer and other treatments.
Members shouldn’t make the decision on using blood products lightly, Paul Gillies, international spokesperson for the Jehovah’s Witnesses, said in an interview.
“What we’re saying is you have to pray about it, you have to study it, you have to see what the Bible has to say about it, because blood in the Bible represents life,” Gillies said. Members need to consider all these factors before reaching “a decision that you feel happy about with your God.”
Jehovah’s Witnesses, who emerged in 19th century America, share many Christian beliefs with other churches but diverge on key theological issues, such as the nature of Jesus and biblical prophecy. They are almost alone in their beliefs about blood transfusions. Jehovah’s Witnesses reported a U.S. membership of 1.3 million in 2025, with a worldwide membership of 9.2 million in more than 200 countries and territories.
— Peter Smith

Mike Rann recalls legacy of Don Dunstan 100 years after his birth
As South Australians commemorate 100 years since their most influential premier was born, a former political heavyweight has recalled his own entry to politics under the man's leadership.
Don Dunstan was SA's trailblazing Labor premier between 1967-68 and 1970-1979, a leader who championed social justice and the arts, and turned Adelaide into a national cultural centre that punched well above its weight.
He died in 1999 aged 72.
Mike Rann was a three-term premier for the state Labor Party between 2002 and 2011, making him the third-longest serving premier in the state's history.
Mr Rann said he had been studying Australian history and politics at university in New Zealand and found Don Dunstan to be somebody who "stood out" among a "fairly deary lot".
He successfully applied to work in SA at the Unit for Industrial Democracy in the premier's department and at the age of 24 was notified that Mr Dunstan's speechwriter had resigned.
"Someone said to me, 'Look, you won't get the job, but he should get to know you, so why don't you apply for the position?'" Mr Rann told 891 ABC Adelaide.
Mr Dunstan ushered him into a room while wearing a white safari suit, before they sat down for a "charming" and "wonderful conversation".
"Then suddenly there was a tap on the door and his secretary said [former Australian prime minister] Gough Whitlam is here," Mr Rann said.
"So I'm being interviewed and terrified, and then I've got Gough Whitlam sitting there as well."
Mr Dunstan had to step out for an ABC interview, leaving Mr Rann with Mr Whitlam, "who turned to me and said, 'Who the hell are you?'"
"I said I was from New Zealand and was applying for a job with Mr Dunstan.
"He said, 'You're wasting your time here, young man. Go east. Go east. Come to Sydney'.
"Dunstan came back and said the interview was concluded, with Gough still there, and then they asked me if I'd like to come out to dinner.
"I didn't think I would get the job but thought it would just be one of the great nights and stories to tell. The next day, I got the job."
Mr Rann was appointed to be Dunstan's press secretary, speechwriter and head of the government's media operations for what he described as a "wild ride".
A true reformer
Emeritus Professor of Politics and International Relations at Adelaide University Clem Macintyre said Mr Dunstan's flagship reforms, first as attorney-general and then as premier, included the nation's first land rights and anti-discrimination laws for Aboriginals, the liberalisation of drinking hours in restaurants and pubs, and the decriminalisation of homosexuality — Australia's first jurisdiction to do so — in 1975.
"He was a transformative premier in South Australia in lots of ways and I think, arguably, set a lead for a number of other states as well in terms of social changes that were coming in the 60s and 70s," Dr Macintyre told 891 ABC Adelaide.
"In many respects, South Australia was a very conservative, inwardly-looking state in the 1950s into the early 1960s under the long-serving premier Tom Playford, who had built some very strong economic foundations.
"Then Dunstan, when he finally became premier in the mid-60s, really began to change the place and, particularly in that second term from 1970 onwards, initiated lots of reforms that really we still see signs of today."
Mr Rann said Mr Dunstan saw that a small jurisdiction like South Australia could be a pace-setter for reform both nationally and internationally and was not afraid to stick his neck out.
"Someone described him as the maestro of the possible, and that's how I saw it,"
"He was prepared to take risks, but he was also prepared to lead, rather than follow, and that's what South Australia was like in the 1890s."
After all, among other reforms, South Australia had been the first jurisdiction in the world to give women the vote in 1894, and the right to stand in parliament on equal terms.
"He wanted us to be a destination again, a place that attracted people from all over who were interested in actual reforms and doing things differently and better," Mr Rann said.
A trained actor, Mr Dunstan was also a champion of the arts and raised money for and overlooked the opening of Adelaide Festival Centre, where the Dunstan Playhouse was later named in his honour, and established the SA Film Corporation.
He also closed a section of Rundle Street to cars and created Rundle Mall, which opened 50 years ago in 1976.
"He was very flamboyant and, while he was interesting, at parties, dinner parties, he would often be the shyest person there," Mr Rann said.
"But when he was on stage or on television, he had this incredible ability to sum up complicated arguments and punch them through."
An exhibition, Don Dunstan: 100 Years, presented by the City of Norwood Payneham & St Peters, Don Dunstan Foundation and Centre of Democracy, is being held at The Gallery adjoining St Peters Library.
With personal items donated by those close to Dunstan, the council says visitors will be able to gain unique insights into his life, passions and personality, and "reflect on the ideas, courage and creativity of a leader whose vision helped shape modern South Australia and continues to inspire today".
The exhibition runs until November 7.

Emily Wilson Wanted to Like Nolan’s Odyssey
The translator of Homer’s epic is done talking about her harsh movie review—but eager to translate the poem again.
Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics. Her 2017 The Odyssey, the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of cultural discourse after she drew her sword and published a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of the ancient work. She didn’t anticipate that she would become part of a pop-culture controversy, and she was reluctant to revisit the episode when we sat down for an interview at this year’s Atlantic Festival. “I really wanted to like the film,” she said, but “it seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth.” Her strong convictions animate a new book of essays, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea, which dissects translations of ancient work with unsparing rigor.
Wilson, who is now working on a second translation of The Odyssey, entertained the idea that there might be something “compulsive” in her art and her approach. Her new essays reveal a translator’s difficult balancing act—between fidelity and originality, and between accessibility and strangeness. In the course of our wide-ranging conversation about the pleasures and blind spots of translation—and, yes, the backlash to her now-notorious movie review—she spoke about the imperative she feels to get that balance exactly right.
The following conversation was condensed and edited for clarity.
Gal Beckerman: You take a pretty hard line in this book about when a text should be retranslated, but you’re translating The Odyssey again. It’s interesting that you should want to go back in again. Have you learned something new about the text or come to see it in a new way that makes it exciting for you to tear it all up and start it from scratch?
Emily Wilson: It’s not tearing it up to do a new one, right? Partly it’s that I’m kind of addicted; I can’t stop doing this. I have several other projects I’m supposed to be doing. I did The Odyssey really prioritizing pacing, because my students would very often show up to class saying, Oh, it was so boring. And I would be like, How can The Odyssey be boring? And then I would realize it’s because the translation was twice as long as the original. Then, with my Iliad translation, I was a little bit looser about not confining myself to the exact same number of lines as the original. I thought there were advantages to doing that. So as soon as I’d finished The Iliad, I wanted to go back to The Odyssey and start all over again to produce one that matches my Iliad. So it’s not that I think there’s anything wrong with my current translation, and I think that there will be readers who will like that one better. It will be snappier and all that.
Beckerman: Do you think that translators have a kind of a compulsion to continue to play with the words, to work this Rubik’s Cube?
Wilson: Yeah, I think it is compulsive, maybe that’s right, but I don’t think that’s just me. I think that is very common, especially for a very long project like this. You’re constantly thinking about, How might I be able to get closer to whatever the vision is?
Beckerman: One of the things I love that you do in the book is demystify translation, and make us understand that these are human beings and that they have biases, that they’re in a specific cultural moment—a certain gender, a certain kind of life experience—and that it shows up in the word choices. When your translation of The Odyssey came out, a lot of the excitement about it was that you were the first woman who was translating The Odyssey in English. And I wonder if you feel like being a woman has affected your translation?
Wilson: I think some of those headlines were kind of bogus, right? I mean, they were suggesting this really simplistic set of ideas about gender: And of course gender will be the only factor that will contribute to how someone writes. And of course all women write in iambic pentameter, just naturally, and all men don’t. Some of it was really silly, I thought.
Beckerman: But do you feel like you understand the particular worldview that you’re bringing to it? None of us fully know the water we’re swimming in, of course, but when you’re translating, are you like, Oh, I think that I’m reading this way or I’m making these choices because I’m a woman of a certain age living in the 21st century in America?
Wilson: You know, I honestly never think that. I mean, I think that when I’m talking to people like you. Well, I don’t mean “people like you”—
Beckerman: Nosey journalist.
Wilson: Exactly. It’s only very belatedly that I feel that I have to prepare an answer for things like this. When I’m actually wrestling with it, I do quite often think, Okay, I’m putting the stress on that, and that syllable and that name; is that because I’m British? To what extent is my approach to the passage informed by that critical study or this critical study? That kind of thing comes into my thinking all the time. But the question is about my lived experience, and do I have this particular relationship to this banquet scene because I don’t eat meat? No.
Beckerman: Right. I mean, meter is important to you, that the sound of the poem or the text in another language have some relationship to the original. For translators 200 years ago, they wouldn’t necessarily care in the same way.
Wilson: Yeah, this is a very old-fashioned choice on my part. I see myself as super retro. I see myself very much as taking a sort of mid-19th-century approach to translation.
Beckerman: How do you think film adaptation is different or similar to literary translation? When you think about a director approaching a text like The Odyssey—wanting to adapt it and making very definite choices about the value system that is underlying the plot that he’s created—is that the same type of thinking through interpretation that a translator does when they approach a text?
Wilson: I would say no. I think it’s a very different kind of thinking. What I’m trying to do as a translator is to get to something equivalent to the experience of the original. I think a good adaptation tries to do the opposite of that. Virgil was certainly doing that in rewriting The Odyssey as The Aeneid. It’s on some level the same story; it’s also the opposite story. So I think the more the adaptation pushes against it, in many cases the more successful it is artistically.
Beckerman: There is this interesting sort of tension through a lot of these essays in your new book, where you want these ancient texts to be popular, to get out there, to have people engage with them and to make new things with them. But on the other hand, that often leads to a kind of a reductive quality. And I feel like it’s a tension that came out around Nolan’s movie. You wrote a very critical review of the film, and I had a moment as I read that when I wondered, Is she trying to distance herself from it as something that has reductive qualities, and is it popular in a way that doesn’t engage with the full texture of the text?
Wilson: I wish I would have liked the film more. I went in hoping to like it and thinking I was going to like it. And it turns out I didn’t. It seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth. There’s another kind of responsibility: that you shouldn’t actually lie about your actual feelings and thoughts. And there’s also a question about: what does it mean to spread the word that everyone should read ancient literature? Everyone should take some kind of interest in history. Everyone should engage with long, difficult books. I really believe in those things, and I don’t believe that the best way to engage with history and to grapple with the essential questions of art and cinema and plays and music and literature is to sort of say, Yay, we love it all.
Beckerman: But what lenses did you put on to critique the film? As a translation or as an adaptation?
Wilson: No. I mean, I say at the start of the review that very often the best adaptations are the ones that are most resistant to the original. The ways that I was critiquing the film were in terms of pacing and characterization and narrative. A satisfying cinematic experience needs to follow through on its own premises. And so if you set us up to think this is going to be the kind of film where we’re supposed to care about the characters, then you need to follow through on that promise.
Beckerman: What did you make of the response to your response—the backlash of sorts? I’m just curious what it told you about people’s relationship to these stories, because there was this real defensiveness about the film, about this effort to make a popular piece of art around The Odyssey. Were you surprised?
Wilson: Yeah, I thought it was really weird. Many people reviewed this film, including other Odyssey translators, and there was no discourse about anyone except for me, which is really weird, I thought. So I’m not sure that I can really comment on what weird people thought. But I feel like this is taking us a bit far from the book? Because I don’t discuss the film in the book. I discuss theater and ancient literature.
Beckerman: I know, I understand. It’s just that it was an interesting cultural moment. It is not every day that my Twitter feed is full of people wanting to debate the finer points of The Odyssey. So I can imagine, for somebody who’s as immersed in it as you are, that it must be unsettling but also exciting.
Wilson: I think it’s wonderful insofar as it is actually substantially about either the film or about the poem, or some combination of the two. I felt that some of the discourse wasn’t about either of those things. I’m, on some level, interested in it because it’s a symptom of some kind of bad stuff in our culture, but I’m not that interested in it, and I’m not going to celebrate it.
Beckerman: Right. So my last question: I’ve thought a lot about the limits to how much we can understand people’s lived experience so far in the past, and as a translator of these texts, you come the closest—you walk right up to that edge—and I’m curious for your thoughts about that. Is it never going to be possible for us to get at what it meant to be living in the time when The Iliad or The Odyssey were written? Or do you see a kind of universality that connects us to the people who wrote those texts?
Wilson: That’s a great question and such a difficult one. I mean, part of my reason for focusing so much on literary form and poetic form is that even if we can’t get the lived, embodied experience of what it means to be going around in your chitons and eating your ancient Greek olives—I’m not sure that we can get to that through texts—I do think we can get quite close to something like the experience of being a fluent listener or reader. I don’t think that means universals, but I think it means we can get to a kind of multicultural imagination that includes going back in time as well as going to different places in space. And if we can do that, there’s a kind of magic in that in itself.

History repeated itself at the Chess Olympiad on Sunday.

POCSO accused teacher in Bengaluru jumps off SP office building, dies
The incident occurred at the Bengaluru South district Superintendent of Police's office complex in Ramanagara on Sunday.
A 49-year-old teacher accused of sexually assaulting children died after jumping from the third floor of the district Superintendent of Police's office complex in Karnataka’s Bengaluru.
According to a report by the news agency PTI, the deceased was a native of Vijayanagara district. Police said that he worked as a physical education teacher at a private school in Channapatna taluk.
The incident occurred at the Bengaluru South district Superintendent of Police's office complex in Ramanagara on Sunday.
The police said that a CCTV video also captured the act, in which he could be seen pushing a constable, running towards the railing and jumping from the third floor of the SP office complex.

After undergoing a medical examination at a government hospital in Bengaluru, the accused was brought to the SP's office on Sunday as part of further procedures before being handed over to judicial custody, the officer said.

‘Caste discrimination a stigma on Hindu society’: RSS' Hosabale says ‘our conduct’ can free us from it
Addressing the issue of caste discrimination, Hosabale stressed that everyone is a child of “Mother India” and “God”.
RSS General Secretary Dattatreya Hosabale said caste-based discrimination is a “stigma on Hindu society” and called for efforts to end such discrimination through individual conduct and behaviour.
Addressing the issue of caste discrimination, Hosabale said there should be no discrimination among people, stressing that everyone is a child of “Mother India” and “God”.
“We are all children of Mother India. We are all children of God. Therefore, there should be no discrimination of any kind among humans,” Hosabale said while speaking at an event in Bhopal on Sunday, according to news agency ANI.
‘Discrimination based on birth not part of Hindu culture’
Hosabale said discrimination based on a person's birth does not form part of Hindu culture.
“Discrimination based on birth is not part of Hindu culture,” he said, adding that different forms of harmful behaviour taking place in society in the name of caste weaken society.
“The various kinds of evil behaviour that occur in society in the name of caste weaken, debilitate and hollow out society,” Hosabale said.
He called upon those who think selflessly about the nation to begin addressing the issue through their own behaviour and within their homes.
“Therefore, those who are selfless and who think selflessly about the nation must begin this practice in their behaviour, in their lives and in their homes,” he said.
‘We will not discriminate on the basis of caste’
Hosabale urged people to make a personal commitment against caste-based discrimination.
“We will not discriminate on the basis of caste. This is a stigma on Hindu society. We need to be free from this stigma,” he said.
He further said that ending the practice would require more than laws or preaching and would depend on people's own conduct.
“This will not happen through law, through the mere incarnation of God, or through someone's preaching. It will happen through our own conduct,” Hosabale said.
“Let us resolve to do so and move forward,” he added.

A fungus that can cause severe pneumonia in people with weaker or weakened immune systems appears to have become resistant to a drug that never intended to kill it, according to the findings of a study by researchers from around the world published in Science Translational Medicine.
The study focused on mycophenolic acid (MPA), an immunosuppressive drug used with people who have received solid-organ transplants. MPA helps keep the immune system from rejecting the organ — but it was also found to affect Pneumocystis jirovecii fungi.
The team analysed 163 P. jirovecii samples from China, Denmark, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and the U.S., of which 96 came from recipients of transplanted organs, most of whom were also involved in pneumocystis pneumonia outbreaks from 2005 to 2019. The remaining samples were controls.
MPA works by inhibiting an enzyme called IMPDH in human immune cells. The fungus possesses a similar enzyme, and the researchers believe this could be the link. The team found six relatively common mutations in the fungal gene that produces IMPDH. Some 86% of samples from transplant recipients contained a mutation in that gene, versus 13% in the non-transplant samples.
The researchers also produced normal and mutated versions of the fungal IMPDH enzyme in the lab and exposed them to MPA. Depending on the mutation, considerably more MPA was required to inhibit the mutated enzymes than the normal enzyme.
The mutations also appeared in at least 11 fungal strains and varied between countries and over time. That is, rather than resistance arising once and spreading from that source, P. jirovecii seem to have evolved similar adaptations as different populations encountered the same selective pressure.
The researchers have acknowledged that they have only established resistance at the enzyme level, rather than in infected patients, and that their cohort sizes and clinical data were limited.
Nonetheless, researchers understand antimicrobial resistance as microorganisms evolving to resist antibiotics, antifungals or other medicines. But in the study, a drug intended to act on the human body was found unintentionally exerting pressure on a pathogen as well. And mutant fungi that could better tolerate MPA may have enjoyed an advantage among transplant recipients taking the drug, allowing them to survive and spread.
The “results challenge the current status quo on P. jirovecii’s unknown resistance,” the study authors wrote, “calling for reevaluating immunosuppressive strategies and infection control measures and highlighting the broader potential for other pathogens to evolve under selective pressures imposed by human-targeted therapies.”

Brisbane Lions players have told ABC Sport that a conversation in July with NBA champion Luc Longley has helped the team in its quest for three consecutive AFL premierships.
The Lions play in the grand final this Saturday against the Fremantle Dockers, the team Longley was the number one ticketholder of in 2006 and 2007.
What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.
If the Brisbane Lions win a third straight AFL premiership on Saturday, they will be thanking a former number one ticketholder for the Fremantle Dockers.
Luc Longley, a three-time NBA champion with the Michael Jordan-led Chicago Bulls, knows what it takes to reach the top and stay there.
Longley, a Fremantle native, was also the Dockers' number one ticketholder in 2006 and 2007.
But a meeting the Olympian had with the Lions in July may be the catalyst for Fremantle's downfall this Saturday.
The Lions are in their fourth consecutive AFL decider, and are trying to complete three premiership triumphs in a row and join the list of all-time great dynasties.
Despite finishing third on the ladder and making it to the final day in September, the Lions' 2026 season has not been smooth sailing.
Brisbane lost their opening two matches of the season, conceded a record 86 points in the third quarter of their loss to GWS, were hammered by 76 points against Carlton, and lost the qualifying final by 53 points to an understrength Sydney.
But they have overcome all obstacles to be in another grand final, with several players telling ABC Sport of a meeting with Longley in July which has spurred them on.
"The ability he had to share some of that wisdom and talk to us about what he went through, it was awesome," Lions star Cam Rayner said.
"Just being able to compare and bounce ideas off him and learn things from him about the ability to keep turning up and find that motivation again has held us in good stead."
The Lions had six wins and six losses through 12 games, but were on a five-match winning streak before meeting Longley ahead of their round 18 clash against West Coast in July.
Rayner said Longley's discussions with the team about keeping the desire to win, despite already experiencing success, resonated with the team as they strived for a third consecutive flag.
"The hunger to want to win and to continue to have that success. At the start of the year there were times that wasn't really there in our performances," he said.
"We were dropping in and out of games and struggling to really perform to the level that we could.
"You can't really question the hunger after the game last week. It's back to a level that it needs to be and it's exciting to bring it to this week.
"That's one of the messages Luc Longley brought to us, he said, 'If the game's not going to get you up, you're probably playing it for the wrong reasons'. I feel like that really resonated with a lot of the boys."
Loading Twitter content
Longley was an important part of the Bulls' 1996-1998 championship run, without being the star player.
Michael Jordan was the star of the NBA, while Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman and Steve Kerr also enjoyed big-name status.
For experienced Lions' midfielder Jarrod Berry, speaking to a champion who was known for his team-first work ethic was exactly what he believed Brisbane's dynasty has been built on.
"He [Longley] was never the big dog, the star, the whatever. He got more satisfaction out of seeing his teammates succeed," Berry told ABC Sport.
"Our squad is so talented and we've got so many stars and whatever, but it's not necessarily those guys that are making the club so special.
"It's the other guys that are doing all the tough work and hard work and selfless stuff.
"It was really nice to highlight that. It's all about being generous to your teammates and doing it for them."
The Lions are attempting to become the sixth team to win three consecutive V/AFL premierships, and the first since Hawthorn, who did it from 2013-15.
The Lions won three premierships on the bounce in 2001, 2002 and 2003, then lost the 2004 grand final.
The only club to have won three consecutive flags twice is Melbourne, which did it from 1939–1941 and 1955–1957.
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.
